title: TAPe+ML: A Compact Structured Representation for Multi-Task Computer Vision
comment: 39 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Project page: https://ml.comexp.net
summary:
We present TAPe+ML v3, a compact computer vision system based on TAPe (Theory of Active Perception), a structured representation that encodes relations among perceptual elements before recognition. Instead of operating directly on pixel tensors, the system uses a shared TAPe representation and a modular recognition architecture for image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation.
  TAPe+ML v3 combines background and contour processing, local object localization, prototype-based classification, and a coordinator for specialized submodels. Across the reported experiments, it uses fewer than 100,000 parameters. On COCO object detection, it obtains 84.7 mAP50 and 65.3 mAP50-95. On COCO instance segmentation, it obtains 80.7 mask mAP50 and 58.4 mask mAP50-95. In classification experiments, it reaches 92 percent validation accuracy on Imagenette under an identical-training comparison with a raw-pixel baseline, and 89.9 percent Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-Real. We also evaluate compactness in video scene detection and adaptation under distribution shift in an industrial pilot. The results suggest that shifting part of the modeling burden from network parameters to a structured input representation can support compact multi-task vision systems with reduced data, memory, and compute requirements.

AI.tldr: A compact, multi-task computer vision system (TAPe+ML v3) that uses a theory of active perception (TAPe) structured input representation to share features across tasks (classification, detection, segmentation) with fewer than 100k parameters, achieving strong results on COCO, Imagenette, and ImageNet-Real, and showing potential efficiency gains by shifting burden from parameters to structured inputs.
AI.motivation: Reduce data, memory, and compute in vision systems by leveraging a structured representation (TAPe) to encode relations among perceptual elements before recognition, enabling a compact, modular, multi-task architecture.
AI.method: Adopt TAPe representation as a shared backbone; incorporate background/contour processing, local object localization, prototype-based classification, and a coordinator coordinating specialized submodels; apply to image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation; maintain a sub-100k parameter budget; evaluate on COCO, Imagenette, ImageNet-Real, with additional experiments in video scene detection and distribution-shift adaptation.
AI.result: Reported results include: COCO object detection 84.7 mAP50 and 65.3 mAP50-95; COCO instance segmentation 80.7 mask mAP50 and 58.4 mask mAP50-95; Imagenette classification 92% validation accuracy; ImageNet-Real 89.9% Top-1; hints of compactness benefits in video scene detection and industrial distribution-shift adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Shifting modeling burden to a structured input representation can yield compact, multi-task vision systems with reduced data, memory, and compute requirements; the approach shows strong multi-task performance with very small parameter counts, though the unusually high COCO metrics would benefit from verification and methodological details.

title: MemeTAG: Keyword-Driven Meme Classification through Tag Embedding Reconstruction
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures; published in the Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV), 2026
summary: The proliferation of harmful internet memes poses a significant societal threat, yet their automated classification remains a formidable algorithmic challenge due to the nuanced, multimodal nature of their content. To address this, we introduce MemeTAG, a novel dual-objective framework that pioneers a keyword-aware approach to meme classification. Our core innovation is a two-part semantic guidance mechanism: first, we leverage a pretrained Vision-Language Model to generate a set of descriptive keywords, that capture the high-level semantics. Second, we introduce the Aggregated Tag Inference Network (ATIN), an attention-based module that distills these keywords into a single, rich semantic embedding. This embedding serves as a target for a novel auxiliary reconstruction loss, which compels the model to learn deeply aligned visual and textual features. This approach, combined with an efficient three-stage training strategy, establishes a new state-of-the-art on the HarMeme, Hateful Memes Challenge (HMC), and PrideMM datasets, decisively outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: MemeTAG introduces a two-stage semantic guidance for meme classification: (1) generate high-level keywords with a pretrained vision-language model, (2) distill them via an Aggregated Tag Inference Network (ATIN) into a single rich semantic embedding, trained with an auxiliary reconstruction loss and a three-stage training regime, achieving state-of-the-art on HarMeme, HMC, and PrideMM datasets.
AI.motivation: Harmful memes are inherently multimodal and semantically nuanced, making robust automatic classification difficult. Existing methods struggle with cross-modal alignment and interpretability. Leveraging keyword-level semantic guidance from a vision-language model aims to improve alignment and provide interpretable, keyword-driven supervision.
AI.method: (1) Use a pretrained Vision-Language Model to generate descriptive keywords capturing high-level semantics of memes. (2) Apply Aggregated Tag Inference Network (ATIN), an attention-based module, to distill these keywords into a single rich semantic embedding. (3) Introduce an auxiliary reconstruction loss that enforces alignment between visual and textual features using the keyword embedding as a target. (4) Employ a three-stage training strategy to integrate these components.
AI.result: Reported state-of-the-art performance on HarMeme, the Hateful Memes Challenge (HMC), and PrideMM datasets, outperforming prior methods.
AI.conclusion: Keyword-aware semantic guidance via ATIN effectively bridges visual and textual modalities in meme classification, yielding robust performance gains and suggesting benefits of explicit keyword-driven representations for multimodal understanding.

title: Image-Derived PM10 Estimation in Cattle Feedlot Using Machine Learning: Addressing Concentration Ranges Beyond Existing Digital Imaging Methods
summary: Affordable dust monitoring remains a pressing need for the cattle feedlot industry, yet camera-based PM estimation, despite its growing body of research in urban air quality settings, has not been evaluated under the extended concentration ranges characteristic of intensive livestock operations. This study developed an image-based approach using contrast panel features and machine learning to estimate PM10 concentrations in a commercial cattle feedlot, where hourly average PM10 ranged from 250 to 1,000 ug/m^-3 and instantaneous concentrations reached 5,000 to 20,000 ug/m^-3. Grayscale images were captured during the evening dust peak period, and features including panel contrast, black and white panel pixel values, and overall image brightness were extracted. The model also incorporated recent past values from preceding images and solar zenith angle as predictors. Among the candidate models evaluated, XGBoost achieved the highest predictive performance, with an R^2 of 0.792 and a median absolute error of 103 ug/m^-3. Feature importance analysis revealed that (a) panels positioned farthest from the camera contributed most strongly to predictions and (b) that black panel pixel values were more sensitive than white panel values to changes in PM10 concentration. Prediction accuracy during the sunset transition, which coincides with the onset of the feedlot evening dust peak, remains an area for further refinement. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of image-based PM10 estimation across PM concentration ranges substantially exceeding those reported in prior urban studies and provide practical guidelines for future deployment in feedlot environments.

AI.tldr: Image-based PM10 estimation in cattle feedlots using contrast-panel features and XGBoost achieves R^2 ~0.79 and MAE ~103 µg/m^3 across high PM ranges; far-from-camera panels and black panel pixels are most informative; sunset transition accuracy remains a challenge.
AI.motivation: Provide affordable, scalable dust monitoring for intensive livestock operations and evaluate camera-based PM estimation across concentration ranges far exceeding urban settings.
AI.method: Capture grayscale images during evening dust peak; extract features from contrast panels (panel contrast, black/white panel pixel values, image brightness); incorporate historical image values and solar zenith angle; evaluate multiple models and select XGBoost for best performance (R^2 and MAE reported).
AI.result: XGBoost achieved R^2 = 0.792 and median absolute error = 103 µg/m^3. Feature importance: panels farther from camera contribute most; black panel pixels are more sensitive to PM10 changes. Sunset transition prediction accuracy not fully resolved.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of image-based PM10 estimation across wide concentration ranges beyond prior urban studies and offers deployment guidelines for feedlot environments, while highlighting specific design and timing considerations (e.g., panel placement, lighting, sunset period) for improved accuracy.

title: Fragment-Aware Vision Transformers for Fresco-Fragment Style Classification
summary: Artistic style classification is usually studied on complete artworks, where models can exploit global composition, spatial organisation, and iconographic structure. In archaeological settings, however, artworks often survive only as fragmented remains, forcing recognition from incomplete, irregular, and context-limited visual evidence. We study fresco-fragment style classification using a progressive transformer-based framework. Starting from a ViT-B/16 baseline, we introduce foreground-guided masking to suppress background-only tokens, inpainting-based geometric regularisation to align irregular fragment supports with the ViT patch grid, and a supervised contrastive objective that operates on predictive distributions through a Kullback-Leibler similarity and consistently improves every branch. We combine the branches with a deliberately simple learnable logit ensemble. Experiments on CLEOPATRA and POMPAAF show that fragment-aware modelling improves over the standard ViT baseline, with the ensemble increasing accuracy from 0.604 to 0.656 and macro-F1 from 0.596 to 0.648 on CLEOPATRA, and outperforming the best single branch in four of six fragmentation settings on POMPAAF. We additionally evaluate a more complex graph-fusion variant and find that it matches the simple ensemble on POMPAAF while offering only a small, dataset-specific gain on CLEOPATRA, which does not justify its added complexity. Beyond these empirical gains, our contribution is twofold: a distribution-level contrastive objective that consistently sharpens single-branch recognition, and an interpretability analysis that verifies the models exploit genuine painted evidence, while quantifying that the inpainting-based branch draws part of its attribution from the synthesised surround.

AI.tldr: A progressive ViT-based framework for fragmentary fresco-style classification that uses foreground-guided masking, inpainting-based geometric regularisation, and a distribution-level contrastive objective, combined with a learnable logit ensemble; achieves notable gains on CLEOPATRA and POMPAAF datasets over a standard ViT baseline, with mixed results for a graph-fusion variant.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of classifying artistic style from fragmented, background-noisy archaeological fragments where global composition is unavailable; aim to leverage fragment-aware modeling and interpretability to ensure reliance on genuine painted evidence.
AI.method: Extend ViT-B/16 with (1) foreground-guided masking to suppress background tokens, (2) inpainting-based geometric regularisation to align irregular fragment supports with the ViT patch grid, (3) a supervised distribution-level contrastive objective operating on predictive distributions via KL similarity, (4) a simple learnable logit ensemble to fuse branches; compare to a more complex graph-fusion variant across fragmentation settings; evaluate on CLEOPATRA and POMPAAF.
AI.result: Fragment-aware modeling improves over ViT baseline; ensemble raises accuracy on CLEOPATRA from 0.604 to 0.656 and macro-F1 from 0.596 to 0.648; on POMPAAF, the ensemble outperforms the best single branch in four of six fragmentation settings; graph-fusion matches the simple ensemble on POMPAAF with limited gains on CLEOPATRA.
AI.conclusion: A distribution-level contrastive objective consistently sharpens single-branch recognition; interpretability analyses show the models use genuine painted evidence and reveal that the inpainting-based branch attributes part of its signal to the synthesized surround; simple ensemble suffices in many settings, with more complex fusion offering limited, dataset-specific gains.

title: On (Directed) Width-Parameters of Geometric Spanners
summary:
To speed up algorithms on geometric graphs, it is common to approximate the complete Euclidean graph while maintaining certain geometric properties. A (directed) $t$-spanner $G$ for a point set $P$ in the Euclidean space is a (directed) graph such that for every pair of points, the shortest path in $G$ is at most a factor $t$ longer than the Euclidean distance between those points.
  In this paper, we investigate $t$-spanners that are bounded by certain graph parameters. Let $κ$ be a graph parameter. We show that for path-width, branch-width and cut-width there is an $\mathcal{O}(n/k^{d/(d-1)})$-spanner $G$ on $P$ with $κ(G)=k$ and that this is asymptotically worst-case optimal. In $\mathbb{R}^2$ we show the same bounds for planar graphs of clique-width or rank-width $k$. In contrast, for tree-depth, we show that there are sets of points for which the dilation cannot be bounded. Therefore, we investigate computing a spanner with tree-depth $k$ and minimum dilation. We show that already for tree-depth $3$ this problem is NP-hard to approximate within any factor strictly less than $\sqrt{2}$, and present an XP-algorithm to compute for a given tree-depth $k$ a graph with dilation at most $2t^*$, where $t^*$ is the minimum dilation.
  We further extend these results to obtain directed $\mathcal{O}(n/k^{d/(d-1)})$-spanners $G$ with $κ(G)=k$ for $κ$ being directed tree-width, directed path-width or DAG-width and show that also in the directed case, this is asymptotically worst-case optimal.

AI.tldr: Near-optimal t-spanners with width-bounded graphs for geometric point sets; extents include path/branch/cut-width and planar-directed width measures; tree-depth presents limits and computational hardness; directed width variants also covered.
AI.motivation: To accelerate geometric-graph algorithms by building sparse spanners that preserve distances within a factor t while respecting graph parameters like path-width, branch-width, cut-width, clique-width, rank-width, tree-depth, and their directed analogues.
AI.method: Construct spanners with dilation O(n / k^{d/(d-1)}) and width parameter κ(G)=k; prove asymptotic optimality via lower bounds; adapt to R^2 planar graphs for clique-/rank-width; analyze tree-depth where dilation cannot be bounded, show NP-hard to approximate dilation for tree-depth 3; devise XP-algorithm to achieve at most 2 t* dilation for given k; extend to directed width notions (directed tree-width, directed path-width, DAG-width) with analogous bounds.
AI.result: Existence of O(n/k^{d/(d-1)})-spanners with κ(G)=k for κ being path/branch/cut-width; similar bounds for planar graphs in the plane with clique-/rank-width k; tree-depth yields unbounded dilation; NP-hardness of achieving close approximation for dilation with tree-depth 3; XP algorithm producing a graph with dilation ≤ 2 t* for given t*, where t* is optimum; directed analogues also hold with corresponding width notions.
AI.conclusion: Width-bounded spanners exist and are near-optimal for several width parameters; tree-depth imposes inherent dilation limits and computational hardness; directed width parameters admit parallel results, confirming a broad, parameterized understanding of spanner quality under graph-structural constraints.

title: Sparse Priors for Efficient Distribution Learning
summary: Despite the widespread use and success of generative AI techniques today, theoretical guarantees on learning a distribution supported in $d$ dimensions from $n$ samples degrade as $O(n^{-1/Θ(d)})$, though shown to be minimax optimal. We hypothesize that present bounds are too pessimistic because smoothness assumptions are not enough to capture the structure of distributions that often appear in real applications. Consequently, we introduce the class of sparse priors and define the "Sparse Dimension" as a measure of sparsity of a prior over the space of all distributions. We show that distribution learning under a $k$-sparse prior achieves a Bayesian risk lower bound of $Ω(\sqrt{k/n})$ under common distance metrics, and show a matching (up to logarithmic terms asymptotically in $n,k$) upper bound for the TV distance under mild additional assumptions. We show the statistical equivalence of distribution learning and learning to sample in the Bayesian setting so that our results apply to learning to sample as well. While $k$ can still depend on the dimension $d$, or a notion of intrinsic dimension, our results show that learning under an appropriate prior overcomes the curse of dimensionality with respect to the dependence on $n$.

AI.tldr: Proposes sparse priors and a Sparse Dimension to improve distribution learning; proves a Bayesian risk lower bound of Ω(√k/n) under a k-sparse prior and a near-matching upper bound for TV distance; establishes an equivalence between learning distributions and learning to sample; suggests sparsity can mitigate the curse of dimensionality in n-dependent rates.
AI.motivation: Traditional smoothness-based guarantees degrade with dimension (n^{-1/Θ(d)}). The authors posit that real distributions exhibit structure not captured by smoothness alone and that sparsity can be exploited to achieve better sample complexity.
AI.method: Introduce a k-sparse prior over the space of distributions and define Sparse Dimension as a sparsity measure. Derive a Bayesian risk lower bound Ω(√(k/n)) under common metrics, and provide a (nearly) matching upper bound for the TV distance under mild extra assumptions. Demonstrate the statistical equivalence between distribution learning and learning to sample in the Bayesian setting.
AI.result: Lower bound scales with sqrt(k/n); upper bound on TV distance matches up to log factors. Equivalence result extends to sampling tasks. k can depend on d or intrinsic dimension; overall, structure-aware priors can beat the generic curse of dimensionality in n-dependent rates.
AI.conclusion: Appropriate priors over distributions, specifically sparse priors leading to Sparse Dimension, can significantly reduce sample complexity in high dimensions. The framework links distribution learning and sampling, motivating structured Bayesian approaches for real-world distributions where sparsity is a natural property.

title: WM-VS: Progress-Aligned World Models for Closed-Loop Visual Servoing
summary: Closed-loop visual servoing requires predictions that indicate whether an action reduces task error, not only whether the action is plausible. We call this gap the prediction-control mismatch and introduce WM-VS, a target-centric progress-aligned world-model framework for closed-loop visual servoing. Offline target-region DINOv2 correspondences define a signed four-dimensional servo coordinate for translation, scale, and in-plane rotation. Stage 1 aligns action-conditioned latent transitions with this coordinate; Stage 2 freezes the world model and trains a reactive joint-velocity policy with action imitation, consequence supervision, and short imagined rollouts that favor error contraction. Deployment is RGB-only and reactive, without online trajectory optimization. On a real 7-DoF eye-to-hand system, WM-VS reaches a corner RMSE no larger than 10 percent of its initial value in 30/30 trials and retains this criterion at the final valid frame in 25/30 (83.33 percent). Removing future-error alignment reduces retention to 26.67 percent. The learned progress signal agrees with an external AprilTag corner error not used for training or control (mean Spearman rho = 0.8778). Without retraining, two unseen 3D targets achieve translation-error reductions of 86.48 percent and 90.27 percent and rotation-error reductions of 70.01 percent and 65.70 percent. These results link progress-aligned action consequences to repeated closed-loop correction and transfer. Code and data will be released as open source.

AI.tldr: A target-centric, progress-aligned world-model for closed-loop visual servoing (WM-VS) that ties action to error reduction, enabling RGB-only, reactive control with strong transfer to unseen targets.
AI.motivation: Addresses prediction-control mismatch in closed-loop visual servoing: predicting action plausibility is insufficient; a signal predicting actual error reduction is needed to guide control.
AI.method: Offline target-region DINOv2 correspondences define a four-dimensional servo coordinate for translation, scale, and in-plane rotation. Stage 1 aligns action-conditioned latent transitions with this coordinate; Stage 2 freezes the world model and trains a reactive joint-velocity policy using action imitation, consequence supervision, and short imagined rollouts that favor error contraction. Deployment is RGB-only and reactive, no online trajectory optimization.
AI.result: On a real 7-DoF eye-to-hand system, corner RMSE ≤ 10% of initial value in all 30 trials; final-frame retention 25/30 (83.3%). Removing future-error alignment drops retention to 8/30 (26.7%). The progress signal aligns with an external AprilTag corner error (mean Spearman ρ = 0.8778). Two unseen 3D targets achieve translation errors reduced by ~86–90% and rotation errors by ~65–70% without retraining. Code and data will be released open source.
AI.conclusion: Progress-aligned action consequences enable repeated closed-loop corrections and transfer to unseen targets without retraining.

title: RBS-Attention: Radius-Bounded Sparse Prefill for Long-Context Large Language Models
summary: Long-context large language model inference is increasingly limited by prefill, where dense self-attention processes the entire prompt before generation begins. Sparse block selection can reduce this cost, but a block centroid may hide a highly relevant token among many irrelevant ones. We call this failure mode mean dilution and propose RBS-Attention, a training-free sparse-prefill method with two complementary selection branches. A centroid base branch captures average relevance, while a rescue branch uses the maximum key-block radius and its prompt-, layer-, and head-dependent distribution to identify blocks at risk of underestimation. Independently thresholding the two branches and combining their masks controls the contribution of rescue blocks while preserving regular block-sparse FlashAttention execution. On H100 GPUs, RBS-Attention achieves 20.65$\times$ standalone prefill-attention speedup, 11.92$\times$ vLLM prefill-attention speedup, and 5.97$\times$ end-to-end time-to-first-token speedup at 128K on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8. On the dense Qwen3-32B model, it obtains 88.65 overall RULER accuracy versus 89.52 for dense attention; LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench, and Video-MME provide additional quality evaluation. Supporting experiments measure actual retention, compare selectors at matched density, and characterize block-size, threshold, and memory behavior. Together, these results support radius-adaptive dual-branch selection as an effective approach to long-context prefill.

AI.tldr: A training-free, radius-adaptive dual-branch sparse-prefill method (RBS-Attention) mitigates mean dilution in long-context LLM inference, delivering substantial speedups with competitive quality.
AI.motivation: Tackle prefill bottlenecks in long-context LLMs caused by processing dense self-attention over the entire prompt; centroid-based selection can miss relevant tokens (mean dilution).
AI.method: Two complementary branches: a centroid base branch tracking average relevance and a rescue branch leveraging the maximum key-block radius with prompt-, layer-, and head-dependent distribution. Independently threshold and combine their masks to preserve regular block-sparse FlashAttention while including rescue blocks.
AI.result: On H100 GPUs: 20.65x standalone prefill-attention speedup, 11.92x vLLM prefill-attention speedup, and 5.97x end-to-end TTF at 128K on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8. On dense Qwen3-32B: 88.65 vs 89.52 RULER accuracy. Evaluated with LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench, Video-MME. Additional experiments cover retention, density-matched selectors, and memory behavior.
AI.conclusion: Radius-adaptive dual-branch selection effectively improves long-context prefill efficiency while maintaining competitive or near-dense-quality results.

title: MAGIC: Marginal-Guided Compression with Optimal Transport for Efficient Visual Document Retrieval
summary: Recent visual document retrieval (VDR) systems such as ColPali use multi-vector page embeddings, in which patch-level vectors enable fine-grained evidence matching but incur substantial index storage and MaxSim scoring overhead. Post-hoc merging offers a practical route to efficient VDR by reducing this cost without retraining the retriever, but its uniform reconstruction objectives are poorly aligned with the sparse, non-uniform patch usage induced by late-interaction retrieval. Under aggressive compression, this misalignment can preserve rarely used patches while concentrating retrieval activity on too few retained representatives. To address this misalignment, we propose Marginal-Guided Compression with Optimal Transport (MAGIC), a training-free post-hoc compressor for efficient retrieval with frozen multi-vector embeddings. MAGIC derives a MaxSim-induced compression surrogate and optimizes it through a two-marginal entropic optimal-transport formulation, where a retrieval-demand source marginal prioritizes high-use patches and a balanced target marginal regularizes retained-facet usage. Across ViDoRe benchmarks, keep ratios, and retrieval backbones, MAGIC consistently outperforms strong post-hoc compressors, with particularly large gains in the aggressive-compression regime; component ablations verify the complementary effects of its two marginals. We release the code at: https://github.com/xandery-geek/MAGIC.

AI.tldr: A training-free post-hoc compressor (MAGIC) uses a two-marginal entropic OT objective to align MaxSim-based compression with fetch-demand in VDR, yielding strong gains under aggressive compression without retraining.
AI.motivation: Reduce index storage and MaxSim scoring overhead of multi-vector page embeddings in visual document retrieval while preserving retrieval effectiveness, avoiding retraining of the retriever.
AI.method: Derive a MaxSim surrogate and optimize via a two-marginal entropic optimal-transport problem: a retrieval-demand source marginal prioritizes high-use patches, and a balanced target marginal regularizes retained-facet usage; compression is applied post-hoc to frozen embeddings.
AI.result: MAGIC consistently outperforms strong post-hoc compressors across ViDoRe benchmarks, keep ratios, and backbones, with the largest gains in aggressive compression; ablations show the two marginals contribute complementarily.
AI.conclusion: MAGIC provides a training-free, effective post-hoc compression method for VDR that aligns with retrieval usage, enabling substantial efficiency gains without retraining; code released.

title: BI-Agent and BI-Bench: Towards Automating End-to-End Business Intelligence
comment: code and data are available at \url{https://github.com/Hu-Chuxuan/bi-agent}
summary:
Business intelligence (BI) is a cornerstone of enterprise decision-making and is widely used by enterprise users in software such as Power BI and Tableau. In traditional BI workflows, users need to prepare data by (1) identifying relevant tables, (2) performing data transformations, and (3) building join relationships, before they can (4) answer their business questions. These steps can be complex and time-consuming, making BI challenging.
  Given the strong capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in working with data, we study their ability to answer BI questions end-to-end, without requiring users to manually perform the tedious preparation steps. To do this, we harvest a large collection of real-world BI projects from public sources, and manually extract pairs of (questions, ground-truth answers) from real user dashboards. The resulting benchmark, BI-Bench, is the first benchmark to systematically study LLMs' ability on end-to-end BI.
  We find that even frontier LLMs perform poorly on BI-Bench, with less than 50% accuracy. To address their limitations, we design a tool-augmented BI-Agent that decomposes BI workflows into subtasks on structured data, such as search, join, and transform, and orchestrates specialized data management methods across BI stages. Furthermore, we develop a post-training framework that synthesizes training trajectories from real BI projects, enabling BI-Agent to be further post-trained using both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). BI-Agent achieves substantial accuracy gains of up to 40 percentage points with vanilla LLMs, and post-trained BI-Agent yields gains of up to 30 points. Our results highlight the importance of combining tool-augmented reasoning with domain-specific post-training in complex BI workflows, and point to promising directions for future research.

AI.tldr: End-to-end BI with LLMs analyzed; introduces BI-Bench benchmark and BI-Agent with tool-augmented reasoning plus post-training to enhance BI workflow performance.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with end-to-end BI tasks due to the need for data preparation (data selection, transformation, joins); a benchmark and targeted methods are needed to study and improve LLM capabilities in BI contexts.
AI.method: Construct BI-Bench from real-world BI projects and extract (question, ground-truth answer) pairs. Propose BI-Agent that decomposes BI workflows into subtasks (search, join, transform) on structured data and orchestrates specialized data-management methods across BI stages. Develop a post-training framework that synthesizes training trajectories from real BI projects and applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) to the BI-Agent.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs achieve <50% accuracy on BI-Bench. BI-Agent with vanilla LLMs yields up to ~40 percentage-point gains. Post-training BI-Agent yields up to ~30-point gains.
AI.conclusion: Combining tool-augmented reasoning with domain-specific post-training is crucial for complex BI workflows and points to promising directions for future research.

title: AeRove: A Compact Bimodal Aerial-Terrestrial Drone with Rapid Bistable Reconfiguration for Close-Range Pipeline Inspection
summary: Close-proximity pipeline inspection is challenging for standard drones due to high hovering power consumption, airflow sensitivity, and propeller wash interference with gas sensing. To address this, we present AeRove, a compact bimodal aerial-terrestrial robot. AeRove uses its propeller guards as wheels to roll along pipes and employs a spring-loaded bistable mechanism to reconfigure between ground and flight modes in 200 ms without continuous actuator power to maintain either state. The converging propeller-guard geometry also improves measured thrust efficiency. By reserving flight for obstacle hopping and using ground rolling for continuous traversal, current draw is reduced 14x compared to continuous flight (0.7 A vs. 10 A), extending estimated travel distance from 144 m to 2057 m. Autonomous trials on a 51 cm diameter steel pipe demonstrated navigation on straight and curved sections, obstacle jumping, and leak detection of simulated inspection markers. Separate CO2 sensing experiments evaluated gas-detection performance under perched and aerial operating conditions. Perched inspection produced a substantially larger concentration response than hovering under the tested conditions. During flight, an underbody propeller-intake configuration produced a faster and stronger gas-detection response than an extended probe by leveraging propeller-induced airflow. Code and designs are released under the CC-BY license.

AI.tldr: AeRove: a bimodal aerial-terrestrial pipe-inspection robot using prop-guard wheels and a bistable reconfig mechanism; 14x lower current draw, longer travel, obstacle hopping, and enhanced gas detection; CC-BY release.
AI.motivation: Close-proximity pipeline inspection is energy-intensive for drones and susceptible to airflow perturbations that affect gas sensing; enabling extended, reliable inspection with integrated sensing is needed.
AI.method: Mechanical design: prop-guards as wheels; spring-loaded bistable mechanism enabling 200 ms ground/flight switching without continuous actuation; converging prop-guard geometry for thrust efficiency; operation strategy: ground rolling for traversal, flight for obstacle hopping; evaluation: current draw, travel distance; autonomous pipe trials on 51 cm diameter steel pipe; CO2 sensing tests in perched vs aerial modes; underbody propeller intake vs extended probe; code released CC-BY.
AI.result: Power: 0.7 A in bimodal vs 10 A in continuous flight; travel distance extended from 144 m to 2057 m; successful navigation on straight and curved pipe segments, obstacle jumping, leak detection markers; perched sensing produced larger gas concentration responses; flight with underbody propeller intake yielded faster/stronger gas detection than extended probe; CC-BY code release.
AI.conclusion: The bimodal design with bistable switching and integrated wheel-wheels enables energy-efficient, capable pipe inspection with improved gas sensing; design choices contribute to thrust efficiency and mission endurance; results support practical deployment and reproducibility.

title: Attention-Aware Routing: Coupling Routing and Attention in MoEs
summary: In Mixture-of-Experts language models, the router typically selects and weights experts based on the token's hidden state, utilizing limited contextual information. We propose Attention-Aware Routing (AAR), which augments the router with temporal and spectral features extracted from a sliding window of attention weights that represent a summary of the model's contextual state, disentangled from the hidden state. Keeping the base transformer entirely frozen, we train only the routing parameters, isolating routing as the sole variable. AAR improves GSM8K by +3.37 pp over a routing-only SFT baseline on OLMoE. Beyond performance, we show that routing and attention form a coupled circuit: routing changes at layer l propagate through the residual stream to amplify attention sinks at layer l+1, reshaping attention without any direct update to the attention mechanism itself. Further, AAR reduces long diverging generation, with incorrect answers getting shorter, while correct answers remain unchanged in length. Finally, AAR is strongly depth-sensitive: applying it indiscriminately across layers can degrade factual retrieval, whereas mathematical reasoning gains persist when it is introduced deeper in the network. This sensitivity exposes a retrieval--reasoning tension across depth and makes layer-selective AAR a controlled probe of the routing-relevant information carried by attention at different layers.

AI.tldr: Attention-Aware Routing (AAR) augments MoE routers with temporal/spectral features from sliding windows of attention weights, trains only routing while freezing the base transformer; yields GSM8K gains (+3.37 pp on OLMoE), reveals coupled routing-attention dynamics, reduces long-divergent generations, and shows depth-sensitive layerwise effects that serve as a probe of routing-relevant information.
AI.motivation: Improve routing decisions in Mixture-of-Experts language models by leveraging richer contextual cues without changing the base model parameters.
AI.method: Extract temporal and spectral features from a sliding window of attention weights to summarize contextual state; freeze the transformer and train only routing parameters; analyze propagation of routing changes through the residual stream and its effect on subsequent attention; evaluate depth sensitivity and layer-selective deployment.
AI.result: Routing augmented with AAR improves GSM8K by 3.37 percentage points over routing-only SFT baseline on OLMoE; demonstrates a coupled routing-attention circuit; reduces long-divergent generations (incorrect answers shorter) without affecting correct answer length; shows strong depth sensitivity where indiscriminate application can hurt factual retrieval but deeper application preserves mathematical reasoning gains; layer-selective AAR provides a probe of routing-relevant information across layers.
AI.conclusion: AAR reveals that routing decisions can be greatly enhanced by incorporating attention-derived contextual summaries while keeping the base model fixed; highlights a retrieval-reasoning tension across depth and suggests layer-wise deployment as both a practical and diagnostic tool for understanding routing-relevant information in attention.

title: MarsFM: Shading-Regularized Flow Matching for Martian Relief Estimation
summary: We present MarsFM, an image-conditioned latent flow-matching model for local Martian relief estimation from single-band HiRISE RED orthoimagery. The method combines a pretrained generative prior with stereo-derived geometric supervision and a differentiable Lunar--Lambert shading objective. Relief, normal, gradient, curvature, and ordinal terms constrain complementary aspects of terrain structure, while a positive-affine-invariant image comparison constrains rendered appearance. An evaluation comprising 2024 gathered patch records per integration-step count yields mean affine-aligned RMSE between 0.0935 and 0.0957 in normalized signed-log relief space for one to twenty Euler steps. These scores measure agreement with VAE-reconstructed references on positive-reference support. Their narrow range supports low-step inference under this protocol. Spatial, differential, and spectral diagnostics show broad terrain correspondence alongside smoothing, amplitude compression, and boundary mismatch. MarsFM provides a framework for combining learned terrain priors with image-based constraints; establishing improved physical terrain resolution requires matched baselines and independent high-resolution reference data. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/SuperComputer/mars_hirise_dtm_processed-6aa9b66ba461e07f; code: https://github.com/Marius-Juston/MarsRecon.

AI.tldr: MarsFM is an image-conditioned latent flow-matching approach to estimate Martian topography from single-band HiRISE imagery, integrating a pretrained generative prior with stereo supervision and differentiable shading, achieving ~0.094 affine-aligned RMSE in normalized log-relief space across 1–20 Euler steps; demonstrates a framework combining priors with image constraints, with caveats on smoothing and boundary artifacts.
AI.motivation: Estimate high-resolution, physically plausible Martian relief from limited single-band imagery by fusing learned terrain priors with geometric and appearance constraints.
AI.method: An image-conditioned latent flow-matching model that uses a pretrained generative prior, stereo-derived geometric supervision, and a differentiable Lunar–Lambert shading objective. It enforces relief, normal, gradient, curvature, and ordinal constraints, plus a positive-affine-invariant image comparison to constrain rendered appearance. Evaluation uses 2024 patch records per integration-step count across 1–20 Euler steps.
AI.result: Mean affine-aligned RMSE between 0.0935 and 0.0957 in normalized signed-log relief space for 1–20 Euler steps, measured against VAE-reconstructed references on positive-reference support; narrow range suggests stable low-step inference. Diagnostics show broad terrain correspondence but with smoothing, amplitude compression, and boundary mismatch.
AI.conclusion: MarsFM provides a framework for combining learned terrain priors with image-based constraints for improved terrain resolution; achieving robust physical terrain resolution requires matched baselines and independent high-resolution reference data; data and code are provided.

title: Elastic Threshold Attention: Learned Contextual Sparsity for Long-Context Decoding
summary: Massive KV caches can cause severe memory-bandwidth bottlenecks during long-context decoding. Sparse attention methods mitigate this via selective loading, but that comes at a cost: rigid heuristics drop necessary context, leading to quality degradation. We introduce \textbf{Elastic Threshold Attention (ETA)}, an end-to-end trainable architecture that achieves hardware-accelerated decoding speed without sacrificing dense model quality. ETA predicts dynamic, contextual thresholds directly from query representations, allowing the model to allocate dense-like context to difficult retrieval or reasoning steps while pruning routine tokens. To learn this policy from scratch without representation collapse, ETA \emph{multiplicatively suppresses} sub-threshold logits toward zero during training rather than deleting them. Training against this smooth uniform attention floor provides a distributed probability reservoir that \textbf{causes localized attention sinks on initial tokens to disappear}. It also enables the model to hard-prune uninformative KV blocks at inference time and absorb incidental tokens co-admitted by coarse GPU block selection. As a result, a 1.45B pretrained ETA model rivals dense attention across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and long-context needle retrieval at $\approx 85\%$ training sparsity and $\approx 38\%$ active decode density. At inference time, we implement a custom decode kernel in Triton that screens KV blocks in $O(1)$ time using cached geometric-probabilistic bounds, delivering up to $2.5\times$ wall-clock decode speedups over FlashAttention-2 on sequences up to 512K tokens. Finally, we introduce an offline calibration algorithm for domain-specific deployments that freezes per-head constant thresholds to eliminate predictor overhead, cutting attention compute by an additional $27\%$.

AI.tldr: ETA is an end-to-end trainable sparse attention mechanism that learns dynamic, context-sensitive thresholds to prune routine tokens while preserving dense-model quality, enabling hardware-accelerated long-context decoding with substantial speedups.
AI.motivation: Massive KV caches cause memory-bandwidth bottlenecks during long-context decoding; rigid heuristic sparse-attention methods degrade quality by pruning essential context. There is a need for an end-to-end trainable, context-aware mechanism that maintains dense-model performance.
AI.method: ETA predicts dynamic, contextual thresholds directly from query representations. It multiplicatively suppresses sub-threshold logits toward zero during training to avoid representation collapse, creating a smooth attention floor. This enables hard pruning at inference and co-admittance of incidental tokens. A custom Triton kernel screens KV blocks in O(1) time using geometric-probabilistic bounds. An offline calibration algorithm freezes per-head constants to remove predictor overhead.
AI.result: A 1.45B pretrained ETA model rivals dense attention in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and long-context needle retrieval at ~85% training sparsity and ~38% active decode density; achieves up to 2.5× wall-clock speedups over FlashAttention-2 for sequences up to 512K tokens; offline calibration reduces attention compute by ~27%.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end trainable, hardware-accelerated long-context decoding with maintained dense-model performance; dynamic thresholds and efficient decoding enable substantial speedups and practical deployment in domain-specific settings.

title: Shake to Learn: Dynamic Interrogation of Hidden Object Physics for Robotic Manipulation with Physical Reservoir Computing
summary: Many physical properties relevant to robotic manipulation are hidden from vision. A sealed object, for example, may reveal little about its center of mass (COM) or internal contents until it is lifted, shaken, or otherwise dynamically perturbed. This study shows that such interactions can enable a new modality of robotic perception and learning, in which interaction-induced dynamic responses are used to infer object physics that is inaccessible to conventional sensing. We implement this idea using an origami-inspired soft robotic arm that functions as a physical reservoir computer. After grasping an object, the arm is excited by a fixed shaking input at its base, and the resulting ringdown response is recorded through either camera tracking or embedded sensors. Because the input is held constant across trials, hidden object properties, such as the COM position, are encoded through their effect on the dynamics of the coupled robot-object system. A lightweight linear readout can then decode these dynamics to recover interpretable information about the hidden object physics. Using this framework, the soft robotic arm reservoir completed three tasks of increasing difficulty: inferring the orientation of the object's hidden COM, inferring the COM distance from the grasp point, and using the inferred COM information to guide a subsequent regrasp. We further develop a dynamic summary representation of the ringdown response that improves prediction accuracy. Together, these results establish shake-to-learn mechanical interrogation as a promising strategy for robotic systems to convert brief physical interactions into actionable cues about hidden object properties for downstream manipulation.

AI.tldr: Soft origami-inspired robotic arm serves as a physical reservoir to infer hidden object physics (e.g., COM) from shake-induced ringdown; a fixed shaker input and linear readout decode dynamics for tasks including COM orientation, COM distance, and guiding regrasp; introduces dynamic summary representation to boost accuracy.
AI.motivation: Reveal hidden object properties not accessible by vision by perturbing the system and exploiting dynamics; leverage reservoir computing in a soft robot to map transient responses to object physics.
AI.method: An origami-inspired soft arm acts as a reservoir. After grasping an object, it is excited by a fixed base shake input; the resulting ringdown is recorded via camera tracking or embedded sensors. The constant input across trials allows hidden properties to be encoded in the dynamics of the coupled robot-object system. A lightweight linear readout decodes these dynamics to infer properties; a dynamic summary representation of the ringdown further improves predictions.
AI.result: The soft-arm reservoir completed three tasks: (1) infer the hidden COM orientation, (2) infer the COM distance from the grasp point, and (3) use the inferred COM information to guide a subsequent regrasp. A dynamic summary representation improved prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Shake-to-learn mechanical interrogation is a promising approach for enabling robotic systems to extract actionable cues about hidden object properties from brief physical interactions for downstream manipulation.

title: CaLR: Causal Latent Revision for Robust Diffusion Reasoning
summary: Autoregressive (AR) models suffer from local greediness, while diffusion language models (DLMs) often lack the strict causal structure required for reasoning. To combine the advantages and overcome the drawbacks of the dual, we propose Causal Latent Revision (CaLR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as constrained latent optimization. By adopting a causal topology matrix (CTM) from an expert model and implicit differentiation, CaLR performs gradient-guided ``thought revision" to enforce logical consistency, enabling dynamic self-correction of intermediate steps during parallel generation. Empirically, CaLR achieves SOTA DLM performance on complex benchmarks, surpassing strong AR baselines and demonstrating superior robustness in constrained tasks like Sudoku.

AI.tldr: CaLR introduces Causal Latent Revision, a framework that couples autoregressive and diffusion-style reasoning by using a causal topology matrix (CTM) and implicit differentiation to perform gradient-guided latent revisions and dynamic self-correction during parallel generation. This yields state-of-the-art performance on complex benchmarks and enhanced robustness in constrained tasks (e.g., Sudoku).
AI.motivation: AR models suffer from local greediness, and diffusion language models lack strict causal structure for reasoning. A framework that preserves causal, corrective dynamics while leveraging the strengths of both paradigms is needed.
AI.method: CaLR reformulates reasoning as constrained latent optimization. It adopts a causal topology matrix (CTM) from an expert model and uses implicit differentiation to perform gradient-guided “thought revisions.” This enables dynamic self-correction of intermediate steps during parallel generation, enforcing logical consistency and maintaining a causal flow.
AI.result: Empirically, CaLR achieves state-of-the-art performance for diffusion-language-model-based reasoning on complex benchmarks, surpassing strong autoregressive baselines and showing superior robustness in constrained tasks like Sudoku.
AI.conclusion: CaLR demonstrates that causal latent revision can combine the strengths of AR and DLMs, addressing local greediness and lack of explicit causal structure, by enabling constrained, self-correcting reasoning during parallel generation.

title: 4DGS-Fixer: Generative Sparse-View 4D Gaussian Splatting with Iterative Refinement Guided by Video Diffusion Priors
summary: This paper addresses the challenges of dynamic scene synthesis from sparse-view videos. Existing methods employ geometric priors, adaptive optimization, or density-control strategies to improve 4D Gaussian modeling under sparse observations. However, they cannot fundamentally resolve the ill-posed problem caused by insufficient observations and missing scene information. Moreover, sparse-view 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) often suffers from poor geometric initialization: with only a few input views, COLMAP typically reconstructs sparse and incomplete point clouds, leaving large scene regions without sufficient Gaussian support and making them difficult to recover through subsequent optimization. To address these limitations, we propose a novel iterative refinement framework based on a video diffusion model to improve the completeness and consistency of dynamic 4D scenes. Specifically, we first estimate multi-view depth maps and fuse them into dense point clouds to provide more complete geometric initialization for a dynamic 4DGS representation. We then employ a pretrained video restoration model to refine sequences rendered along novel camera trajectories at different time steps. The restored sequences serve as pseudo-supervision to regularize and iteratively refine the 4DGS representation. Experiments on a widely used benchmark dataset demonstrate that our method substantially outperforms existing baselines, achieving nearly a 2 dB PSNR improvement over the previous best-performing method.

AI.tldr: An iterative refinement framework enhances sparse-view dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) by integrating multi-view depth-based dense geometry with a video diffusion-based restoration, using pseudo-supervision to iteratively refine 4DGS, achieving ~2 dB PSNR gains on a standard benchmark.
AI.motivation: Sparse-view dynamic scene synthesis with 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) is ill-posed due to insufficient observations and weak geometric initialization (COLMAP yields sparse/incomplete point clouds). Existing priors and optimization can't fully resolve missing scene information.
AI.method: Compute multi-view depth maps and fuse into dense point clouds to improve geometric initialization for 4DGS. Render sequences along novel camera trajectories, refine them with a pretrained video restoration model, and use the restored sequences as pseudo-supervision to regularize and iteratively refine the 4DGS representation.
AI.result: The approach substantially outperforms existing baselines, achieving nearly a 2 dB PSNR improvement over the previous best-performing method on a widely used benchmark dataset.
AI.conclusion: An iterative diffusion-informed refinement strategy can improve completeness and consistency of dynamic 4D scenes under sparse observations, by combining dense geometric initialization with pseudo-supervised sequence refinement.

title: Bio-MF: Low-Latency and High-Fidelity EEG-to-fNIRS Cross-Modal Generation for Hybrid Motor-Imagery Brain--Computer Interfaces
summary: Hybrid motor-imagery brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) combining EEG and fNIRS can outperform EEG-only systems by exploiting complementary electrophysiological and hemodynamic information. To obtain such hybrid information when paired EEG-fNIRS acquisition is unavailable or inconvenient, recent studies have focused on EEG-to-fNIRS cross-modal generation. However, existing methods still suffer from slow generation and often require pretraining, limiting their use in real-time MI-BCI scenarios. Although one-step generative models offer an attractive route to low-latency synthesis, removing the iterative refinement process can reduce generation fidelity and introduce non-physiological artifacts. To address these problems, this paper proposes Bio-MF, a latent-free one-step MeanFlow framework for EEG-conditioned fNIRS generation. Bio-MF performs direct signal-space x-prediction, converts this signal-space output into MeanFlow velocity supervision, and completes inference with one network evaluation. To preserve task-relevant hemodynamic structure under heterogeneous sensor layouts, Bio-MF integrates Spatial-Temporal Interactive 4D Encoding, cross-modal classifier-free guidance, and noise-level-gated FFT regularization. On Dataset 1, EEG + synthetic fNIRS improves ACC over EEG-only by 3.37 and 4.15 percentage points for HbR and HbO, respectively. On Dataset 2, the corresponding gains remain 2.98 and 2.50 percentage points under the unseen 64-channel EEG montage. On an RTX PRO 6000 GPU, Bio-MF generates one fNIRS trial in 7.0 ms, corresponding to an 857x speedup over the 1000-step SCDM latency. These results show that Bio-MF enables fast EEG-to-fNIRS synthesis while preserving task-relevant generation quality for downstream hybrid MI decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/psychosiwa/Bio-MF.

AI.tldr: Bio-MF is a latent-free one-step EEG-conditioned fNIRS generation framework (MeanFlow) that enables fast, high-fidelity cross-modal synthesis for EEG-to-fNIRS in hybrid MI-BCIs, achieving large accuracy gains and substantial speedups while handling heterogeneous sensor layouts.
AI.motivation: Hybrid motor-imagery BRNs interfaces can outperform EEG-only systems by leveraging complementary EEG and fNIRS signals. When paired EEG-fNIRS data aren't available, cross-modal EEG-to-fNIRS generation enables real-time HD hybrid decoding, but existing one-step methods trade fidelity for speed or require pretraining. A fast, faithful one-step method that preserves physiological structure under varying sensor layouts is needed.
AI.method: Bio-MF adopts a latent-free one-step pipeline with direct signal-space x-prediction, then converts this to MeanFlow velocity supervision, enabling one-network inference. It integrates Spatial-Temporal Interactive 4D Encoding to preserve hemodynamic structure across heterogeneous sensor layouts, classifier-free guidance for cross-modal generation, and noise-level-gated FFT regularization to stabilize training. Output is generated in one network evaluation (one-shot), with x-space prediction guiding the MeanFlow supervision.
AI.result: Quantitative gains: Dataset 1 - HbR: +3.37 percentage points; HbO: +4.15 pp in ACC over EEG-only. Dataset 2 (unseen 64-channel EEG montage) - HbR: +2.98 pp; HbO: +2.50 pp. Speed: on RTX PRO 6000, one fNIRS trial generated in 7.0 ms, about 857x faster than the 1000-step SCDM latency. The method maintains task-relevant generation quality for downstream hybrid MI decoding; code available at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: Bio-MF demonstrates that fast, one-step EEG-to-fNIRS generation can achieve high fidelity and robustness across sensor layouts, enabling practical real-time hybrid MI-BCIs. The approach offers substantial time savings without sacrificing performance, making real-time EEG-conditioned fNIRS synthesis feasible.

title: ForeTac-VLA: A Forecasting-Based Tactile-Vision-Language-Action Model for Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on visual perception limits robustness in contact-rich environments, where critical physical interaction states may not be visually observable. Existing tactile-enhanced VLA methods improve physical grounding using observed tactile feedback, but most remain largely reactive rather than explicitly modeling how contact may evolve. Therefore, we propose ForeTac-VLA, a forecasting-based tactile-vision-language fusion model that predicts future tactile states to guide action generation. Specifically, ForeTac-VLA encodes recent tactile observations into temporal representations and integrates them with vision-language features through bidirectional cross-attention. Further, a transformer-based forecasting module predicts multi-step future tactile states, enabling the model to reason jointly over observed and anticipated contact. Finally, the fused multimodal representations and predicted future tactile states are fed into the VLA backbone to condition action generation. To stabilize training, a ground-truth-to-prediction curriculum is employed when early forecasts are unreliable. Across four real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, ForeTac-VLA achieves an average success rate of 95%, outperforming the fine-tuned VLA model by 36.25 percentage points and state-of-the-art tactile-enhanced VLA baselines by over 22 percentage points. ForeTac-VLA also maintains strong performance under low-illumination and visually cluttered conditions. Video demonstrations can be found on https://foretac-vla.github.io/

AI.tldr: ForeTac-VLA forecasts future tactile states to guide action in vision-language-action robotics, integrating tactile, vision, and language through cross-attention and a transformer forecaster; achieves 95% average success across four contact-rich tasks and outperforms baselines, robust to low-light and clutter.
AI.motivation: Robust manipulation requires grounding in tactile/contact states not always visible; existing tactile-VLA methods are largely reactive and do not model how contact evolves over time.
AI.method: Encode recent tactile observations into temporal representations; fuse with vision-language features via bidirectional cross-attention; use a transformer-based module to predict multi-step future tactile states; feed fused multimodal representations and predicted tactile states into the VLA backbone for action generation; stabilize training with a ground-truth-to-prediction curriculum.
AI.result: Achieves 95% average success across four real-world tasks; outperforms fine-tuned VLA by 36.25 percentage points and state-of-the-art tactile-enhanced VLA baselines by >22 points; maintains performance under low illumination and clutter.
AI.conclusion: Forecasting future tactile states enhances VLA for contact-rich manipulation by enabling joint reasoning over observed and anticipated contact; curriculum aids training stability; supports robust, real-time manipulation with multimodal fusion.

title: LoRA Enhanced Contrastive Learning with SAS Vision Transformers
summary: Automatic target recognition (ATR) with synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) supports advanced naval capabilities, but deep learning is constrained by scarce target imagery, background clutter, and human-in-the-loop assessment. We adapt DINOv3 Vision Transformer (ViT) models to underwater SAS ATR using a three-stage parameter-efficient framework. Stage 1 uses Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) while freezing the ViT backbone, bridging the gap between natural-image pretraining and underwater acoustic propagation. Stage 2 uses hard-negative mining to strengthen the decision boundary against acoustic mimics, including rocks and sediment formations resembling man-made targets. Stage 3 uses Supervised Contrastive Learning (SupCon) to separate target and clutter representations. We evaluate at-sea SAS data using a mission-level geographic split, compare all arms at 85 percent test recall, and repeat each comparison over three random seeds. LoRA accounts for the primary effect, increasing area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) from 0.300 to 0.679 +/- 0.027 using the same frozen backbone. Rank 4 achieves this result while training only 0.26 percent of weights. Neither refinement stage exceeds its matched control: hard-negative mining changes AUPRC by -0.0045 +/- 0.0119 versus an equal-size random curriculum, and SupCon changes AUPRC by +0.0002 +/- 0.0096 versus the preceding stage. These null results indicate that mining occurred on data the encoder had already fit and that supervised stages had already imposed most target-clutter geometry. One efficient adaptation stage is sufficient; stacked refinement is not.

AI.tldr: LoRA-enabled, frozen ViT fine-tuning for SAS ATR yields major gains; subsequent refinement stages offer negligible improvement.
AI.motivation: Overcoming scarcity of target imagery and prevalence of clutter in underwater SAS ATR using a parameter-efficient transfer approach that minimizes retraining while adapting to acoustic propagation differences.
AI.method: Three-stage framework: Stage 1 LoRA with frozen ViT backbone; Stage 2 hard-negative mining to tighten decision boundary against acoustic mimics; Stage 3 SupCon to separate target vs clutter. Evaluation on at-sea SAS data with mission-level geographic split; comparisons at 85% test recall; three random seeds; measure AUPRC.
AI.result: LoRA with frozen backbone increases AUPRC from 0.300 to 0.679 ± 0.027 using the same backbone; trains 0.26% of weights (Rank 4). Stage 2 and Stage 3 refinements yield negligible improvements: -0.0045 ± 0.0119 and +0.0002 ± 0.0096 respectively, indicating no meaningful gains beyond the single adaptation stage.
AI.conclusion: A single efficient adaptation stage suffices; stacked refinement does not improve performance. The encoder appears to have already captured target–clutter geometry; LoRA offers the primary benefit while additional stages provide minimal value.

title: OnomatoBridge: Onomatopoeia Translation and Rendering Pipeline in Manga
summary: Manga is a comic drawn by black and white paints gaining popularity around the world. Onomatopoeia in Manga specifically appeals to the audience with its unique visual styles, which convey sound, motion, and emotion. Visual onomatopoeia translation requires the clean replacement of Japanese onomatopoeia with onomatopoeia in the other language while preserving their visual style. Existing approaches often produce residual artifacts or style inconsistency when removing the Japanese onomatopoeia and rendering stylized English onomatopoeia. To approach these problems, we present OnomatoBridge, a filtering pipeline for visual onomatopoeia translation. We evaluate OnomatoBridge from Japanese to English on the Manga109 onomatopoeia dataset and compare it with baseline image editing models. Experimental results show that the filtered outputs by the proposed method outperform those of conventional methods. OnomatoBridge improves English text correctness by roughly 10 to 25 points and reduces residual Japanese text by about 20 to 50% in relative terms.

AI.tldr: A filtering pipeline, OnomatoBridge, translates visual onomatopoeia in Manga from Japanese to English, reducing artifacts and improving style coherence; outperforms baselines on Manga109 with 10–25 point gains in English text correctness and 20–50% reduction in residual Japanese text.
AI.motivation: Visual onomatopoeia is a key narrative device in manga; translating it requires removing Japanese text cleanly while rendering stylized English equivalents that match the visual style. Existing methods often leave artifacts or style inconsistencies.
AI.method: Proposes OnomatoBridge, a filtering pipeline that detects and removes Japanese onomatopoeia regions and overlays stylized English onomatopoeia to preserve the original visual appearance; evaluated on the Manga109 onomatopoeia dataset against baseline image editing models.
AI.result: The filtered outputs from OnomatoBridge outperform conventional methods, with English text correctness improving by ~10–25 points and residual Japanese text reduced by ~20–50% (relative).
AI.conclusion: OnomatoBridge effectively mitigates artifacts and maintains visual coherence during translation, enhancing the quality and readability of translated visual onomatopoeia in manga.

title: Continuous Delayed-Memory Stochastic Gradient Descent and Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning from History of Astrophysical Time Series Studies
comment: Keywords: Stochastic process, Stochastic gradient descent, Continuous-Delayed-Memory Stochastic Gradient Descent, Stochastic Delay Differential Equation, Reinforcement Learning, Adjoint method
summary: Quasars are luminous objects in the universe that exhibit stochastic brightness variations encoding information about the supermassive black holes powering them, and modeling these variations from ground-based survey data time series, known as light curves, is a statistical challenge. This paper reviews how stochastic differential equations (SDEs) have been adapted with neural network parameterizations to overcome this challenge in history. We create the Continuous-Delayed-Memory Stochastic Gradient Descent which depend on the past state of the discrete iteration process. We performed the simulation on some 2-dimensional landscape and observed some wider-exploration and more precise convergent behavior compared to Vanilla SGD by adjusting hyperparameters. Besides, we proposed a reinforcement learning structure with continuous time policy gradients for exploratory policies without solving HJB PDE, and we show that its optimality conditions recover the Gibbs policy of previous works.

AI.tldr: The abstract surveys SDE-based neural modeling of quasar light curves and introduces a novel past-state dependent SGD (Continuous-Delayed-Memory SGD) with empirical gains in exploration and convergence, plus a continuous-time policy-gradient RL framework whose optimality conditions align with Gibbs policies.
AI.motivation: Quasar brightness variations are stochastic, and modeling them from ground-based light curves is statistically challenging. Integrating stochastic differential equation models with neural parameterizations and developing tractable, effective optimization and RL methods is desirable for better inference and control.
AI.method: 1) Propose Continuous-Delayed-Memory SGD that depends on past states of the discrete iteration process; test on a 2D landscape showing broader exploration and more precise convergence versus Vanilla SGD by tuning hyperparameters. 2) Propose a reinforcement learning structure with continuous-time policy gradients for exploratory policies without solving the HJB PDE, and prove that its optimality conditions recover the Gibbs policy of previous works.
AI.result: Empirical results on a 2D landscape indicate improved exploration and convergence behavior for the proposed CDM-SGD compared to Vanilla SGD. The continuous-time RL framework yields theoretical optimality conditions that converge to the Gibbs policy known from prior literature.
AI.conclusion: The work combines SDE-based neural parameterizations for astrophysical time-series modeling with a novel past-state optimization scheme and a continuous-time RL formulation that links to Gibbs policies, offering methodological advances in stochastic optimization and RL for continuous-time systems.

title: PIVOT: Physically Informed Vision-Language Off-Road Traversability for Field Robot Navigation
summary: Terrain assessment is a critical capability for off-road mobile robots, enabling safe and reliable navigation through unstructured and geometrically complex environments. Conventional geometry-based terrain assessment is fast to compute but often overly conservative in unstructured environments. We present PIVOT: a Physically Informed Vision-Language Off-Road Traversability navigation system that augments conventional geometry-based planning with vision-language-model (VLM)-based semantic reasoning for field robots. To physically ground this assessment, we quantify how strongly the VLM's predicted traversal energy cost, robot vibration, and wheel slip correlate with real-world measurements and introduce a unified traversability score that weights each modality by its prediction-measurement correlation. For efficiency, we design a two-level navigation architecture that retains geometry-based planning as the nominal mode and invokes semantic replanning only when that mode fails to find a path. Across five repeated closed-loop trials on a mixed-terrain route totalling around $6.4$ km, the proposed system increases overall autonomy from $59.6\%$ to $97.0\%$, reduces human interventions from $11$ to $3$, and increases the mean distance between interventions (MDBI) from $69.2$ m to $412.9$ m compared with geometry-only navigation. These results demonstrate that physically grounded VLM-based terrain assessment can substantially extend autonomous navigation beyond the limitations of geometry alone, while preserving efficient geometric planning as the nominal mode.

AI.tldr: Physically grounded VLM-based terrain assessment augments geometry-based planning with semantic reasoning to improve off-road traversal in unstructured environments, using a two-level architecture and multimodal traversability scoring; results show large autonomy gains and fewer interventions.
AI.motivation: Geometry-based terrain assessment is fast but conservative in unstructured environments. Incorporating perceptual semantics can enable better path selection, but must be physically grounded and efficiently integrated with existing planning.
AI.method: Quantify correlations between VLM-predicted traversal energy cost, vibration, and wheel slip with real-world measurements; compute a unified traversability score weighting modalities by their prediction–measurement correlation; implement a two-level navigation system with geometry-based planning as the nominal mode and semantic replanning when needed; validate on five repeated closed-loop trials totaling ~6.4 km.
AI.result: Autonomy increased from 59.6% to 97.0%; human interventions decreased from 11 to 3; mean distance between interventions (MDBI) increased from 69.2 m to 412.9 m across ~6.4 km of mixed-terrain trials; geometry-only navigation baseline performance substantially surpassed.
AI.conclusion: Physically grounded VLM-based terrain assessment can substantially extend autonomous navigation beyond the limitations of geometry alone while preserving efficient geometry-based planning as the default mode.

title: Detecting Hallucination in LLMs: Tracing the Topological Signatures of Impaired Context Sharing
summary: In this work, we examine the topology of information flow patterns within attention graphs to effectively distinguish hallucinated from non-hallucinated responses. We analyze the Forman-Ricci curvature to identify structural patterns indicating information bottlenecks in attention graphs. We then introduce a method that captures both semi-local and global information-flow characteristics of attention heads associated with hallucinated responses. We evaluate our approach extensively across several LLMs and established benchmarks. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed single-pass approach provides consistent improvements over existing attention-based and multi-response baselines across two hallucination-detection benchmarks, while achieving competitive performance across diverse LLM architectures. Further analysis reveals that impaired context sharing among tokens during causal generation is strongly associated with hallucination occurrences in LLMs. In particular, hallucinated responses are consistently characterized by an over-reliance on self-attention, diffused context retrieval from earlier tokens, or information over-squashing, especially in the final transformer layer.

AI.tldr: A single-pass method using Forman-Ricci curvature on attention graphs to detect hallucinations by capturing semi-local and global information-flow patterns, identifying bottlenecks and context-sharing impairments, and outperforming existing baselines on hallucination-detection benchmarks with robust cross-architectural performance.
AI.motivation: To understand and detect hallucinations in LLM outputs by analyzing the topology of information flow in attention networks, addressing limitations of existing attention-based and multi-response baselines, and achieving an efficient single-pass detection method.
AI.method: Compute Forman-Ricci curvature on attention graphs to identify information bottlenecks; extract semi-local and global information-flow features from attention heads associated with hallucinated responses; evaluate across multiple LLMs and standard benchmarks in a single-pass framework; compare against attention-based and multi-response baselines.
AI.result: The proposed single-pass approach yields consistent improvements on two hallucination-detection benchmarks and competitive performance across diverse LLMs, outperforming existing attention-based and multi-response baselines.
AI.conclusion: Structural patterns in attention-flow, such as impaired context sharing, over-reliance on self-attention, diffused context retrieval, and information over-squashing—especially in the final transformer layer—are strongly associated with hallucinations; the method effectively captures these patterns to improve detection and generalizes across architectures.

title: Hand-Aware Transition Modeling for Bimanual Procedural Anomaly Detection
summary: Procedural anomaly detection in bimanual assembly requires judging each hand action against the execution so far. A corrective action may look unusual in isolation, while a visually plausible action can violate the order of the procedure. We present HACT, a transition model over predicted per-hand events. A role-preserving history keeps the concurrent responsibilities of both hands, and a marked temporal point process assigns each observed transition a semantic and temporal surprisal. A supervised evidence head and a two-state filter convert these surprisals into per-hand anomaly posteriors. A recovery-aware protocol on predicted events and participant-disjoint folds reports the recovery false-positive rate at an operating point selected on validation participants. On two bimanual power-tool procedures HACT has the highest AUPRC and F1 among the compared methods and the fewest recovery alarms. Applied without retraining to a different assembly order of the same product, it retains the highest AUPRC and F1. The source code is available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/HACT.

AI.tldr: HACT is a transition-model-based detector for procedural anomalies in bimanual assembly that uses a role-preserving history and a marked temporal point process to compute per-hand anomaly posteriors, achieving state-of-the-art AUPRC/F1 with low recovery alarms and robust cross-order transfer; code available.
AI.motivation: Detect procedural anomalies in bimanual assembly where wrong actions may be visually plausible but violate procedure order. Reduce false alarms while maintaining sensitivity, and enable cross-order robustness without retraining.
AI.method: HACT constructs a transition model over predicted per-hand events. It uses a role-preserving history to maintain concurrent hand responsibilities, a marked temporal point process to assign semantic and temporal surprisal to observed transitions, and a supervised evidence head with a two-state filter to produce per-hand anomaly posteriors. A recovery-aware evaluation protocol with participant-disjoint folds reports recovery false-positive rates at a chosen operating point.
AI.result: In two bimanual power-tool procedures, HACT achieves the highest AUPRC and F1 among compared methods and the fewest recovery alarms. It also retains the top AUPRC and F1 when applied to a different assembly order of the same product without retraining.
AI.conclusion: HACT effectively models inter-hand procedural transitions with role-preserving history and temporal surprisal, delivering accurate, robust anomaly detection with low false alarms and cross-order generalization; code is publicly available.

title: Do Quantum Models Scale Like LLMs?
summary: In this work, we study the neural scaling laws of RydbergGPT, an autoregressive transformer model trained on qubit projective measurement data gathered from interacting Rydberg atom arrays. The quantum system is known to exhibit a finite-size remnant of a critical point as the laser detuning parameter is varied. We find that near the critical point the transformer loss as a function of training dataset size is well described by a power-law with a loss floor correction. However, away from criticality the quality of the power-law description is substantially reduced. We then compare the statistical structure of both Rydberg measurements and natural-language corpora using an entropy-normalised, finite sample corrected mutual information "two-point" function. We find that near-critical statistics of the two point functions are closest to those observed in natural-language, whilst other qubit configurations far from the critical point have two-point functions that decay more rapidly. This supports the hypothesis that multi-scale dependence contributes to stable neural scaling, and that scaling behaviour should be viewed as a property of the model-data pair.

AI.tldr: Near-critical Rydberg data enable stable neural scaling in RydbergGPT; loss follows a power-law with a floor and matches natural-language statistics in two-point mutual information, while away from criticality the scaling is poorer.
AI.motivation: Understand how criticality and multi-scale dependencies affect neural scaling laws in transformer models trained on quantum measurement data, and compare with natural language to probe universality of scaling.
AI.method: Train an autoregressive transformer (RydbergGPT) on qubit projective measurements from interacting Rydberg atom arrays.
