Analyze loss versus dataset size with power-law fits including a floor term; compute entropy-normalised, finite-sample corrected mutual information two-point functions for both quantum measurements and natural-language corpora; compare the two-point statistics across near-critical and off-critical regimes.
AI.result: Loss adheres to a power-law with a floor near the critical detuning; away from criticality the power-law description weakens. Near-critical statistics of the two-point function resemble natural language more closely, while far-from-critical data exhibit faster decay. This suggests multi-scale dependence underpins stable neural scaling and that scaling is a property of the model-data pair.
AI.conclusion: Scaling behavior in this setting is not universal but emerges from the interaction between model and data, with near-critical quantum statistics aligning with natural-language patterns and upholding robust neural scaling due to multi-scale dependencies.

title: Do Spinning Radar Doppler Velocity Measurements Improve Vehicle Detection and Tracking?
summary: Spinning frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radars have been gaining popularity in autonomous vehicle perception on account of their robustness to adverse weather conditions and 360° field of view. Recently, scanning radars have also been shown capable of generating per-azimuth Doppler velocity. In this paper, we investigate whether these Doppler velocity measurements improve spinning radar vehicle detection and tracking performance. For detection, we estimate the ego motion and use it to undo the Doppler range distortion of the radar image before passing it to a network. For tracking, we propose a new way to estimate a per-vehicle velocity and use it as a prior for the tracker's motion model. Since Doppler-enabled spinning radar data is not available in any dataset with ground-truth dynamic object labels, our first contribution is an automatic labelling pipeline that uses an ensemble of fine-tuned off-the-shelf lidar detectors to label all 643 km of the Boreas Road Trip dataset. We then transfer detections to radar, and use over 250 km of vehicle-dense sequences as ground-truth training data. By training and evaluating two state-of-the-art detectors, we show that Doppler undistortion can improve detection accuracy by up to $2.37$ points on mean average precision. Furthermore, we show that the Doppler velocity prior can improve tracking accuracy by $13.68$ points on multi-object tracking accuracy (MOTA) versus the zero-velocity initialization baseline, while achieving $99.7\%$ of the MOTA obtained using ground-truth velocities as the prior.

AI.tldr: Doppler-enabled spinning FMCW radar improves vehicle detection and tracking via Doppler undistortion and per-vehicle velocity priors; an automatic labeling pipeline on the Boreas dataset enables radar training; reported gains include up to 2.37 mAP and 13.68 MOTA points, approaching the performance with ground-truth velocities.
AI.motivation: To leverage per-azimuth Doppler measurements from spinning FMCW radars to boost perception (detection and tracking) in autonomous driving, addressing the lack of labeled radar data with Doppler and the need for velocity-aware tracking.
AI.method: 1) For detection: estimate ego motion to undo Doppler range distortion in the radar image, then pass to a detector. 2) For tracking: estimate a per-vehicle velocity to serve as a prior in the tracker’s motion model. 3) Develop an automatic labeling pipeline using ensembles of fine-tuned LiDAR detectors to label the Boreas Road Trip dataset (643 km), transfer detections to radar, and use 250+ km of vehicle-dense sequences as ground truth. 4) Train/evaluate two state-of-the-art detectors on this setup.
AI.result: Doppler undistortion improves detection accuracy by up to 2.37 percentage points in mean average precision (mAP). The Doppler-velocity prior improves multi-object tracking accuracy (MOTA) by 13.68 points over a zero-velocity initialization baseline, achieving 99.7% of the MOTA that would be obtained with ground-truth velocities as prior.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating per-azimuth Doppler information via Doppler undistortion and velocity-informed tracking substantially enhances spinning radar perception. The proposed automatic labeling pipeline enables radar-ground-truth training data creation, though results are dataset-specific and depend on accurate ego-motion estimation.

title: Decoupling Internal Representational Changes and Causal Importance in Fine-Tuned Large Language Models
summary: Fine-tuning has emerged as a widely adopted approach for adapting LLMs to a variety of downstream tasks. However, how it reshapes their internal mechanisms remains poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how fine-tuning alters internal representations in LLMs, including attention patterns and layer-wise activations, and examine whether these changes are linked to task-relevant components identified by EAP (e.g., attention heads and logit-level activations) that drive task performance. We find that EAP-identified components are concentrated within specific layers, indicating a degree of functional localisation in how models internalise task-specific behavior. Notably, the distribution of these components across layers is largely uncorrelated with the layers undergoing the most substantial representational changes during fine-tuning. Furthermore, we observe that overlap in EAP-identified components across tasks does not translate into cross-task performance transfer if the tasks are different in nature (e.g. classification vs. generative tasks). More specifically, fine-tuning on one task can lead to a degradation of performance on another when the two tasks exhibit a high degree of overlap in their EAP-identified components.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning reshapes internal representations and attention-related mechanisms; EAP-identified components are concentrated in specific layers, showing functional localization. However, where these components are distributed across layers does not align with the largest representational changes during fine-tuning. Overlap of EAP components across tasks does not ensure cross-task transfer; in fact, high overlap can lead to negative transfer when tasks differ in nature (e.g., classification vs. generation).
AI.motivation: To understand how task-specific fine-tuning reshapes LLM internal mechanisms and whether EAP-identified components predict transferability or cause interference across tasks.
AI.method: Analyze fine-tuning effects on attention patterns and layer-wise activations; identify task-relevant components using EAP (attention heads and logit-level activations) and map their layer distribution; assess correlations with representational changes, cross-task overlap, and cross-task transfer across tasks of different natures (e.g., classification vs. generative).
AI.result: EAP-identified components are concentrated in particular layers, indicating functional localization. The distribution of these components across layers is largely uncorrelated with the layers that undergo the most substantial representational changes during fine-tuning. Overlap of EAP-identified components across tasks does not predict cross-task transfer when tasks differ in nature; fine-tuning on one task can degrade performance on another if the tasks share high EAP overlap.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning induces localized, task-specific component changes; EAP-based components reflect functional localization rather than global representational shifts, and cross-task transfer is limited and can be negative when EAP components overlap substantially.

title: Multi-viewpoint Geo-localization with Event Cameras
summary: Robot localization is an ongoing challenge that demands mapping and positioning systems that are tolerant to viewpoint change. Event cameras are attracting increasing interest and adoption in robotics; however, dealing with viewpoint variance is an under-investigated problem in existing event-based localizers. In addition, event-based datasets that emphasize viewpoint variance for challenging localization situations are scarce. Here, we introduce an event-based visual place recognition (VPR) system that performs robustly under viewpoint changes. We converted five large-scale geo-tagged datasets, conventionally used to train frame-based localization systems, into synthetic event streams using Image-to-Event (I2E) conversion, and used them to fine-tune a pre-trained event-based vision transformer backbone with a multi-loss function, yielding a system we call MegaEvent that learns viewpoint-robust features for place recognition. We achieved an average Recall@1 of 82% across three existing event-based localization datasets, leading the next best event-based method by 20 recall points, and frame-based VPR models applied directly to event frames by 8 to 26 recall points. We introduce a new, challenging dataset - Springfield-Event-VPR - which features a 3.7km walking route recorded in three camera orientations for a total of 11.1km, which MegaEvent outperforms the strongest baseline by 9 recall points. The code for MegaEvent is available at https://github.com/AdamDHines/megaevent.

AI.tldr: An event-based visual place recognition system (MegaEvent) learns viewpoint-robust features by converting geo-tagged datasets into synthetic event streams via Image-to-Event (I2E) and fine-tuning a vision transformer; it achieves strong recall and introduces Springfield-Event-VPR for evaluation.
AI.motivation: Tolerance to viewpoint change is critical for robot localization; event cameras are promising but viewpoint variance is under-explored, and datasets emphasizing this are scarce. The work aims to enable robust, viewpoint-invariant place recognition from event data.
AI.method: Convert five large-scale frame-based datasets into synthetic event streams using I2E; fine-tune a pre-trained event-based vision transformer with a multi-loss function; evaluate on three event-based localization datasets; introduce Springfield-Event-VPR (3.7 km route, three orientations, 11.1 km total); release code.
AI.result: MegaEvent achieves average Recall@1 = 82% across three event-based datasets, outperforming the next-best event-based method by ~20 points and frame-based VPR on event frames by 8–26 points; Springfield-Event-VPR yields MegaEvent +9 Recall points over strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MegaEvent provides robust viewpoint-robust event-based VPR, demonstrates the value of I2E-generated training data for viewpoint generalization, and contributes a challenging dataset and open-source code.

title: When AI Reviews Train AI Reviewers: Scientific-Judgment Collapse and Mitigation
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly participate in scientific evaluation, both as automated reviewers and as assistants to human reviewers. As model-generated reviews enter public data and future training corpora, AI peer review can become recursive: later reviewers learn from judgments produced by earlier models. We study one step of this feedback loop in a controlled setting. Starting from Llama 3.1 8B, we first fine-tune a reviewer on official ICLR reviews from 2018--2023 and then train four successor models on ICLR 2024 data with systematically varied mixtures of official and model-generated reviews. Our study shows that introducing synthetic reviews compresses rating distributions and reduces both same-paper and corpus-level semantic diversity. We call this pattern $\textbf{scientific-judgment collapse}$.
  To mitigate this failure mode, we introduce $\textbf{TrustReviewer}$, an open-source LLM-based system for generating peer reviews of AI and machine learning papers. TrustReviewer intervenes at two complementary stages. For training-time prevention, we train the core reviewer in a single stage on a curated corpus designed to reduce low-quality and semantically degenerate supervision. For test-time correction, paired activation steering aims to further mitigate residual tendencies toward collapsed judgments without further training or additional expert annotation. Together, these results characterize a concrete risk of recursive reviewer training and provide practical interventions for preserving judgment diversity and improving recommendation alignment in AI-assisted scientific evaluation.

AI.tldr: A study on recursive AI peer review shows that synthetic reviews induce a “scientific-judgment collapse” by compressing rating distributions and reducing semantic diversity; it also proposes TrustReviewer, a two-stage mitigation (training-time corpus curation and test-time activation steering) to preserve judgment diversity and alignment in AI-assisted review.
AI.motivation: To assess risks of recursive reviewer training in AI-assisted scientific evaluation and to develop practical methods to preserve diversity of judgments and alignment with human standards.
AI.method: Fine-tune a reviewer from Llama 3.1 8B on official ICLR reviews (2018–2023). Train four successor models on ICLR 2024 data with varying mixtures of official vs. model-generated reviews. Evaluate effects on rating distributions and semantic diversity. Introduce TrustReviewer: (1) training-time prevention via a curated corpus designed to reduce low-quality/degenerate supervision; (2) test-time correction via paired activation steering, no extra training or annotation. Open-source release claimed.
AI.result: Synthetic reviews lead to compressed rating distributions and reduced same-paper and corpus-level semantic diversity (scientific-judgment collapse). TrustReviewer mitigates collapse through the proposed dual-stage approach, suggesting a path to preserve judgment diversity and improve alignment in AI-assisted peer review.
AI.conclusion: Recursive reviewer training poses a concrete risk to scientific evaluation quality; the paper offers practical interventions (curated training data and activation steering) to maintain diversity of judgments and better alignment with human standards in AI-assisted review.

title: Project SCOUT: Interceptor Drone for Perimeter Defense
summary: The rapid proliferation of unauthorized unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has created a growing need for robust, jamming-resistant counter-UAV systems for perimeter defense. This paper presents \textbf{SCOUT} (Spatial Computation for Optimized UAV Tracking), a ROS-integrated onboard perception and control framework for real-time aerial defense against incoming UAVs. SCOUT performs visual detection, target association, track filtering, and control command generation directly onboard the defender UAV, without relying on external sensing infrastructure or ground-station computation. To provide stable control inputs, the perception pipeline combines TensorRT-accelerated drone detection with ByteTrack-based association and a lightweight track-retention state machine. The state machine rejects abrupt target jumps and maintains short-term target continuity during temporary detection degradation, reducing unstable control responses caused by false detections or target switching. We evaluate the proposed architecture through an integrated hardware deployment executing a planar ``goalkeeping'' interception strategy. In this setting, the defender UAV tracks the incoming target and adjusts its motion to maintain a blocking configuration near the protected boundary. Real-world flight results show that SCOUT maintains valid target detections for 92.2\% of frames while operating at real-time onboard detection rates, demonstrating the feasibility of visual tracking and closed-loop control for UAV perimeter defense. A video demonstration of the end-to-end perimeter defense operation is available online. https://figshare.com/s/497befc033091fc0b84f

AI.tldr: SCOUT is a ROS-integrated onboard perception-control framework for real-time UAV perimeter defense, fusing TensorRT-accelerated detection with ByteTrack data association and a lightweight track-retention state machine to achieve onboard tracking at real-time rates with 92.2% frame-level target maintenance in a planar interception scenario.
AI.motivation: Address the need for robust, jamming-resistant counter-UAV systems that operate fully onboard without reliance on external sensors or ground stations.
AI.method: Perception pipeline combines TensorRT-accelerated drone detection, ByteTrack-based data association, and a lightweight track-retention state machine; ROS integration; onboard control commands; hardware deployment for a planar goalkeeping interception strategy.
AI.result: Real-world flight results show 92.2% valid target detections across frames at real-time onboard rates, demonstrating feasibility of visual tracking and closed-loop control for UAV perimeter defense; a video demonstration is available online.
AI.conclusion: SCOUT demonstrates feasible, self-contained onboard visual tracking and control for UAV perimeter defense with robust target continuity and reduced control instability due to false detections.

title: TinyCeNN-LM: Quality-Gated Conversion of Pretrained Attention with CeNN-Inspired Cellular-Recurrent Layers
summary: Replacing attention in a pretrained language model is a compatibility problem: a plausible substitute may alter representations expected by later layers. TinyCeNN-LM introduces a \emph{quality-gated post-training conversion} framework using CeNN-inspired cellular-recurrent layers with bounded local processing, compact recurrent memory, routing, fusion, and accept-or-rollback validation. Three implementations are studied: Integrated Memory, MemoryFusion, and PDelta3-GDN2-CLVR+Local32. Strict PDelta3 conversion accepts a layer only when representation and NLL criteria pass fixed thresholds. On SmolLM2-135M, layers 0-2 are accepted with cumulative $Δ\mathrm{NLL}=+0.01209$, while layer 3 is rejected despite acceptable NLL because representation fidelity fails. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, full-attention layers 3, 7, and 11 are accepted with final $Δ\mathrm{NLL}=+0.02073$. Integrated Memory keeps perplexity within $-0.07\%$ to $+0.93\%$ while reducing total cache by up to $6.01\%$. A sampled 200-item downstream sanity check gives $28.5\%$--$32.0\%$ overall accuracy for converted Qwen releases. The results support conservative, quality-gated structural conversion rather than universal attention replacement or speedup.

AI.tldr: Conservative, quality-gated post-training conversion replaces attention with CeNN-inspired cellular-recurrent layers in pretrained LMs, selectively and only when representation fidelity and NLL criteria pass thresholds.
AI.motivation: Replacing attention in pretrained LMs risks representation drift in later layers; a gating mechanism is needed to preserve performance while enabling possible speedups or memory reductions.
AI.method: Introduce TinyCeNN-LM framework with CeNN-inspired cellular-recurrent units featuring bounded local processing, compact memory, routing/fusion, and accept-or-rollback validation. Implement Integrated Memory, MemoryFusion, and PDelta3-GDN2-CLVR+Local32. Use strict PDelta3 conversion with fixed representation- and NLL-threshold checks. Evaluate on SmolLM2-135M and Qwen3.5-0.8B for ΔNLL, perplexity, cache reduction, and downstream sanity accuracy (200-item sample).
AI.result: On SmolLM2-135M, layers 0–2 accepted (ΔNLL=+0.01209); layer 3 rejected due to representation fidelity. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, layers 3, 7, 11 accepted (ΔNLL=+0.02073). Integrated Memory maintains perplexity within -0.07% to +0.93% and reduces total cache by up to 6.01%. A 200-item sanity check yields 28.5–32.0% accuracy for converted Qwen releases.
AI.conclusion: The results support a conservative, quality-gated substitution approach over universal attention replacement or speedups, balancing representation fidelity, NLL impact, and resource savings.

title: VGGT-CAD: Reconstructing Parametric CAD 3D Model with Geometric Grounding
summary: Parametric CAD reconstruction requires recovering both precise geometry and editable modeling operations from visual observations, making it challenging under limited and ambiguous views. Existing methods mainly rely on 2D appearance cues and lack strong multi-view geometric priors. In this work, we present VGGT-CAD, a geometry-aware framework for parametric CAD reconstruction from single- and multi-view observations. We transfer pretrained 3D geometric priors into CAD reconstruction by encoding camera parameters as condition tokens and jointly modeling them with image tokens. To handle varying numbers of viewpoints, we introduce a variable-view cross-view context aggregation module that adaptively fuses multi-view features. We further develop a training-free geometry-aware view selection strategy to select complementary and reliable frames during inference. The resulting representation is decoded into CAD command sequences using a non-autoregressive decoder. We also develop VideoCAD, a large-scale multi-view video benchmark derived from existing CAD data through multi-view re-rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of VGGT-CAD for visual CAD reconstruction under different observation configurations.

AI.tldr: A geometry-aware, priors-informed framework for parametric CAD reconstruction from single- and multi-view data, VGGT-CAD, coupling 3D priors with camera-conditioned tokens, variable-view fusion, and a training-free view selection, decoded into CAD commands; accompanied by VideoCAD benchmark.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of recovering precise geometry and editable CAD operations from limited or ambiguous views by leveraging pretrained 3D geometric priors and robust multi-view fusion.
AI.method: Encode camera parameters as condition tokens aligned with image tokens; employ a variable-view cross-view context aggregation to adaptively fuse features from varying numbers of viewpoints; implement a training-free geometry-aware view selection strategy to pick complementary frames; decode the representation with a non-autoregressive CAD command decoder; create VideoCAD, a large-scale multi-view video benchmark by re-rendering existing CAD data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate effectiveness of VGGT-CAD across different observation configurations, showing improved reconstruction quality and robustness relative to baselines (specific metrics not provided in the abstract).
AI.conclusion: VGGT-CAD provides a geometry-aware pipeline that leverages 3D priors and flexible multi-view fusion to recover accurate and editable parametric CAD representations from diverse observation setups, and VideoCAD offers a scalable benchmark for multi-view CAD reconstruction.

title: Efficient Bayes-Adaptive Reinforcement Learning with Temporal Logic Specifications
comment: ©~2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary: We present a novel end-to-end model-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithm for efficient policy synthesis under given Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications (e.g., safety or reachability) in unknown environments. To do so, a Limit-Deterministic B{ü}chi Automaton (LDBA) representation of the LTL task is synchronised with a Bayes-Adaptive Markov Decision Process (BAMDP) representation of the environment, which allows us to leverage an enhanced exploration-exploitation trade-off that is achieved via Bayesian RL, as opposed to traditional non-Bayesian approaches. We further propose a novel Bayes-Adaptive Monte-Carlo Planning (BAMCP) algorithm to allow for approximate Bayes-optimal strategy synthesis in the synchronised BAMDP construct. A range of finite- and infinite-horizon task experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in terms of both property satisfaction and sample efficiency, when compared to traditional model-free approaches. Additional ablation studies also successfully highlight the value of the novel BAMCP algorithm in comparison to classical BAMCP for LTL task satisfaction. Finally, we also showcase a successful application of our approach for \textit{cautious} RL, namely to reduce the number of task violations incurred during policy training.

AI.tldr: End-to-end model-based RL for LTL-constrained policy synthesis in unknown environments by synchronizing a Limit-Deterministic B{"u}chi Automaton (LDBA) with a Bayes-Adaptive MDP (BAMDP) and using Bayes-Adaptive Monte-Carlo Planning (BAMCP); demonstrates improved property satisfaction and sample efficiency, with ablations and cautious RL benefits.
AI.motivation: Develop a principled framework for efficient, correct-by-construction policy synthesis under temporal logic constraints in unknown environments by leveraging Bayesian exploration-exploitation and planning in a BAMDP/LTL setting.
AI.method: Represent the LTL task with an LDBA and synchronize it with the environment's BAMDP. Introduce BAMCP for approximate Bayes-optimal planning in the synchronized model. Evaluate on finite- and infinite-horizon tasks, conduct ablations against classical BAMCP and non-Bayesian baselines, and demonstrate cautious RL to reduce task violations.
AI.result: Shows improved satisfaction rates and sample efficiency over traditional model-free approaches. Ablations validate the added value of BAMCP in LTL task satisfaction. Demonstrates practical cautious RL benefits by reducing violations during training.
AI.conclusion: The proposed BAMDP-LTL framework with BAMCP offers a principled, sample-efficient, end-to-end solution for LTL-constrained policy synthesis in unknown environments, with demonstrated gains in safety (fewer violations) and theoretical alignment to Bayes-optimal planning.

title: SPARROW: Survival-POMCP for Adaptive Robot Routing, Observation, and Waiting
summary: Temporary obstacles that may block a robot's planned route create a sequential navigation problem: a robot must decide whether to wait for a blockage to clear, reroute, or acquire more information about the obstacle before acting. We formulate graph navigation among temporary obstacles as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process and introduce SPARROW, a belief-space planner built on Partially Observable Monte Carlo Planning (POMCP). SPARROW searches over traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting actions while maintaining a particle belief over latent obstacle classes and clearance times. Class-conditioned survival models are learned online from both clearance observations and right-censored encounters where the robot reroutes before clearance is observed. A generative model simulates obstacle arrivals and clearances as each action unfolds, so the planner can account for blockages that may occur along alternative routes. We further introduce a value-of-learning criterion that trades the immediate cost of collecting labelled survival data against its expected reduction in future navigation regret. Across two simulation graphs and multiple obstacle-class settings, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 12-26% relative to OSCAR, a recent survival-based method for the same problem. On a physical mobile robot, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 20.5% relative to OSCAR while selectively observing, waiting, and rerouting as environment conditions change.

AI.tldr: SPARROW is a POMCP-based planner for graph navigation with temporary, classifiable obstacles, using online learned survival models and a value-of-learning criterion to decide between traversal, waiting, and observation; it reduces time-to-goal versus OSCAR in simulations (12-26%) and on a real robot (20.5%).
AI.motivation: Address sequential navigation with temporary blockages by integrating planning under partial observability for obstacle clearance times and classes, enabling decisions on waiting or information gathering to minimize navigation time.
AI.method: Formulate as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process (POSMDP). SPARROW is built on Partially Observable Monte Carlo Planning (POMCP). It searches over actions including traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting while maintaining a particle belief over latent obstacle classes and clearance times. Online learning yields class-conditioned survival models from clearance observations and censored encounters. A generative model simulates obstacle arrivals and clearances to account for blockages along alternative routes. A value-of-learning criterion balances immediate data collection costs against expected reductions in future navigation regret.
AI.result: SPARROW achieves 12-26% reductions in mean time-to-goal over OSCAR across two simulation graphs and multiple obstacle-class settings. On a real mobile robot, it reduces mean time-to-goal by 20.5% relative to OSCAR, by selectively observing, waiting, and rerouting as environment conditions change.
AI.conclusion: Integrating online survival learning, latent obstacle-class beliefs, and a learning-aware planning objective enables effective navigation under temporary obstacles, yielding substantial navigation-time improvements over a recent survival-based baseline (OSCAR) in both simulation and physical experiments.

title: Clinician-Grounded Quality Assurance for AI-Assisted Psychiatric Intake
summary: Before patients can use AI-assisted psychiatric intake systems, health systems need practical ways to routinely evaluate these tools against their clinical standards for quality assurance. Because clinicians may use different intake styles, evaluation for this task must (1) support comparison across interviewing approaches, (2) minimize clinician burden, and (3) measure clinically relevant performance for health systems deploying these technologies. We present a clinician-grounded evaluation platform built around a memory-augmented patient simulator for open-ended AI interviewing, InterviewPlayground. We created interactive patients using InterviewPlayground with our expert-authored vignettes, constructed a simulated intake platform for the interviews, and designed evaluation modalities relevant to intake. In a pilot of 6 clinicians in a 25-minute assessment compared to a GPT-based LLM intake interviewer, the LLM recovered more of the clinically relevant items embedded in the patient vignettes (88.0% vs. 38.9%), but made more clinical inferences not based on the interview (56.8% vs. 27.8%), and characterized identified safety concerns less often (33.3% vs. 66.7%), setting the stage for deployed quality assurance for this task.

AI.tldr: Introduces InterviewPlayground, a clinician-grounded platform with a memory-augmented patient simulator to evaluate open-ended AI psychiatric interviewing, enabling cross-study comparison and reduced clinician burden; a 6-clinician pilot shows an LLM interviewer retrieves more clinically relevant items but makes more non-grounded inferences and detects safety concerns less often.
AI.motivation: To provide practical, low-burden, clinically meaningful evaluation of AI-assisted psychiatric intake tools that can be used across different interviewing styles and integrated into health-system quality assurance.
AI.method: Developed InterviewPlayground with expert-authored vignettes, a simulated intake platform, and evaluation modalities; conducted a 25-minute pilot with 6 clinicians comparing a GPT-based LLM intake interviewer to human-driven evaluation using the platform.
AI.result: LLM recovered 88.0% of clinically relevant items embedded in patient vignettes vs. 38.9% for the comparator; LLM made more clinical inferences not grounded in the interview (56.8% vs. 27.8%); LLM identified safety concerns less often (33.3% vs. 66.7%).
AI.conclusion: The platform supports deployed quality assurance for AI-assisted psychiatric intake, elucidating trade-offs between comprehensive item recovery and risk/ safety assessment, and enabling standardized evaluation across interviewing approaches.

title: Multiclass Semantic Segmentation of Wildland Fire Images Using Context-Aware Centralized Copy-Paste Data Augmentation
summary: Producing accurate annotations for deep learning based image segmentation is both costly and labor intensive. This challenge is especially evident in wildland fire applications, where accurately labeled datasets are scarce due to the difficulty of collecting and annotating dynamic fire scenes. To address this problem, our previous work introduced the Centralized Copy-Paste Data Augmentation (CCPDA) method for semantic segmentation of wildland fire imagery, which generates artificial training samples by randomly pasting fire clusters from source images onto target images. However, random placement can produce contextually unrealistic scenes, such as fire burning on asphalt. In this paper, we present a context-aware strategy designed specifically to improve data quality and realism in small multiclass wildland fire datasets, ensuring that augmented samples remain contextually meaningful. The proposed method restricts fire placement to semantically valid target regions and selects the location whose Ash-Vegetation composition most closely matches the source context. This approach preserves existing fire regions in the target image, prevents unrealistic placements, and maintains contextual accuracy by generating images that resemble real wildland fire scenes. We evaluate the Context-Aware CCPDA strategy through numerical analysis and comparisons with other augmentation methods by a weighted sum-based multi-objective optimization (MOO) approach. The results confirm that the context-aware data augmentation strategy leads to improved segmentation performance and contextual realism, outperforming other augmentation procedures.

AI.tldr: Context-aware CCPDA improves realism and segmentation performance for wildfire imagery by semantically restricting and context-matching fire augmentation, outperforming random placement augmentations under a multi-objective optimization evaluation.
AI.motivation: Address the scarcity and labor-intensive annotation of wildland fire datasets and the limitations of random data augmentation that can create unrealistic scenes, hindering model performance on small, multiclass datasets.
AI.method: Develop a context-aware extension to Centralized Copy-Paste Data Augmentation (CCPDA): restrict fire placements to semantically valid regions and choose locations whose Ash-Vegetation composition matches the source context; preserve existing fire regions; evaluate via a weighted sum-based multi-objective optimization (MOO) and comparisons with other augmentation methods.
AI.result: The context-aware strategy yields improved segmentation performance and more realistic augmented images, outperforming other augmentation procedures.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware augmentation enhances data quality and model performance for wildland fire semantic segmentation on small multiclass datasets, validating its effectiveness and potential for broader application.

title: From Switching to Dynamic Regret: A Simple Reduction via Unbiased Random Sequences
summary: In non-stationary online learning, dynamic regret has attracted increasing attention as a measure of how well an online learner performs against a time-varying comparator sequence. Despite considerable advances, attaining optimal bounds for strongly convex and exp-concave losses often involves intricate analysis. In this paper, we present a \textit{simple} framework that reduces dynamic regret minimization to switching regret minimization. As a result, we can derive dynamic regret bounds by using off-the-shelf algorithms with switching regret guarantees. The key idea of our reduction is to construct, for \textit{any} comparator sequence, an auxiliary random sequence that is unbiased at each round, with the controlled variance and a manageable number of switches. Combining this construction with suitable surrogate losses, we can decompose dynamic regret into the expected switching regret against the random sequence and its controlled variance. Theoretically, for strongly convex and exp-concave losses, we establish the $\widetilde{O}(T^{1/3}P_T^{2/3})$ dynamic regret bounds, where $T$ denotes the time horizon and $P_T$ denotes the path-length of the comparator sequence. Moreover, for general convex losses, the same reduction also recovers the $O(\sqrt{T(1+P_T)})$ dynamic regret bound. Notably, all our findings match the minimax optimal results for these three types of losses, highlighting the versatility of our proposed framework.

AI.tldr: A simple reduction framework that converts dynamic regret minimization to switching regret via an auxiliary randomized comparator; yields minimax-optimal dynamic regret bounds for strongly convex/exp-concave and general convex losses.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of achieving optimal dynamic regret in non-stationary online learning, especially for strongly convex and exp-concave losses, by introducing a universal, simple reduction to switching regret that leverages existing switching-regret algorithms.
AI.method: Construct an unbiased auxiliary random sequence for any comparator with controlled variance and a bounded number of switches; pair this with surrogate losses to decompose dynamic regret into the expected switching regret against the random sequence plus its variance; apply off-the-shelf switching-regret guarantees.
AI.result: Dynamic regret bounds: O(T^{1/3} P_T^{2/3}) for strongly convex/exp-concave losses; O( sqrt{T(1+P_T)}) for general convex losses; all achieving minimax-optimal rates.
AI.conclusion: The framework is simple and versatile, reducing dynamic regret to switching regret and enabling optimal rates for multiple loss classes by leveraging existing switching-regret guarantees and surrogate losses.

title: Towards Effective Visual-Inertial SLAM with Passive-Only Sensors for Low-Cost Autonomous Underwater Vehicles
summary: Improvements to Visual-Inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (VI-SLAM) for low-cost autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are critical for transitioning advanced marine robotics from specialized labs to broader research and hobbyist applications. While high-end AUVs typically rely on expensive sensor suites - such as Doppler Velocity Logs (DVLs) and Ultra-Short Baseline (USBL) systems - this work demonstrates that robust, high-quality navigation is achievable using a sub-$10, 000(USD) platform equipped only with inexpensive consumer-grade sensors. By leveraging a similarly priced, open-source AUV, we evaluate the performance of stereo cameras, Micro-electromechanical System (MEMS)-based IMUs, and depth sensors in a fully unconstrained 6-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) underwater environment. We analyze the efficacy of off-the-shelf SLAM packages and propose optimizations for sensor fusion to mitigate the visual and physical challenges of untethered underwater operation. Our results prove that a usable SLAM solution can be accessible to the masses, providing a benchmark for expectations in demanding, real-time maritime missions without the financial barrier of industrial-grade hardware.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates viable VI-SLAM on a sub-$10k AUV using consumer sensors, suggesting affordable, real-time underwater navigation without high-end hardware.
AI.motivation: Lower the cost barrier for robust underwater SLAM and enable broader adoption in academia and hobbyist robotics by evaluating off-the-shelf sensors and open-source SLAM pipelines.
AI.method: Use an open-source, similarly priced AUV with stereo cameras, MEMS IMUs, and depth sensors; perform a fully unconstrained 6-DOF underwater test; assess off-the-shelf SLAM packages and propose sensor-fusion optimizations for underwater challenges.
AI.result: Shows that usable, real-time VI-SLAM is achievable with inexpensive hardware; provides benchmarks and optimization strategies for unfettered underwater operation, illustrating practical viability.
AI.conclusion: Affordable VI-SLAM on low-cost AUVs is feasible, widening access to advanced marine robotics while maintaining performance; further work could refine fusion strategies and extend robustness in challenging underwater conditions.

title: Can Agents Design Better Chips with a Higher Level Abstraction?
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly being explored for chip design, but most existing approaches operate directly at RTL. We ask whether agents can design better chips by leveraging higher-level abstractions. We compare Direct RTL Design, Agent-based HLS Design, Post-Compiler HLS Refinement, and Post-HLS RTL Refinement, and combine Agent-based HLS Design with Post-HLS RTL Refinement as Agent-based HLS with RTL Refinement (AHRR). We use FPGAs as a practical, easy-to-deploy platform for end-to-end evaluation, but note that the design-flow tradeoffs we study are largely independent of the target technology. Across a diverse 11-tasks benchmark suite, AHRR achieves a 2.6$\times$ geometric-mean speedup over Direct RTL Design across our benchmark suite. Case studies show that HLS distills design knowledge into abstractions that agents can leverage, while RTL refinement recovers lower-level optimization opportunities. Together, these results make AHRR a promising workflow for agentic chip design. The code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/ZijD/AHRR.

AI.tldr: AHRR combines agent-based high-level synthesis (HLS) with post-HLS RTL refinement to outperform direct RTL design, achieving 2.6x geometric-mean speedup across 11 FPGA-based tasks; HLS distills design knowledge into abstractions for agents, while RTL refinement recovers low-level optimizations, making agentic chip design more effective.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether higher-level abstractions and agent-based design can outperform traditional RTL-driven design, to improve efficiency and exploration in chip design with LLM-enabled agents.
AI.method: Compare four workflows—Direct RTL Design, Agent-based HLS Design, Post-Compiler HLS Refinement, Post-HLS RTL Refinement—then combine Agent-based HLS Design with RTL Refinement to form AHRR; evaluate on FPGA across 11 tasks; conduct case studies; provide code/artifacts at the referenced GitHub.
AI.result: AHRR yields a 2.6x geometric-mean speedup over Direct RTL Design across the 11-task benchmark; case studies show HLS distills design knowledge into high-level abstractions for agents, while RTL refinement uncovers low-level optimization opportunities.
AI.conclusion: Agent-based HLS with RTL refinement is a promising end-to-end workflow for agentic chip design, with broadly technology-agnostic implications and available evaluation artifacts.

title: SafeStyle: Calibrated Style Residual Injection for Controllable Style-Leakage Trade-off in Diffusion Stylization
summary: Reference-guided diffusion stylization aims to transfer visual style from a reference image while preserving the semantics specified by a text prompt. However, image conditioning often entangles transferable style cues with reference-specific content, leading to an inherent trade-off: stronger conditioning improves style fidelity but increases content leakage, whereas aggressive suppression reduces leakage at the cost of style expression. This challenge is further complicated by the distinct spatial organization of texture- and geometry-dominant styles. To address these issues, we propose SafeStyle, a training-free framework for calibrated style residual injection in frozen diffusion models. SafeStyle first estimates style-supported and content-associated subspaces from compact calibration sets, preserving their informative overlap while suppressing useless content variations. It then transports the purified style evidence over adaptive spatial granularity and constrains its effective influence through an explicit residual-norm budget. Experiments across texture- and geometry-dominant styles show that SafeStyle achieves a DINO style similarity of 0.432 while maintaining competitive text alignment. On a semantically disjoint leakage-stress benchmark, it further achieves a DINO style similarity of 0.474 with only 0.8\% semantic leakage, demonstrating an effective balance between style fidelity and reference-content suppression.

AI.tldr: SafeStyle is a training-free framework that calibrates style residuals in frozen diffusion models by separating style-supported and content-associated subspaces and controlling influence via a residual-norm budget, enabling improved style fidelity with reduced content leakage.
AI.motivation: Reference-guided diffusion stylization faces a fundamental trade-off: stronger conditioning yields better style but more content leakage; this is compounded by the distinct spatial organization of texture- vs geometry-dominant styles. A training-free method to calibrate style evidence is needed.
AI.method: Estimate style-supported and content-associated subspaces from compact calibration sets to preserve informative overlap while suppressing irrelevant content variations. Transport purified style evidence over adaptive spatial granularity and constrain its influence with an explicit residual-norm budget.
AI.result: Evaluations show DINO style similarity of 0.432 for texture- and geometry-dominant styles, with competitive text alignment. On a semantically disjoint leakage-stress benchmark, DINO style similarity reaches 0.474 with only 0.8% semantic leakage, indicating strong balance between style fidelity and content suppression.
AI.conclusion: SafeStyle provides a training-free, calibrated style residual injection that achieves effective style transfer while suppressing reference-content leakage across style types, through subspace disentanglement, adaptive granularity, and residual budgeting.

title: Generative inversion for early ranking of competing geologic interpretations
summary: High-consequence subsurface decisions are often made under severe data scarcity. Experts may arrive at competing interpretations of the same subsurface system, yet early in a project there is rarely a practical way to determine which one is most realistic. This uncertainty can persist until several wells are drilled, often costing millions of dollars. Existing approaches for evaluating geologic interpretations rely either on subjective judgment or on dense data that are rarely available in early-stage investigations. We present a workflow that addresses this challenge by translating competing geologic interpretations into alternative spatial priors and ranking them according to their consistency with hydraulic-head observations. For each interpretation, a text-to-image foundation model generates an ensemble of 1600 geologic images, and a separately trained variational autoencoder provides an interpretation-specific latent representation. A supervised inverse network maps the head observations into this latent space, and the frozen decoder produces an image that is mapped to a log-conductivity field. Steady-state flow simulation then provides predicted heads, and the resulting mismatch is converted into a Gaussian-form compatibility score. We evaluate the framework using a synthetic benchmark based on the Johansen Formation and three interpretations of decreasing consistency with the reference representation. Across 925 test cases, the mean head RMSE increases from 0.197 for the Precise \& Accurate interpretation to 0.227 for the Accurate interpretation and 0.280 for the Mismatched interpretation. We subsequently apply the workflow to two published conceptual models of the Culebra Dolomite Member at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant. The revised model receives a compatibility weight of 0.991, compared with 0.009 for the original model, consistent with the independent evidence.

AI.tldr: A data-scarce workflow ranks competing subsurface interpretations by converting each into a spatial prior, generating 1,600 geologic image realizations per interpretation via a text-to-image model, and using a latent-space surrogate (VAE and supervised inverse map) to map head observations to log-conductivity fields. Steady-state flow and head misfit yield a Gaussian compatibility score to rank interpretations; validated on a synthetic Johansen benchmark and two published Culebra models at WIPP, correctly prioritizing the revised model.
AI.motivation: Early-stage subsurface decisions suffer from sparse data and multiple plausible interpretations; there is a need an objective, data-efficient framework to compare interpretations and guide drilling without requiring dense data.
AI.method: For each interpretation: generate an ensemble of 1,600 geologic images with a text-to-image foundation model; obtain an interpretation-specific latent representation via a variational autoencoder; map head observations into this latent space with a supervised inverse network; use a frozen decoder to produce an image that maps to a log-conductivity field; run steady-state flow to predict heads and convert misfit into a Gaussian-form compatibility score; evaluate on 925 synthetic test cases with increasing inconsistency (Precise & Accurate, Accurate, Mismatched); apply to two WIPP Culebra Model interpretations and assign compatibility weights.
AI.result: Synthetic benchmark shows RMSE of predicted heads rising with decreasing consistency: 0.197 (Precise & Accurate), 0.227 (Accurate), 0.280 (Mismatched) across 925 tests. In WIPP applications, revised model receives a compatibility weight of 0.991 versus 0.009 for the original, aligning with independent evidence.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an objective, data-efficient approach to rank competing geological interpretations by translating them into spatial priors and evaluating consistency with hydraulic-head observations, demonstrated on both synthetic and real-world conceptual models.

title: Catch Me If You Can: Real-Time Feedback Denoising for Responsive VLAs
comment: 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin TX, USA
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by combining semantic knowledge from pretrained vision-language models with expressive action-generation policies. Diffusion-based action generators are particularly effective for modeling temporally coherent action chunks, but these chunks are typically executed open-loop after inference. This limits responsiveness when objects move, contacts change, or the scene evolves during execution. We propose VLA-Feedback, a two-timescale architecture that combines low-frequency diffusion planning with high-frequency visual feedback. Rather than fully denoising an action chunk before execution, VLA-Feedback retains its final denoising step as a lightweight feedback interface, allowing each action to be corrected using the latest observation before it is executed. This design preserves the expressiveness of the diffusion planner while enabling real-time action correction without rerunning the full vision-language diffusion model. VLA-Feedback matched GR00T on static LIBERO tasks while improving average success on dynamic simulation tasks from 27.5% to 85.0%. On real-robot tasks, it improved average success from 51% to 73%. Additional materials can be found on our project page: https://vla-feedback.github.io.

AI.tldr: A two-timescale diffusion-based planning framework (VLA-Feedback) for Vision-Language-Action models in robotic manipulation; it adds high-frequency visual feedback to correct actions during execution without full re-planning, improving dynamic task performance while preserving planner expressiveness.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based action planners offer expressive, temporally coherent actions but are typically executed open-loop. In dynamic environments, corrections based on new observations are essential for robustness and responsiveness without incurring full re-inference costs.
AI.method: A two-timescale architecture that couples low-frequency diffusion planning with high-frequency feedback. Instead of completing full denoising of an action chunk, the terminal denoising step is retained as a lightweight feedback interface to adjust the action using the latest observation before execution. Integrates diffusion-based planning with perception-driven feedback within a Vision-Language-Action framework.
AI.result: On static LIBERO tasks, VLA-Feedback matched GR00T. On dynamic simulation tasks, average success rose from 27.5% to 85.0%. On real-robot tasks, average success rose from 51% to 73%.
AI.conclusion: Retaining the final denoising step as a feedback interface preserves diffusion planner expressiveness while enabling real-time action correction, yielding substantial gains in dynamic scenarios without re-running the full model; promising for robust, responsive manipulation in changing environments.

title: SpecOpt: Contact-Diff Reasoning for Agentic Molecule Optimization Toward Binding Specificity
summary: Off-target protein binding is a major source of adverse effects for small-molecule drugs, yet most structure-based molecular design methods focus on generating selective compounds de novo rather than improving the selectivity of existing, well- characterized drugs. We introduce specificity optimization (SpecOpt), a molecular design task that seeks constrained structural modifications to an existing compound that increase its binding preference for an intended target over known off-targets while preserving its structural identity and drug-like properties. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct a ChEMBL-derived benchmark from compound-target interaction data, identifying intended targets through curated drug-mechanism annotations and off- targets through measured activities. We then develop an agentic framework that docks each compound against its intended target and off-targets, compares the resulting poses through residue-aware atom-protein contacts, and provides these differential interactions to a large language model to propose targeted structural modifications. Candidates are retained only if they satisfy molecular similarity, ADMET, and target-off-target docking selectivity criteria. On 915 compounds, the agent improves the target- off-target binding gap for 84.8% of compounds, shifting the mean gap from -0.72 to +0.47 kcal/mol while maintaining a mean Tanimoto similarity of 0.72 to the starting compounds. Ablation studies identify residue-specific contact information as the critical optimization signal: replacing residue identities with binary contact indicators eliminates improvement on all 29 ablation compounds. These results establish SpecOpt as a distinct molecular design problem and demonstrate residue-aware differential interactions as an effective signal for improving the specificity of existing compounds.

AI.tldr: SpecOpt designs constrained edits to existing drugs to boost target selectivity over off-targets while preserving similarity and drug-like properties; builds a ChEMBL-derived benchmark; uses docking-based residue-aware differential interactions fed to an LLM to propose modifications; achieves improved specificity on 84.8% of 915 compounds with mean target-off-target Δbinding +0.47 kcal/mol and mean Tanimoto similarity 0.72.
AI.motivation: Reduce adverse effects from off-target binding by optimizing existing drugs instead of only de novo design; create a benchmark for systematic evaluation of selectivity improvements.
AI.method: Construct a ChEMBL-derived benchmark of drug–target interactions, identify intended vs off-targets; dock each compound against both; compare residue-level protein contacts to obtain differential interaction signals; use an agentic framework with an LLM to propose targeted modifications; apply filters for molecular similarity, ADMET, and docking selectivity.
AI.result: For 915 compounds, target–off-target binding gap improved in 84.8% of cases (mean shift from -0.72 to +0.47 kcal/mol); mean Tanimoto similarity maintained at 0.72; ablation shows residue identities are essential; replacing with binary contacts eliminates improvements across 29 ablation compounds.
AI.conclusion: SpecOpt establishes a new molecular design problem—residue-aware differential interactions as a key signal for enhancing the specificity of existing compounds.

title: Geometry-Aware Diffusion Guidance via Curvature-Adaptive Tubular Correction
summary: Gradient-guided diffusion samplers provide flexible priors for inverse problems and conditional generation, but strong guidance can move the sampling trajectory into regions where the learned score is poorly supported. Existing tangent-projection strategies limit first-order departure from an iso-density surface, yet discard potentially useful normal motion and overlook the second-order departure induced by tangent motion on a curved surface. We introduce curvature-adaptive tubular correction (CAT), a training-free plugin that regulates both effects within a shared, noise-dependent geometric budget. CAT decomposes the guidance gradient into normal and tangent components, charges normal displacement at first order and tangent displacement according to directional curvature, and obtains their jointly optimal magnitudes from a one-dimensional dual equation. Armijo backtracking calibrates the resulting finite step against the actual guidance objective, while matrix-free directional derivatives avoid constructing the full score Jacobian. We establish local guarantees for the tubular approximation, uniqueness of the correction, and sufficient objective decrease. Across seven inverse problems on FFHQ and ImageNet, CAT improves the evaluated pixel- and latent-space host samplers, with particularly consistent gains in perceptual metrics. It also improves black hole reconstruction on InverseBench and yields the lowest FID among the compared methods at every tested classifier-free guidance scale, while maintaining stable saturation and contrast. These results support curvature-aware tubular control as a reusable mechanism for stabilizing diffusion guidance.

AI.tldr: A training-free curvature-adaptive tubular correction (CAT) for diffusion-guided inverse problems and conditional generation, decomposing guidance into normal and tangent components, applying curvature-based scaling to tangent motion, and using Armijo backtracking with matrix-free derivatives to ensure stable, convergent updates; yields local guarantees and improved performance across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Guide diffusion samplers more robustly without discarding useful tangent/normal motions or second-order effects, addressing failures where strong guidance departs from well-supported score regions.
AI.method: CAT decomposes the guidance gradient into normal and tangent components. It applies first-order normal displacement and tangent displacement scaled by directional curvature, with magnitudes determined by a one-dimensional dual optimization problem. Armijo backtracking calibrates the step against the objective, and matrix-free directional derivatives compute needed sensitivities without constructing the full score Jacobian. The approach is training-free and provides local tubular-approximation guarantees, uniqueness of the correction, and objective decrease.
AI.result: Empirically, CAT improves both pixel- and latent-space samplers across seven inverse problems on FFHQ and ImageNet, with consistent gains in perceptual metrics. It enhances black-hole reconstructions on InverseBench and achieves the lowest FID among compared methods at all guidance scales while maintaining stable saturation and contrast.
AI.conclusion: Curvature-aware tubular control is a reusable mechanism for stabilizing diffusion guidance, offering theoretically-grounded corrections and practical performance gains.

title: ASGARD: Action-Space Guard for UAV Resilience via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) controllers have been recently adopted for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) navigation and control. However, they are susceptible to action-space attacks that overwrite the action commands after the policy generates them and before the actuators execute them. While most existing defenses target attacks on the policy's inputs, those addressing action-space attacks retrain the policy at training time and are not resilient to corrupted actions at runtime. We propose ASGARD, a two-phase teacher-student pipeline for making RL-based UAV control resilient to action-space attacks. In the teacher phase, an encoder combines the UAV's physical state with action-attack-related privileged information to produce an action-attack-aware latent that trains the RL control policy and a monitor that outputs corrected action commands to the actuators. In the student phase, both the encoder and the monitor are trained via supervised learning from their teacher counterparts to run on-board using only the UAV's physical state history. We evaluate ASGARD across attack scenarios targeting different action commands on UAV. We find that ASGARD is resilient to action-space attacks and completes the missions despite the attack. We further find that ASGARD generalizes to unseen attacks and remains resilient against stealthy attacks.

AI.tldr: ASGARD: a two-phase teacher-student framework that makes RL-based UAV control robust to action-space attacks by learning an attack-aware latent in a teacher phase and distilling it for onboard use; effective against seen, unseen, and stealthy attacks.
AI.motivation: Action-space attacks overwrite actuator commands in RL UAV controllers. Existing defenses mainly focus on input defenses or require retraining and are not resilient to runtime corrupted actions; a runtime, onboard defense is needed.
AI.method: Two-phase approach: (1) teacher phase combines the UAV's state with privileged attack-related information to produce an action-attack-aware latent, training the RL policy and a monitor that outputs corrected actuator commands; (2) student phase trains encoder and monitor via supervised learning from their teacher counterparts to operate on-board using only physical state history.
AI.result: ASGARD demonstrates resilience across varied action-space attack scenarios, enabling mission completion despite attacks, and generalizes to unseen and stealthy attacks.
AI.conclusion: ASGARD provides an effective, generalizable runtime defense for RL-based UAV control against action-space manipulation, enabling onboard deployment without sacrificing resilience.

title: Adapting Rigid-Body Dynamics Derivatives for Constraint Embedding Closed-Chain Models
summary: This paper extends an existing algorithm for the first-order derivatives of rigid-body dynamics to the case of closed-chain kinematic systems modeled using constraint embed- ding. Many standard dynamics algorithms apply to both open- chain and constraint-embedded models, but existing efficient derivative methods assume joint velocity effects are locally config- uration invariant. We remove this assumption and derive adapted algorithms that extend dynamics derivatives to more general joint types, including those arising in constraint-embedded closed- chain models. Our results compare conventional pin-joint robot models with more complete actuation models that capture local closed chains. We show that the additional terms introduced by these generalizations have low computational impact when mod- eling actuation kinematics alone, but can incur higher cost when additional rigid bodies, such as motor rotors, are included in the actuation chain, or when considering non-local loops. Overall, these results enable more accurate dynamics computations for constraint-embedded actuation submechanisms to be adopted in model-predictive control and differentiable simulation.

AI.tldr: Extends first-order derivatives in rigid-body dynamics to constraint-embedded closed-chain systems via constraint embedding; removes the assumption of locally configuration-invariant joint velocities; offers generalized algorithms for diverse joint types; modest overhead for actuation-kinematics, higher when more bodies are included or loops are non-local; enables accurate dynamics for MPC and differentiable simulation.
AI.motivation: Address the limited applicability of existing derivative methods to open-chain models when applied to closed-chain, constraint-embedded systems. The goal is to derive derivatives for more general joint types within closed chains and improve accuracy of actuation dynamics in simulations and control.
AI.method: Derive adapted algorithms that remove the assumption of local configuration invariance for joint velocity effects, extend dynamics derivatives to general joint types in constraint-embedded closed chains, and compare traditional pin-joint models with more complete actuation models that include local closed chains.
AI.result: Additional terms from generalization have low computational impact when modeling actuation kinematics alone; higher cost arises when additional rigid bodies (e.g., motor rotors) are included in the actuation chain or in non-local loops; the work enables more accurate dynamics computations for constraint-embedded actuation submechanisms in MPC and differentiable simulation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed generalizations enable more accurate and broadly applicable dynamics derivatives for constraint-embedded actuation submechanisms, supporting their use in model-predictive control and differentiable simulation.

title: Implicit Rule Induction with Test-Time Task Embeddings in ARC-like Tasks
summary: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus and related benchmarks evaluate whether AI models can solve novel reasoning tasks, but often leave unclear whether success reflects inference of the intended underlying rule or reliance on shortcuts. We address this gap by studying test-time task embeddings in Vision ARC (VARC), a model in which a pre-trained backbone is complemented by a trainable embedding representing the transformation rule. In the original VARC, test-time training (TTT) is jointly applied to the backbone and task embedding. Here we introduce a novel two-step TTT protocol: first finetune only the task embedding (Embed-TTT), then freeze it and finetune the backbone. Across ARC-AGI-1, ConceptARC, and two controlled datasets with known rules, Embed-TTT consistently yields improved task embeddings, ones that align better with underlying task rules, improve embedding-based retrieval, and enable accurate linear probing of known rules. Qualitatively, Embed-TTT identifies more semantically meaningful relations between test and train tasks on ARC-AGI-1. We also show that optimizing only task embeddings (less than 0.01% of model parameters) already solves a non-trivial fraction of ARC-AGI-1, ConceptARC, and Mini-ARC tasks, while the full two-step pipeline improves final performance. Finally, we show that Embed-TTT recovers the underlying geometric structure of parametric rules and learns compositional capabilities that enable rule-wise interpolation, but not extrapolation. These findings support a clearer separation between rule induction and rule execution in ARC-like evaluations, motivating benchmarks that better distinguish in-distribution from out-of-distribution rules.

AI.tldr: Two-step test-time training (Embed-TTT) for VARC improves task embeddings, aligning with underlying rules, enhancing retrieval and rule probing, enabling rule-wise interpolation but not extrapolation, and highlighting a separation between rule induction and execution in ARC-like benchmarks.
AI.motivation: ARC-like benchmarks struggle to distinguish genuine rule induction from shortcut strategies. The study investigates whether test-time embeddings capture the intended transformation rules in VARC and how training order affects this.
AI.method: Introduce a two-step TTT protocol: (1) finetune only the task embedding (Embed-TTT) while keeping the backbone fixed, (2) freeze the task embedding and finetune the backbone. Evaluate on ARC-AGI-1, ConceptARC, and two controlled datasets with known rules, comparing against joint TTT. Analyze embedding quality via retrieval, linear probing, and qualitative task relation analysis; assess contributions from small task-embedding updates (<0.01% of parameters).
AI.result: Embed-TTT consistently produces task embeddings that align better with underlying task rules, improves embedding-based retrieval, and enables accurate linear probing of rules. It yields more semantically meaningful relations between test and train tasks and, with minimal parameter updates, solves a non-trivial fraction of tasks. The full two-step pipeline further improves final performance and reveals the underlying geometric structure of parametric rules and compositional capabilities supporting rule-wise interpolation (but not extrapolation).
AI.conclusion: Separating rule induction from rule execution in ARC-like evaluations clarifies the source of success and motivates benchmarks that distinguish in-distribution from out-of-distribution rules.

title: Edit-VAR: Taming Visual Autoregressive Model for Precise Video Editing
summary: Text-guided video editing modifies target content while preserving the appearance and temporal coherence of unedited regions. Training-based approaches provide strong control but demand substantial data and computation. Training-free methods fall into inversion-free and inversion-based paradigms. Inversion-free approaches avoid trajectory recovery, but their source-preserving guidance can limit editing strength and leave semantic changes incomplete. Inversion-based approaches recover a latent trajectory before regeneration, where approximation errors can accumulate and cause source-content drift and temporal inconsistency. We introduce Edit-VAR, the first training-free and inversion-free framework for text-guided video editing with a pretrained visual autoregressive video model. Edit-VAR directly encodes the source video into multi-scale discrete tokens and performs probability-guided conditional token replacement for source preservation. Attention-guided token-wise and scale-aware modulation selectively relaxes source constraints over edit-relevant positions and generation stages. Scale-Decoupled Generation, implemented as late-scale constraint release, regenerates motion-consistent details and reduces texture fragmentation. Residual-guided token pruning further exploits redundancy at the final two high-resolution scales to reduce inference cost. Extensive experiments and a blind user study demonstrate that Edit-VAR outperforms existing training-free video editing methods overall in editing fidelity, source preservation, temporal coherence, and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: Proposes Edit-VAR, a training-free, inversion-free framework for text-guided video editing using a pretrained autoregressive video model with discrete tokens, leveraging attention-guided, scale-aware token modulation and token pruning to preserve source content while enabling edits; reports superior editing fidelity, source preservation, temporal coherence, and efficiency vs. existing training-free methods.
AI.motivation: Overcome the data/computation demands of training-based video editing methods and the limitations (weak edits, source drift, temporal inconsistency) of existing training-free approaches by enabling direct source-to-edit token manipulation without latent trajectory optimization.
AI.method: Encode source video into multi-scale discrete tokens. Perform probability-guided conditional token replacement for source preservation. Use attention-guided token-wise and scale-aware modulation to relax source constraints only at edit-relevant positions and stages. Employ Scale-Decoupled Generation with late-scale constraint release to regenerate motion-consistent details. Apply residual-guided token pruning at the final two high-resolution scales to reduce inference cost.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and a blind user study show Edit-VAR outperforms existing training-free video editing methods in editing fidelity, source preservation, temporal coherence, and inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Edit-VAR is the first training-free and inversion-free approach for text-guided video editing using a pretrained visual autoregressive video model, achieving strong performance with improved efficiency and better source preservation and temporal coherence compared to prior methods.

title: From Stress to Affect: Multimodal Deep Learning for Physiological Emotion Recognition Across Wearable Sensor Modalities
summary: Physiological emotion recognition using wearable sensors has important applications in mental health monitoring, affective computing, and human-computer interaction. However, existing studies typically evaluate a single model, sensing configuration, or dataset, limiting our understanding of how these factors influence recognition performance. We present a comparative study of temporal deep learning architectures for physiological emotion recognition using two multimodal wearable datasets: WESAD and EmoWear. Bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM), temporal convolutional network (TCN), and Transformer models are evaluated under wrist-only, chest-only, and multimodal sensing configurations using participant-independent leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV). We also investigate soft-voting ensembles, sensor ablation, sampling frequency, and gradient-based saliency. The Transformer achieved the highest multimodal accuracy on WESAD (99.02% +/- 0.51%), whereas the LSTM achieved the best multimodal accuracy on EmoWear for both arousal (91.80% +/- 1.06%) and valence (89.96% +/- 0.36%). These results show that relative architecture performance depends on dataset characteristics rather than one architecture being uniformly superior. Multimodal sensing consistently outperformed wrist-only and chest-only configurations across both datasets. Sampling-frequency analysis showed that 4 Hz provides a practical operating point, with performance comparable to higher frequencies at substantially lower training cost. These findings provide guidance for selecting architectures, sensing modalities, and sampling frequencies for wearable physiological emotion recognition.

AI.tldr: Comparative evaluation of BiLSTM, TCN, and Transformer for physiological emotion recognition across WESAD and EmoWear shows dataset-dependent architecture performance; multimodal sensing improves accuracy; 4 Hz sampling is efficient.
AI.motivation: To understand how model architecture, sensing modality, and sampling rate affect wearable-based emotion recognition across datasets and to provide actionable guidance.
AI.method: Evaluate BiLSTM, TCN, and Transformer on wrist-only, chest-only, and multimodal configurations using LOSO-CV on WESAD and EmoWear; test soft voting, sensor ablation, sampling frequency, and gradient-based saliency; compare across datasets.
AI.result: Transformer yields top multimodal accuracy on WESAD; LSTM yields top multimodal accuracy on EmoWear for arousal and valence; multimodal outperforms uni-modal; 4 Hz closely matches higher frequencies with lower cost.
AI.conclusion: Dataset characteristics govern relative architecture performance; adopt multimodal sensing and consider 4 Hz sampling for practical deployments; results guide architecture and modality selection in wearable emotion recognition.

title: MAPLE-RF: Efficient Probabilistic RF Source Localization in Partially Explored Environments
summary: Localizing a radio-frequency (RF) transmitter from received signals often requires a model of the environment to predict how obstacles block and reflect the signal. In many robotic applications, however, only a partial map is available, particularly when a robot localizes the source while exploring with simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). We study single-snapshot transmitter localization on such partially explored maps and compare two approaches that output a posterior over transmitter locations. The first extends a digital-twin method, which ray-traces every candidate location, to partial maps by treating unexplored space as free and training on mixed map coverage. The second, MAPLE-RF, encodes estimated path angles of arrival and signal-to-noise ratios as grid channels aligned with map knownness, occupancy, and line-of-sight visibility, and a U-Net scores all candidate positions in one pass without simulating propagation at inference. Ray-tracing simulations of indoor environments indicate that training on mixed map coverage is essential for both approaches. The digital-twin approach is more accurate on most single-snapshot metrics, while MAPLE-RF comes close at a query cost that does not depend on the propagation model and is more than two orders of magnitude below a fresh full-grid query with general-purpose ray tracing. Both outperform Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture baselines, and on exploration routes guided by its own estimates, fused MAPLE-RF posteriors place more probability near the source than the compared methods. Code and data will be released.

AI.tldr: Two methods for single-snapshot RF transmitter localization on partially explored maps: (i) a digital-twin ray-tracing approach using mixed map coverage; (ii) MAPLE-RF, a CNN-based method using grid channels for AoA and SNR. Training with mixed map coverage is crucial; digital-twin is generally more accurate, MAPLE-RF is faster and nearly as good, with significant inference cost savings; both beat Gaussian baselines, and MAPLE-RF fused posteriors concentrate near the source on exploration routes.
AI.motivation: Enable RF transmitter localization with partial maps during SLAM, where unexplored regions must be accounted for without costly full-propagation at inference. Compare a physics-based ray-tracing approach with a learned, inference-efficient model to understand tradeoffs in accuracy and compute for single-shot localization.
AI.method: Digital-twin approach: extend ray-tracing to candidate transmitter locations while treating unexplored space as free; train using mixed map coverage. MAPLE-RF: encode estimated angles-of-arrival and SNR as grid channels aligned with map certainty, occupancy, and LOS; use a U-Net to score all candidate positions in a single pass without propagating signals at inference.
AI.result: Ray-tracing simulations show training on mixed map coverage is essential for both methods. The digital-twin approach is more accurate on most single-snapshot metrics, while MAPLE-RF closely approaches it. MAPLE-RF offers a substantial reduction in inference cost, being independent of the propagation model and more than 100× cheaper than a fresh full-grid ray-tracing query. Both methods outperform Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture baselines. On exploration routes guided by MAPLE-RF posteriors, fused MAPLE-RF posteriors place more probability near the source compared to the baselines.
AI.conclusion: Both approaches advance single-shot RF localization under partial maps: the digital-twin method yields higher accuracy but with higher compute, while MAPLE-RF delivers faster, model-agnostic inference with competitive accuracy. Training with mixed map coverage is critical. The study suggests complementary strengths and indicates potential for combined use and future releases of code and data.

title: AI-GRACE: A Use-Case Operationalization Framework for Agentic AI: From Organizational Objectives and Obligations to Deployment Capabilities and Architecture
