summary: Organizations deploying agentic artificial intelligence must determine more than whether a model is trustworthy; they must establish what to validate, control, and observe for a use case to deliver its intended outcome while meeting applicable obligations. This paper proposes AI-GRACE (Agentic Intelligence-Governance, Risk, Assurance, Controls, and Evidence) as a use-case operationalization framework connecting organizational governance with technical implementation. The proposal draws on professional observations and a purposive synthesis of standards and literature, using design science to frame the method contribution and situational method engineering to guide contextual tailoring and reuse. The framework establishes objectives and obligations and then assesses risks in seven proposed domains, including mission and value realization. It derives requirements for assurance before deployment, runtime controls, and evidence, which guide capability qualification, gap assessment, and a logical architecture. An Agent Operating Envelope specifies permitted actions and escalation conditions, while Risk-Aligned Independence Levels (RAIL) summarize the authorized independence. A fictional retail banking application illustrates the method. The contribution is a traceable basis for deciding what an organization must implement, what it already supports, and what remains unresolved. Empirical evaluation must establish whether it improves deployment decisions, efficiency, and reuse.

AI.tldr: AI-GRACE: a governance-to-implementation framework for agentic AI that connects organizational obligations with technical controls, using design science and situational method engineering; includes seven risk domains, Agent Operating Envelope, and RAIL; illustrated by a banking use case; empirical validation pending.
AI.motivation: Organizations deploying agentic AI must decide not just trustworthiness but what to validate, control, and observe to achieve outcomes while satisfying obligations; a practical bridge between governance and deployment is lacking.
AI.method: Design science research to define the method contribution; situational method engineering to tailor to context; purposive synthesis of standards and literature; development of risk domains, assurance requirements, runtime controls, evidence, architecture, Agent Operating Envelope, and Risk-Aligned Independence Levels (RAIL).
AI.result: A concrete framework (AI-GRACE) with operational components and a banking case study; provides a traceable basis for decision-making, gap assessment, and deployment planning; sets the stage for evaluation of benefits.
AI.conclusion: AI-GRACE offers a structured basis for determining what to implement and what remains unresolved; empirical evaluation is required to confirm improvements in deployment decisions, efficiency, and reuse.

title: Beyond Exact Match: Task-Aware GRPO for Cross-Domain PCBA Visual Question Answering
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026)
summary: In automated Printed Circuit Board Assembly (PCBA) inspection, standards-guided decisions require systems to jointly reason over fine-grained visual cues, component semantics, and manufacturing knowledge. Although large vision-language models (VLMs) provide a promising foundation, their deployment is hindered by the domain shift between standards-derived samples and real-world production-line imagery, together with heterogeneous output spaces spanning choice-based and numerical counting tasks. To address these challenges, we propose a multimodal reasoning framework for cross-domain PCBA visual question answering. The framework converts standards-derived, real-world, and auxiliary PCB-domain data into a unified instruction format and constructs verified reasoning traces aligned with visual evidence, question semantics, candidate options, and ground-truth answers. We further introduce Task-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which moves beyond exact-match supervision by integrating multi-component semantic rewards for choice-based questions, distance-aware rewards for counting questions, and an auxiliary format reward for valid outputs. During inference, answer-option semantic consistency correction, self-consistency voting, and multi-model arbitration are combined to improve prediction robustness. The proposed system achieves an Overall Score of 83.24 on the official PCBA Standard-to-Real Grand Challenge leaderboard, demonstrating the effectiveness of task-aware reward design and robust inference for cross-domain PCBA visual question answering.

AI.tldr: A multimodal reasoning framework for cross-domain PCBA VQA that unifies standards-derived, real-world, and auxiliary PCB-domain data into a single instruction format, with verified reasoning traces and a task-aware GRPO that uses semantic, counting, and validity rewards, plus robust inference strategies; achieves 83.24 Overall Score on the PCBA Standard-to-Real Grand Challenge.
AI.motivation: Domain shift between standards-derived samples and real-world production-line PCBA imagery; heterogeneous output spaces (multiple-choice and numerical counting); need for robust cross-domain reasoning and guidance grounded in standards to improve automated inspection.
AI.method: Convert standards-derived, real-world, and auxiliary PCB-domain data into a unified instruction format; construct verified reasoning traces aligned with visual evidence, question semantics, candidate options, and ground-truth answers; introduce Task-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that combines multi-component semantic rewards for choice questions, distance-aware rewards for counting questions, and an auxiliary format reward for valid outputs; during inference apply answer-option semantic consistency correction, self-consistency voting, and multi-model arbitration for robustness.
AI.result: Achieves an Overall Score of 83.24 on the official PCBA Standard-to-Real Grand Challenge leaderboard, demonstrating the effectiveness of task-aware reward design and robust inference for cross-domain PCBA VQA.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware reward design combined with robust inference significantly improves cross-domain PCBA visual question answering, highlighting the value of unified instruction-format data, traceable reasoning, and multi-model arbitration for domain adaptation in multimodal QA.

title: MOSAIC-SR: Transformer-Guided Symbolic Regression for Scientific Equation Recovery
summary: Symbolic regression aims to recover closed-form equations from observations, providing interpretable models for scientific discovery. Existing approaches struggle to combine flexible structural search with efficient inference. Search-based methods can refine expression structure but often rely on costly combinatorial optimization with random initialization. Pretrained neural models generate formulas almost instantly, but their predictions often contain symbolic errors. We introduce MOSAIC-SR, which uses a pretrained Transformer to propose multiple initial sketches. These sketches initialize searches in several promising regions, avoiding random starts in the vast expression space. Each search jointly recovers structure and constants through scale-aware constant optimization and local symbolic repair. We evaluate MOSAIC-SR on the SRSD-Feynman dataset with and without dummy variables and on six additional benchmarks. MOSAIC-SR obtains the highest symbolic solution rate on every dataset while ranking among the top two methods in predictive accuracy. This advantage persists in the presence of irrelevant dummy inputs. The results show that learned priors can focus search on promising equation structures, and that numerical optimization and symbolic repair are important for recovery.

AI.tldr: MOSAIC-SR combines a pretrained Transformer with search-based symbolic regression to propose multiple initial sketches, guiding structure search and constants optimization for robust, interpretable equation recovery across benchmarks; it achieves state-leading symbolic solution rate while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy, even with dummy inputs.
AI.motivation: To overcome the trade-off between flexible, expensive search-based SR and fast, but error-prone neural formula generation; inject learned priors to steer searches toward promising expression structures while maintaining exact symbolic recovery.
AI.method: Use a pretrained Transformer to generate multiple initial sketches (structure proposals). Run parallel, scale-aware optimization to jointly infer structure and constants, followed by local symbolic repair to fix remaining issues. Evaluate across SRSD-Feynman dataset (with/without dummy variables) and six other benchmarks.
AI.result: MOSAIС-SR achieves the highest symbolic solution rate on every dataset and remains in the top two for predictive accuracy; performance persists when dummy inputs are present, indicating robustness to irrelevant inputs and effective use of priors to steer search.
AI.conclusion: Learned priors from the Transformer effectively focus structural search on promising equation forms; combined with scale-aware constant optimization and symbolic repair, this yields accurate symbolic recovery with strong interpretability, suggesting a productive direction for combining neural priors with search-based SR.

title: DEXTERA: From a Single Image to Deployable Dexterous Manipulation via Real-to-Sim-to-Real
summary: Collecting real-world robot data for dexterous manipulation is costly and time-consuming. While high-fidelity physics simulators enable scalable data synthesis and policy learning, constructing deployment-ready digital twins manually remains labor-intensive, and residual visual, geometric, and dynamics gaps hinder reliable sim-to-real transfer. We present DEXTERA, an automated real-to-sim-to-real framework that transforms a single RGB image into deployable policies for dexterous manipulation across four unified stages: (1) single-image scene factorization into a static Gaussian background and interactive rigid or articulated assets with VLM-inferred physical parameters; (2) metric scene global alignment, object canonicalization, and morphology-balanced robot calibration; (3) scalable simulator task primitive construction, VR teleoperation, and object-centric trajectory synthesis; and (4) a shared multimodal policy interface supporting both imitation learning and reinforcement learning. We evaluate DEXTERA across 13 task-embodiment pairs, 2 dexterous robot platforms, and 6 policy architectures. Experimental results demonstrate that DEXTERA achieves superior visual fidelity and 3D geometric reconstruction compared to generative baselines, while cross-domain trajectory replays validate strong physical interaction consistency. Furthermore, simulation-only trained policies enable viable zero-shot real-robot deployment, while simulation-real co-training substantially improves mean physical policy success from 29.2% to 61.9% across diverse policy architectures.

AI.tldr: DEXTERA converts a single RGB image into deployable dexterous manipulation policies via a four-stage real-to-sim-to-real pipeline, enabling zero-shot deployment and data-efficient sim-to-real co-training with substantial policy performance gains.
AI.motivation: Reduce the cost and time of collecting real-world robot data and manual creation of deployment-ready digital twins, while closing sim-to-real gaps for dexterous manipulation.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline: (1) single-image factorization into static background and interactive assets with VLM-derived physical parameters; (2) metric global alignment, object canonicalization, and morphology-balanced robot calibration; (3) scalable simulator task primitive construction, VR teleoperation, and object-centric trajectory synthesis; (4) a shared multimodal policy interface supporting imitation learning and reinforcement learning.
AI.result: DEXTERA achieves superior visual fidelity and 3D reconstruction relative to generative baselines; cross-domain trajectory replays demonstrate physical interaction consistency. Simulation-only training enables viable zero-shot real-robot deployment, and simulation-real co-training substantially improves mean physical policy success from 29.2% to 61.9% across diverse policy architectures.
AI.conclusion: DEXTERA offers a fully automated, single-image-to-deployable-digital-twin workflow for dexterous manipulation that delivers high-fidelity scene reconstruction and robust sim-to-real transfer, reducing manual effort and enabling substantial policy performance gains through sim-real co-training.

title: Information-Gain Rewards over Diversity-Pruned Tests: GT-Anchored Verifier Co-Training for Reliable Code Generation
summary: Self-play methods that co-train a single language model as both coder and test author promise to move code-generation RL beyond fixed test suites, but they suffer from two coupled pathologies: permissiveness collapse, where pass-rate rewards are maximised by trivial, non-discriminative tests, and concentration bias, where i.i.d. sampled tests cluster on modal inputs and inflate estimator variance. We introduce CoVer (Co-trained Coder and Verifier), a single-policy GRPO framework that addresses both failure modes. First, an information-gain (IG) reward scores each self-generated test by the mutual information between its pass/fail vector and a graded, ground-truth-anchored correctness signal y [0, 1] m, gated by the sign of their covariance so that only positively discriminative tests receive reward. Second, a three-stage diversity-aware selection step prunes a candidate pool to a behaviourally non-redundant suite (invalidity, input-string, execution-profile filtering), raising the effective sample size of the IG estimator at fixed execution budget. On five benchmarks (LiveBench, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, Code-Forces), CoVer raises one-shot pass@1 by +5.8 points at 7B and +7.1 points at 14B over the Qwen2.5-Instruct backbone, and achieves the highest macro-average among all compared methods at both scales. As a drop-in backbone inside the CodeT ranking pipeline, CoVer-7B adds +3.5 points, demonstrating the dual benefit of co-training for both generation and selection.

AI.tldr: CoVer introduces an information-gain reward and a three-stage diversity-aware test selection to co-train a single policy as both coder and verifier, improving pass@1 across multiple benchmarks and boosting CodeT rankings.
AI.motivation: Address two coupled pathologies in self-play co-training with a single LM: permissiveness collapse (trivial tests maximize passes) and concentration bias (tests cluster on modal inputs, inflating estimator variance).
AI.method: Propose CoVer, a single-policy GRPO framework. Use an information-gain (IG) reward that scores self-generated tests by the mutual information between their pass/fail vector and a graded ground-truth-anchored correctness signal y in [0,1], gated by the sign of their covariance to reward only positively discriminative tests. Apply a three-stage diversity-aware test selection (invalidity, input-string, execution-profile filtering) to prune a candidate pool into a non-redundant, diverse test suite, increasing the effective IG estimator sample size under a fixed execution budget.
AI.result: Empirical gains on five benchmarks (LiveBench, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, Code-Forces): +5.8 pass@1 at 7B and +7.1 at 14B over the Qwen2.5-Instruct backbone; highest macro-average among all compared methods at both scales. When used as a drop-in backbone in the CodeT ranking pipeline, CoVer-7B adds +3.5 points.
AI.conclusion: CoVer demonstrates that co-training for generation and verification with an information-gain reward and a diversity-aware test-selection strategy can mitigate permissiveness and concentration issues, yielding strong cross-benchmark gains and practical integration benefits in CodeT ranking pipelines.

title: Combining Object Detection with Geometry-Aware Clustering to Distinguish Overlapping Plants in UAV Imagery
summary:
Reliable plant-level information from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery is important for automated crop monitoring. However, in dense crop canopies, adjacent plants frequently overlap and are detected as a single object, reducing the reliability of plant-level measurements. This study presents a geometry-aware post-detection framework for resolving overlapping plant instances using standard RGB UAV imagery.
  The framework combines object detection with geometric clustering of plant components. Leaves or branches detected within each bush-level region are represented using two complementary geometric features: component centroids and radial intersection points (RIPs) derived from detected plant structures. K-means and Gaussian mixture models determine whether a detected region contains a single plant or two overlapping plants. Density filtering suppresses spurious radial intersections, and a post-pipeline ensemble combines spatial and directional geometric information.
  The framework was evaluated using UAV imagery of eggplant and tomato crops under field conditions. Centroid-based clustering achieved an F1-score of 0.89 for eggplant, while the combined centroid-RIP approach achieved the best tomato performance, with an accuracy of 0.80, precision of 1.00, and F1-score of 0.75 using K-means. Density filtering substantially improved RIP-based clustering for tomato.
  The proposed approach provides a lightweight, modular engineering solution that can be integrated with existing RGB UAV monitoring pipelines without additional depth sensors, pixel-level segmentation, three-dimensional reconstruction, or retraining of the primary bush detector. The results demonstrate that geometric reasoning applied to existing detector outputs can complement deep-learning-based object detection and improve plant-level interpretation in dense agricultural canopies.

AI.tldr: A geometry-aware post-detection framework to separate overlapping plant instances in dense canopies from RGB UAV imagery, using centroid and radial intersection points, with clustering (K-means or Gaussian mixture) to decide single vs two plants, improving plant-level accuracy without extra sensors or retraining.
AI.motivation: Reliable plant-level measurements are hindered by adjacency/overlap of plants in dense canopies; standard detectors often merge neighboring plants. There is a need for a lightweight, RGB-only method that leverages geometric cues to disambiguate overlapping individuals without depth data or retraining.
AI.method: Represent leaves/branches within each bush-level region by two geometric features: component centroids and radial intersection points (RIPs) derived from detected plant structures. Use K-means and Gaussian mixture models to determine whether a region contains a single plant or two overlapping plants. Apply density filtering to suppress spurious RIPs. Use a post-pipeline ensemble combining spatial and directional geometric information. Evaluated on UAV imagery of eggplant and tomato under field conditions. No depth sensors, pixel-level segmentation, 3D reconstruction, or retraining of the primary bush detector.
AI.result: Centroid-based clustering achieved F1-score of 0.89 for eggplant. The combined centroid-RIP approach with K-means achieved best tomato performance: accuracy 0.80, precision 1.00, F1-score 0.75. Density filtering substantially improved RIP-based clustering for tomato.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a lightweight, modular solution that can be integrated with existing RGB UAV pipelines without depth sensing or retraining. Geometry-based reasoning on detector outputs complements deep learning-based detection, improving plant-level interpretation in dense canopies.

title: On the Limits of Maximal Coding Rate Reduction for Out-of-Distribution Generalisation
summary: Substantial efforts have been devoted to making deep learning objectives, representations, and architectures interpretable, with the goal of improving the safety, robustness, and generalisation of learning systems in diverse real-world applications. The recently proposed maximal coding rate reduction ($\mathrm{MCR}^{2}$) offers a promising information-theoretic framework for learning structured, discriminative representations of class-wise submanifolds and has inspired interpretable white-box architectures. However, we observe that $\mathrm{MCR}^{2}$ can completely fail under distribution shift, motivating our study of its out-of-distribution (OOD) generalisation limits. We establish two limitations of $\mathrm{MCR}^{2}$ for OOD generalisation. First, the $\mathrm{MCR}^{2}$ objective alone can admit complete prediction failure: a representation based entirely on unstable environmental features can achieve the global coding optimum yet fail completely after correlation reversal, despite an available perfectly stable feature. This exact-optimum example includes test inputs that cannot occur during training. Even when every possible test input can also occur during training, coding quality can be arbitrarily close to optimal while prediction error is arbitrarily close to 100%. Second, directly incorporating the invariance principle underlying widely successful invariant risk minimisation (IRM) and risk extrapolation (REx) does not eliminate this failure. The failing representation admits the same optimal coding operator across training environments, showing that shared coding optimality does not ensure stable prediction. Reliable OOD guarantees for $\mathrm{MCR}^{2}$ therefore require additional new assumptions or learning principles that establish stable predictive relationships across environments.

AI.tldr: MCR^2-based representations can fail OOD; two limits: (1) the objective can optimize to unstable features causing prediction failure under correlation reversal; (2) invariance principles (IRM/REx) do not fix this; stable predictive relationships require new assumptions or learning principles.
AI.motivation: Assess OOD robustness of MCR^2 and its suitability for interpretable representations across environments.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis constructing worst-case scenarios: an exact-optimum representation based on unstable environmental features that remains optimal under training but collapses under correlation shift; also analyze compatibility with IRM/REx invariance.
AI.result: Identified two fundamental limitations: (i) global coding optimum can coincide with complete prediction failure under distribution shift; (ii) invariance-based training does not remove this, since the same optimal coding operator can hold across environments.
AI.conclusion: MCR^2 lacks reliable OOD guarantees; additional assumptions or learning principles are required to ensure stability of predictions across environments.

title: Constraint-Unified MPC for Over-Actuated Surface Vehicles with Post-Detection Fault Reconfiguration
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for the International Symposium of Robotics Research (ISRR) 2026
summary: Choreographed aquatic performances require small autonomous surface vehicles to track precise paths under per-thruster force and rate limits, including after thruster failures. We report a deployed system in which trajectory tracking, thrust allocation, and the per-thruster force and rate limits are resolved in a single quadratic program over the per-thruster commands, with fault reconfiguration entering through one binary flag per thruster from an external detector. The system has driven a fleet in live performances on Lake Zürich and at the Time Space Existence 2025 exhibition in Venice. The field campaign measures 1.6 cm root mean square position error in a 10-minute hold and 4.3 cm over a 10 m square at 0.6 m/s. At 0.5 m/s, losing the front thruster increases the error to 11.6 cm, while losing the starboard-side thruster increases it to 11.5 cm. Losing two thrusters simultaneously leaves the craft tracking a 0.4 m/s square with a root mean square position error of 1.25 m. Compared to our own cascaded baseline, the unified formulation tracks the nominal square to the same few centimeters and holds station more tightly with roughly half the thruster force. The architectures separate after a thruster failure, where the unified controller stays within 24 cm of the reference path while the cascade leaves it.

AI.tldr: A unified quadratic-program-based control approach simultaneously handles trajectory tracking, per-thruster thrust allocation, and fault reconfiguration for small autonomous surface vehicles, achieving robust cm-level tracking under single- and multi-thruster failures, with better efficiency than a cascaded baseline, demonstrated in live performances.
AI.motivation: The need for precise, fault-tolerant path tracking in choreographed aquatic performances where individual thrusters are rate-limited and can fail; existing architectures separate control tasks, leading to degraded performance after failures.
AI.method: Formulate a single quadratic program that computes per-thruster commands subject to per-thruster force and rate limits and incorporate fault reconfiguration via binary flags per thruster from an external detector; solve online to produce feasible commands that track a reference path while respecting limits and handling faults.
AI.result: Field deployment yields RMS position errors of 1.6 cm for 10-minute hold, 4.3 cm for a 10 m square at 0.6 m/s; under single thruster loss errors ~11-12 cm; double thruster failure yields 1.25 m RMS on 0.4 m/s square; compared to cascaded baseline, the unified approach tracks with a few cm error and uses ~50% of the thrust; after failures, unified remains within 24 cm of reference, while cascade deviates.
AI.conclusion: Unified QP-based controller provides robust, efficient, fault-tolerant trajectory tracking for ASV fleets in real-world performances, outperforming cascaded architectures and enabling live, multi-vehicle shows with better path adherence and lower propulsion demand.

title: Ability-Residual Decoupled Modeling for Affective Cognitive Diagnosis
summary: Cognitive diagnosis infers students' concept mastery from response logs. However, students' responses are not determined by mastery alone: non-cognitive factors such as emotion, engagement, and fatigue can also affect performance. Affective cognitive diagnosis therefore extends conventional cognitive diagnosis by incorporating affective states. Existing methods often assume that the cognitive diagnosis backbone has already explained ability, item, and concept effects, so the remaining errors can be attributed mainly to affect. We argue that this assumption can be insufficient in real educational data: item calibration bias, systematic concept bias, personalized student-concept deviations, and latent student-item matching can form stable cognitive residuals. Without an explicit modeling pathway, these residuals may leak into affective representations, producing affect contamination. To address this problem, we propose an ability-residual decoupled framework for affective cognitive diagnosis. The model first captures unmodeled cognitive residuals through student, item, concept, student-concept, and low-rank student-item components, and then uses an affective module to modulate guess/slip effects. A Q-matrix-constrained concept residual attention mechanism adaptively aggregates only item-relevant concept residuals. Experiments on ASSIST2017, ASSIST2012, ASSIST2009, and Junyi with six cognitive diagnosis backbones show response-prediction gains across the reported comparisons and generally improved affect alignment when affect labels are available. Ablation studies, leakage probes, principal component analysis visualization, long-tail analysis, and case studies further indicate that ability residuals absorb stable cognitive bias, reduce cognitive contamination in the affective branch, and enhance the robustness and predictive accuracy of cognitive diagnosis models.

AI.tldr: An ability-residual decoupled framework improves affective cognitive diagnosis by explicitly modeling cognitive residuals (student/item/concept and cross-influence residuals, plus low-rank terms) before an affective module; a Q-matrix constrained residual attention then aggregates item-relevant concept residuals, yielding better response prediction and affect alignment across several datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing affective cognitive diagnosis often assumes the cognitive backbone already accounts for ability, item, and concept effects, leaving residual errors attributed to affect. However, stable cognitive residuals (calibration bias, concept bias, personalized deviations, and latent matching) can contaminate affective representations. There is a need to explicitly model these residuals to prevent affect contamination and improve robustness.
AI.method: Proposes an ability-residual decoupled framework: (1) capture unmodeled cognitive residuals via explicit components (student, item, concept, student-concept, and low-rank student-item) to model residuals; (2) an affective module modulates guess/slip effects based on these residuals; (3) a Q-matrix-constrained concept residual attention mechanism adaptively aggregates only item-relevant concept residuals; (4) evaluated with six cognitive diagnosis backbones on ASSIST2017, ASSIST2012, ASSIST2009, and Junyi datasets.
AI.result: Across datasets and backbones, the model achieves response-prediction gains and generally improved affect alignment when labels are available. Ablation studies and diagnostics show ability residuals capture stable cognitive biases, reduce cognitive contamination in the affective branch, and enhance robustness and predictive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Modeling cognitive residuals explicitly before affective processing improves prediction and affect alignment in cognitive diagnosis, reducing contamination and increasing robustness across diverse datasets and backbones.

title: S3VD: Semantic-Guidance Spatio-Temporal Scanning for Video Deraining
summary: Heavy rainfall severely degrades outdoor videos by corrupting high-frequency details and introducing motion blur, critically undermining the reliability of visual tasks. Recently, State Space Models (SSMs), particularly Mamba, have emerged as efficient alternatives for vision tasks with their linear complexity and ability to model long-range dependencies. However, when confronted with the poor visual representations in rainy videos, Mamba still faces difficulties in preserving the integrity of 2D spatial semantics and modeling 3D spatio-temporal correlations. To break these limitations, we introduce S3VD, a Semantic-Guidance Spatio-Temporal Scanning framework for video deraining, featuring two key innovations: Multi-Scale Semantic Fusion (MSSF) Module and Spatio-Temporal Scanning Fusion (STSF) Module. The former integrates temporal semantic priors from DINOv2 to guide precise feature representation and counteract the loss of local semantic context inherent to Mamba's 1D flatten operation, enhancing robustness against extreme degradation. The latter introduces a spatio-temporal scanning mechanism and devises a Decoupled-Gating Mamba (DG-Mamba) layer, which employs two independent gates to adaptively control preceding and subsequent contextual information within the input clip, optimizing intra-frame and inter-frame correlation modeling. Experiments on video deraining benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of S3VD, achieving state-of-the-art performance with an average 0.84 dB PSNR improvement over Mamba-based baselines.

AI.tldr: S3VD proposes Semantic-Guided Spatio-Temporal Deraining with MSSF and STSF, using DG-Mamba, to outperform Mamba baselines in rain artifact removal.
AI.motivation: Heavy rain corrupts high-frequency details and induces motion blur, degrading visual tasks. Mamba-like State Space Models struggle to preserve 2D spatial semantics and model 3D spatio-temporal correlations under severe degradation.
AI.method: S3VD comprises two modules: (1) Multi-Scale Semantic Fusion (MSSF) that injects temporal semantic priors from DINOv2 to stabilize feature representations and counteract information loss from Mamba's 1D flattening; (2) Spatio-Temporal Scanning Fusion (STSF) with a Decoupled-Gating Mamba (DG-Mamba) layer that uses two independent gates to adaptively control preceding and subsequent context, enhancing intra-frame and inter-frame modeling.
AI.result: On video deraining benchmarks, S3VD achieves state-of-the-art performance, with an average of 0.84 dB PSNR improvement over Mamba-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: S3VD robustly preserves 2D spatial semantics and captures 3D spatio-temporal dependencies in rain-affected videos, delivering superior deraining performance over prior Mamba-based approaches.

title: Scaling Discovery through Test-Time Communication
summary: Science advances not in isolation but through collaboration, yet existing agentic systems capture little of this. Whether communicating agents help remains an open question with mixed prior results. We show that test-time communication can substantially outperform independent parallel attempts on challenging tasks, where sharing a breakthrough can push the whole group forward. We first study the effect of scaling multi-agent test-time communication, where agents have no predefined roles and communicate via a shared directory, on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark requiring novel problem solving. We find that a team of $k$ communicating agents, team@$k$, matches the success rate of $4k$ independent agents, and this advantage grows with $k$, suggesting gains compound with scale. The effect is not merely efficiency: a task that no single agent can solve, a team of agents can solve reliably. Furthermore, these gains transfer to research-oriented tasks, given sufficient compute. On polyomino packing, communicating agents outperform best@$k$ and exceed the prior best-known score. On MNIST classifier compression, communication surpasses the best-known human solution. A team of four agents produced a 1,957-byte classifier submission achieving 99.4% test accuracy, smaller than both the best-known human solution and the best single-agent result. These gains are not unconditional. Independent agents may outperform communication when compute is limited or when a clear measure of progress is absent. However, under sufficient compute and clear feedback, multi-agent communication consistently yields stronger results.

AI.tldr: Test-time communication among teams of agents yields substantial performance gains over independent agents on challenging tasks; scaling benefits compound; communication enables solving tasks unreachable by single agents; results generalize across domains; with sufficient compute, multi-agent communication outperforms independent approaches.
AI.motivation: To determine whether agent communication during test time can improve collaborative problem solving, quantify scalability benefits, and resolve mixed prior results on the efficacy of communicating agents.
AI.method: Empirically evaluate teams of k communicating agents (team@k) who share a common directory for communication, without predefined roles, on ARC-AGI-3 (novel problem solving) and additional tasks (polyomino packing, MNIST classifier compression). Compare performance against best@k independent agents and analyze scaling effects and compute requirements.
AI.result: Team@k matches the performance of 4k independent agents on ARC-AGI-3; advantages of communication grow with k. Communication enables solving tasks no single agent can. Results transfer to other tasks: in polyomino packing, communicating agents exceed best@k and prior scores; in MNIST compression, a four-agent team produced a 1,957-byte classifier with 99.4% accuracy, outperforming both the best-known human solution and the best single-agent result.
AI.conclusion: Under sufficient compute and clear feedback, multi-agent test-time communication yields stronger results than independent efforts; independence-based approaches may still win under limited compute or ambiguous progress signals.

title: PlantShade: Predicting Plant Shadows for Lighting-Aware Robotic Agricultural Operation
comment: This paper has been accepted by the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Plant growth and agricultural production form the foundation of a country's sustainable development and directly impact human livelihoods. Recent advances in frontier artificial intelligence have enabled scientific agriculture with strong potential to improve crop productivity. In this paper, we identify the importance and inherent complexity of plant shade simulation, as shading is a critical factor influencing plant growth. To advance this field and promote broader societal benefits, we focus on two main contributions. First, we introduce a comprehensive plant growth and shade dataset covering four plant species, including soybean, tomato, sugarbeet, and strawberry. The dataset includes top-down viewpoints with a supplementary light along a circular trajectory, casting dynamic shadows across multiple growth stages and diverse observation complexities. Second, we propose generative shade simulation based on diffusion models, enabling realistic shade generation for unseen plants and supporting downstream robotic tasks such as perception, lighting control, and view planning. The model incorporates temporal conditioning to facilitate flexible shade simulation across different time stages. We conduct both quantitative and qualitative evaluations to assess model performance. This work provides a foundational study for plant-aware shade modeling and has meaningful implications for broader agricultural and robotic applications.

AI.tldr: Diffusion-based generative shade simulation plus a four-species plant shade dataset for temporally conditioned, realistic shade across growth stages, aiding agriculture and robotics tasks.
AI.motivation: Shading is a complex, impactful factor in plant growth. The work provides datasets and models to enable AI-assisted agriculture, perception, lighting control, and planning in robotics.
AI.method: Dataset: four species (soybean, tomato, sugarbeet, strawberry); top-down views with a supplemental light along a circular trajectory to cast dynamic shadows across growth stages and observation conditions. Model: diffusion-based generative shade simulation with temporal conditioning to enable realistic, time-aware shade for unseen plants and support downstream tasks (perception, lighting control, view planning).
AI.result: Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate realism and usefulness for downstream robotics and agricultural tasks; establishes a foundational study for plant-aware shade modeling.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a foundational resource and methodology for plant-aware shade modeling with broad implications for agricultural productivity and robotic applications.

title: A Fully Differentiable Neuro-Soft-Symbolic Framework for Perceptual Task Planning
summary: Perceptual planning tasks require two key capabilities: accurately perceiving uncertain scenes and planning valid action sequences following logical rules. Conventional methods convert perception into discrete symbolic facts and then plan, discarding perceptual uncertainty and severing task-level feedback to perception. We introduce a generic, fully differentiable neuro-soft-symbolic framework that connects visual perception and task planning within a single computational graph. The framework maintains a continuous soft symbolic state, lifts domain rules into a differentiable soft-$T_P$ transition operator, and optimizes action logits over a short planning horizon. Gradients from the planning objective can also update the perception parameters, allowing task-relevant perceptual representations to be refined during planning. On Blocksworld, our method solves 40/40 LatPlan-40 tasks and 596/600 PlanBench-600 tasks, compared with 33/40 for LatPlan and 587/600 for the reasoning-model baseline, while requiring substantially less computation and time. In the perceptual-uncertainty ablation, our method improves the success rate from 59\% with frozen perception to 83\%. We further conduct task-and-motion simulations on Blocksworld scenes, providing an execution-level validation of the compatibility between decoded task plans and downstream robotic motion execution.

AI.tldr: A differentiable neuro-soft-symbolic framework links perception and planning with soft symbolic state and differentiable transition rules, enabling robust planning under perceptual uncertainty and achieving state-of-the-art task success on Blocksworld/PlanBench with end-to-end gradient updates to perception.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between perceptual uncertainty and symbolic task planning, enabling task-driven perceptual refinement rather than treating perception separately and discarding uncertainty.
AI.method: Introduce a continuous soft symbolic state; lift domain rules into a differentiable soft-T_P transition operator; optimize action logits over a short planning horizon; propagate planning gradients back to perception to refine perceptual representations during planning.
AI.result: On Blocksworld, achieves 40/40 LatPlan-40 and 596/600 PlanBench-600 (vs 33/40 and 587/600 baselines), with substantially less computation/time; perceptual-uncertainty ablation raises success from 59% (frozen perception) to 83%; includes execution-level task-and-motion simulations validating plan-to-motion compatibility.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end differentiable neuro-soft-symbolic integration effectively unites perception and planning under uncertainty and is feasible for downstream robotic execution, improving robustness and efficiency compared to conventional pipelines.

title: VeriFuse: Bounded Vision-Language Arbitration and Reason-Guided Refinement for Cooperative 3D Perception
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong scene understanding and semantic judgment across diverse tasks, but their appropriate role in cooperative perception remains unclear. Directly asking a VLM to regress 3D detections is unreliable and computationally expensive, whereas using it to select the output of a single source discards useful information from other agents. We introduce VeriFuse, a bounded arbitration framework for vehicle-infrastructure cooperative 3D detection. Each agent first produces detections independently. Around each vehicle and roadside proposal, VeriFuse generates source-conditioned geometric candidates and combines the original detections, their perturbations, and cross-source hypotheses into a unified candidate pool. A frozen VLM then chooses among three admissible actions: SELECT an adequate candidate; REFINE an existing anchor when an object is supported but all candidates are geometrically inadequate; or REJECT an unsupported infrastructure-only proposal. Experiments on the DAIR-V2X dataset show that VeriFuse achieves 0.494/0.357 cooperative 3D AP50/AP70 and limits the relative vehicle-side BEV AP50 drop under a 300 ms delay to 1.7%. Overall, VeriFuse assigns the VLM a clear and constrained role in cooperative perception: semantic reasoning resolves ambiguity among cross-agent hypotheses, while deterministic constraints determine the final 3D geometry.

AI.tldr: A frozen vision-language model acts as a bounded arbiter in VeriFuse, a cooperative perception framework that fuses vehicle–infrastructure detections via source-conditioned candidates; it selects, refines, or rejects proposals to achieve cooperative 3D detection with competitive AP and low latency.
AI.motivation: To address the mismatch between VLMs' strengths in semantic reasoning and the need for precise 3D geometry in cooperative perception; avoid expensive direct regression and preserve cross-agent information by bounding the VLM's role.
AI.method: Independent detections per agent; generate source-conditioned geometric candidates around each vehicle/roadside proposal; assemble a unified candidate pool including original detections, their perturbations, and cross-source hypotheses; a frozen VLM selects among: SELECT, REFINE, or REJECT; REFINE used when supported but geometry is inadequate; REJECT for infrastructure-only proposals.
AI.result: On DAIR-V2X, VeriFuse achieves cooperative 3D AP50 0.494 and AP70 0.357; vehicle-side BEV AP50 drop under 300 ms latency is limited to 1.7%.
AI.conclusion: VeriFuse offers a clear, constrained role for VLMs in cooperative perception: semantic reasoning resolves ambiguity among cross-agent hypotheses, while deterministic geometry constraints finalize the 3D outputs.

title: Stiefel-AdamW: Geometry-Aware AdamW for Linear Factorization Blocks
summary: A pervasive structural pattern in modern deep learning is the linear factorization block: a submodule of the form $W = BA$ in which two parameter matrices are multiplied directly, with no intervening nonlinearity. Such blocks appear in LoRA adapters, low-rank compressed layers, query-key products of self-attention, and share a common pathology: the factorization is non-unique, which can destabilize training and limit usable learning rates. Despite this, factorization blocks are typically optimized with standard Euclidean methods that ignore the underlying geometry. We introduce Stiefel-AdamW, a near drop-in replacement for AdamW for use wherever such blocks appear. By constraining one factor on the Stiefel manifold while leaving the other Euclidean, Stiefel-AdamW relaxes the full $\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{R}^r)$ gauge symmetry to a compact orthogonal symmetry, ruling out factor blow-up while retaining the coordinate-wise diagonal preconditioning that gives AdamW its practical strength. Moment estimation is performed in the ambient Euclidean space, with geometry entering only through a tangent-space projection and a manifold retraction. The implementation overhead over AdamW is minimal, and we show that the resulting optimizer inherits both the stability benefits of Riemannian methods and standard convergence guarantees. We validate Stiefel-AdamW on LoRA-style fine-tuning of GPT2, ViT, and Mistral 7B and on full pretraining of GPT2 on OpenWebText, showing consistent improvements over strong baselines at essentially no additional cost over AdamW.

AI.tldr: Stiefel-AdamW constrains one factor of linear factorization blocks to the Stiefel manifold, stabilizing training and enabling larger learning rates with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Non-uniqueness of linear factorization blocks W=BA causes instability and can bottleneck learning rates; standard Euclidean optimizers ignore the underlying geometry.
AI.method: Constrain one factor on the Stiefel manifold while keeping the other Euclidean. Use ambient Euclidean moment estimation with tangent-space projection and a manifold retraction. Minimal overhead over AdamW; preserves diagonal preconditioning.
AI.result: Empirical improvements on LoRA-style GPT‑2, ViT, and Mistral 7B fine-tuning and GPT-2 pretraining on OpenWebText, with improved stability and performance at essentially no extra cost.
AI.conclusion: Geometric constraints on factorized blocks yield stability benefits of Riemannian methods while retaining AdamW advantages; applicable to various LoRA-style and low-rank factorization blocks and show practical gains with modest implementation effort.

title: Design of Adaptive PID Controller Based On Asynchronous Advantage Actor Critic Learning Method for QuadCopter Control
summary: Quadcopters offer great utility in many applications, but their nonlinear nature and disturbance sensitivity present great control challenges. Basic PID controllers are generally not sophisticated enough to cope with these complexities. This paper suggests a control system that integrates the Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) algorithm with a PID controller for quadcopter attitude and trajectory tracking. The A3C controller uses parallel agents to optimize PID parameters dynamically using a neural network. A system identification module for the complementary system makes predictions about system states for optimal control policy. The proposed framework was compared with a standard actor-critic (A2C) model. Simulation results verify that they both track accurately. However, the A3C-based controller converges much more for the loss function, as evidenced by reward figures and loss curves, demonstrating better parameter optimization. This shows that A3C-based approach results in improved performance for the control of quadcopter, effectively integrating reinforcement learning and traditional control to achieve higher adaptability.

AI.tldr: Proposes an A3C-based PID tuning framework for quadcopter attitude/trajectory control, integrating parallel RL agents with a PID controller and a system identification module; shows improved loss convergence vs A2C in simulations.
AI.motivation: PID controllers struggle with nonlinear quadcopter dynamics and disturbances; adaptive learning-based tuning via reinforcement learning can enhance performance and robustness.
AI.method: Use asynchronous A3C to tune PID gains in real-time for quadcopter attitude and trajectory control; parallel agents optimize the PID parameters; includes a system identification module to predict system states to inform policy; compare to a standard A2C approach; evaluated in simulations.
AI.result: Both A3C and A2C track trajectories accurately; A3C converges more strongly in the loss function and reward curves, indicating better parameter optimization and adaptability.
AI.conclusion: An A3C-based RL approach integrated with traditional PID control improves quadcopter control performance in simulations, highlighting the potential of combining reinforcement learning with classical control for increased adaptability.

title: CogGym: Towards Large-Scale Comparative Evaluation of Human and Machine Cognition
summary: Understanding and modeling human intelligence are parallel goals shared by artificial intelligence (AI) and cognitive science. As AI systems grow increasingly capable, in what ways do model responses resemble human responses, and where do they systematically diverge? The sheer breadth and diversity of the tasks humans can perform and think about pose a challenge for scalable and rigorous comparison between humans and models. We introduce CogGym, a scalable, unified framework grounded in cognitive science for systematically comparing model and human behavior on matched experimental trials. CogGym uses a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop pipeline to standardize diverse experimental paradigms into a task-agnostic Experiment Markup Language (EML), enabling reproducible and faithful comparison at scale. For initial release, we curate and standardize 258 cognitive experiments from 100 papers that focuses on human commonsense reasoning, and evaluate 50 large language models against human responses. We find a clear scaling trend where larger and more recent AI models better reproduce human judgments. Yet AI models' improvement on such common reasoning tasks is considerably slower than the gains observed on formal-reasoning benchmarks like math and coding, and model--human fit remains well below human splithalf reliability ($R^2 = 0.93$ on text, $0.95$ on image, and $0.92$ on video) with the best models achieving $R^2 = 0.59$ on text, $0.58$ on image, and $0.43$ on video experiments. We intend for CogGym to provide a living evaluation framework that continually incorporates new cognitive science experiments to characterize where model behavior resembles human behavior, where it systematically diverges, and how those patterns change as models and experiments evolve.

AI.tldr: CogGym provides a scalable framework using an Experiment Markup Language to standardize 258 cognitive experiments across 100 papers, enabling large-scale comparison of 50 LLMs with humans; finds scaling trends with model size but model-human fit remains below human reliability and improves slower than formal reasoning benchmarks; positions CogGym as a living evaluation framework.
AI.motivation: To enable rigorous, scalable comparison between human cognition and AI model behavior across diverse cognitive tasks by standardizing experiments and enabling reproducible cross-model evaluation.
AI.method: Semi-automated, human-in-the-loop pipeline; standardization into a task-agnostic Experiment Markup Language (EML); aggregation of 258 experiments from 100 papers; evaluation of 50 large language models against human responses; analysis of model–human fit (R^2) across modalities.
AI.result: Scaling: larger and more recent models better reproduce human judgments; improvements on commonsense tasks are slower than gains on formal-reasoning benchmarks (math, coding); model–human fit remains well below human split-half reliability (R^2 = 0.93 text, 0.95 image, 0.92 video for humans) with best models achieving R^2 = 0.59 text, 0.58 image, 0.43 video.
AI.conclusion: CogGym establishes a living evaluation framework that continually incorporates new cognitive science experiments to characterize where model behavior resembles human behavior, where it diverges, and how those patterns evolve as models and experiments evolve.

title: Cube-Splat: High-Fidelity 360° Gaussian Splatting SLAM via Cubemap Factorization and Adjoint-Consistent Optimization
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Source code : https://github.com/guoxf304/CubeSplat
summary: Recent progress in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has enabled dense visual SLAM with pinhole cameras, yet most pipelines are not designed for panoramic imagery. We present Cube-Splat, the first panoramic GS-SLAM framework that factorizes each 360° frame into a cubemap of four fixed-orientation virtual pinhole views sharing a single optical center. By designating the front face as the primary pose state, we accumulate gradients from all faces via an adjoint mapping, thereby enabling multi-face observations to coherently update a single state while strictly preserving cross-view geometric consistency. Concurrently, our mapping module densifies and optimizes anisotropic Gaussians using aggregated cubemap rays for high-fidelity, dense reconstruction. Furthermore, to rigorously evaluate panoramic SLAM under diverse and challenging conditions, we introduce SynPano, a highly scalable, photorealistic synthetic dataset featuring parameterized complex trajectories and multi-modal ground truth. Extensive evaluations on two public benchmarks (PALVIO and OmniBlender) and our SynPano dataset, collectively encompassing both indoor and outdoor scenes, demonstrate that Cube-Splat achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in tracking accuracy and reconstruction fidelity. Both the source code and the SynPano dataset are available at https://github.com/guoxf304/CubeSplat.

AI.tldr: Cube-Splat is a panoramic 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM method that fuses four fixed-orientation views into a single state via adjoint gradients, with a high-fidelity dense mapping module and a photorealistic synthetic SynPano benchmark, achieving SOTA on PALVIO/OmniBlender.
AI.motivation: Extend dense GS-SLAM from pinhole cameras to panoramic imagery, ensuring cross-view geometric consistency and accurate dense reconstruction, and provide a scalable panoramic SLAM benchmark.
AI.method: Represent 360° frames as a cubemap of four fixed-orientation virtual pinhole views sharing one optical center. Treat the front face as the primary pose state and back-propagate gradients from all faces to this state through an adjoint mapping to maintain cross-view consistency. Densify and optimize anisotropic Gaussians using aggregated cubemap rays for high-fidelity reconstruction. Introduce SynPano as a photorealistic synthetic dataset with parameterized trajectories and multi-modal ground truth.
AI.result: Cube-Splat attains state-of-the-art tracking accuracy and reconstruction fidelity on PALVIO and OmniBlender benchmarks, over indoor and outdoor scenes, and demonstrates strong performance on the SynPano dataset.
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes a practical, coherent panoramic GS-SLAM pipeline with robust multi-face fusion and high-quality dense reconstruction, complemented by a scalable synthetic panorama benchmark (SynPano).

title: A Lightweight Plug-in Gate for Transformer-Based Time-Series Forecasters
summary: Covariate-rich time-series forecasting requires deciding how external variables enter the target forecasting path. Existing Transformer-based forecasters usually build a covariate representation and pass it to the encoder without an explicit admission stage. This paper studies pre-encoder covariate admission as an input-side interface that regulates that representation immediately before encoder processing. We implement the interface with a lightweight representation-level pre-encoder gate that assigns sigmoid scores to representation units, and we also study a usage-regularized variant that penalizes average admission. The interface is evaluated as a plug-in module for TimeXer, Inverted Transformer (iTransformer), and Patch Time Series Transformer (PatchTST) under a zero-extra-tuning protocol, where each gated model inherits the corresponding baseline configuration. Experiments on the Electricity Transformer Temperature minute-level (ETTm1 and ETTm2) datasets, Traffic, Energy, and influenza-like illness (ILI) include paired forecasting comparisons, gate-placement ablation, initialization ablation, controlled covariate-admission analysis, and a variance inflation factor (VIF)-informed permutation feature importance (PFI) diagnostic case study. In the tested settings, the gate is competitive with the corresponding baselines, and the usage penalty reduces average admission scores while keeping forecasting errors close to the unpenalized TimeXer setting.

AI.tldr: Introduces a pre-encoder covariate admission gate for time-series transformers to regulate external variable representations before encoding, evaluated as a plug-in across multiple architectures with a regularized variant.
AI.motivation: To control when and how covariates influence the forecasting path, potentially improving interpretability and robustness of covariate-rich time-series forecasting.
AI.method: Add a lightweight representation-level pre-encoder gate that assigns sigmoid scores to representation units; include a usage-regularized variant that penalizes average admission. Implement as a plug-in for TimeXer, iTransformer, and PatchTST under a zero-extra-tuning protocol; conduct extensive ablations and diagnostic analyses (gate placement, initialization, covariate-admission control, VIF-informed PFI).
AI.result: The gate is competitive with baselines; the usage penalty reduces average covariate admission while keeping forecasting errors close to the unpenalized TimeXer setting. The approach yields interpretable admission patterns and maintains performance across diverse datasets (ETTm1/ETTm2, Traffic, Energy, ILI).
AI.conclusion: Pre-encoder admission gates are a viable plug-in mechanism for covariate-rich forecasting, offering a tunable trade-off between covariate usage and predictive accuracy with interpretability benefits; further work could explore generalization, initialization strategies, and alternative regularizers.

title: Dynamic Modeling and LQR Control of a Single Coaxial Drone with 2DOF Thrust Vectoring Mechanism
summary: Coaxial rotor drones have generated considerable interest because of energy efficiency and small size, but they are afflicted with inherent underactuation for roll and pitch control, although systems like swashplates have circumvented this limitation at the cost of greater mechanical complexity. This work presents a novel coaxial drone supplemented by a two-degreesof-freedom pendulum mechanism for active thrust vectoring that offers a less mechanically complicated alternative. We develop a comprehensive Lagrangian dynamic model that does not ignore the inertial contributions of all the components, including body, servo arms, and motor assembly. A Linear Quadratic Regulator(LQR) is designed based on the linearized dynamics around the hover equilibrium. High-fidelity simulations taking actuator dynamics and sensor noise into account validate the proposed architecture. An Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) blends GPS, barometer, and IMU estimates with high accuracy for state estimation. The findings verify the potential and reliability of this approach for power-saving, rapid coaxial UAVs.

AI.tldr: A coaxial drone variant uses a 2-DOF pendulum for active thrust vectoring to address roll/pitch underactuation with lower mechanical complexity. It employs a full Lagrangian dynamic model, an LQR controller around hover, and an EKF for sensor fusion, validated in high-fidelity simulations.
AI.motivation: Coaxial rotors suffer from underactuation for roll and pitch, and traditional fixes (e.g., swashplates) add mechanical complexity. The work seeks a simpler, energy-efficient thrust-vectoring solution.
AI.method: Derive a comprehensive Lagrangian dynamic model including inertial effects of the body, servo arms, and motor assembly. Design an LQR controller based on linearized dynamics around hover. Validate with high-fidelity simulations incorporating actuator dynamics and sensor noise. Use an Extended Kalman Filter to fuse GPS, barometer, and IMU data for state estimation.
AI.result: High-fidelity simulations validate the proposed architecture. The EKF achieves high-accuracy state estimates. The approach supports power-saving and rapid maneuvering in coaxial UAVs.
AI.conclusion: The 2-DOF pendulum thrust-vectoring concept offers a less mechanically complex alternative to swashplates for actively controlling coaxial rotors, with demonstrated theoretical and simulated feasibility and potential energy efficiency benefits; hardware implementation and real-world testing remain for future work.

title: PlaceReasoner-Beta: Reasoning-Driven Macro Placement and Benchmarking
summary: Automated macro placement remains a fundamental challenge in VLSI physical design. Despite decades of research, existing approaches predominantly optimize hand-crafted proxy objectives, such as estimated wirelength, and typically produce placements through one-shot numerical optimization, limiting their ability to incorporate visual layout context, codified design expertise, and downstream physical-design feedback in a unified loop. We present PlaceReasoner-Beta, a verifier-guided multi-agent framework that reformulates macro placement as a closed-loop reasoning problem rather than black-box optimization. A vision-language model (VLM) planner generates candidate placements from the floorplan image, macro specifications, and connectivity structure; a geometric verifier enforces physical legality and expert placement principles; a physical verifier refines candidates using early implementation feedback; and a post-route optimizer further improves promising layouts using final PPA. To enable reproducible evaluation, we introduce PlaceReasoner-Bench, a fully open end-to-end benchmark built from open RTL designs, EDA tools, and technology libraries. It comprises 8 designs at two aspect ratios, yielding 16 tasks with fixed floorplans and I/O assignments, so methods differ only in macro positions and orientations and are evaluated using routed PPA and DRC rather than pre-route proxies. Across the benchmark, PlaceReasoner-Beta achieves the best timing among DRC-clean methods on all square tasks, reducing post-route TNS by 61.2% at 1:1 and 53.0% at 2:1 relative to the classical baseline field. It also shortens routed wirelength on most designs despite never explicitly optimizing it, demonstrating that reasoning over spatial structure under physical-design feedback can improve end-to-end layout quality beyond proxy-objective optimization.

AI.tldr: PlaceReasoner-Beta reframes macro placement as a closed-loop reasoning task using a vision-language model planner and sequential verifiers with a post-route optimizer, achieving state-of-the-art timing and reduced TNS with DRC-clean layouts on a new open benchmark.
AI.motivation: Addresses the limitations of hand-crafted proxy objectives and one-shot optimization in macro placement by incorporating visual layout context, domain expertise, and downstream physical-design feedback in a unified loop.
AI.method: A verifier-guided multi-agent framework: a vision-language model planner proposes candidate placements from floorplan images, macro specs, and connectivity; a geometric verifier enforces physical legality and placement principles; a physical verifier refines candidates using early implementation feedback; a post-route optimizer improves promising layouts using final PPA. Evaluation uses PlaceReasoner-Bench, an open end-to-end benchmark with 8 designs at two aspect ratios (16 tasks) and fixed floorplans/I/O, comparing routed PPA and DRC instead of proxy objectives.
AI.result: PlaceReasoner-Beta achieves the best timing among DRC-clean methods on all square tasks, reducing post-route test-not-specified (TNS) by 61.2% at 1:1 and 53.0% at 2:1 relative to a classical baseline; it also reduces routed wirelength on most designs despite not explicitly optimizing it.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning over spatial structure with physical-design feedback in a closed-loop, multi-agent framework can surpass proxy-objective optimization and yield improved end-to-end layout quality.

title: PrismAlign: Prior-Steered Multi-View VLM Alignment for Hallucination-Robust Table OCR
summary: Table extraction suffers from frequent structural errors and semantic hallucinations. We propose PrismAlign, a multi-VLM framework aligning diverse visual perspectives to resolve ambiguity. It integrates priors of table logic to assess output plausibility, decoupling structural alignment from cell content alignment. A Bayesian decision strategy maximizes alignment accuracy by exploiting the correlation between extraction errors and computable rule violations. Evaluated on open-source and custom VLMs, PrismAlign reduces hallucinations and achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniDocBench 1.5, as well as on the table category of CC-OCR and PureDocBench.

AI.tldr: PrismAlign is a multi-VLM framework for robust table extraction that decouples structural alignment from cell content alignment, uses table-logic priors, and employs a Bayesian decision strategy to reduce semantic hallucinations; it achieves state-of-the-art results on OmniDocBench 1.5 and other benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Table extraction from VLMs suffers from structural errors and semantic hallucinations due to ambiguity in visual table representations. There is a need to enforce table-consistent structure and content through priors and principled decision rules to improve plausibility.
AI.method: Introduce PrismAlign, a multi-VLM framework that aligns multiple visual perspectives to resolve ambiguity. It decouples structural alignment from cell content alignment, integrates priors of table logic to assess output plausibility, and uses a Bayesian decision strategy that exploits the correlation between extraction errors and rule violations to maximize alignment accuracy.
AI.result: PrismAlign reduces hallucinations and achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniDocBench 1.5 and on the table category of CC-OCR and PureDocBench, demonstrated across open-source and custom VLMs.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling structure and content alignment, together with priors on table logic and Bayesian decision-making, yields more accurate and plausible table extraction, enabling SOTA results on multiple benchmarks.

title: FedeRage: Provably Convergent Agnostic Federated Learning under General Client Drift
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data, but its performance degrades under non-IID data and stochastic client participation. Remedies built on classical Federated Averaging (FedAvg) typically presuppose that client participation probabilities are known to the server, which is rarely the case in deployed systems. We first discuss and then characterize the optimization problem that \emph{distributionally agnostic} FedAvg actually solves when participation is entirely unknown, possibly highly skewed, and of variable size across rounds: uniform aggregation is shown to minimize a well-defined stochastic objective, weighted by the participation-induced marginal, at a standard $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ rate for convex and possibly nonsmooth losses. Building on this characterization, we propose \emph{Federated Risk-Averse Averaging} (\textsc{FedeRage}), a risk-averse extension of FedAvg that embeds the \emph{Conditional Value-at-Risk} (CVaR) into the local objective within a natural distributionally robust optimization (DRO) framework. \textsc{FedeRage} implicitly upweights high-loss and infrequently participating clients while adding only a \emph{single scalar per-client}, and admits an $\mathcal{O}(κ/\sqrt{T})$ rate in which the factor $κ$ is the upper bound on the ``price" of risk aversion. In contrast with aggregation-alignment schemes based on optimal transport, which require the availability distribution as an input, \textsc{FedeRage} remains agnostic to it. Several experiments on three heterogeneous benchmarks indicate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, fairness, and convergence speed.

AI.tldr: Uniform aggregation is optimal under unknown participation probabilities in FedAvg, and a CVaR-based DRO extension (FedeRage) improves accuracy, fairness, and convergence in non-IID, variable-participation FL with minimal per-client overhead.
AI.motivation: Address FL under non-IID data and stochastic client participation when participation probabilities are unknown or highly skewed. Traditional FedAvg assumes known participation, which is impractical in deployed systems, and can lead to degraded performance and fairness.
AI.method: 1) The paper characterizes the optimization problem solved by distributionally agnostic FedAvg under entirely unknown participation, showing that uniform aggregation minimizes a stochastic objective weighted by the participation marginal. 2) Proposes FedeRage, a risk-averse extension of FedAvg that embeds Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) into the local objective within a distributionally robust optimization framework. 3) FedeRage adds only a single scalar per client and yields an O(κ/√T) convergence rate, where κ bounds the price of risk aversion. 4) Unlike optimal-transport aggregation schemes, FedeRage does not require the input participation distribution.
AI.result: Empirical validation on three heterogeneous benchmarks shows that FedeRage consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, fairness, and convergence speed, indicating robustness to participation uncertainty and data heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a principled understanding of distributionally agnostic FedAvg, showing that uniform aggregation is optimal under unknown participation. It introduces FedeRage, a CVaR-based DRO method that improves performance with minimal per-client overhead and is distribution-agnostic, offering a scalable and robust solution for FL with uncertain participation.

title: Dynamics-Induced Commitment in Learning-Based Robotic Penalty Kicks
summary: Learning in robotic games is constrained not only by strategic information but also by what the body can still execute. We study this coupling in a hierarchical humanoid-quadruped penalty system in which game-level self-play policies command fixed soccer whole-body controllers (S-WBCs). The humanoid shooting skill is initialized from self-collected motion-capture data, whereas the quadruped saving skill is learned by reinforcement learning. We introduce dynamics-induced commitment mapping (DIC-Map), a body-grounded analysis that estimates continuation capability, identifies the first persistent loss of a terminal alternative, and tests whether the remaining interaction admits a reduced zero-sum game. For symmetric terminal alternatives, the reduced game yields a closed-form bound on optimal strategy concentration determined by the responder's value of deferring. We further show that, when the responder acts through an estimator, equal response values eliminate the direct terminal-allocation gradient and leave an estimator-mediated first-order learning channel. Experiments locate commitment about 0.29 s before contact, and changing only ball speed shifts deferral coverage. Across four responder policies, replacing the estimator raises save rate from 0.240 to 0.472, whereas a comparable gain in read accuracy obtained by waiting raises it only to 0.246. Posterior analysis is used for the equilibrium comparison because the available coverage terms are observational proxies. Project website: https://chris-ruizegeng.github.io/penaltykick/

AI.tldr: Introduces dynamics-induced commitment mapping (DIC-Map) to link strategy with body-grounded fixed controllers in a hierarchical humanoid-quadruped penalty game, deriving bounds on optimal strategy concentration in reduced zero-sum settings and showing estimator-mediated learning channels; experiments reveal commitment ~0.29 s before contact and large gains in save rate when replacing the estimator, with sensitivity to ball speed.
AI.motivation: To understand how execution constraints of a robot's body limit strategic self-play in robotic games and to provide a body-grounded framework for continuation analysis, commitment timing, and equilibrium reasoning.
AI.method: A hierarchical setup where game-level self-play policies command fixed soccer whole-body controllers (S-WBCs); humanoid shooting initialized from motion-capture data while quadruped saving is learned via reinforcement learning. Introduces DIC-Map to estimate continuation capability, detect the first persistent loss of a terminal alternative, and assess whether the residual interaction forms a reduced zero-sum game. For symmetric terminal alternatives, derives a closed-form bound on strategy concentration; analyzes estimator-mediated learning when the responder acts through an estimator; conducts experiments across four responder policies in a penalty-kick style task and uses posterior analysis for equilibrium comparison due to observational proxies.
AI.result: Commitment located about 0.29 s before contact; changing ball speed shifts deferral coverage. Replacing the estimator raises save rate from 0.240 to 0.472, while a similar read-accuracy gain by waiting reaches only 0.246. Across responder policies, estimator removal substantially improves defense performance, and posterior analysis supports equilibrium comparisons though coverage terms are observational proxies.
AI.conclusion: DIC-Map offers a body-grounded lens to bound strategic concentration and reveal learning channels mediated by estimators; results demonstrate notable sensitivity to agent configuration and input variations. The study provides empirical evidence for the role of body constraints in strategic execution, with equilibrium claims limited by observational proxies and the need for further validation across tasks.

title: Efficient Benchmarking in Production: A Study of an Evolving LLM Agent
comment: A study of efficient recurring evaluation of a production LLM agent based on real-world historical data
summary: Production LLM agents are evaluated repeatedly as they evolve, but full agent benchmarks are costly to rerun. We study efficient recurring evaluation for a production analytics agent serving tens of thousands of monthly active users and report first-hand deployment experience. Using 574 historical runs of the production benchmark, split chronologically into calibration and held-out periods, we compare random sampling, historical caching, fixed representative subsets, and IRT-based adaptive testing. The results show that multidimensional 2PL adaptive testing achieves the best overall score fidelity: executing 200 questions, 38.5% of a full run, yields 1.03 pp of MAE. We nevertheless deployed difficulty-stratified fixed subsets because of their operational simplicity, and show they transfer without recalibration to five other agent families and remain stable across calibration windows as short as one day. Drawing on this deployment experience, we report practical recommendations for recurring production-agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: Efficient recurring evaluation for production LLM agents using historical runs shows multidimensional 2PL adaptive testing yields best fidelity with ~38.5% of a full test (200 items) achieving ~1.03 percentage points MAE; fixed difficulty-stratified subsets offer simpler, transferable evaluation across agent families; practical recommendations for production-agent evaluation.
AI.motivation: Production analytics agents serve many users and require ongoing performance monitoring, but full re-benchmarks are expensive. The study seeks efficient, recurring evaluation strategies that preserve fidelity.
AI.method: Analyzed 574 historical runs, chronologically split into calibration and hold-out periods. Compared random sampling, historical caching, fixed representative subsets, and IRT-based adaptive testing (multidimensional 2PL). Measured score fidelity via MAE, and tested transferability across agent families and calibration window stability.
AI.result: Multidimensional 2PL adaptive testing with 200 questions (38.5% of a full run) achieves 1.03 percentage points MAE. Fixed difficulty-stratified subsets, despite not beating adaptive testing, transfer to five other agent families without recalibration and remain stable with calibration windows as short as one day.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive testing offers best fidelity with substantial efficiency gains, but simpler fixed subsets provide robust, transferable deployment. The study provides practical guidance for recurring production-agent evaluation.

title: Field Tracking of Insects Using a Stereoscopic Event-Based Camera Setup
summary: High-speed tracking of small, fast-moving organisms in their natural environments is important to better understand their behavior and ecology. Traditional frame-based imaging suffers from motion blur due to low temporal resolution, and data storage limitations, propelling a search for more adaptive solutions. Event cameras, which capture changes in brightness at pixel level instead of entire frames, have emerged as a promising solution by increasing temporal resolution and data efficiency. Here, we demonstrate the use of event-based imaging with standard video-based processing methods by converting the asynchronous events into conventional video formats, allowing us to leverage the event camera's enhanced temporal detail to capture intricate insect flight movements and apply established image analysis techniques. Coupling this conversion process with a stereoscopic configuration provides continuous, low-latency, three-dimensional tracking of fast-moving subjects in field conditions. As a result, we substantially mitigate motion artifacts and achieve more accurate representations of animal movements. By making event-based imaging more readily applicable in natural field settings, our method support broader applications across animal behavior and ecological research, agricultural management, and other fields requiring high-fidelity object tracking in the wild.
