AI.tldr: Event cameras are converted to conventional video to enable frame-based analysis, enabling high-tempo, low-latency 3D tracking of small, fast insects in natural environments using stereo setups.
AI.motivation: Overcome motion blur and data-storage limitations of traditional frame-based imaging to study fast insect flight in the wild, requiring high temporal resolution and robust 3D tracking.
AI.method: Capture with event cameras and convert asynchronous events into video-like streams, then apply standard video-based processing; employ a stereoscopic configuration for continuous 3D tracking in field conditions.
AI.result: Mitigated motion artifacts, more accurate representations of rapid movements, and continuous low-latency 3D tracking in natural settings; demonstrated applicability of standard image analysis techniques to event data.
AI.conclusion: Event-based imaging can be made compatible with conventional pipelines, expanding the reach of high-temporal-resolution tracking to ecology, agriculture, and other field applications.

title: Toward individual-level calibration in affect recognition with perceptual adjustment queries
comment: 14 pages, 13 figures. Accepted as a poster at IEEE ACII 2026
summary: Behavioral tasks measuring facial affect perception assume that identical stimuli impose equivalent perceptual difficulty across participants. However, this assumption is systematically violated by individual differences in perceptual sensitivity. Using an affective perception task as our testbed, we propose a framework to normalize for perceptual difficulty that directly estimates each participant's Just Noticeable Difference (JND) along the facial affect spectrum via cognitively lightweight perceptual adjustment queries (PAQs). We use these PAQ-inferred JNDs to re-express stimulus distances, constructing difficulty-equated tasks in perceptual space. We validate the framework in a Two-Alternative Forced-Choice (2AFC) task using two complementary behavioral measures: binary metacognitive difficulty judgments and response time variance decomposition. We find that PAQ calibration significantly equalizes perceived task difficulty at an individual level when compared to both the non-calibrated baseline and population-level Weibull calibration, while also reducing mean response time and between-subject variance in response time. These results establish PAQ as a principled and practical instrument for individualized perceptual calibration in facial affect recognition.

AI.tldr: PAQ-based JND calibration normalizes perceptual difficulty in facial affect recognition, enabling individualized task difficulty and reduced RT variance in 2AFC tasks.
AI.motivation: Perceptual sensitivity varies across individuals, making identical stimuli inequitable; need for individualized perceptual calibration to equalize task difficulty in facial affect perception.
AI.method: Estimate each participant's Just Noticeable Difference (JND) along the facial affect spectrum using cognitively lightweight perceptual adjustment queries (PAQs); re-express stimulus distances in perceptual space; construct difficulty-equated tasks; validate in a 2AFC task with binary metacognitive difficulty judgments and RT variance decomposition.
AI.result: PAQ calibration equalizes perceived task difficulty at the individual level more effectively than non-calibrated baseline and population-level Weibull calibration; also reduces mean response time and between-subject variance in response time.
AI.conclusion: PAQ constitutes a principled and practical instrument for individualized perceptual calibration in facial affect recognition.

title: Learning Scene-Aware Humanoid Locomotion through 3D Clutter from Immersive Human Demonstrations
summary: While learning from human motions has enabled highly dynamic humanoid skills such as dancing and martial arts in obstacle-free space, traversal through densely cluttered environments remains underexplored. These spaces are three-dimensional and geometrically constrained, requiring scene-aware locomotion that tightly couples whole-body motion with scene geometry for obstacle avoidance. To address these challenges, we present Moving Through Clutter (MTC), a learning-from-demonstration framework for scene-aware humanoid locomotion. To bypass costly physical scene construction, MTC uses procedurally generated Virtual Reality environments for immersive data collection. To transform these human motions into training-ready humanoid motions, we propose a scene-aware motion retargeting algorithm that converts human demonstrations into humanoid trajectories while strictly enforcing robot-scene clearance to guarantee collision-free traversal. These reference trajectories are then used to train a scene-aware locomotion policy that deploys on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Evaluated on our proposed MTC-Challenge for multi-obstacle traversal, the policy demonstrates a 70.2% collision-free rate across diverse scenarios, successfully traversing complex environments through diverse whole-body skills, including crawling through low-clearance passages and squeezing through narrow gaps.

AI.tldr: A learning-for-demonstration framework (MTC) enabling scene-aware humanoid locomotion in cluttered 3D spaces via VR data collection and a scene-aware retargeting pipeline, achieving 70.2% collision-free traversal on a multi-obstacle benchmark with complex whole-body skills.
AI.motivation: Overcoming obstacle-rich, 3D environments requires tight coupling of locomotion with scene geometry; existing learning-from-demonstration approaches largely focus on obstacle-free spaces and do not ensure robust collision-free traversal in clutter.
AI.method: MTC uses procedurally generated VR environments to collect immersive demonstrations; applies a scene-aware motion retargeting algorithm that enforces strict robot-scene clearance to convert human motions into humanoid trajectories; trains a scene-aware locomotion policy on the retargeted trajectories and deploys on a Unitree G1.
AI.result: The policy yields a 70.2% collision-free rate across diverse multi-obstacle scenarios, enabling complex whole-body maneuvers such as crawling through low-clearance passages and squeezing through narrow gaps.
AI.conclusion: MTC demonstrates the feasibility of scene-aware, collision-free humanoid locomotion in cluttered 3D environments by integrating VR-based data collection, tight robot-scene retargeting, and learning-based control on a real humanoid platform; further work is needed to improve robustness and generalization.

title: GameASG-Bench: Benchmarking Autonomous Software Generation for Game Development
summary: Autonomous software generation (ASG) aims to turn human requirements into executable applications, but delivering these applications does not necessarily establish that their interacting components satisfy the specified behavioral requirements. We introduce GameASG-Bench, a benchmark that makes behavioral testability part of the generation task for game development. Our design declares an evaluation interface specification before generation, fixing legal starting scenarios, player-level actions, stable snapshots, rejection behavior, and invariants while leaving private implementations open. Concretely, we include: (i) static L1 checks that assess source-level compliance; and (ii) browser-executed L2 checks that combine semantic observations with real input and runtime evidence. We implement this protocol as 47 browser-native game-generation tasks spanning 12 primary genres and both 2D and 3D interaction, each with executable checks and an independently verified reference implementation. Our experiments answer four key questions about end-to-end agent performance, tool access and nominal turn budget, reasoning effort, and harness choice. Across nine agent stacks, the highest observed mean L2 check pass rate is 93.2%, yet the highest observed strict task success rate, requiring all L1 and applicable L2 prerequisite and core requirement checks, is only 55.3% (26/47 tasks). For DeepSeek-V4-Flash, full tool access and larger nominal turn budgets yield more strict task successes, while the strict task success rate is not monotonic in reasoning effort. Both tested harnesses achieve 18 strict task successes, but only ten tasks succeed under both. These results expose task-level compliance gaps that high average check pass rates actually obscure.

AI.tldr: Behavioral testability is integrated into ASG benchmarks for games; high L2 pass rates mask limited strict task success, revealing task-level compliance gaps across 47 tasks, two harnesses, and nine agent stacks.
AI.motivation: Ensure that autonomous game-generators satisfy behavioral requirements, not just source-level style, by making behavioral testability an explicit part of the generation task and by exposing gaps between high-level checks and strict task success.
AI.method: Prototype GameASG-Bench with an evaluation interface specification for starting scenarios, actions, snapshots, rejection behavior, and invariants. Includes: (i) static L1 checks for source-level compliance; (ii) browser-executed L2 checks using real input and runtime evidence. Implemented as 47 browser-native game-generation tasks across 12 genres (2D/3D) with executable checks and a verified reference, plus experiments over nine agent stacks to assess end-to-end performance, tool access, nominal turns, reasoning effort, and harness choice.
AI.result: Mean L2 check pass rate across tasks: 93.2%. Strict task success rate (requiring L1 plus applicable L2 prerequisites and core requirements): 55.3% (26/47). DeepSeek-V4-Flash with full tool access and larger nominal budgets yields more strict task successes; strict success rate is not monotonic with reasoning effort. Both tested harnesses achieve 18 strict task successes, but only 10 tasks succeed under both; task-level compliance gaps are revealed by high average check pass rates.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral testability reveals gaps between high average L2 pass rates and strict task-level compliance; integrating behavioral checks into generation benchmarks is essential to uncover and address task-level requirements in autonomous game generation.

title: Hiding in Plain Sight: A Diffusion-based Mitigation of Geolocation Privacy Leakage in Vision-Language Models
summary: Multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex visual understanding. However, this very power introduces a critical yet underexplored privacy threat: adversaries can exploit MLRMs to precisely infer users' geographic locations from casually shared photographs, by performing structured reasoning over subtle visual cues such as architectural styles, vegetation, and lighting conditions. In this work, we present a systematic study of MLRM-driven geolocation privacy leakage. We first reveal that refusal-based safeguards are critically insufficient, as carefully crafted jailbreak prompts can raise model response rates to 100%. We further identify that existing defenses, which inject imperceptible perturbations into shared images, suffer from structural limitations intrinsic to their pixel-space optimization, resulting in degraded black-box transferability and pronounced visual artifacts. Motivated by these findings, we propose a diffusion-based framework that provides targeted, proactive defense against geolocation privacy leakage. By injecting perturbations into the latent space of a diffusion model during reverse sampling, our method operates directly on high-level semantic representations, thereby resolving the effectiveness-utility bottlenecks by construction. We further ground our optimization with GeoCLIP, a model explicitly aligned with GPS coordinates, as a surrogate to pinpoint and disrupt the geographic signals that MLRMs exploit for location inference. This targeted semantic disruption yields significantly stronger black-box transferability while preserving perceptual image quality, offering a seamless integration on social media platforms.

AI.tldr: Diffusion-based latent-space perturbations defend against geolocation privacy leakage in multimodal large reasoning models by semantic disruption of geographic signals, outperforming pixel-space defenses and jailbreak countermeasures; uses GeoCLIP as surrogate to guide perturbations while preserving perceptual quality.
AI.motivation: Address a significant privacy risk: MLRMs can infer users' geographic location from casual photographs. Refusal-based safeguards are easily bypassed; pixel-space perturbations degrade utility and have limited transferability. A proactive, semantics-aware defense is needed.
AI.method: Inject perturbations into the latent space of a diffusion model during reverse sampling, acting on high-level semantic representations. Optimize perturbations guided by GeoCLIP, a GPS-aligned surrogate, to disrupt geographic cues while preserving perceptual image quality.
AI.result: Improved black-box transferability of the defense; stronger disruption of geographic signals with fewer perceptual artifacts; practical integration for social media platforms.
AI.conclusion: A targeted semantic perturbation framework provides robust defense against geolocation privacy leakage in MLRMs, addressing shortcomings of prior safeguards and offering a deployable solution.

title: REFINEPPO: Learning Continuous Control Policies by Iterative Action Refinement
summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved strong performance across a wide range of continuous-control problems. These continuous-control policies, however, are often defined as direct mappings from an observed state to an action or action distribution, requiring a single feed-forward network to construct an optimal control decision in one pass. While effective, this formulation leaves little opportunity for the policy to reconsider or progressively improve an action once an initial prediction has been formed. In this work, we explore an alternative approach: rather than learning only to directly predict an action, can a policy learn to iteratively improve one, and can this iterative process provide advantages during policy learning? We introduce Iterative Action Refinement (IAR), an iterative action-construction method that constructs control actions through a sequence of learned residual corrections. Starting from an initial proposal, a shared refinement network repeatedly conditions on the observed state and the current action proposal, allowing each refinement step to revise the action constructed by preceding steps. The final refined proposal is then used to determine the action executed by the agent. We integrate this iterative action-construction mechanism with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), yielding REFINEPPO. We evaluate REFINEPPO across 14 benchmark control tasks, complemented by controlled ablations of refinement depth and update schedules and analyses aimed at understanding why iterative refinement is effective. Across these environments, REFINEPPO matches or exceeds the performance of standard PPO while demonstrating faster convergence on several tasks.

AI.tldr: Iterative action refinement (IAR) builds actions via a sequence of learned residuals, integrated with PPO as REFINEPPO. It matches or surpasses PPO on 14 tasks and often converges faster.
AI.motivation: Addresses the limitation of single-pass action prediction in continuous-control policies by enabling iterative reconsideration and refinement of actions, potentially improving learning efficiency and performance.
AI.method: Propose IAR: start with an initial action proposal, then apply a shared refinement network that conditions on the state and the current action to produce residual corrections. Repeat for multiple refinement steps to produce a final refined action, which is executed. Integrate IAR with Proximal Policy Optimization to form REFINEPPO; perform controlled ablations on refinement depth and update schedules; analyze reasons for effectiveness.
AI.result: REFINEPPO achieves comparable or superior performance to standard PPO across 14 benchmark tasks and demonstrates faster convergence on several tasks; ablations clarify how refinement depth and update schedules influence performance; analyses provide insights into why iterative refinement helps policy learning.
AI.conclusion: Iterative action refinement is a viable and effective enhancement to policy architectures for continuous control, offering stability and potential speedups in learning without sacrificing final performance, and is compatible with existing policy-gradient algorithms like PPO.

title: Demonstration Synthesis from a Single Scan via Gaussian Splatting for Visuomotor Policy Learning
summary: Training a visuomotor policy calls for abundant demonstrations that closely match the target environment, yet collecting them anew remains expensive. Existing demonstration synthesis methods reduce this cost but remain constrained by high manual effort, limited visual fidelity, or heavy reliance on physics simulators. This paper introduces GaussianFactory, a high-fidelity data engine that mass-produces demonstrations with a single video scan as its only human input and no physics engine in the generation loop. Specifically, GaussianFactory reconstructs the scene as an editable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) replica and samples from the object-combination tasks the scene affords. For each task, it plans grasps and trajectories purely kinematically on the geometric reconstruction, rendering photorealistic demonstrations that visually match the target environment. Physical dynamics enter the pipeline only where contact force interactions dictate the outcome---during grasp formation, via a learned contact model pretrained once on an interaction dataset. To evaluate the downstream utility of the synthesized demonstrations, we implement an end-to-end scan-to-deployment workflow in two setups: a simulated scene that stands in for the real world to enable reproducibility, and a real-world workspace with a physical UR10e robot. In each setup, a standard diffusion policy trained solely on the synthesized demonstrations achieves 95.1% and 84.2% success rates, respectively.

AI.tldr: GaussianFactory offers high-fidelity, scalable demonstration synthesis from a single video input by reconstructing scenes with 3D Gaussian Splatting and using kinematic planning with a learned contact model; achieved strong sim-to-real performance without a full physics loop.
AI.motivation: To reduce the cost and effort of collecting demonstrations for visuomotor policies while achieving high visual fidelity and avoiding heavy reliance on physics simulators.
AI.method: Reconstruct the scene as an editable 3D Gaussian Splatting replica, sample object-combination tasks, plan grasps and trajectories kinematically on the geometric reconstruction, render photorealistic demonstrations, and apply a learned contact model only for dynamics during grasp formation; train a diffusion policy solely on synthesized data; validate in simulated and real UR10e setups.
AI.result: End-to-end scan-to-deployment workflow yields a policy achieving 95.1% success in simulation and 84.2% in the real world when trained only on GaussianFactory-generated demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: Shows that high-fidelity, low-human-input demonstration synthesis is feasible without a physics engine in the generation loop, enabling scalable visuomotor policy training across sim-to-real pipelines.

title: LEGIT: Credentialing Protocol for Trustworthy AI Agent Marketplaces
summary: Agentic marketplaces are emerging where AI agents with varying capabilities autonomously complete specialized tasks for buyers. A major challenge of such marketplaces is that buyers cannot easily determine which agent will perform best on their tasks. Reported benchmark scores may be difficult to verify or compare across tasks, software, and budgets. We introduce LEGIT, a credentialing protocol connecting certification, reputation, and proposed marketplace allocation. Certification binds measured quality and cost per solved task to an agent configuration, task domain, evaluation budget, and evidence through a signed record. Reputation links records of past task outcomes to the same identity, subject to the reliability of the reported feedback. Buyers and agents can verify credential records and inspect optional visual profiles. Evaluations reveal cost differences between agent configurations with similar observed task success, and show that comparisons depend on the evaluation budget. These results support binding performance measurements to the tested configuration and resource limits. A complementary analysis quantifies the deposits and fees required for reputation manipulation under a stated Sybil attack model.

AI.tldr: LEGIT is a credentialing protocol for AI agent marketplaces that ties evaluation outcomes to a specific agent configuration, task domain, and evaluation budget via signed certifications and linked reputation records, enabling verifiable comparisons and reducing manipulation. It also analyzes deposits and fees to deter reputation manipulation under a Sybil attack model.
AI.motivation: To address verifiability and comparability challenges in agent marketplaces, where buyers can't easily identify the best-performing agent and benchmark scores are hard to verify across tasks, software, and budgets.
AI.method: Introduce Certification (a signed record binding measured quality and cost per solved task to an agent configuration, task domain, evaluation budget, and evidence), Reputation (records of past outcomes linked to the same identity with reliability-weighted feedback), optional visual profiles; conduct evaluations showing cost differences across configurations and budget-dependent comparisons; analyze deposits/fees to deter reputation manipulation under a stated Sybil model.
AI.result: Evaluations demonstrate that performance measurements can be bound to the tested configuration and resource limits; reveal cost differences between agent configurations with similar observed task success and show that comparisons depend on the evaluation budget; complementary analysis quantifies deposits and fees required to deter reputation manipulation under Sybil attacks.
AI.conclusion: LEGIT binds performance measurements to tested configurations and resource limits, improving verifiability and trust in AI agent marketplaces; it also provides a framework to deter reputation manipulation via deposits/fees under a Sybil attack model.

title: RobotEQ-Video: A Video-Centric Benchmark for Social Proactive Intelligence with World-State Taxonomy
summary: Social Proactive Intelligence (SPI) extends proactive assistance beyond task completeness to consider social appropriateness in diverse embodied scenarios. However, prior SPI research faces two key limitations. First, existing work focuses on static images, whereas dynamic videos provide crucial cues for inferring human states and needs, offering richer information than isolated images. Second, prior work often relies on free-form data collection pipelines, which fail to guarantee comprehensive coverage of diverse scenarios. To address these gaps, we introduce RobotEQ-Video, shifting the focus from image-centric to video-centric analysis. To ensure comprehensive video coverage, we construct a hierarchical world-state taxonomy organized into a four-level coarse-to-fine structure, comprising 6 domains, 20 dimensions, 142 level-1 attributes, and 816 level-2 attributes. The resulting benchmark comprises 2K+ videos with 100K+ human annotations and 16K+ labels for assessing behavior properness. Benchmark evaluation reveals that current systems remain unreliable and fall short of human performance. We further explore how world models can help tackle this task. This work advances SPI research from static images to dynamic videos and ensures more comprehensive scenario coverage during benchmarking.

AI.tldr: Introduces RobotEQ-Video, a video-centric benchmark for Social Proactive Intelligence (SPI) with a four-level world-state taxonomy (6 domains, 20 dimensions, 142 level-1 attributes, 816 level-2 attributes), spanning 2K+ videos and 100K+ human annotations plus 16K+ behavior-appropriateness labels; finds existing systems are unreliable and fall short of human performance; investigates world models to address SPI tasks.
AI.motivation: Addresses two limitations of prior SPI work: (1) reliance on static images rather than dynamic videos, which provide richer cues about human states and needs; (2) free-form data pipelines that fail to guarantee diverse, comprehensive scenario coverage.
AI.method: Video-centric extension of SPI with a hierarchical, four-level world-state taxonomy; construction of RobotEQ-Video benchmark comprising 2K+ videos with 100K+ human annotations and 16K+ labels for behavior properness; evaluation of current systems against human performance; exploration of world-model approaches to SPI.
AI.result: Benchmark reveals current systems are unreliable and significantly underperform humans in judging social appropriateness; world models show potential to enhance SPI capabilities in dynamic video contexts.
AI.conclusion: Shifts SPI research from static images to dynamic videos, enabling richer scenario coverage for benchmarking; provides a comprehensive taxonomy and dataset; highlights the need for improved models (potentially world-model-based) to reach human-level performance in social proactive intelligence.

title: Talk to Me, Jarvis: An Open-Source Edge-Deployable Voice Assistant Framework for Autonomous Racecars
summary: Recent advances in large language models have improved their effectiveness as back-end components for voice assistants, particularly in intent understanding and context-aware input classification. However, online-hosted models introduce network dependency and variable inference latency, limiting their suitability for time-critical autonomous driving applications. In this work, we address these issues by developing Jarvis, an offline voice assistant for high-level behavioral commands of autonomous vehicles. Its architecture integrates speech recognition and synthesis with natural language command classification into a lightweight, local framework. Jarvis core component is a text-to-command classifier, built using a domain-specific fine-tuning of the Mistral 7B model, demonstrating low-latency inference. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that our solution outperforms larger online-hosted models, achieving 97.63 % intent recognition accuracy with an average processing latency of 1.39 s, making it well-suited for operations requiring quick response times. To support further research and fine-tuning, we provide an open-source implementation.

AI.tldr: Offline, domain-tuned Mistral 7B for text-to-command classification in autonomous driving; low latency and high accuracy (97.63%); open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Mitigate network dependency and high inference latency of online LLMs in time-critical autonomous driving by providing an offline voice assistant that handles high-level behavioral commands.
AI.method: Integrates ASR, TTS, and a domain-specific fine-tuned Mistral 7B model to perform text-to-command classification in a compact, local framework.
AI.result: Outperforms larger online models in intent recognition accuracy (97.63%) with real-time-like processing latency (~1.39 s), making it suitable for time-critical tasks.
AI.conclusion: An open-source offline voice assistant demonstrates that domain-specific fine-tuning of mid-sized LLMs can meet latency and accuracy requirements for AV command interpretation; provides a resource for further research.

title: Noctif3R: Feed-Forward Monocular Real-Time SLAM for Photon-Limited Scenes on Embedded Hardware
summary: Robots carrying out tasks in dark environments need to localize from a single RGB camera, in light so low that the per-pixel signal approaches the sensor's own noise, on a power-constrained onboard computer, in real time. Each of these constraints has matured pipelines, but the intersection does not. Offline low-light reconstruction now recovers structure below -4 dB but is far too slow to run in real time, while the real-time monocular systems a robot can actually carry (DROID-SLAM, DPV-SLAM, etc.) degrade or fail when SNR gets low. We measured how they fail: across the nine lowest darkness levels of our scenes, DROID-SLAM returns a full-length trajectory carrying no information about the camera's motion on all nine, VGGT-SLAM and CUT3R on eight, pi^3 on seven, and DPV-SLAM on four. We present SYS, a monocular pipeline built on a low-light feed-forward pointmap front end with an explicit match gate, which returns three tracked trajectories and no uninformative ones, at the lowest error of any method where it tracks (24-47% of the no-information ceiling against 56-73% for the strongest baseline), and at the narrowest coverage. On a real robot video take in which 86.5% of delivered frames are entirely black, every configuration of ours stops after the lit beginning, while DROID-SLAM and DPV-SLAM each emit a pose for all 1178 frames. Our method contribution is an embedded execution path for the Jetson AGX Orin: running the map, keyframes and backend at 384 pixels with tracking at 256, together with two fixes to the per-frame pose solve, is a replicated Pareto improvement, 1.28x throughput at 0.964x error on one scene and 1.42x at 0.68x on a second, with 47% less peak GPU memory and 29% less energy per pose. We evaluate on a calibrated, bit-exact regenerable noise ladder, on relabelled real-world dark exposures, and on a new dark-room video ladder recorded from a Boston Dynamics Spot robot.

AI.tldr: SYS: a monocular low-light SLAM pipeline with a feed-forward pointmap frontend and explicit match gate, achieving robust tracking under extreme darkness on Jetson, with improved Pareto efficiency over DROID-SLAM/DPV-SLAM, validated on synthetic and real dark sequences.
AI.motivation: Address real-time monocular localization in ultra-dark, power-constrained onboard robotics. Existing real-time SLAM degrades under low SNR; offline low-light methods are too slow for real-time operation.
AI.method: A forward-pointmap frontend with an explicit match gate (SYS) producing three tracked trajectories and no uninformative ones. Embedded execution path on Jetson AGX Orin with map/keyframes and backend at 384 px and tracking at 256 px. Two fixes to per-frame pose solve. Evaluated on calibrated, regenerable noise ladder, relabeled real-world dark exposures, and a new dark-room video ladder from a Boston Dynamics Spot.
AI.result: SYS achieves lowest error among tracking-methods when it tracks (24-47% of the no-information ceiling vs 56-73% for strong baselines) and the narrowest coverage. On a real robot video with 86.5% frames entirely black, it stops after illumination ends while others produce poses for all frames. In embedded Jetson deployment, SYS yields 1.28x throughput at 0.964x error on one scene and 1.42x throughput at 0.68x error on another, with 47% less peak GPU memory and 29% less energy per pose.
AI.conclusion: SYS offers a replicated Pareto improvement for ultra-low-light monocular SLAM on embedded hardware, enabling robust, real-time tracking with reduced resource usage, validated across synthetic and real darkness datasets.

title: Offline Multimodal Large Language Models for Decision Support in Air Operations
summary: Air operations rely on complex rules, established procedures, and time-critical analysis under limited connectivity and strict security constraints. In such environments, analysts must combine written doctrine with images, often without access to external computing resources. This paper studies offline large language models as decision support tools, deployed in isolated and restricted environments to give analysts access to doctrinal knowledge that remains traceable to its original sources through natural language interaction. We describe a modular retrieval-augmented architecture suitable for operation without Internet connectivity, supporting both text and image input from technical manuals. As a first step toward evaluating this architecture, we report a pilot study with four image analysts of the Brazilian Air Force, combining (i) a doctrinal knowledge assessment based on their electronic-target identification doctrine, comparing human and proposed system performance on the same test, and (ii) a measurement of the cognitive workload involved in manually producing a reconnaissance target report (Relatório de Missão de Reconhecimento - REMIR) without AI assistance. The results show a demanding manual task, especially in terms of mental demand (6.0/7) and effort (5.0/7), while the proposed system matches the human score (8/10) and completes the assessment in 7.1 minutes (compared to a human average of 26.5 minutes), establishing a baseline for future AI-assisted evaluation. Finally, we describe a future evaluation protocol to systematically compare manual and AI-assisted workflows.

AI.tldr: Offline retrieval-augmented LLM architecture for decision support in restricted, internet-isolated air operations; pilot study shows potential efficiency gains and comparable performance to humans in doctrinal assessment.
AI.motivation: Enable access to doctrinal knowledge and decision-support in environments with no Internet access and strict security constraints, while preserving traceability to original sources through natural language interaction.
AI.method: Develop a modular retrieval-augmented architecture operable offline that can ingest text and images from technical manuals. Conduct a pilot study with four image analysts from the Brazilian Air Force to (i) compare doctrinal knowledge assessment performance against the same test, and (ii) measure cognitive workload in producing a reconnaissance mission report (REMIR) without AI assistance. Metrics include performance scores, completion time, and workload indicators.
AI.result: The system achieved parity with humans on the doctrinal assessment (both 8/10) and completed the task in 7.1 minutes versus an average human of 26.5 minutes. The manual task is cognitively demanding (mental demand 6.0/7, effort 5.0/7). The study establishes a baseline for future AI-assisted evaluation.
AI.conclusion: An offline, modular retrieval-augmented architecture is a viable decision-support tool in constrained environments. The paper outlines a future evaluation protocol to systematically compare manual and AI-assisted workflows.

title: JEPA Guided Diffusion: Predictive Vision-Language Conditioning for Generative Traffic Forecasting
comment: ECCV Workshop 2026, AI City Challenge 2026 Track 5
summary: Accurate traffic forecasting requires both understanding scene dynamics and synthesizing realistic future observations. Recent diffusion-based video generation models produce visually plausible predictions but require expensive end-to-end training and often entangle scene understanding with image synthesis. In this work, we propose a decoupled forecasting framework that separates future representation learning from video generation. A frozen V-JEPA encoder first extracts predictive latent representations from the observed traffic videos, capturing the underlying scene dynamics in a semantic latent space. A lightweight latent alignment module then projects these representations into the conditioning space of a frozen Cosmos diffusion module, enabling future video synthesis without retraining the large generative model. By freezing all foundation models and training only the lightweight alignment module, the proposed framework substantially reduces optimization complexity while preserving forecasting capability. Experimental results on the AI City Challenge 2026 Track 5 benchmark demonstrate that the proposed method achieved a score of 75.1297, ranking third in the competition. These results suggest that predictive world representations learned by V-JEPA can effectively guide downstream video generation, providing a practical and efficient alternative to end-to-end diffusion-based forecasting.

AI.tldr: A decoupled forecasting framework for traffic video prediction using frozen encoders and a lightweight alignment module to condition a diffusion generator, reducing training complexity while maintaining performance (3rd place, AI City Challenge 2026 Track 5, score 75.1297).
AI.motivation: Address the high cost and entanglement of end-to-end diffusion-based forecasting by decoupling scene understanding from video generation. Leverage frozen foundation models to learn predictive latent representations andguide downstream synthesis with minimal additional training.
AI.method: Use a frozen V-JEPA encoder to extract predictive latent representations from observed traffic videos. Introduce a lightweight latent alignment module to map these representations into the conditioning space of a frozen Cosmos diffusion module. Train only the alignment module while keeping all foundation models frozen.
AI.result: On AI City Challenge 2026 Track 5, the method achieved 75.1297 and ranked third. The results indicate that predictive world representations learned by V-JEPA can effectively guide downstream video generation, offering a practical alternative to end-to-end diffusion-based forecasting.
AI.conclusion: Freezing foundation models and training only a lightweight alignment module can substantially reduce optimization complexity without sacrificing forecasting performance, validating the use of predictive latent representations to steer diffusion-based video synthesis.

title: Signal-Centric Remote Sensing via Alternative Preprocessing and Acoustic Processing for ML-Driven Applications
comment: 7 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Published in Proc. IEEE SoutheastCon 2025, pp. 1078-1084, doi: 10.1109/SoutheastCon56624.2025.10971547
summary: The dominant method of processing sonar data is using image-based representations, requiring the preprocessing of image data on autonomous systems. We propose an alternative data processing method for remote sensing applications via the use of data in Comma-Seperated Value format. Experimentation on our alternative approach shows a reduction of processing time by 91.18%, an improvement in accurate object detection by Machine Learning, and an increase in SNR (Signal-to-noise ratio), PSNR (Peak signal-to-noise ratio), and other evaluation metrics.

AI.tldr: CSV-based data representation for sonar/remote sensing improves processing speed and ML performance compared to image-based preprocessing.
AI.motivation: Image-based preprocessing for sonar data is computationally heavy on autonomous systems; a lightweight, structured data representation (CSV) could reduce latency while preserving or enhancing detection performance.
AI.method: Propose using data in CSV format for remote sensing sonar data; conduct experiments comparing the CSV-based approach with traditional image-based preprocessing; evaluate processing time, ML-based object detection accuracy, and quality metrics such as SNR and PSNR.
AI.result: Reported 91.18% reduction in processing time; improved ML-based object detection accuracy; increased SNR, PSNR, and other evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: CSV-based data representation is a viable alternative to image-based preprocessing for sonar/remote sensing tasks, offering substantial speedups and accuracy gains; further validation across datasets and setups is recommended.

title: MetaPusher: Meta Learning and Planning for Nonprehensile Manipulation of Unseen Objects with Rapid Online Adaption
summary: Manipulating previously unseen objects remains challenging, as their dynamics depend on latent physical properties, such as friction and mass distribution, that cannot be inferred from perception alone. Prior experience across objects can provide an initial estimate of unseen object dynamics, but this estimate remains uncertain and can degrade further during sim-to-real transfer. Adapting the dynamics through interaction can progressively refine the estimation, however, updating the model may invalidate the planned trajectory. Successful and efficient manipulation therefore requires both rapid dynamics adaptation and a planning strategy that can incorporate this evolution. In this work, we introduce MetaPusher, a meta-learning and adaptive planning framework for nonprehensile manipulation of unseen objects without prior object-specific interactions. A meta-learned dynamics model rapidly adapts from interactions during task execution, while an adaptive kinodynamic planner updates long-horizon plans by reusing and refining its existing search tree. This coupling enables manipulation and adaptation without a separate data collection phase. We evaluate MetaPusher on unseen objects in simulation and in sim-to-real scenarios, comparing against fine-tuning and active learning methods, MPPI-based control, and a reinforcement learning policy. It achieves lower prediction error and improves task success rate by up to 20%.

AI.tldr: MetaPusher combines meta-learning for rapid online adaptation of unseen-object dynamics with an adaptive kinodynamic planner that reuses/refines its search tree during task execution, eliminating a separate data-collection phase.
AI.motivation: Manipulating unseen objects requires handling latent physical properties (e.g., friction, mass distribution) not inferable from perception. The sim-to-real gap and evolving dynamics during interaction demand fast adaptation plus planning that can update plans as the model evolves.
AI.method: A meta-learned dynamics model rapidly adapts from interactions during task execution. An adaptive kinodynamic planner updates long-horizon plans by reusing and refining its existing search tree, enabling continual planning while the model evolves. No separate data collection phase is required.
AI.result: Evaluated on unseen objects in simulation and sim-to-real scenarios, comparing against fine-tuning, active learning, MPPI-based control, and an RL policy. MetaPusher achieves lower prediction error and increases task success rate by up to 20%.
AI.conclusion: Coupling meta-learning with an adaptive planner yields rapid dynamics adaptation and robust planning for nonprehensile manipulation of unseen objects, reducing the need for data collection and improving success in unseen-object tasks.

title: DENSE: Distilling Agent Trajectories into Evidence-Grounded Shortcut Trees for Self-Refinement
summary: Online agent deployments produce abundant execution traces, while task-specific verification and expert annotation are costly to scale. We study how to distill these traces into reusable feedback without post-hoc outcome labels, drawing on their evidence of local progress, recovery, and unfinished requirements. We introduce DENSE (Distilling Evidence from Nested Subtask Executions), which organizes this evidence into evidence-grounded nested shortcut trees. DENSE compresses redundant attempts, reconciles issues across levels using recovery evidence, and summarizes completed branches while expanding unresolved ones, linking reusable progress to remaining obligations. We introduce REFIT, a source-paired protocol comparing feedback from shared initial trajectories under post-hoc outcome blindness, with environments and model contexts reset for fresh attempts at the same tasks. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, DENSE achieves the highest strict pass rate among tested non-privileged feedback methods across four recipient models. Relative to initial executions, strict pass rate improves by 7.12-15.64 pp, with 19.0-43.6% fewer observed recipient tokens in reruns. GPT-5.5 ablations support combining nested subtask analysis with shortcut construction and issue reconciliation. These findings point toward agent self-refinement through evidence-grounded trajectory reuse with less reliance on external supervision.

AI.tldr: DENSE builds evidence-grounded, nested shortcut trees to distill execution traces into reusable feedback without post-hoc outcome labels; REFIT evaluates feedback under outcome blindness by resetting environments; results show higher strict pass rates and substantial token-efficiency, supporting self-refinement with less external supervision.
AI.motivation: The abundance of execution traces from online agent deployments makes post-hoc labeling costly; there is a need for scalable, reusable feedback derived directly from traces.
AI.method: DENSE organizes trace evidence into nested shortcut trees, compresses redundant attempts, reconciles multi-level issues via recovery evidence, and summarizes completed branches while expanding unresolved ones. REFIT compares feedback from shared initial trajectories under post-hoc outcome blindness with environment resets for fresh attempts. Evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 across four recipient models, plus GPT-5.5 ablations.
AI.result: DENSE achieves the highest strict pass rate among tested non-privileged feedback methods across four recipient models. Strict pass rate improves by 7.12-15.64 percentage points relative to initial executions, with 19.0-43.6% fewer observed recipient tokens in reruns. GPT-5.5 ablations support the combination of nested subtask analysis with shortcut construction and issue reconciliation.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-grounded trajectory reuse enables agent self-refinement with less reliance on external supervision, through structured trace distillation and outcome-blind evaluation.

title: AgentVidBench: A Multi-Hop Video Question Answering Benchmark for Evaluating MLLM Agents
summary: Comprehensive video understanding is crucial for advancing artificial intelligence toward the intricate dynamics of the physical world. While recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in video understanding, existing benchmarks remain confined to simple scene-level queries or global summaries that require only single-step inference. Real-world video understanding involves more challenging tasks that require multi-hop multimodal reasoning, and there is a critical absence of video benchmarks equipped to rigorously evaluate these agentic capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce AgentVidBench, a multi-hop video question answering benchmark focused on evaluating the spatial, temporal, and causal reasoning capabilities of MLLM agents. Beyond standard question-answer pairs, AgentVidBench provides step-by-step solution traces to support trajectory evaluation that assesses whether agents explicitly acquire the evidence needed to justify their answers. Experiments with 12 proprietary and open-source MLLMs show that single-turn performance remains limited on AgentVidBench, while integrating these models into state-of-the-art agentic workflows generally improves performance with respect to both accuracy and trajectory scores. We further present a simple yet effective agentic strategy that serves as a competitive baseline on AgentVidBench, establishing our benchmark as a holistic testbed for future research on agentic video understanding. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/krafton-ai/agentvidbench and https://huggingface.co/datasets/agentvidbench/agentvidbench.

AI.tldr: AgentVidBench is a multi-hop video QA benchmark for evaluating MLLM agents, featuring spatial, temporal, and causal reasoning tasks plus step-by-step solution traces. It reveals limited single-turn performance but shows that integrating models into agentic workflows improves accuracy and trajectory scores; a simple competitive baseline is proposed. Code and data are released.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of benchmarks that rigorously evaluate agentic, multi-hop multimodal reasoning in video understanding. Real-world video tasks require tracing evidence and justifications across space, time, and causal relationships, which current benchmarks largely overlook.
AI.method: Introduce AgentVidBench focused on multi-hop reasoning in videos. Each task requires spatial/temporal/causal inference. The benchmark provides step-by-step solution traces to support trajectory evaluation, assessing whether agents gather the necessary evidence. The authors evaluate 12 MLLMs, study their integration into agentic workflows, and propose a simple competitive agentic strategy as a baseline.
AI.result: Single-turn performance of MLLMs on AgentVidBench is limited. However, when incorporated into agentic workflows, models show improved accuracy and trajectory scores. A straightforward agentic strategy yields competitive results, establishing a baseline for future work.
AI.conclusion: AgentVidBench offers a comprehensive, holistic testbed for evaluating agentic video understanding. The benchmark enables rigorous assessment of reasoning traces and evidence gathering, and code/datasets are publicly available for reproducibility and future research.

title: Layerwise Decoupling for Stable Structured Sparsification of Fully Connected Layers
summary: We propose a decoupled, layerwise method for structurally sparsifying the fully connected layers of pretrained neural networks. Rather than penalizing all layers jointly, our approach extracts shallow two-layer subnetworks, normalizes the inner weights, and applies a structured group penalty to the outer weight matrix of each block, processing layers sequentially to prune neurons and reduce the width of each layer. We prove that the constrained decoupled objective is equivalent at optimality to a specific joint penalty on the inner and outer weights, for any positively homogeneous activation, and thus admits a clean projected and proximal formulation. Our central finding is that this decoupled reformulation is more robust than coupled methods. In numerical experiments it provides a wider usable range of the regularization strength and a lower rate of catastrophic over-pruning than the tested joint baseline while maintaining comparable accuracy. We establish these properties in controlled classification and sparse-recovery studies, and examine their scope in a high-dimensional PINN stress test and in the feed-forward layers of OPT-1.3B.

AI.tldr: A decoupled, layerwise sparsification method for pretrained neural networks' fully connected layers, using two-layer subnetworks, normalization, and structured group penalties per block; shown to be equivalent to a joint penalty at optimality and more robust than coupled methods. Keeps accuracy with a wider regularization range and less over-pruning, demonstrated in classification, sparse recovery, a high-dimensional PINN test, and OPT-1.3B feed-forward layers.
AI.motivation: To sparsify pretrained dense networks by decoupling layerwise regularization to improve robustness and reduce catastrophic pruning, without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: Process layers sequentially: extract shallow two-layer subnetworks, normalize inner weights, apply a structured group penalty to the outer weight matrix of each block; prove equivalence to a joint penalty for positively homogeneous activations; employ a clean projected/proximal optimization framework.
AI.result: Decoupled reformulation is more robust, offering a wider usable range of regularization strengths and a lower rate of catastrophic over-pruning while maintaining comparable accuracy; validated in controlled classification and sparse-recovery tests, a high-dimensional PINN stress test, and in OPT-1.3B feed-forward layers.
AI.conclusion: The decoupled, layerwise sparsification approach provides theoretical and empirical robustness advantages over joint-penalty methods, enabling effective pruning of large pretrained networks with preserved accuracy across diverse tasks.

title: SAGE: Safety-Aligned Gradient Enforcement for Human--Robot Collaboration
summary: Multi-party human-robot collaboration poses a dual challenge: robot decisions should remain interpretable and auditable, while executed actions must satisfy safety constraints during physical interaction. Combining explainable decision-tree policies with control-barrier-function (CBF) filtering provides a promising architecture but creates two learning mismatches in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Safety projection changes the action applied to the environment, while the coupled proposal graph can misalign independently optimized actor updates with a team-level update. We present safety-aligned gradient enforcement (SAGE) to address both mismatches. Its shield-annealed internalization layer (SAIL) uses a differentiable finite-penalty proposal map while retaining the exact CBF quadratic program for execution, preserving constraint-normal sensitivity to internalize repeatedly active safety constraints. Team-averaged Lyapunov policy optimization (TALO) constructs a team-aware update reference and applies a Lyapunov half-space correction to regulate independent actor updates. Physical experiments with two humanoid robots and a human partner demonstrate deployment feasibility. Across nine simulation scenarios, SAGE achieves a 71.0% success rate with 0.5 collision steps per thousand environment steps. Ablations show that direct CBF filtering reduces collision frequency by 98.5% but decreases success from 67.3% to 59.3%. SAIL reduces proposal violation by 48.8% and proposal-execution correction by 85.2%, while TALO reduces the update-consistency gap by 50.8%.

AI.tldr: SAGE addresses two learning mismatches in multi-agent human-robot collaboration by combining safety-aligned gradient enforcement with a two-layer structure (SAIL for differentiable, exact-CBF execution; TALO for team-aware policy updates). It yields improved safety and consistency, validated in simulations and real-robot experiments, with notable trade-offs between safety and task success.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent human-robot systems, decisions must be interpretable and auditable while ensuring safety during physical interaction. Safety filtering (CBF) can alter environment actions, and coupled multi-agent updates can misalign independent learning signals with team-optimal behavior.
AI.method: SAIL uses a differentiable finite-penalty proposal map to internalize safety constraints while preserving the exact CBF quadratic program for execution. TALO constructs a team-aware update reference and applies a Lyapunov half-space correction to regulate independent actor updates. The framework is evaluated through physical experiments with two humanoid robots and a human partner and nine simulation scenarios.
AI.result: 9 simulations show 71.0% success with 0.5 collision steps per 1000 environment steps. Ablations: direct CBF filtering reduces collisions by 98.5% but lowers success from 67.3% to 59.3%. SAIL reduces proposal violations by 48.8% and proposal-execution corrections by 85.2%. TALO reduces update-consistency gap by 50.8%. Physical experiments demonstrate deployment feasibility.
AI.conclusion: SAGE effectively mitigates both learning mismatches in multi-agent human-robot collaboration, balancing safety and performance while preserving constraint-sensitive execution; the approach is validated across simulations and real-world experiments.

title: GVPO++: Group Variance Policy Optimization for LLM Post-Training and On-Policy Distillation
comment: Extended version of the NeurIPS 2025 paper "GVPO: Group Variance Policy Optimization for Large Language Model Post-Training"
summary:
Post-training plays a pivotal role in enhancing the reasoning capabilities and task-specific expertise of large language models (LLMs). Despite recent advances in post-training methods, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), their practical deployment remains impeded by training instability arising from the reliance on importance sampling.
  We introduce Group Variance Policy Optimization (GVPO), a novel post-training method that integrates the analytical solution of KL-constrained reward maximization into its gradient weighting scheme. This formulation provides an intuitive interpretation: GVPO's gradient corresponds to the mean squared error between the central distance of implicit rewards and that of actual rewards. GVPO offers two key advantages: (1) it guarantees a unique optimal solution, exactly to the KL-constrained reward maximization objective, and (2) it enables flexible sampling distributions without requiring importance sampling.
  Beyond general post-training, we show that GVPO naturally extends to on-policy distillation (OPD). Furthermore, GVPO enables the optimization of a broad family of extended OPD objectives, providing a principled foundation for diverse objective design. By unifying theoretical guarantees with practical adaptability, GVPO establishes a new paradigm for reliable and versatile LLM post-training and on-policy distillation.

AI.tldr: GVPO provides a unique-optimal KL-constrained reward optimization for post-training, removes importance-sampling instability, and extends to on-policy distillation with flexible objectives.
AI.motivation: Address training instability in post-training methods (e.g., GRPO) caused by reliance on importance sampling; the goal is a stable, principled framework for LLM post-training and distillation.
AI.method: Introduce GVPO by integrating the analytical solution of KL-constrained reward maximization into gradient weighting; the gradient equals the mean-squared error between the central distance of implicit rewards and actual rewards; enables flexible sampling distributions without importance sampling; guarantees a unique KL-constrained optimum.
AI.result: GVPO guarantees a unique optimal solution to KL-constrained reward maximization, supports flexible sampling without importance sampling, naturally extends to on-policy distillation (OPD) and extended OPD objectives, and provides both theoretical guarantees and practical adaptability for reliable post-training and distillation.
AI.conclusion: GVPO unifies theory and practice to establish a new paradigm for reliable and versatile LLM post-training and on-policy distillation.

title: A Scene Language Model for Open-Vocabulary Scene Mapping
summary: Open-vocabulary 3D scene mapping aims to build a persistent representation of the objects in an environment. Existing systems typically rely on engineered mapping pipelines to associate observations, merge information across views, and maintain a consistent scene representation over time. Many additionally store feature-rich object representations, such as embeddings or image crops, increasing the size and complexity of the persistent memory. We introduce SceneLM, a Scene-Language Model that directly maintains a textual scene map. The full scene is represented as a structured text list of objects, which serves as the model's only persistent memory. For each input image, the model reads the current scene state and updates the map by adding, editing, and removing objects. To learn this behavior, we introduce supervision tasks for iterative scene map maintenance together with an automatic annotation pipeline that generates training data from images without human labels. We evaluate SceneLM on both a language-grounded retrieval benchmark and a localization benchmark. Across both benchmarks, the model produces a scene map that achieves competitive performance with complete mapping systems built from dedicated perception and geometric modules while producing a scene representation that is 6-12x more compact. We further show that SceneLM can be run online on an edge device through experiments on a quadruped. These results show that a persistent open-vocabulary 3D scene map can be maintained directly by a single vision-language model using only a lightweight text representation. Training and inference code is available on https://goldengait.github.io/scenelm/.

AI.tldr: A vision-language model maintains a compact, textual 3D scene map, enabling online updates on edge devices with competitive performance and significantly reduced memory compared to traditional pipeline-based methods.
AI.motivation: Open-vocabulary 3D scene mapping currently relies on modular perception and geometry with large, feature-rich representations. A persistent, compact memory that supports open vocabulary would simplify pipelines and enable online deployment.
AI.method: Train SceneLM, a scene-language model that stores the full scene as a structured text list and updates it per image by adding, editing, or removing objects. Use supervised tasks for iterative maintenance and an automatic annotation pipeline to generate training data from unlabeled images. Evaluate on language-grounded retrieval and localization benchmarks; demonstrate online edge deployment on a quadruped.
AI.result: SceneLM achieves competitive performance with full mapping systems on both benchmarks while using 6–12× less persistent memory. It can run online on edge hardware, showing feasibility of a single vision-language model maintaining a persistent textual scene map.
AI.conclusion: A persistent open-vocabulary 3D scene map can be effectively maintained by a single vision-language model using a lightweight textual representation, enabling compact, online scene understanding without traditional perception/geometry modules.

title: EnSol: an environment-aware graph neural network for molecular solubility prediction
summary: Molecular solubility directly affects key aspects of molecular development such as reaction feasibility, formulation performance, separation efficiency, and solvent selection. However, experimental measurement across solutes, solvents, and temperatures remains costly and sparsely sampled. Existing computational models often rely on fixed-solvent assumptions, deterministic formulations, or simplified representations of solute-solvent interactions, limiting their ability to capture complex molecular interactions, continuous temperature effects, and experimental uncertainty. Here, we introduce EnSol, an environment-aware probabilistic framework for molecular solubility prediction. EnSol represents the solute and solvent as molecular graphs and learns separate representations for each before bringing them together through cross-attention to capture solute-solvent interactions. Temperature is incorporated directly into the solvent environment through feature-wise modulation, and a mixture density network predicts full solubility distributions to capture both temperature-dependent behavior and experimental uncertainty. On the independent SolProp and Leeds benchmark datasets, EnSol achieved Spearman correlations of 0.876 and 0.601, respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art solubility prediction models across both benchmarks. Beyond computational benchmarking, experimental validation across chemically diverse solute-solvent pairs showed that EnSol maintained strong predictive performance and supported reliable solvent ranking, achieving a Spearman correlation of 0.715. These results show that EnSol can support reliable solubility prediction and solvent selection across diverse chemical systems while accounting for predictive uncertainty.

AI.tldr: EnSol: environment-aware probabilistic solubility predictor using graph representations for solute/solvent, cross-attention coupling, temperature-conditioned solvent environment, and a mixture density network to model full solubility distributions and uncertainty; achieves state-of-the-art on SolProp (0.876) and Leeds (0.601) benchmarks and strong experimental validation (Spearman 0.715).
AI.motivation: Solubility prediction is essential for reaction feasibility, formulation, and solvent choice, but experimental data is sparse and noisy. Existing models struggle with solvent effects, temperature dependence, and uncertainty quantification due to fixed solvent representations and deterministic outputs.
AI.method: Represent solute and solvent as molecular graphs with separate embeddings; cross-attention fuses solute–solvent interactions; incorporate temperature via feature-wise modulation of the solvent environment; predict solubility distributions with a mixture density network to capture temperature effects and experimental uncertainty; evaluate on SolProp and Leeds benchmarks and validate with diverse experimental data.
AI.result: On SolProp and Leeds, EnSol achieved Spearman correlations of 0.876 and 0.601, respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art models across both benchmarks. Experimental validation showed Spearman correlation of 0.715, indicating reliable solvent ranking and uncertainty-aware predictions.
AI.conclusion: EnSol demonstrates reliable, uncertainty-aware solubility prediction across diverse chemical systems and thermodynamic conditions, enabling improved solvent selection and modeling of temperature-dependent solvation phenomena.

title: Diverse and Adaptable Arm Coordination for Octopus-Crawling via Diffusion-Based Uncertainty-Aware Optimization
summary: Octopus crawling motivates soft robots that exploit redundancy, yet discovering and organizing diverse coordination modes for adaptation remains challenging. To address this, we introduce a Diffusion-based Uncertainty-aware Optimization (DUO) algorithm that learns demonstration-free crawling controllers for a simulated, muscle-actuated CyberOctopus. This work represents the first application of diffusion-based control to soft multi-arm robots in contact-rich simulations. By embedding a variety of locomotion behaviors within a shared control distribution, this approach enables the simulated octopus to navigate dynamic physical constraints, demonstrating that learned coordination diversity inherently facilitates robust adaptation. The main contributions include: (i) a symmetry-structured policy representation that folds radially equivalent controllers into a canonical directional sector, (ii) an online black-box optimization strategy, the DUO algorithm, that discovers and retains diverse coordination modes, and (iii) a control editing technique that adapts existing controllers to novel actuator constraints without retraining. These results show how learned coordination diversity makes motor abundance a practical resource for adaptation in soft multi-arm robots.

AI.tldr: DUO learns diverse, demonstration-free crawling strategies for a soft, multi-arm robot via diffusion-based, uncertainty-aware optimization.
AI.motivation: To enable robust, adaptable locomotion in soft, multi-arm robots by discovering diverse coordination modes that can adapt to changing contact-rich constraints.
AI.method: Proposes DUO: symmetry-structured policy representation that normalizes controllers, online black-box optimization to discover and retain diverse coordination modes, diffusion-based control to encode coordination diversity, and a control-editing technique to adapt controllers to new actuator constraints without retraining.
AI.result: First diffusion-based control for soft multi-arm robots in contact-rich simulations; demonstrates navigation of dynamic physical constraints; coordination diversity improves robustness; online optimization retains diverse modes; editing enables adaptation to actuator changes.
AI.conclusion: Coordination diversity provides a practical resource for motor abundance in soft robots; diffusion-based, demonstration-free control offers scalable, adaptable locomotion across constraints.

title: Risk-Aware Occupancy for Safety-Oriented End-to-End Autonomous Driving
comment: The first version of this research was completed in early 2025
summary: Sparse representation formulates the environment perception for the end-to-end driving system as a set of discrete elements like objects and lane lines. This formulation meets safety risks in crowded, occluded scenes dealing with unstructured obstacles, uncertain regions, and intricate interactions. In this paper, we propose a dense representation, risk-aware occupancy, to characterize planning-relevant risks in an explicit and uniform manner. It jointly encodes global scene occupancy, map-derived traffic constraints, and future dynamic agent occupancy into a unified BEV map. The unified BEV map captures the risk evidence for trajectory planning in both spatial and temporal dimensions. We design an E2E network, ROIDrive, to realize risk-aware occupancy. It predicts risk-aware occupancy with an independent branch and injects it into planning queries for safety-oriented trajectory generation. In addition, to quantify the safety problem, we introduce RiskOcc4D-nuScenes built upon nuscenes and occ3d-nuscenes. Our risk-aware occupancy yields relative open-loop collision reductions of 52.9% under the UniAD metric and 35.0% under the ST-P3 metric on nuScenes.

AI.tldr: A dense risk-aware occupancy representation in BEV is proposed to improve planning safety in end-to-end driving. It unifies global scene occupancy, map constraints, and future dynamic occupancy, via an ROIDrive network with a separate risk-branch that informs planning queries. A new RiskOcc4D-nuScenes dataset is introduced for evaluation. Reported results show substantial collision reductions on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Sparse representations struggle in crowded, occluded, and unstructured environments. A dense, explicit risk representation could better quantify planning risks across space and time, improving safety without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: Introduce Risk-aware Occupancy Dense- BEV (Risk-aware occupancy) that encodes global occupancy, map constraints, and future dynamic occupancy into a unified BEV map. Develop ROIDrive, an end-to-end network with an independent risk-branch that injects risk features into planning queries. Create RiskOcc4D-nuScenes on nuScenes and occ3d-nuscenes for evaluation.
AI.result: Risk-aware occupancy enables significant open-loop collision reductions: 52.9% under UniAD metric and 35.0% under ST-P3 metric on nuScenes.
AI.conclusion: Dense risk-aware occupancy improves planning safety for end-to-end driving. The accompanying RiskOcc4D-nuScenes dataset facilitates standardized evaluation across planning frameworks.

title: SIRA: Reasoning-Aware Surgical Instrument Segmentation via Query-Anchored Alignment
summary: Surgical instrument segmentation (SIS) plays a critical role in robotic assistance and surgical workflow analysis. However, most existing SIS methods formulate segmentation as a category-driven localization problem, limiting their ability to capture procedural context and task-dependent semantics in surgical workflows. We introduce Reasoning-Aware Surgical Instrument Segmentation (RA-SIS), a task formulation that frames segmentation as query-conditioned inference under surgical context. To benchmark this setting, we construct SurgRS, a surgical reasoning segmentation dataset consisting of 41,000 image-text pairs, which aligns instance-level masks with structured query-answer supervision to enable semantic grounding at the pixel level. Based on SurgRS, we propose Surgical Instrument Reasoning and Segmentation Assistant (SIRA), a multimodal framework that disentangles target-level and query-level semantics and integrates them with visual features through query-anchored dual alignment. By aligning query semantics with spatial features and segmentation prompts, SIRA enhances semantic-visual consistency in mask prediction. Extensive experiments on SurgRS demonstrate improvements over existing reasoning-aware baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/linxir226/SIRA.

AI.tldr: RA-SIS reframes surgical instrument segmentation as query-conditioned inference using a multimodal framework SIRA on SurgRS, achieving semantic grounding and improved accuracy with a 41k image-text dataset; code available.
AI.motivation: Current SIS largely treats segmentation as category-driven localization, missing procedural context and task-dependent semantics in surgical workflows.
AI.method: Propose RA-SIS as query-conditioned inference; construct SurgRS with 41,000 image-text pairs aligning masks with structured query-answer supervision; introduce SIRA that disentangles target- and query-level semantics and uses query-anchored dual alignment to fuse semantics with visual features.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on SurgRS show improvements over existing reasoning-aware baselines.
AI.conclusion: RA-SIS with SurgRS and SIRA enables semantic grounding at pixel level and advances visual-semantic alignment in surgical instrument segmentation; code released.

title: HMB-GAN: Hybrid Multi-Bézier GAN for Vector Shape Synthesis
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Published in the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Software (QSW)
summary: We explore the use of hybrid quantum-classical generative adversarial networks for synthesising CAD-ready vector geometries. Unlike prior work that operates in rasterised or single-Bézier domains, we introduce HMB-GAN (Hybrid Multi-Bézier GAN), an end-to-end differentiable generative framework that constructs closed shapes through stitched multi-segment Bézier representations with geometric continuity enforced by construction. We compare a quantum-enhanced generator with a classical generator within this architecture and evaluate them across point cloud distribution metrics and geometric shape statistics. Results show that despite faster convergence, a reduction in model parameter count, and slightly improved performance on point cloud metrics, the quantum generator suffers from excessive simulator overhead and thus classically-simulated evaluation suffers from hardware constraints. These results demonstrate the feasibility of modelling structured geometries through hybrid quantum architectures whilst highlighting contemporary hardware limitations.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum-classical GAN (HMB-GAN) for generating CAD-ready vector Bézier geometries, comparing a quantum-enhanced generator to a classical one. Demonstrates feasibility of structured geometry modelling with hybrids, but hardware/simulator limits impede practical evaluation.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of generating precise, CAD-ready vector geometries by combining quantum and classical generative models, and to evaluate whether quantum components offer advantages in convergence or parameter efficiency for structured geometry tasks.
AI.method: Propose HMB-GAN—an end-to-end differentiable framework that builds closed shapes from stitched multi-segment Bézier curves with continuity constraints. Implement and compare a quantum-enhanced generator vs. a classical generator within the same architecture. Assess using point cloud distribution metrics and geometric shape statistics.
AI.result: Quantum generator exhibits faster convergence and reduced parameter count with slight gains in point cloud metrics, but suffers from significant simulator overhead and hardware constraints when evaluated in classical simulators. Classical generator remains more practical given current hardware, though benefits of quantum component are limited by tooling.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid quantum architectures can model structured geometries like vector Bézier shapes, but contemporary hardware and simulation overhead limit practical evaluation; further hardware and algorithmic advances are needed to realize tangible benefits.

title: Same World, Different Knowledge: When Isolated Audits Misjudge World-Model Repairs
summary:
A repair favored under an isolated input fault can be inferior when deployed modules share the faulty information. We introduce an information-interface
  audit for world models, distinguishing fidelity gaps, where exact inputs become estimates, from availability gaps, where inputs are missing. Fixed-weight
  interventions measure prediction error, input dependence, and paired closed-loop benefit, including dependencies introduced by reconstruction. In
  simulated quadrotor model predictive control, coupled, opposite-sign 10% mass/thrust calibration errors reduce a physics-anchored model's success from 69%
  to 8%; uncertainty training restores 65%. Wind reconstruction recovers control benefit but inherits calibration dependence. For a positive calibration
  offset, reconstruction-only corruption favors uncertainty-trained reconstruction, whereas shared corruption favors the baseline. Acceleration diagnostics
  reveal compensation between reconstruction bias and nominal-model error, also observed with a disturbance observer. Repair selection therefore depends on
  the information paths used in deployment.

AI.tldr: Proposes an information-interface audit to diagnose fidelity vs availability gaps in world-model deployments; reports that reconstruction and calibration errors can dramatically affect repair performance, with uncertainty training improving robustness; repair choice becomes path-dependent on information flows.
AI.motivation: To explain why repairs that look good under isolated faults can underperform when modules share faulty information, by separating fidelity gaps (inputs become estimates) from availability gaps (inputs missing) and by quantifying how reconstruction and information paths influence deployment.
AI.method: Introduce information-interface audit for world models; distinguish fidelity vs availability gaps; use fixed-weight interventions to quantify prediction error, input dependence, and paired closed-loop benefit; account for dependencies from reconstruction; test in simulated quadrotor MPC with coupled 10% mass/thrust calibration errors; analyze effects of uncertainty training, wind reconstruction, and corruption types; employ acceleration diagnostics and a disturbance observer to study compensation.
AI.result: In the quadrotor MPC, coupled 10% mass/thrust calibration errors reduce success from 69% to 8%; uncertainty training restores to 65%. Wind reconstruction recovers control benefit but inherits calibration dependence. For a positive calibration offset, reconstruction-only corruption favors uncertainty-trained reconstruction, whereas shared corruption favors the baseline. Acceleration diagnostics indicate compensation between reconstruction bias and nominal-model error, observed also with a disturbance observer.
AI.conclusion: Repair selection is contingent on the information paths used in deployment. An information-interface audit helps identify when reconstruction- or calibration-induced dependencies will degrade or enhance performance, guiding robust repair decisions.

title: Driving on Registers, Reasoning on Risk: Risk-Aware Occupancy for Register-Based End-to-End Autonomous Driving
comment: This version of this research was completed in early 2026
summary: Multimodal trajectory prediction improves behavioral coverage in end-to-end autonomous driving, but existing methods remain limited by sparse scene representations. Incomplete evidence leads to low-quality candidate generation and unreliable ranking among geometrically similar trajectories. On a register-based baseline, bad and poor candidates constitute 19.74% of the candidate set, while the oracle-best candidate ranks only 33.9th on average. We propose RRDrive, which introduces risk-aware occupancy as a dense, temporally aligned, and trajectory-queryable representation. Its global structure guides high-quality multimodal generation, while candidate-conditioned risk queries support fine-grained selection. We further construct RiskOcc4D-NAVSIM with automatic risk annotations. RRDrive achieves a selected-trajectory PDMS of 0.951, representing a 1.5% relative improvement over the baseline (0.937), and improves the average candidate PDMS by 7.7%. In challenging scenes, it improves candidate PDMS by 30.2% and increases the Spearman correlation among good candidates by 0.41, from 0.26 to 0.67.
