AI.tldr: A Python library FairLMs unifies fairness evaluation and mitigation for language models by declaring model capabilities, offering extensive metrics, mitigations, diagnostics, and adapters, enabling standardized, comparable workflows across models and datasets.
AI.motivation: Fairness research in LMs suffers from fragmented tools with incompatible interfaces and evidence formats, hindering method comparison and reproducibility.
AI.method: FairLMs provides explicit declarations of model capabilities and input requirements; implements 33 intrinsic/extrinsic metrics, 14 mitigation components across four intervention categories, 14 dataset/scoring diagnostics, adapters for three Transformer architectures and hosted completion APIs, and benchmark loaders; declarations are checked before execution; results include the configuration used.
AI.result: An integrated, extensible toolkit enabling reproducible, comparable fairness evaluations and mitigations, with provenance of results and a common protocol.
AI.conclusion: FairLMs offers a unified platform to reconcile heterogenous fairness tools, easing method comparison and extension to new models/datasets.

title: Fewer Steps, Better Actions: Rethinking Flow-Matching Inference for VLA Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies based on flow matching generate action chunks through repeated evaluations of an action expert. Increasing the number of integration steps raises inference cost, but does not necessarily improve closed-loop success. We propose Coda, which reallocates part of this integration budget to a single learned endpoint correction. A frozen policy first completes a few-step noise-to-action trajectory; a lightweight Transformer then predicts a demonstration-supervised residual using the candidate action, source noise, and shared observation-prefix cache. Only the corrector is trained. On 50 RoboTwin Easy tasks, five-step Coda improves success from 71.64% to 74.68% over the matched five-step baseline, while reducing forward latency by 30.2% relative to the default ten-step policy. A two-step configuration achieves 71.88% success with a 2.12$\times$ speedup. An independent 13-task control shows a 5.69-percentage-point gain at nearly equal latency, supporting correction as an effective alternative to additional integration. The same design also improves frozen official SmolVLA, raising two-step success from 60.8% to 69.4%. These results show that endpoint correction improves the quality-latency trade-off of frozen flow-matching policies.

AI.tldr: Endpoint correction via a lightweight learned corrector improves the efficiency and success of flow-matching vision-language-action policies, achieving better quality-latency trade-offs than additional integration steps.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching VLA policies rely on multiple integration steps; more steps raise inference cost and do not always boost closed-loop success. A single learned endpoint correction could reallocate computation to improve performance per unit latency.
AI.method: Freeze the base policy and perform a few-step noise-to-action trajectory. Introduce a lightweight Transformer as an endpoint corrector that predicts a demonstration-supervised residual using the candidate action, source noise, and a shared observation-prefix cache. Train only the corrector while keeping the policy frozen. Compare five-step and ten-step baselines on RoboTwin Easy tasks and SmolVLA, evaluating success and latency.
AI.result: Five-step Coda improves success on RoboTwin Easy tasks from 71.64% to 74.68% and reduces forward latency by 30.2% relative to the ten-step baseline. A two-step configuration yields 71.88% success with 2.12× speedup. An independent 13-task control shows a 5.69-percentage-point gain at nearly equal latency. On SmolVLA, two-step success grows from 60.8% to 69.4%. Overall, endpoint correction enhances the quality-latency trade-off compared to further integration steps.
AI.conclusion: Endpoint correction is an effective alternative to adding integration steps in frozen flow-matching policies, improving both success rates and latency and strengthening the policy’s quality-latency trade-off.

title: Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education
summary: Access to academic support is a key determinant of student success, yet students experience it unequally: some readily seek help from lecturers or tutors, while others hesitate due to anxiety, fear of judgement, uncertainty about expectations, or low confidence in their understanding. This may be especially evident in computing education, where programming tasks are cumulative and cognitively demanding. Although students increasingly turn to general-purpose generative AI tools, these can produce responses that are inaccurate, insufficiently contextualised, or misaligned with module expectations. This study presents and evaluates Beacon, a course-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system providing private, immediate, module-aligned academic support. Grounding responses in approved teaching materials, Beacon was designed to lower barriers to help-seeking while encouraging independent learning. Using a design-based research approach, Beacon was developed iteratively and evaluated via mixed methods, combining questionnaires and semi-structured interviews with students and staff at a Higher Education institution. Students described Beacon's responses as closely aligned with module content and more trustworthy than unrestricted generative AI tools, valuing its use of pseudocode and scaffolded explanations over direct solutions. Although participants remained cautious about trusting AI-generated responses without verification, they viewed the system as a valuable first point of support before consulting lecturers or official resources. The findings suggest that carefully designed course-specific AI systems may reduce barriers to academic support by occupying an intermediary space between independent study and formal support. Rather than replacing educators, educational AI may be most valuable when it broadens access to guidance while preserving the pedagogical role of lecturers.

AI.tldr: Beacon is a course-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system that provides private, module-aligned academic support grounded in approved materials, designed to lower help-seeking barriers and complement traditional teaching rather than replace educators.
AI.motivation: To address unequal access to academic support and the limitations of general-purpose AI (inaccuracy, contextual misalignment) by delivering a trusted, module-aligned assistant that encourages independent learning.
AI.method: Design-based research with iterative development and evaluation through mixed methods (surveys and semi-structured interviews) involving students and staff at a Higher Education institution; Beacon uses approved teaching materials to ground responses.
AI.result: Participants found Beacon's outputs closely aligned with module content and more trustworthy than unrestricted AI, valued pseudocode and scaffolded explanations, but remained cautious about verification; seen as a valuable initial support before consulting lecturers/resources.
AI.conclusion: Course-specific AI like Beacon can reduce barriers to accessing guidance, occupying an intermediary space between independent study and formal support; rather than replacing educators, it broadens access to guidance while preserving the pedagogical role of lecturers.

title: SkillIR: Evolving Scene-Aware Skills for Agentic Image Restoration
summary: This paper studies agentic image restoration, in which multimodal agents coordinate specialized restoration tools to recover images affected by complex degradations. Existing restoration agents often derive complete tool-use plans from the original degraded image or retrieve previously successful trajectories, providing limited support for adapting individual actions to evolving intermediate restoration states. We find that accepted tool executions can change the residual degradation state and, consequently, the applicability of subsequent tools. To address this issue, we propose SkillIR, a skill-guided framework that represents restoration experience as degradation-centered action evidence rather than complete tool-use trajectories. SkillIR consolidates context-dependent action outcomes into scene-aware restoration skills that characterize applicable conditions, expected effects, and attributable failure cases. Instead of prescribing a complete restoration plan, the retrieved skills guide one bounded action at a time within a verified residual-state loop: each tool output is treated as a candidate, committed only after transition verification, and followed by reassessment of the active residual degradations. After each rollout, the resulting evidence is used to create, refine, or patch dynamic skills, enabling accumulated restoration experience to improve decision-making for subsequent inputs. Experiments on synthetic and real-world multi-degradation datasets demonstrate that SkillIR improves restoration quality and enables more reliable and effective tool use.

AI.tldr: SkillIR introduces a degradation-centered, skill-based policy for stepwise tool use in multimodal image restoration, replacing full-trajectory plans with verifiable, evolving skills learned from restoration outcomes.
AI.motivation: Current restoration agents rely on complete tool-use plans or retrieved trajectories, which fail to adapt when residual degradations evolve; tool outcomes can change what tools remain applicable.
AI.method: Represent experience as scene-aware restoration skills detailing conditions, effects, and failure modes. Operate in a residual-state loop: propose a tool output as a candidate, commit only after transition verification, then reassess residual degradations and update skills after each rollout.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world multi-degradation datasets show SkillIR improves restoration quality and enables more reliable and effective tool use.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, evidence-based skill consolidation enables accumulated experience to improve decision-making for future inputs and adapt restoration behavior to evolving degradation states.

title: Fast And Accurate Text Content File Type Identification
comment: To appear in The 13th IEEE International Conference on Data Science and Advanced Analytics (DSAA 2026)
summary: A common requirement across organizations is to have a tool that can identify file types based on their contents, particularly in the cybersecurity domain where magic numbers and file extensions can not be trusted. While existing tools work well in practice, there is plenty of room for improvement either in terms of computational load and time for detection in the case of model based tools like Magika or in terms of accuracy of detection in the case of file parsing tools that use programming language constructs. In this study, we propose a neural network model for identification of types of text content files, especially source code, that is more accurate and faster than other available tools. Our experiments on open-source files indicate that it is not only more accurate on average for text-content file-type identification, but also approximately four times faster than Magika, while being 28% smaller in size.

AI.tldr: A neural network model for text-content file-type identification (notably source code) outperforms Magika in accuracy and speed, and is smaller in size, demonstrated on open-source data.
AI.motivation: Reliably identifying file types by content is essential in cybersecurity; traditional magic-number/extension heuristics are unreliable, and existing model-based or parser-based tools have limitations in speed or accuracy. The work aims to improve accuracy and speed while reducing model size.
AI.method: Develop a neural network model for identifying text-content file types, especially source code; train/evaluate on open-source files; compare against Magika and multi-tool baselines; report performance in accuracy, speed, and model size.
AI.result: The proposed model achieves higher average accuracy for text-content file-type identification, runs about four times faster than Magika, and has a size reduction of roughly 28%.
AI.conclusion: Neural-network-based content-type identification can outperform existing tools in accuracy and efficiency, with smaller footprint, making it attractive for cybersecurity workflows. Further work could explore generalization to broader file domains and robustness across datasets.

title: Safe Real-Time Policy Steering via Noise-Space Trajectory Optimization for One-Step Generative Policies
summary: Generative robot policies can represent diverse, multimodal behaviors, but adapting pretrained policies to deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance remains challenging. Existing inference-time steering methods typically apply gradient guidance through iterative diffusion or flow processes, which can be computationally expensive for real-time control. We propose INSPO, which formulates inference-time steering of one-step generative policies as trajectory optimization in the policy's input noise space. By optimizing the input noise while evaluating constraints on the induced state trajectory, INSPO searches the policy-induced behavior space without directly modifying generated actions. The optimization includes a regularization term that encourages solutions to remain consistent with the policy's input distribution and is solved online using population-based particle optimization. We evaluate INSPO on state- and image-based task-specific policies and generalist vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial. INSPO improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, while comparing favorably with gradient-guided generation at lower runtime.

AI.tldr: One-step trajectory optimization in the policy's input-noise space (INSPO) enables online constraint-aware steering of generative policies by optimizing noise while enforcing state-trajectory constraints, using population-based particle optimization.
AI.motivation: Adapting pretrained generative policies to deployment-time constraints (e.g., collision avoidance, orientation maintenance) is difficult; gradient-guided inference methods (diffusion/flow) are computationally heavy for real-time control.
AI.method: Formulate steering as online trajectory optimization in the policy input-noise space. Optimize the noise to satisfy constraints on the induced state trajectory, without modifying actions directly. Include regularization to stay close to the policy's input distribution and solve online via population-based particle optimization.
AI.result: Assessed on state- and image-based task-specific policies and generalist vision-language-action policies (Push-T, Can pick-and-place, LIBERO-Spatial). INSPO yields higher task success and constraint satisfaction than best-of-N sampling and action projection, and competes favorably with gradient-guided generation at lower runtime.
AI.conclusion: INSPO enables real-time, constraint-aware steering of generative policies by searching in the input-noise space, across both specialized and generalist policies, offering improved performance with lower computational cost.

title: Calibrating Teacher--Student Discrepancy for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves reasoning models by learning the token-level discrepancy between a stronger teacher and an on-policy student. However, this discrepancy does not purely reflect the capability gap between the teacher and the student: it also contains deviations arising from the teacher itself, which are consequently mixed into the observed teacher--student discrepancy and indiscriminately learned by standard OPD during training. This issue is further exacerbated by privileged OPD, where privileged information induces larger teacher-side likelihood shifts, thereby encouraging the student to learn more of the teacher's own deviation. We introduce \textbf{Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (Cal-OPD)}, which estimates the teacher's self-deviation region through positive and negative privileged interventions and calibrates the original teacher--student discrepancy by retaining only the component that lies beyond this region. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that, while retaining only about 52--65\% of the original teacher--student discrepancy as the optimization signal, Cal-OPD consistently outperforms standard OPD and its variants across model scales.

AI.tldr: Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (Cal-OPD) isolates the true teacher–student capability gap by filtering out the teacher’s own deviations using positive/negative privileged interventions, retaining only the portion of the discrepancy beyond the calibrated region; this yields improved reasoning performance, even when only a subset of the original discrepancy is used.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) conflates the teacher–student gap with deviations arising from the teacher itself, a problem amplified under privileged OPD where teacher-side likelihood shifts increase. The result is suboptimal guidance and learning.
AI.method: Cal-OPD estimates the teacher’s self-deviation region via positive and negative privileged interventions and calibrates the teacher–student discrepancy by retaining only the component that lies beyond this region, effectively removing the teacher’s own deviations from the optimization signal.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, Cal-OPD retains about 52–65% of the original teacher–student discrepancy yet consistently outperforms standard OPD and its variants across model scales.
AI.conclusion: Cal-OPD provides a robust calibration mechanism that disentangles true capability gaps from teacher-side noise, leading to improved reasoning models and better cross-scale performance.

title: MT-WAM: Reorienting the One-Pass Predictive Representation Toward Action Generation
summary: Fast-WAM shows that video-action co-training improves control without generating future video at inference, making the representation from a single video diffusion Transformer forward central to action generation. However, future-observation prediction does not explicitly prioritize the future dynamics and visual structure needed for control. We present MT-WAM, which retains the original training objectives and adds complementary supervision for future two-dimensional point trajectories and visual features. A lightweight dual-stream branch copied from the video backbone's final blocks provides target-specific processing, while a structured attention mask prevents cross-stream attention. Motion-stream tokens supply additional dynamics conditions to the action expert. Future visual-feature prediction provides supervision in a feature space that captures object and spatial structure. This supervision trains the video backbone to provide more informative visual context for action generation under changing visual conditions, without adding visual-feature-stream tokens to action conditioning. At inference, MT-WAM uses video and motion caches computed once per replan and skips future-video prediction. Without additional embodied policy pretraining, MT-WAM achieves 98.2% success on LIBERO and 73.7% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding Fast-WAM by 23.8 percentage points on the latter. On RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Rand, Random success increases from 6.30% to 19.40%; across four real-world tasks, average success increases from 67.0% to 77.8%.

AI.tldr: MT-WAM extends Fast-WAM by adding complementary supervision for future 2D trajectories and visual features, plus a lightweight dual-stream branch and structured attention to improve control-driven action generation without future video at inference; uses caches for inference.
AI.motivation: to align future-observation supervision with control needs, emphasizing future dynamics and visual structure rather than simply predicting future frames, enabling more informative context for action generation under changing visuals.
AI.method: MT-WAM retains Fast-WAM objectives and adds two components: (1) a lightweight dual-stream branch from the video backbone’s final blocks for target-specific processing, with a structured attention mask to prevent cross-stream attention; (2) supervision on future 2D point trajectories and visual features; motion-stream tokens provide additional dynamics to the action expert; future visual-feature prediction operates in a feature space capturing object/space structure; at inference, video/motion caches are computed per replan and future-video prediction is skipped.
AI.result: MT-WAM achieves 98.2% success on LIBERO and 73.7% on LIBERO-Plus (exceeding Fast-WAM by 23.8 points on LIBERO-Plus). On RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Rand, Random success rises from 6.30% to 19.40%; across four real-world tasks, average success improves from 67.0% to 77.8%.
AI.conclusion: By preserving training objectives while introducing complementary future-dynamics/visual-structure supervision, a dual-stream, masked-attention design, and motion-conditioned tokens, MT-WAM delivers substantial gains in action generation accuracy and robustness with cache-based inference and without requiring embodied-policy pretraining.

title: An Introduction to Compression-Based Machine Learning
comment: To appear in The 13th IEEE International Conference on Data Science and Advanced Analytics (DSAA 2026)
summary: Any lossless compression algorithm (like gzip) may be converted into a machine learning method, via either Normalized Compression Distance or the Minimum Description Length principle. Any auto-regressive model may be converted into a lossless compression method via entropy coding. This seemingly circular dependence has unrealized potential in modern artificial intelligence and machine learning, and we survey and formalize the various strategies that have been used to leverage compression for machine learning. We introduce and empirically validate a design framework for compression-based ML, finding compression-based methods competitive with conventional baselines and decisively stronger on malware. We find that varying these design choices yields accuracy gains of up to 0.62.

AI.tldr: Compression-based ML is a viable paradigm: a survey and a formal design framework show competitive performance with conventional baselines and clear gains in malware detection, with accuracy improvements up to 0.62 by design choices.
AI.motivation: Investigate the circular relationship between compression and learning (via MDL, NCD, and entropy coding) and assess whether compression principles can yield practical ML methods beyond traditional approaches.
AI.method: Survey and formalize existing strategies that convert compression into ML; introduce a design framework for compression-based ML; empirically validate it by comparing to standard baselines and testing on malware detection tasks.
AI.result: Compression-based methods are competitive with conventional baselines and markedly stronger on malware data; varying design choices yields accuracy gains up to 0.62.
AI.conclusion: Compression-based ML is a promising direction. A formal design framework can guide development, with notable gains in domain-specific settings (e.g., malware) and potential broader applicability.

title: SafeStage: Evaluating Safety Before, During, and After Vision-Language-Conditioned Robot Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-conditioned robot policies integrate perception, language understanding, and control for general-purpose manipulation. However, existing evaluations often focus on task success, isolated physical constraints, semantic refusal, or realized physical damage, providing limited insight into where safety fails during closed-loop manipulation. We introduce SafeStage, a lifecycle-structured benchmark for evaluating manipulation safety before, during, and after task execution. SafeStage contains 97 purpose-built risk scenarios organized into three stages. Initial-State Hazards captures safety-relevant relations that must be resolved before manipulating the target. Execution-Time Safety evaluates unsafe contacts, trajectories, region entries, and object interactions during execution. Final-State Hazards capture unstable or otherwise unsafe conditions remaining after nominal task completion. The benchmark evaluates realized interactions using event-based and state-based checks and reports native task success independently from stage-specific safety outcomes. We evaluate representative direct-action Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies and policies with world-model-based policies under a common closed-loop protocol. Our results demonstrate that nominal task completion frequently coexists with safety violations and that different policies exhibit distinct failure profiles across the three stages. By separating task success from safety and localizing when violations occur, SafeStage provides a unified diagnostic testbed for evaluating and improving vision-language-conditioned robot manipulation policies.

AI.tldr: SafeStage introduces a lifecycle-structured benchmark with 97 risk scenarios across Initial-State Hazards, Execution-Time Safety, and Final-State Hazards to evaluate safety independently of task success in vision-language-conditioned manipulation policies; reveals safety failures co-occur with task completion and policy-dependent failure profiles.
AI.motivation: To diagnose where safety fails in closed-loop vision-language manipulation and to separate safety evaluation from nominal task success.
AI.method: Design of SafeStage: 97 scenarios organized into three stages; event-based and state-based safety checks; common closed-loop protocol; evaluation of direct-action VLA and world-model-based policies; native task success reported separately.
AI.result: Task success often coexists with safety violations; policies exhibit distinct safety failure profiles across stages; SafeStage enables diagnosis and improvement by localizing violations.
AI.conclusion: SafeStage is a unified diagnostic testbed for evaluating and improving vision-language-conditioned robot manipulation policies by decomposing safety across the lifecycle of manipulation.

title: One Prompt Does Not Fit All: Self-Meta-Evolve for Personalized Information Extraction
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for enterprise information extraction (IE), where the same document must be reorganized differently for each user. Existing prompt optimization methods, however, rely on a single prompt optimized against a global objective, which is misaligned with the inherent user heterogeneity of real workplaces. We formulate enterprise IE as per-user prompt adaptation under interaction feedback and propose Self-Meta-Evolve, a hierarchical framework that maintains a dedicated prompt for each user and continuously refines it through a dual-loop process: an inner loop that edits structured prompts based on persona-conditioned feedback, and an outer loop that evolves the meta-prompt itself by distilling successful editing patterns. To enable scalable training and evaluation, we release a persona-driven IE benchmark of 292 simulated enterprise users, paired with a reproducible persona-generation pipeline grounded in O*NET occupational taxonomies. On this benchmark, Self-Meta-Evolve achieves a 74.58% success rate, outperforming the strongest prompt-optimization baseline by 13.56 absolute points, and reaches 52.54\% within only two iterations. A double-blind human study with twenty real professionals further confirms that prompts adapted by our framework win against static baselines in 71% of pairwise comparisons.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical per-user prompt adaptation for enterprise IE via Self-Meta-Evolve; inner-loop edits prompts per user with persona feedback; outer-loop meta-prompt evolution through distilling editing patterns; benchmark on 292 simulated users; strong empirical gains and positive human study.
AI.motivation: Enterprise IE requires accommodating user heterogeneity; global prompts misalign objectives; propose per-user adaptation with interaction feedback and scalable evaluation via persona-driven benchmark built on O*NET.
AI.method: Self-Meta-Evolve framework with two-loop structure: inner loop edits structured prompts conditioned on persona feedback; outer loop distills successful editing patterns to evolve meta-prompt; maintain a dedicated prompt per user; use 292 simulated users and a reproducible persona-generation pipeline; two-iteration evaluation; double-blind human study.
AI.result: Promising performance: 74.58% success rate, +13.56 absolute points over strongest baseline; 52.54% achieved in two iterations; human study shows 71% preference over static baselines.
AI.conclusion: Per-user prompt adaptation with meta-prompt evolution improves enterprise IE and scales via persona-driven benchmarks; validated by simulated-user experiments and human evaluation.

title: OpenSAL360: Open-Source Crowdsourcing Platform for Omnidirectional Video Saliency Collection
summary: Omnidirectional video saliency prediction plays an important role in many immersive multimedia applications, including viewport-adaptive streaming and compression, foveated rendering, mesh simplification, perceptual quality assessment. Yet progress in this area remains constrained by the cost and complexity of collecting eye-tracking data with VR headsets, which makes large-scale dataset creation difficult to extend. We present OpenSAL360, the first open-source platform for scalable, low-cost 360° video saliency collection. Unlike conventional VR-based protocols, it requires only a standard screen, mouse, and internet connection, enabling parallel saliency data collection from common crowdsourcing assessors without specialized hardware. We validate our collection protocol against seven well-established VR eye-tracking datasets and conduct ablation studies on key interface, pre-, and post-processing parameters. To demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed methodology, we collect and publicly release a saliency dataset covering 500 omnidirectional videos annotated by 2,000+ crowdsourcing assessors, making it, to the best of our knowledge, the largest dataset in this field. We make OpenSAL360 publicly available at https://github.com/msu-video-group/OpenSAL360.

AI.tldr: OpenSAL360: the first open-source, scalable, low-cost platform for collecting 360° video saliency data using standard hardware; validated against VR eye-tracking datasets and released a large crowdsourced dataset.
AI.motivation: Reducing cost and complexity of collecting eye-tracking data for omnidirectional video; traditional VR headset-based methods limit dataset size and accessibility.
AI.method: Web-based interface using a standard screen, mouse, and internet; enables parallel crowdsourcing data collection without specialized hardware; validation against seven VR eye-tracking datasets; ablation studies on interface, pre-, and post-processing parameters; public release of the collected dataset (500 videos, 2,000+ assessors).
AI.result: Public release of OpenSAL360 dataset: 500 omnidirectional videos with 2,000+ crowd assessors; claimed as the largest, to date, in 360° saliency research; OpenSAL360 codebase/dataset publicly available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Crowdsourced, hardware-free data collection is viable for large-scale 360° saliency datasets; the proposed protocol aligns well with VR-ground-truth datasets and enables scalable advancement in omnidirectional video saliency research.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Buffered Quantile Objectives
summary: Quantile-based reinforcement learning provides an interpretable approach to risk-sensitive decision-making by optimizing a prescribed quantile of the cumulative-return distribution. Despite this appeal, learning under a point quantile objective is challenging: quantiles can change abruptly under small perturbations of the return distribution, and exact quantile-sensitive planning requires computationally demanding distributional optimization. Lower-buffered quantiles alleviate the former difficulty by averaging neighboring quantiles immediately below the target level, providing a smoother surrogate while preserving the underlying point-quantile objective. Existing methods based on this principle, however, remain model-based and rely on explicit return-law planning, limiting their applicability beyond small tabular problems. We develop Deep-BQRL, a model-free distributional reinforcement-learning framework that extends buffered-quantile learning to neural function approximation. The method learns conditional return quantiles directly from sampled transitions, constructs buffered action scores from the relevant region of the learned quantile function, and uses ensemble disagreement to guide exploration. An augmented input representation allows the learned policy to respond to trajectory information without explicitly reproducing the quantile-state recursion required by exact planning. Experiments on an asset-selling optimal-stopping problem and slippery FrozenLake compare Deep-BQRL with model-based UCB-BQRL and tabular PPO and TRPO implementations. In asset selling, Deep-BQRL attains smaller mean cumulative point-quantile policy gaps than PPO and TRPO at the reported target levels, while UCB-BQRL retains the smallest gaps. The learned stopping decisions also vary with the target quantile, providing an interpretable illustration of the method's risk-sensitive behavior.

AI.tldr: A model-free distributional RL method (Deep-BQRL) learns buffered quantiles via neural nets, uses ensemble disagreement for exploration, and augments input to capture trajectory information, enabling risk-sensitive decision-making with interpretable stopping decisions; it matches or surpasses tabular PPO/TRPO and some baselines on benchmark tasks but is outperformed on gaps by the model-based method UCB-BQRL in some cases.
AI.motivation: Quantile-based objectives offer risk-sensitive control but are brittle under small distribution perturbations; exact quantile planning is computationally intensive and existing buffered-quantile methods are largely model-based and limited to tabular settings. A model-free, neural approach is needed to scale to complex environments while preserving interpretability.
AI.method: Learn conditional return quantiles directly from sampled transitions (distributional RL). Build buffered action scores from the relevant region of the learned quantile function. Use ensemble disagreement to drive exploration. Introduce augmented input representation so the policy can respond to trajectory information without requiring exact quantile-state recursion, enabling end-to-end learning with neural networks.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on an asset-selling optimal-stopping problem and slippery FrozenLake shows Deep-BQRL achieves smaller mean cumulative point-quantile policy gaps than PPO and TRPO at reported target levels, with UCB-BQRL achieving the smallest gaps overall. The learned stopping decisions depend on the target quantile, illustrating the method’s interpretability and risk-sensitive behavior.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of a model-free, buffered-quantile RL framework with neural function approximation that yields interpretable, risk-sensitive policies and competitive performance against model-based baselines and tabular methods; supports extension to non-tabular, real-world decision problems requiring risk-aware control.

title: AirSplan: Risk-Aware Motion Planning for Quadrotors in Cluttered 3D Gaussian Splats
comment: To appear in the proceedings of IROS 2026
summary: Quadrotors are increasingly deployed in applications such as agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and maintenance. In each of these applications, the robot must navigate complex scene geometry while remaining strictly collision-free. Unlike in ground domains, even minor collisions for aerial vehicles can result in the loss of the robot. This safety requirement induces a pair of technical challenges. First, the environment must be represented with sufficient fidelity to encode complex structure, even when no ground-truth obstacle data is available. Second, a motion planner must leverage this representation to determine a collision-free path to the goal. This paper proposes a system that addresses these complementary challenges. The proposed method, AirSplan, adopts a normalized variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that encodes high-fidelity scene geometry. It then applies a novel reachability-based motion planner that leverages the differential flatness of quadrotors to compute continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate the robot's occupancy. Experiments demonstrate that AirSplan successfully finds a path in 81.2% of challenging test cases, a significant improvement over the nearest baseline method's 51.2%.

AI.tldr: AirSplan combines normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting for high-fidelity 3D scene geometry with a reachability-based, continuous-time collision planner that uses quadrotor differential flatness to compute tight occupancy constraints; achieves 81.2% success in challenging cases, outperforming a baseline at 51.2%.
AI.motivation: Safe, collision-free navigation for aerial robots in cluttered 3D environments where obstacle data may be incomplete or unavailable; requires accurate scene representation and an effective planner to avoid collisions.
AI.method: Use normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting to encode high-fidelity scene geometry. Develop a reachability-based motion planner that leverages quadrotor differential flatness to generate continuous-time collision constraints, which tightly overapproximate the robot's occupancy during planning.
AI.result: Path is found in 81.2% of challenging test cases, significantly better than the nearest baseline method (51.2%).
AI.conclusion: Integrating a high-fidelity geometric representation with a tight, continuous-time collision-aware planner yields substantial improvements in path-finding success for quadrotors in challenging environments; highlights the benefit of combining expressive scene representations with reachability-based planning.

title: Accelerating Dense LLMs via L0-regularized Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance but suffer from slow and costly inference. Existing acceleration methods often lead to noticeable performance degradation, while Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models require extensive computational resources. In this paper, we propose L0-MoE, a lightweight MoE approach using L0-regularization to accelerate dense LLMs nearly without performance loss. Our method introduces a cluster confusion matrix for domain-aware dataset curation and applies dynamic batching for efficient training. Experiments show that L0-MoE achieves up to 2.5x speedup over dense models while maintaining competitive performance, outperforming existing LLM acceleration baselines.

AI.tldr: A lightweight MoE framework (L0-MoE) using L0-regularization to prune and route computations in dense LLMs, augmented by a cluster confusion matrix for domain-aware data curation and dynamic batching, achieving up to 2.5x speedup with minimal performance loss and beating baseline accelerators.
AI.motivation: To reduce inference cost and latency of LLMs while avoiding significant accuracy degradation; standard acceleration methods either harm quality or demand huge resources (MoE).
AI.method: Apply L0-regularization to gate or experts to encourage sparse usage; incorporate cluster confusion matrix to curate training data across domains; use dynamic batching to improve training efficiency; align with domain-aware dataset curation to train efficient routing.
AI.result: Up to 2.5x speedup over dense models; competitive performance; outperforms existing LLM acceleration baselines in experiments.
AI.conclusion: L0-MoE demonstrates that combining L0 sparsity with domain-aware data curation and dynamic batching can yield practical, fast LLMs with minimal performance loss; offers a viable path for efficient inference.

title: VoxelTTO: Voxel-Aligned Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Test-Time Optimization
summary: Recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods typically regress pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives, often causing excessive overlap and artifacts, while inaccuracies in predicted camera poses can lead to misalignment in novel-view synthesis (NVS). We present VoxelTTO, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing geometrically accurate 3DGS scenes from an arbitrary number of images and optional camera parameters. VoxelTTO aggregates dense image features into a global voxel representation and decodes Gaussians from voxel features, breaking the pixel-to-Gaussian correspondence. To exploit known camera parameters while keeping the pretrained visual foundation model (VFM) parameters frozen, we introduce test-time optimization (TTO) that adapts lightweight LoRA modules using pose supervision. We further replace vanilla 3DGS rasterization with stochastic solid volume rendering during training and inference, improving geometric fidelity. Training updates only the voxel-aligned Gaussian reconstruction modules, requiring 80 GPU hours. Experiments on Replica, Tanks and Temples, and DTU demonstrate improved RGB-D NVS and camera-pose estimation relative to prior methods.

AI.tldr: VoxelTTO enables geometrically accurate 3D Gaussian Splatting by aggregating dense image features into a global voxel grid, decoding Gaussians directly from voxel features, and using test-time LoRA-based pose supervision with stochastic volume rendering. It decouples pixel-Gaussian correspondence, improves NVS and pose estimation, and trains only a small module in ~80 GPU hours.
AI.motivation: Address the main limitations of current feed-forward 3DGS: excessive Gaussian overlap from pixel-aligned regressors and pose misalignment causing novel-view artifacts. A voxel-based global representation can enforce geometric fidelity while leveraging known camera parameters.
AI.method: Build a global voxel feature grid that aggregates dense image features and decodes Gaussians from voxel features (breaking pixel-to-Gaussian correspondence). Apply test-time optimization (LoRA adapters) with pose supervision while freezing the pretrained visual foundation model. Replace rasterization with stochastic solid volume rendering during training and inference. Train only the voxel-aligned Gaussian reconstruction modules (~80 GPU hours).
AI.result: On Replica, Tanks and Temples, and DTU, the approach yields improved RGB-D NVS and camera-pose estimation compared to prior 3DGS methods.
AI.conclusion: VoxelTTO demonstrates that voxel-based feature aggregation plus lightweight TTO and stochastic volume rendering can achieve geometrically faithful 3D Gaussian Splatting with efficient training and compatibility with pretrained visual models, outperforming pixel-aligned regressor approaches.

title: Routine Blood Tests Outperform CRP for Distinguishing Bacterial From Viral Infection in Children
summary: Acute infectious diseases are among the leading causes of medical consultations and hospitalizations in children worldwide. These infections are predominantly caused by viruses or bacteria, yet differentiating between the two remains a common clinical challenge. As a result, pediatricians often default to the safer option of prescribing antibiotics contributing to the growing problem of antimicrobial resistance. The objective is to assess the additional predictive value of CBC towards determining the current infection. This retrospective study used data from 906 pediatric patients aged between 2 and 14 years who were tested positive either for viral or bacterial infection between 2022 and 2026. Inclusion criteria further required availability of CBC results and CRP level measurements. These laboratory parameters as well as age were used as input features for several supervised classification models. Model performance was evaluated using AUC, sensitivity and specificity. The best performing model is XGBoost, which included all features, achieving out of-sample performance of AUC of 81.7% and sensitivity of 70.8%, specificity of 79.2%. All trained models outperform a CRP-based only decision-rule model in terms of AUC. We suggest that the decision to prescribe antibiotics should be based on a number of factors, including but not limited to CBC, some of which are not currently incorporated into routine practice.

AI.tldr: Using CBC and CRP with ML to distinguish viral vs bacterial infections in children; XGBoost with all features achieves AUC 0.817, sensitivity 0.708, specificity 0.792; all models beat CRP-only baseline.
AI.motivation: Addressing diagnostic uncertainty in pediatric infections to curb unnecessary antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance; explore predictive value of CBC alongside CRP.
AI.method: Retrospective study of 906 pediatric patients (ages 2–14) with confirmed viral or bacterial infection (2022–2026). Included if CBC and CRP data available. Features: CBC parameters, CRP, and age. Supervised classification models evaluated by AUC, sensitivity, specificity. XGBoost with all features performed best.
AI.result: Best model (XGBoost with all features) yielded out-of-sample AUC 81.7%, sensitivity 70.8%, specificity 79.2%. All trained models exceeded CRP-only decision-rule model by AUC.
AI.conclusion: CBC adds predictive value alongside CRP for differentiating viral vs bacterial infections; antibiotic prescribing decisions should consider multiple factors, including CBC, beyond current practice.

title: FOCAL-VLA: Subtask-Guided Geometry Distillation and Implicit World Modeling for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models built on pretrained vision-language models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. However, VLA models that directly map current 2D observations to actions often lack sufficient spatial and temporal understanding, limiting their performance in precise and long-horizon manipulation. Recent methods enhance VLA models through geometric supervision and future-state prediction across the entire scene. However, these methods can suffer from redundant scene information, distracting the model from learning the geometry and dynamics relevant to the current interaction. To address this issue, we propose FOCAL-VLA, a framework that combines subtask-guided geometry distillation with implicit world modeling to learn representations of current spatial structure and future interaction dynamics. To focus geometric learning on the current subtask, we transfer geometric knowledge from VGGT to the VLA model by aligning geometry latents with features from subtask-relevant image regions. To capture the future 3D evolution of the current interaction, we incorporate implicit world modeling using Track4World features from current and future demonstration frames. The two complementary representations jointly guide action generation without running VGGT or Track4World at inference time. Experiments show that FOCAL-VLA outperforms baselines on both simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. Project website: https://zhiyuan-gao.github.io/FOCAL-VLA/.

AI.tldr: FOCAL-VLA combines subtask-guided geometry distillation from VGGT with implicit world modeling (Track4World) to enhance vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation, focusing geometry learning on the current subtask and modeling future interaction dynamics without runtime VGGT/Track4World, yielding improved performance on both simulation and real tasks.
AI.motivation: Current VLA models that map 2D observations to actions lack precise spatial/temporal understanding. Global geometric supervision can introduce redundant information that distracts from task-relevant geometry and dynamics. A focused, subtask-guided approach combined with implicit future dynamics can improve performance.
AI.method: 1) Distill geometry latent representations from VGGT and align them with features from subtask-relevant image regions to focus geometry learning on the current interaction. 2) Employ implicit world modeling via Track4World features to capture the future 3D evolution of the current interaction from current and future frames. 3) Jointly train the two representations to guide action generation, with no VGGT or Track4World computation required at inference time. 4) Validate on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks; provide project website.
AI.result: FOCAL-VLA outperforms baselines on both simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Integrating subtask-guided geometry distillation with implicit world modeling yields stronger VLA performance by concentrating geometric learning on the relevant current subtask and encoding future dynamics, while maintaining efficient inference since VGGT/Track4World are not used at test time.

title: GUARD: Natural Forgetting in Large Reasoning Models via Guided Answer-Reasoning Distillation
summary: Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) have made machine unlearning more challenging, as protected facts or unsafe rationales may surface in intermediate chain-of-thought (CoT) traces before the final answer is produced. Existing unlearning objectives typically suppress the target content or redirect internal representations, but they never specify how the post-forgetting trajectory should continue, which can lead to hallucinated substitutes, malformed boundaries, or repetitive outputs. We argue that LRM unlearning should instead learn a natural forgetting trajectory: a coherent non-disclosing CoT followed by a stable refusal-style answer that replace the original disclosure. To this end, we propose Guided Answer-Reasoning Distillation (GUARD), which converts model-generated unsafe disclosures into safe-exit trajectories, aligns a frozen LRM via guidance tokens, and distills the guided behavior into model parameters.To address the lack of metrics for replacement quality beyond leakage, we further introduce Natural Forgetting Reasoning Score (NFRS), which captures structural stability, fluency, and unsupported substitutes in forgotten outputs. Extensive experiments on R-TOFU and a STAR-1-derived harmful-intent setting show that GUARD substantially reduces unsafe and privacy disclosures across two widely adopted distilled LRMs while preserving reasoning utility. Codes are available at https://github.com/zeyu-Yan/GUARD

AI.tldr: GUARD distills safe exit trajectories from unsafe chain-of-thought in large reasoning models, aligning a frozen LRM with guidance tokens and distilling the policy into parameters; introduces NFRS to measure replacement quality; shows reduced unsafe disclosures on R-TOFU and STAR-1 with preserved reasoning utility; code released.
AI.motivation: LRMs can leak protected facts or unsafe rationales during intermediate CoT traces; existing unlearning methods suppress content but do not define a coherent post-forgetting trajectory, risking hallucinated substitutes or repetitive outputs.
AI.method: 1) Transform model-generated unsafe disclosures into safe-exit trajectories (safe CoT plus a refusal). 2) Align a frozen LRM via guidance tokens. 3) Distill the guided behavior into model parameters (fine-tuning). 4) Propose Natural Forgetting Reasoning Score (NFRS) to evaluate structure, fluency, and absence of unsupported substitutes.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on R-TOFU and STAR-1 harmful-intent settings shows GUARD substantially reduces unsafe/privacy disclosures for two distilled LRMs, while preserving reasoning utility.
AI.conclusion: GUARD provides a coherent forgetting trajectory and a quantitative replacement-quality metric (NFRS); applicable to post-forgetting safety in LRMs, with publicly available code; further work could broaden tasks and models and refine evaluation.

title: Adaptive World Memory 3D Foundation Model for Scalable 3D Mapping, Localization, and Rendering
summary: Recent 3D foundation models enable generalizable geometric reasoning from RGB images but remain limited in persistent memory, scalability, and renderable scene modeling. We present a memory-centric 3D foundation model for scalable robotic localization, reconstruction, and Gaussian rendering. Its core is an adaptive world memory mechanism that combines transformer-based gated updates with test-time temporal-spatial regulation. Learned gates control recurrent memory propagation, while temporal state evolution and spatial observation-state consistency regulate token-wise updates and forgetting over long image sequences. To support large-scale mapping, we organize memory into local submaps and integrate progressive mapping and tracking, loop closure, and SL(4)-based global refinement to maintain local accuracy and global consistency. A Gaussian reconstruction head decodes memory-enhanced features into renderable primitives, unifying camera pose estimation, dense point-cloud reconstruction, and photorealistic rendering within a single model. Experiments on public benchmarks and self-collected datasets from diverse robotic platforms demonstrate improved trajectory accuracy, reconstruction completeness, and rendering quality over existing 3D foundation reconstruction and SLAM baselines. These results support adaptive memory as a foundation for persistent robotic world modeling. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/dtc111111/AWM-3DFM}{https://github.com/dtc111111/AWM-3DFM}.

AI.tldr: Memory-centric 3D foundation model for scalable, persistent robotic localization, reconstruction, and rendering using adaptive world memory with gated transformer updates, temporal-spatial regulation, local submaps, loop closure, and GL refinement.
AI.motivation: 3D foundation models excel at reasoning from RGB but struggle with persistent memory, scalability, and renderable scene modeling for long-term robotic operation. A memory-based approach aims to unify localization, reconstruction, and rendering while maintaining global consistency across large environments.
AI.method: An adaptive world memory mechanism couples transformer-based gated updates with test-time temporal-spatial regulation. Learned gates control memory propagation; temporal evolution and spatial observation-state consistency regulate updates/forgetting. Memory is organized into local submaps; progressive mapping/tracking, loop closure, and SL(4)-based global refinement ensure local accuracy and global consistency. A Gaussian reconstruction head decodes memory-enhanced features into renderable primitives, unifying camera pose estimation, dense point-cloud reconstruction, and photorealistic rendering in a single model.
AI.result: Experiments on public benchmarks and diverse robotic datasets show improved trajectory accuracy, reconstruction completeness, and rendering quality compared with existing 3D foundation reconstruction and SLAM baselines. The approach demonstrates enhanced persistent world modeling capabilities; dataset and code will be released publicly.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive memory provides a foundation for persistent robotic world modeling by unifying localization, mapping, and rendering in a scalable, memory-driven 3D foundation model.

title: IntBMoE: Integrating Block-Level Conditioning into Expert Composition for Full-Participation Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales capacity, but existing designs cannot set three quantities independently. For a single token, participation is how many experts contribute knowledge to its output, execution is how many are actually computed (compute cost), and materialization is how many expert-sized parameter sets must be built and stored (memory cost). Sparse routing keeps execution and materialization low, but shrinks participation: for each token, only a few experts contribute. Dense output-mixing restores full participation, but its execution grows with the number of experts. Parameter-merging keeps execution at one expert, but its materialization grows with the number of routing decisions. We propose IntBMoE, a block-conditioned MoE that decouples all three by pairing dense expert composition with sparse block execution. Its blocks come from a small learned codebook, one per entry. At each internal layer, a lightweight hypernetwork merges all expert bases in that layer's pool into one composed expert. Participation is full, because every composed expert draws on the entire pool. Execution stays sparse, because a router sends each token to only a few blocks. Materialization is bounded, because the codebook, not the input, fixes how many blocks exist. Dual-Path Residual Gating (DPRG) further couples two independently composed paths through multiplicative gating. Experiments on image classification show consistent gains over representative sparse and dense MoE baselines. Additional experiments on language modeling and sequential recommendation validate its generalization beyond vision. IntBMoE is fully deployed in AMap's generative recommendation system, serving hundreds of millions of users under a 60ms latency budget, with a 2.4% relative UVCTR gain in online A/B testing. Our code is available at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/DreamX-Rec/.

AI.tldr: IntBMoE is a block-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts that decouples participation, execution, and materialization by using a dense composed expert path via a small codebook of blocks, sparse routing, and a per-layer hypernetwork. It achieves gains across vision, language, and recommendations, with practical deployment in a 60ms latency system.
AI.motivation: MoE designs trade off participation (how many experts contribute), execution (compute cost), and materialization (memory cost). Existing approaches cannot independently control all three, limiting scalable capacity with low latency. IntBMoE decouples these factors to enable full participation with sparse execution and bounded materialization.
AI.method: Introduce IntBMoE: blocks derived from a learned codebook; at each layer a lightweight hypernetwork merges all expert bases in the layer's pool into a single composed expert. Participation is full (every composed block uses the full pool), execution is sparse (router sends tokens to only a few blocks), and materialization is fixed by the codebook. Dual-Path Residual Gating (DPRG) couples two independently composed paths via multiplicative gating. Evaluated on image classification (and generalization to language modeling and sequential recommendation); deployed in AMap's generative recommendation system with a 60 ms latency budget.
AI.result: IntBMoE shows consistent gains over representative sparse and dense MoE baselines in image classification; generalizes to language modeling and sequential recommendation. In online A/B tests within AMap, it yields a 2.4% relative UVCTR gain with 60 ms latency and hundreds of millions of users affected; code is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: IntBMoE provides independent control over participation, execution, and materialization in MoE, achieving high-capacity models with efficient inference and proven real-world impact. The approach generalizes across modalities and tasks and is accompanied by open-source code.

title: KnowDemo: Knowledge-Guided Robot Demonstration Generation from Human Videos
summary: Learning robot manipulation policies typically requires substantial demonstration data, which are costly to collect on real robots. Recent methods generate robot demonstrations from human videos by adapting recovered motion and validating the resulting trajectories in simulation. However, methods centered on motion-reference adaptation can limit behavioral diversity by retaining the demonstrated contact strategies and subtask orders, while insufficient understanding of task requirements and scene relations can reduce demonstration generation efficiency by generating invalid candidates. To address these limitations, we propose KnowDemo, a framework that uses structured manipulation knowledge from human videos to generate diverse robot demonstrations for a target workspace. To distinguish task requirements from demonstration-specific choices, we develop a knowledge extraction and reasoning module based on a vision-language model (VLM) that associates object and action descriptions with inferred task conditions, demonstration references, and permissible execution variations. To translate this knowledge into executable demonstrations, we resolve the descriptions against target-scene entities and geometry to guide candidate generation and screening before motion planning and simulation. The resulting demonstrations exhibit multimodal behavior through alternative contact strategies and valid subtask orders, with structured execution labels. Experiments demonstrate additional verified execution modes beyond a reference-only configuration and improved candidate planning success through task-guided grasp sampling. To validate the generated data for policy learning, we fine-tune the pretrained $π_{0.5}$ model on simulation data, achieving sim-to-real transfer across three tasks. Project page: https://zhiyuan-gao.github.io/knowdemo/

AI.tldr: KnowDemo creates diverse robot demonstrations from human videos by extracting structured knowledge with a vision-language model to guide generation, enabling multimodal behaviors and better sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Collecting substantial real-robot demonstrations is costly. Motion-reference adaptation can limit behavioral diversity and may fail to capture task requirements and scene relations, reducing generation efficiency and validity of candidates.
AI.method: Build a knowledge extraction and reasoning module using a vision-language model to link object/action descriptions with inferred task conditions, demonstration references, and permissible execution variations. Resolve descriptions against target scene entities and geometry to guide candidate generation and screening before motion planning and simulation. Enable multimodal demonstrations with alternative contact strategies and subtask orders, and provide structured execution labels. Use task-guided grasp sampling.
AI.result: Demonstrations exhibit multimodal behavior and additional verified execution modes beyond a reference-only configuration. Planning success improves with task-guided grasp sampling. Fine-tuning the pretrained π0.5 model on simulation data yields sim-to-real transfer across three tasks.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-guided demonstration generation enhances diversity and planning efficiency, aiding policy learning and sim-to-real transfer. A project page provides further resources and results.

title: Listen Before You Speak: Response Planning from Listener Facial Reactions for Conversational Speech Generation
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 2026 ECCV Workshop (11th ABAW) Best Student Paper Award
summary: Conversational speech depends on dialogue context and the listener's immediately preceding behavior. We propose ReACT-TTS, a two-stage framework that uses a one-second pre-response listener facial sequence to plan the next utterance's emotion and prosody before speech realization. On a strict dyadic MELD protocol, Temporal conditioning yields higher mean macro-F1 and VAD concordance than Text-only across ten seeds, while accuracy remains essentially unchanged. Ablations show that temporal modeling performs best among the visual variants and that an explicit early-to-late difference is unnecessary; correct listener reactions also outperform cyclic mismatches on average. In a contextual-appropriateness study with 20 speech researchers, 76% of judgments prefer Temporal, 9% Text-only, and 15% report no preference. We further connect the predicted response style to a Grad-TTS backbone for end-to-end speech realization. Overall, the results support pre-response listener dynamics as complementary cues for conversational response planning. The source code is available at https://github.com/CYJ1/ReACT-TTS_public.

AI.tldr: A two-stage ReACT-TTS uses a one-second pre-response listener facial sequence to plan emotion/prosody for the next utterance; temporal conditioning improves MELD protocol metrics versus text-only; ablations favor temporal modeling; listener reactions outperform mismatches; 76% of experts prefer Temporal; Grad-TTS enables end-to-end synthesis; code available.
AI.motivation: To enhance conversational speech by incorporating the listener's immediately preceding visual behavior into planning the speaker's next utterance, aiming to improve emotional alignment and prosodic naturalness.
AI.method: A two-stage framework (ReACT-TTS) that conditions on a one-second pre-response listener facial sequence to plan emotion and prosody before speech realization. Evaluations on a strict dyadic MELD protocol compare Temporal conditioning to Text-only across multiple seeds; ablations assess visual variants and the necessity of early-to-late differences; a contextual-appropriateness study with 20 speech researchers assesses human judgments. End-to-end realization via a Grad-TTS backbone.
AI.result: Temporal conditioning yields higher mean macro-F1 and VAD concordance than Text-only across ten seeds; accuracy is unchanged. Temporal modeling outperforms other visual variants; explicit early-to-late separation is unnecessary. Correct listener reactions outperform cyclic mismatches. In a study with 20 researchers, 76% prefer Temporal, 9% Text-only, 15% no preference. End-to-end realization with Grad-TTS is demonstrated. Source code available at the referenced GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Pre-response listener dynamics serve as complementary cues for conversational response planning, improving prosodic and emotional alignment with the listener. This approach supports more natural, contextually appropriate dialogue and can be integrated end-to-end with TTS backbones.

title: 2D GauSS-MI: Efficient Active Scene Reconstruction with Balanced Visual and Geometric Quality
summary: Active reconstruction requires efficient active view selection to achieve high-quality reconstruction within limited onboard computational resources. Existing methods face challenges in adequately balancing visual and geometric quality with the computational efficiency required for real-time operation. In this work, we present an active reconstruction framework based on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). We develop an efficient online 2DGS mapping pipeline for incremental RGB-D observations and introduce a probabilistic reliability model that characterizes the view-dependent reconstruction quality of individual 2D Gaussian splats. Building on this model, we formulate 2D Gaussian Splatting Shannon Mutual Information (2D GauSS-MI), a mutual-information-based metric that exploits the explicit surface orientation of 2DGS to evaluate the expected information gain of candidate views. The proposed metric enables active view selection to account for both visual and geometric reconstruction quality. We evaluate the proposed system against three state-of-the-art baselines on eight Replica scenes. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a favorable balance between visual and geometric reconstruction quality with substantially lower computational cost and competitive model storage.

AI.tldr: 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) for active reconstruction with MI-based view selection (2D GauSS-MI); an efficient online RGB-D mapping pipeline, a probabilistic reliability model for splats, and a mutual-information criterion that accounts for surface orientation to balance visual and geometric quality under limited onboard resources; evaluated on Replica scenes with favorable results and lower compute/storage.
AI.motivation: To achieve high-quality 3D reconstruction under real-time constraints by balancing visual fidelity and geometric accuracy with computational efficiency, via an active view selection framework.
AI.method: Develop an online 2DGS mapping pipeline for incremental RGB-D data; introduce a probabilistic reliability model for view-dependent splat quality; formulate 2D GauSS-MI mutual-information metric that uses explicit surface orientation of 2DGS to estimate expected information gain of candidate views and guide active view selection.
AI.result: The proposed method demonstrates a favorable balance between visual and geometric reconstruction quality with substantially lower computational cost and competitive model storage, outperforming baselines on eight Replica scenes.
AI.conclusion: A geometry-aware, computationally efficient active reconstruction framework based on 2D Gaussian splatting and MI-based view selection, enabling effective real-time reconstruction with good visual/geometry quality and lower resource usage.

title: Knowledge-Graph-Augmented Chronos-2 for HEC-RAS Surrogate Forecasting
summary: We investigate whether coupling a time-series foundation model to hydraulic project knowledge improves surrogate forecasting of HEC-RAS water-surface elevation (WSE). We present KG-Chronos-2, which combines a frozen Chronos-2 predictor with exact-state residual decoding, graph-conditioned historical retrieval, and input-aligned correction. We compare the method with persistence, a residual LSTM, project-conditioned recurrent GeoFNO, a hydraulic DCRNN-style model, and frozen Chronos-2. Task-specific fitting uses the 2008 simulation. Evaluation covers 64 fixed 24-hour windows from the 2011 and 2002 simulations at 4,675 cross sections in 71 reaches on a shared geometry. KG-Chronos-2 achieves event-balanced root-mean-square error 0.246970 in native WSE units. It reduces RMSE by 14.13% relative to frozen Chronos-2, 29.38% relative to the hydraulic DCRNN-style model, and 39.54% relative to recurrent GeoFNO. The 95% hierarchical-bootstrap interval for its event-balanced RMSE difference from frozen Chronos-2 is [-0.075177, -0.016317]. KG-Chronos-2 also achieves the lowest active-window and final-lead RMSE among the six completed systems. These results support coupling a frozen temporal predictor to project knowledge for warm-start HEC-RAS forecasting on the fixed benchmark.

AI.tldr: A frozen temporal predictor augmented with hydraulic knowledge improves HEC-RAS WSE forecasting; KG-Chronos-2 outperform baselines on a fixed benchmark with strong RMSE gains.
AI.motivation: Improve surrogate WSE forecasting by fusing data-driven temporal models with project-specific hydraulic knowledge to leverage complementary strengths.
AI.method: KG-Chronos-2 combines a frozen Chronos-2 predictor with exact-state residual decoding, graph-conditioned historical retrieval, and input-aligned correction. Training uses a 2008 simulation; evaluation spans 64 fixed 24-hr windows from 2011 and 2002 simulations across 4,675 cross sections in 71 reaches on a shared geometry.
AI.result: Event-balanced RMSE of 0.246970 (native WSE units). RMSE reductions: 14.13% vs frozen Chronos-2; 29.38% vs hydraulic DCRNN-style model; 39.54% vs recurrent GeoFNO. 95% hierarchical-bootstrap interval for RMSE difference vs frozen Chronos-2: [-0.075177, -0.016317]. KG-Chronos-2 achieves the lowest active-window and final-lead RMSE among six systems.
AI.conclusion: Coupling a frozen temporal predictor with project knowledge yields improved warm-start HEC-RAS forecasting on a fixed benchmark, supporting hybrid data-driven/physics-based surrogate modeling for hydraulic forecasting.

title: VLA-Scope: Shift-Aware Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robotic actions, but distribution shifts can compromise their reliability. Because these models may still succeed under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, detecting OOD inputs alone is insufficient to predict execution failure. In this paper, we introduce VLA-Scope, a two-stage framework that combines input-shift characterization with execution history to predict failure during OOD rollouts. The first stage uses pooled image and language representations to detect OOD inputs and classify their shift categories. For inputs flagged as OOD, the second stage combines the predicted category, action-prefix features, and execution progress features. A logistic regression model shared across shift categories updates failure risk as execution proceeds. We evaluate the framework with OpenVLA on ten LIBERO-Spatial tasks using leave-one-group-out cross-validation. OOD detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.9454, and shift classification achieves 91% accuracy. Evaluated independently of the OOD gate on all 1,400 OOD rollouts, the failure predictor achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.8497 after 60 executed actions, compared with 0.7906 without execution progress features. It also achieves a higher ROC-AUC than the evaluated ActProbe and SAFE-MLP baselines. These results suggest that combining action features with temporally aggregated execution step representations improves failure prediction under input shifts.

AI.tldr: VLA-Scope presents a two-stage framework to predict failures of Vision-Language-Action models under input shifts by combining input-shift characterization with execution-history features, improving failure prediction beyond baseline methods.
AI.motivation: VLA models often encounter distribution shifts that degrade reliability. Detecting OOD inputs alone does not guarantee failure prediction; leveraging execution history could better anticipate failures during rollouts.
AI.method: Stage 1: pool image/text representations to detect OOD and classify shift type. Stage 2: for OOD inputs, fuse predicted shift category with action-prefix and execution-progress features, using a shared logistic regression predictor updated across shift categories to estimate failure risk as rollout progresses. Evaluation uses OpenVLA on LIBERO-Spatial tasks with leave-one-group-out CV; OOD detection ROC-AUC=0.9454; shift classification accuracy=91%; failure predictor ROC-AUC=0.8497 after 60 actions; comparisons show improvement over baselines ActProbe and SAFE-MLP.
AI.result: The framework achieves strong OOD detection and shift classification, and a notable improvement in failure prediction when incorporating execution-progress features, outperforming relevant baselines on 1,400 OOD rollouts.
AI.conclusion: Combining input-shift characterization with temporally aggregated execution features yields more reliable failure prediction for VLA policies under distribution shifts, suggesting a viable path to safer and more dependable robots in OOD settings.

title: World Modeling in Transformers
summary: Behavioral failures can make a transformer appear to lack a world model even when it has learned faithful representations of its environment. We demonstrate this in TaxiGPT, a transformer trained on random walks through Manhattan whose failures have been interpreted as evidence of an incoherent internal map. Through mechanistic analysis and causal interventions, we show that the model represents intersections and streets, tracks its position, and uses a goal compass to navigate. We trace its failures to interference between superposed intersection features, which disrupts localization within the internal map. Affordance packing, which groups representations of intersections with the same legal moves, helps limit the consequences of these errors. Finally, we propose mechanistic indicators that we use to compare models and show that world-modeling capacities emerge at different stages of training. Our findings motivate a shift from asking whether a model has a world model to mechanistically studying its world modeling: the interacting capacities through which it represents its environment and uses those representations to guide behavior.

AI.tldr: The TaxiGPT study shows a transformer trained on random walks through Manhattan develops an internal map of streets and intersections; apparent world-model failures arise from interference between overlapping features; affordance packing mitigates errors; mechanistic indicators enable comparison and reveal world-modeling emerges at different training stages.
AI.motivation: To move beyond a binary question of whether models have world models and instead mechanistically dissect the interacting capacities through which a model represents its environment and uses those representations to guide behavior.
AI.method: Mechanistic analysis and causal interventions on TaxiGPT, examining representations of intersections and streets, tracking position, and a goal compass for navigation; identifying interference between superposed intersection features as the source of localization errors; introducing affordance packing to group representations by legal moves.
AI.result: The model develops map-like representations with localization capabilities; failures are due to interference between superposed features; affordance packing reduces error propagation; proposed mechanistic indicators allow cross-model comparisons; world-modeling capabilities emerge at different points during training.
AI.conclusion: Encourage a shift from asking whether a model has a world model to mechanistically studying the interacting capacities that constitute world modeling and guide behavior; provide indicators to compare models and track the emergence of world-modeling during training.

title: VidOmni-Bench: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Video Understanding via Spatio-Temporal Event Verification across Complexity and Duration
summary: While Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have recently demonstrated strong performance, reliably evaluating their fine-grained video understanding remains challenging. Existing benchmarks often rely on question answering or ground-truth caption matching, where models may succeed through superficial cues and incomplete annotations. To this end, we introduce VidOmni-Bench, a benchmark that requires models to verify whether each event in dense video captions is supported by the video. VidOmni-Bench consists of 500 videos spanning five complexity types and diverse durations from 4 seconds to 90 minutes. After collecting videos along these axes, we use diverse Video-LLMs to generate dense captions and obtain human-verified sentence-level labels, where sentences containing incorrect events serve as hard negatives for evaluation. Our experiments on VidOmni-Bench reveal three key findings: (i) Video-LLMs frequently generate hallucinated descriptions in dense video captioning; (ii) they also struggle as verifiers, failing to reliably detect plausible but incorrect event descriptions; and (iii) model weaknesses vary across video complexity and duration, revealing diverse, model-specific bottlenecks in current Video-LLMs.

AI.tldr: VidOmni-Bench is a dense-caption verification benchmark for video understanding that exposes hallucinations and verification weaknesses in Video-LLMs, revealing model-specific bottlenecks across complexity and duration.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks rely on QA or caption matching and can be gamed by superficial cues; a fine-grained, sentence-level verification test is needed to assess true understanding of video events.
