AI.method: Construct 500 videos across five complexity types and durations 4s–90min; generate dense captions with Video-LLMs; collect human-verified sentence-level labels; use incorrect-event sentences as hard negatives; evaluate LLMs on their ability to verify each event's support from the video.
AI.result: Three key findings: (i) widespread hallucinations in dense captions; (ii) verifiers struggle to reject plausible but incorrect events; (iii) weaknesses are context-dependent, varying with video complexity and duration, indicating model-specific bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: VidOmni-Bench reveals gaps in current Video-LLMs and provides a challenging evaluation paradigm to push robust, verifiable video understanding with hard negatives; potential to guide future model and dataset design.

title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Business Process Executions with Neural Temporal Point Processes
summary: Operators of service-based systems act on forecasts of how a running execution will continue, and such a forecast is actionable only if its reliability is known. Mainstream deep-learning models for this task are discriminative and deterministic: they emit a single next activity and a single remaining-time estimate, without a distribution to reason over. We instead cast the problem as generative sequence modelling with marked temporal point processes, which define a joint density over the next mark and its inter-event time and therefore deliver predictive distributions by construction. Real event logs violate the simple-point-process assumption these models rest on, since consecutive events frequently carry identical timestamps; we handle such ties explicitly and combine a transformer encoder with a mixture decoder over inter-event times, trained by exact log-likelihood. On ten public logs, the resulting model matches discriminative baselines on point accuracy, dominates them on the calibration and sharpness of remaining-time distributions, and is the cheapest at inference, since a full predictive distribution is obtained in a single forward pass without sampling.

AI.tldr: Generative sequence model for service-based forecasts using marked temporal point processes (TPP) with a Transformer encoder and mixture decoder, handling timestamps ties, yielding a full predictive distribution in one forward pass and improving calibration/sharpness over discriminative baselines while retaining point accuracy and reducing inference cost.
AI.motivation: Provide actionable forecasts with calibrated predictive distributions for remaining time and next event in running processes, addressing the lack of uncertainty in discriminative models and the mismatch between real event logs (with tied timestamps) and simple-point-process assumptions.
AI.method: Define a joint density over the next event and its inter-event time via marked temporal point processes. Use a Transformer encoder to summarize history and a mixture-decoder over inter-event times. Explicitly handle ties in timestamps. Train with exact log-likelihood. Inference yields a full predictive distribution in a single forward pass (no sampling).
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on ten public logs shows parity with discriminative baselines on point accuracy, superior calibration and sharpness of remaining-time distributions, and lower inference cost due to one-pass generation of the full distribution without sampling.
AI.conclusion: A generative TPP approach with proper handling of timestamp ties provides well-calibrated, sharp predictive distributions for service-based process forecasting while maintaining competitive point accuracy and offering efficient inference compared to sampling-based methods.

title: LOInK: Learned Optimal Inverse Kinematics via Structured Neural Surrogate Models
summary: We introduce Learned Optimal Inverse Kinematics (LOInK), a method to generate approximately optimal solutions to an inverse kinematics problem. When trained on data consisting of sampled configurations and associated task variables and a given cost function, LOInK learns a bi-Lipschitz invertible mapping from configuration space to a decoupled task/latent space, and moreover, the latent space is structured so as to place cost-minimizing solutions at the origin. This enables efficient sampling of cost-minimizing solutions via a network-inversion algorithm based on operator splitting. We demonstrate the proposed approach on three problems: an illustrative three degree-of-freedom manipulator problem; a quadrupedal climbing robot for which LOInK can generate near-optimal solutions on average 31 times faster and up to 100 times faster than a constrained optimization approach; and a simulated soft actuator as a purely data-driven example, in which LOInK can explicitly generate high-quality solutions, unlike existing generative approaches that require diverse sampling and evaluation of candidate solutions.

AI.tldr: A data-driven method (LOInK) learns a bi-Lipschitz inverse mapping from configuration space to a decoupled task/latent space, with cost-minimizers placed at origin, enabling fast network-inversion via operator splitting to generate near-optimal IK solutions; demonstrated with three robotic systems, showing large speedups over constrained optimization and explicit high-quality solutions without dense sampling.
AI.motivation: Efficiently producing cost-minimizing inverse kinematics solutions in high-dimensional robots; overcome slow optimization by learning structured latent space where cost-minimizing configurations concentrate at the origin.
AI.method: Train a neural mapping that is bi-Lipschitz invertible from configuration space to a decoupled task/latent space; structure latent space so cost-minimizers map to origin; use a network-inversion algorithm based on operator splitting to sample solutions; trained on data of configurations, task variables, and a given cost function.
AI.result: Illustrative 3-DOF manipulator; quadrupedal climbing robot with 31x faster on average and up to 100x faster than constrained optimization; simulated soft actuator where LOInK yields explicit high-quality solutions, outperforming generative baselines requiring diverse sampling.
AI.conclusion: LOInK provides near-optimal IK solutions efficiently via learned invertible mapping and operator-splitting inversion; achieves substantial speedups and accurate solutions across diverse robotic problems; suggests broad applicability to data-driven IK with cost functions.

title: ECG Mirage: Revealing and Mitigating the Underutilisation of ECGs in Vision-Language Models for Clinical Prediction
summary: Emergency department (ED) decision-making relies on heterogeneous clinical information, including patient history, vital signs, laboratory results, and electrocardiograms (ECGs). Vision--language models (VLMs) can jointly process these modalities, but strong predictive performance does not necessarily imply meaningful use of the correct patient's ECG. We term this failure mode ECG Mirage: apparent multimodal capability without useful dependence on patient-specific ECG information. We distinguish two forms: ECG neglect, where ECGs provide little predictive benefit, and ECG confusion, where matched ECGs outperform no-image inputs but not mismatched ECGs. To evaluate these behaviours, we compare predictions obtained with matched ECGs, outcome-discordant mismatched ECGs, and no-image inputs while holding the clinical text and prediction targets fixed. Across four VLMs on MDS-ED, matched ECGs provide no consistent advantage for either ICU admission or clinical deterioration prediction. We then train four restricted visual prompts using supervised learning followed by conditional direct preference optimisation, while keeping the VLM backbone frozen. The resulting models achieve balanced accuracies of 70.6% for ICU admission and 67.5% for deterioration and increase the matched-versus-mismatched performance gap to approximately 16.5 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively. Overall, our study identifies ECG Mirage in multimodal clinical prediction and introduces visual prompt tuning as an efficient mitigation strategy.

AI.tldr: Defines 'ECG Mirage' as a failure mode in multimodal ED prediction where ECGs do not meaningfully contribute; identifies ECG neglect and ECG confusion; finds matched ECGs offer no consistent benefit; shows visual prompt tuning mitigates this and yields competitive accuracies.
AI.motivation: To determine whether vision-language models truly leverage patient-specific ECG information in multimodal ED prediction and to prevent reliance on spurious multimodal cues.
AI.method: Evaluate four VLMs on MDS-ED using matched ECGs, outcome-discordant mismatched ECGs, and no-image inputs; hold clinical text and targets fixed; train four restricted visual prompts with supervised learning and conditional direct preference optimization while freezing the backbone; compare ICU admission and deterioration predictions.
AI.result: Matched ECGs provide no consistent advantage; ECG Mirage identified (two forms: ECG neglect and ECG confusion). Prompt tuning increases gap between matched and mismatched ECG performance (≈16.5pp for ICU, ≈5.5pp for deterioration); final balanced accuracies: 70.6% (ICU) and 67.5% (deterioration).
AI.conclusion: ECG Mirage limits the presumed multimodal advantage of ECGs in VLM-based ED predictions; visual prompt tuning offers an efficient mitigation strategy without altering the backbone.

title: Refine Then Fusion: Training-Free 3D Point Cloud Adaptation with Priority Refinement and Multi-Modal Knowledge Fusion
summary: Recent pre-trained foundation models provide rich multi-modal priors for downstream 3D vision tasks. However, the effectiveness of these representations in few-shot scenarios is limited by two fundamental challenges: High-dimensional features often contain substantial channel redundancy and task-irrelevant noise, while the reliability of different modalities varies across samples. Consequently, direct aggregation of heterogeneous representations overlooks sample-dependent modality reliability and may obscure the discriminative cues essential. To address these limitations, we propose Refine Then Fusion(RTF), a training-free framework for few-shot 3D recognition. RTF first identifies discriminative feature channels by jointly modeling inter-class similarity and intra-class stability, thereby decoupling domain-specific knowledge refinement from the cached representations of pre-trained models. It then introduces a reliability-aware fusion mechanism that estimates sample-wise modality reliability from the distribution shifts induced by feature refinement, enabling adaptive aggregation of multi-modal representations. Furthermore, RTF constructs a memory cache that integrates instance-level support features with class-level prototypes to infer query labels. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that RTF consistently outperforms single-modal baselines, partial-fusion variants, and existing lightweight adaptation methods, achieving state-of-the-art few-shot 3D recognition performance without gradient optimization, additional training data, auxiliary training, or parameter updates.

AI.tldr: RTF is a training-free, multi-modal fusion framework for few-shot 3D recognition that refines discriminative feature channels and uses reliability-aware fusion, plus a memory cache, achieving state-of-the-art performance without gradient updates.
AI.motivation: In few-shot 3D vision, high-dimensional features exhibit channel redundancy and task-irrelevant noise, and modality reliability varies across samples. Direct heterogeneous fusion can obscure discriminative cues. A training-free approach is needed to exploit pre-trained multi-modal priors while adapting to sample-specific reliability.
AI.method: RTF consists of two stages: (1) channel refinement by jointly modeling inter-class similarity and intra-class stability to identify discriminative feature channels, decoupling domain refinement from cached representations; (2) reliability-aware fusion that estimates sample-wise modality reliability from distribution shifts induced by refinement, enabling adaptive aggregation of multi-modal features. A memory cache combines instance-level support features with class prototypes to infer query labels. No gradient updates or extra training data required.
AI.result: Experiments on five benchmarks show RTF consistently surpasses single-modal baselines, partial-fusion variants, and existing lightweight adaptation methods, achieving state-of-the-art few-shot 3D recognition performance without gradient optimization, additional training data, auxiliary training, or parameter updates.
AI.conclusion: RTF provides a training-free, reliability-aware, multi-modal fusion framework for few-shot 3D recognition that effectively leverages pre-trained representations, yielding robust improvements across benchmarks without additional training.

title: Tracing the Evidence Behind Zero-Shot Time-Series Forecasting: A Source-First Taxonomy and Audit Framework
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to ACM AI Summit 2026 (Visionary Papers)
summary: Zero-shot time-series forecasting (TSF) is often described as forecasting without target-specific parameter updates, but that training-status condition does not specify what evidence the system may use. A frozen language model prompted with serialized values, a time-series model pretrained on broad forecasting corpora, and a retrieval-augmented forecaster may all satisfy the no-update condition while drawing on different transferable evidence. This paper argues that zero-shot TSF should therefore be governed as an evidence-access claim. We propose a source-first taxonomy that separates three primary evidence sources---frozen LLM prior reuse, parametric time-series pretraining, and retrieval-augmented external memory---from the architectures that implement them. After the source is identified, four additional audit questions remain: task interface, forecast object and scoring, prediction-time context, and resource budget. The resulting agenda is to make zero-shot leaderboards auditable by reporting evidence boundaries and interface assumptions alongside scores, so that benchmark progress reflects transferable forecasting capability rather than undisclosed changes in context, memory, or budget.

AI.tldr: A source-first taxonomy for zero-shot time-series forecasting (TSF) that identifies three evidence sources (frozen LLM prior reuse, parametric TS pretraining, retrieval-augmented external memory) and four audit questions to make zero-shot benchmarks auditable by reporting evidence boundaries and interface assumptions alongside scores.
AI.motivation: To clarify what counts as zero-shot in TSF, avoid conflating no-update with transferable evidence, and ensure benchmarking progress reflects genuine transferable forecasting capability rather than undisclosed context/memory/budget changes.
AI.method: Proposes a taxonomy that separates evidence sources from architectures, detailing three primary evidence sources; and outlines four audit questions (task interface, forecast object and scoring, prediction-time context, resource budget) to guide auditing and leaderboard reporting.
AI.result: A framework for auditing zero-shot TSF benchmarks; guidance for reporting evidence sources and interface assumptions to accompany performance scores, enabling fair comparisons across methods with different inference-time contexts.
AI.conclusion: Auditable zero-shot TSF benchmarks should disclose evidence sources and interface assumptions; progress should reflect transferable forecasting ability rather than undetected changes in context, memory, or budget.

title: Stability-aware Residual Reinforcement Learning Framework for Robotic Manipulator Disturbance Compensation
summary: Although conventional controllers and disturbance observers (DOBs) are the standard for precision tracking in manipulators, they suffer from parameter uncertainty, nonlinear friction, and compound disturbances. This study proposes a residual reinforcement learning DOB framework that pairs an analytical observer with an RL policy. The deterministic baseline operates within a reliable region, whereas the RL policy explicitly targets the residuals that the model cannot capture. To make this compensation disturbance-aware, an estimator network aligns the observation history with a privileged disturbance context, organizing the latent space by disturbance regime and enabling rapid adaptation across disturbance transitions. To guarantee stability, we derived and enforced a state-dependent action bound on the RL policy from an input-to-state stability (ISS) analysis such that the closed loop provably confines the tracking error to a certified envelope for arbitrary policy outputs. Experiments on a 6-DOF manipulator demonstrated consistent improvements in disturbance estimation and tracking, including a 27.8% tracking-error reduction on real hardware under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and a 38.0% reduction under a base-vibration disturbance that was not observed during training.

AI.tldr: Residual RL-based disturbance observer augments an analytical DOB with a residual policy to handle parameter uncertainty and disturbances in 6-DOF manipulator tracking, with ISS-based stability guarantees and state-dependent action bounds, yielding notable tracking improvements including zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Conventional DOBs struggle with model mismatches, nonlinear friction, and compound disturbances, leading to degraded precision. A framework that leverages RL to compensate residual dynamics while guaranteeing stability and disturbance sensitivity is sought.
AI.method: Combine a deterministic analytical observer with a reinforcement learning policy that targets residual dynamics. An estimator network maps observation history to a privileged disturbance context, organizing latent space by disturbance regime for fast adaptation. An ISS-based analysis yields a state-dependent action bound for the RL policy to ensure the closed-loop tracking error remains within a certified envelope under arbitrary policy outputs.
AI.result: Experimental validation on a 6-DOF manipulator shows consistent improvements in disturbance estimation and tracking. Notably, 27.8% reduction in tracking error on real hardware under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and 38.0% reduction under a base-vibration disturbance not seen during training.
AI.conclusion: The residual RL DOB framework provides stable, disturbance-aware compensation that improves precision and generalizes across disturbance transitions, with provable envelope-bounded tracking and practical success on real hardware.

title: LLM-Generated Feature Pools for Time Series Anomaly Detection
summary: We study how far a simple statistical pipeline can go on univariate time series anomaly detection under a strict selection protocol. The method extracts a small pool of statistics over sliding windows, scores each window with a transductive robust (MAD) model, and selects a feature subset per domain on a held-out tuning split. On TSB-AD-U it reaches $0.529$ per-series VUS-PR, above the best neural ($0.45$) and statistical ($0.44$) entries on the public leaderboard and within $0.06$ of the strongest pretrained foundation model, several of which use more supervision than ours. Ablations locate the cause: across three selection strategies and a hindsight oracle the score moves by $0.031$, and across the aggregation grid by $0.096$, while changing the candidate pool moves it by $0.226$. The candidate pool sets the ceiling; the search over it is second-order. We therefore generate a pool per domain by prompting a multimodal LLM with in-context example windows from that domain. The generated pools match the hand-crafted one under matched selection, and the two cover different domains: selecting over their union improves on the generated pool in all twelve generator-seed pairs and lifts the pipeline to $0.588$, matching the performance of the best entry on the leaderboard.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, statistics-based anomaly detection pipeline with domain-specific feature selection and LLM-generated candidate pools can reach state-of-the-art performance on univariate time series anomaly detection under strict selection.
AI.motivation: Evaluate how far simple statistical methods can go under a strict selection protocol and compare to neural and foundation models.
AI.method: Extract a small pool of statistics over sliding windows; score windows with a transductive robust (MAD) model; perform per-domain feature subset selection on a held-out tuning split; generate a domain-specific candidate pool by prompting a multimodal LLM with in-context example windows; evaluate on TSB-AD-U with ablation studies.
AI.result: On TSB-AD-U, 0.529 per-series VUS-PR, beating best neural (0.45) and statistical (0.44); within 0.06 of the strongest pretrained foundation model; ablations show the score is most sensitive to candidate pool choice (0.226 effect) and aggregation (0.096), while selection strategies and hindsight oracle contribute 0.031; generating pools per domain yields performance close to hand-crafted pools; union of generated and hand-crafted pools yields 0.588, matching the leaderboard best.
AI.conclusion: The candidate pool quality caps the ceiling; the search is secondary. Generating domain-specific pools via LLM prompts can match hand-crafted pools and, when combined across domains, achieve leaderboard-level performance with relatively lightweight supervision.

title: Purification and Regulation: Comorbidity-Aware Multi-Label Few-Shot Learning for Medical Image Classification
summary: Multi-label few-shot learning (MLFSL) remains a significant challenge in medical image analysis (MIA). Current metric-based meta-learning methods face two critical limitations in MIA. First, conventional prototype generation often entangles irrelevant disease information, leading to contaminated prototypes and degraded performance. Second, prior studies typically enforce inter-class separability in embedding space, largely neglecting the inherent correlations among diseases. To overcome these challenges, we propose Prototype Purification and Regulation (PPR), a novel MLFSL framework for MIA. PPR first performs prototype purification by leveraging sample-level comorbidity scores to emphasize disease-specific features, producing purified prototypes that better characterize each disease. Building upon these purified prototypes, PPR further addresses the underexplored problem of inter-class prototype distance in MIA by incorporating disease-level comorbidity statistics to adaptively regulate inter-class similarity, forming a comorbidity-aware embedding space. Overall, PPR sequentially enables the model to capture pure disease features and inter-class relationships for reliable MLFSL in MIA. Extensive experiments across four chest X-ray benchmark datasets, including cross-domain evaluation, show that PPR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly improving disease detection while demonstrating robust generalization and clinical applicability.

AI.tldr: A framework (PPR) for multi-label few-shot learning in medical image analysis that purifies prototypes via sample-level comorbidity scores and regulates inter-class similarity with disease comorbidity statistics, achieving state-of-the-art performance and robust cross-domain generalization on chest X-ray data.
AI.motivation: MLFSL in medical imaging suffers from contaminated prototypes that embed non-disease information and ignores disease correlations; need purer, more semantically meaningful prototypes and a space that reflects disease comorbidity.
AI.method: Prototype purification using sample-level comorbidity scores to emphasize disease-specific features; followed by comorbidity-aware embedding space where inter-class distances are adaptively regulated using disease-level comorbidity statistics; sequentially learns pure features and relationships.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four chest X-ray datasets, including cross-domain evaluation, show PPR consistently outperforms SOTA methods, with notable improvements in disease detection and good generalization/clinical applicability.
AI.conclusion: PPR demonstrates that incorporating purification at the prototype level and disease comorbidity-guided regulation yields more reliable MLFSL performance in medical imaging, suggesting practical impact and potential for broader adoption.

title: Decision-Focused Learning for Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization via KKT-Based Reformulation
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Accepted at PRICAI 2026 (Pacific Rim International Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
summary: Mean-variance portfolio optimization (MVO) is a central framework in data-driven asset management. A widely adopted approach is a two-stage framework that first predicts expected returns and then solves the optimization problem based on these predictions, with the predictive models trained by minimizing prediction errors. However, this objective of prediction is not aligned with the quality of the downstream portfolio decision. Decision-focused learning (DFL), which directly minimizes the downstream decision loss within the learning process, has thus emerged as a promising direction. However, existing DFL approaches to MVO rely on surrogate losses or constraint relaxations for tractability, creating a structural mismatch between predictive model training and the constrained MVO solved at evaluation. We propose a single-level optimization formulation that incorporates the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions of the lower-level MVO into the upper-level learning problem. This formulation explicitly preserves the budget and short-sale constraints while remaining tractable for standard nonlinear optimization solvers. Rolling-window experiments on real-world ETF (Exchange Traded Funds) data across two asset universes with different correlation structures show that our method achieved the best performance on multiple investment metrics and also demonstrated performance improvement due to the proposed regularization.

AI.tldr: Introduces a single-level decision-focused learning framework for MVO by embedding KKT conditions of the lower-level optimization into the upper-level learning problem, preserving budget and short-sale constraints; empirically outperforms surrogate-based DFL approaches and benefits from a regularization term.
AI.motivation: To align predictive training with the quality of the downstream mean-variance portfolio decision, addressing the misalignment in standard two-stage MVO where predictions minimize prediction error rather than downstream loss.
AI.method: Formulate a single-level optimization by incorporating the KKT optimality conditions of the lower-level mean-variance optimization into the learning objective, explicitly enforcing budget and short-sale constraints, and maintaining tractability with standard nonlinear solvers; include a regularization term to improve generalization.
AI.result: Rolling-window experiments on real-world ETF data across two asset universes with different correlation structures show the proposed method achieves best performance on multiple investment metrics, with additional gains attributable to the proposed regularization.
AI.conclusion: Embedding the KKT conditions into a single-level decision-focused learning framework for MVO preserves feasibility and improves decision quality, with empirical evidence of superior performance and beneficial regularization effects.

title: NaViRrator: Robot Navigation from Human-Readable Maps through a Learned Visual Route
summary: Human-readable maps provide an intuitive interface for specifying robot destinations, but connecting their schematic geometry to egocentric observations remains challenging. We present NaViRRator, a framework that translates user-specified start and goal locations on such maps into navigation instructions for a pretrained vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policy. Its core method, RouteScribe, separates route inference from verbalization by first generating an explicit route scaffold in map-image coordinates, which a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) converts into a navigation instruction. We construct the scaffold with start--goal line conditional flow matching (SGL-CFM), which deforms a straight start--goal waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route. During execution, the VLN policy receives only the instruction and egocentric observations, while the map and scaffold remain upstream, allowing executor replacement without retraining the map-to-language modules. Real-world experiments show higher success rates and success weighted by path length (SPL) than direct map-to-instruction generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source conditional flow matching. Qualitative results further show clearer salient turns and better preservation of the intended maneuver sequence, supporting route-grounded language as a modular interface between human-readable maps and pretrained navigation policies.

AI.tldr: NaViRRator translates user-specified map locations into VLN instructions by generating a map-based route scaffold with SGL-CFM, then verbalizes via a pretrained VLM, enabling a modular, updatable interface between human maps and navigation policies; it outperforms baselines on real-world tasks and preserves maneuver sequences.
AI.motivation: Bridge human-readable schematic maps with egocentric, vision-language navigation policies by decoupling map-to-language from policy execution, enabling modular replacement of components and improved interpretability.
AI.method: RouteScribe first constructs a map-conditioned route scaffold by deforming a straight start–goal waypoint sequence using start–goal line conditional flow matching (SGL-CFM). The scaffold, created in map-image coordinates, is converted into a navigation instruction by a pretrained vision-language model, while the executing policy only uses the instruction and egocentric observations; the map/scaffold are upstream, allowing component replacement without retraining.
AI.result: Real-world experiments show higher success rates and SPL than direct map-to-instruction generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source conditional flow matching. Qualitative results show clearer salient turns and better preservation of the intended maneuver sequence, supporting route-grounded language as a modular interface between maps and pretrained navigation policies.
AI.conclusion: Route-grounded language via a modular RouteScribe pipeline improves robustness and flexibility of map-guided navigation by decoupling route inference from language generation, enabling reuse of pretrained VLN policies with human-readable maps and potential for component substitution without retraining.

title: MIST: Multimodal Survival Prediction with Genomic-Guided Histology Attention
comment: Accepted at the COMPAYL 2026 Workshop on Computational Pathology and Multimodal Data at MICCAI 2026. 11 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables
summary: Multimodal survival models can combine complementary prognostic information from whole-slide images and genomic profiles, but effective fusion remains challenging amid external cohort shift and computational complexity. To address these challenges, we propose MIST, multimodal survival prediction with genomic-guided histology attention. MIST represents genomic features as tokens and allows them to query compact foundation-model-derived histology context tokens before survival prediction. This design enriches molecular information with histology context rather than merging separately encoded modalities only at the final stage. Training combines discrete-time survival prediction with genomic feature masking, WSI dropout, and paired WSI-genomics contrastive alignment. Across four external evaluations in colon, renal, lung, and glioblastoma cohorts, MIST improves external C-index over standard fusion baselines in the primary comparisons. These results support genomic-guided histology attention as a compact and effective strategy for multimodal oncology outcome prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/samiyavuuz/MIST .

AI.tldr: Introduces MIST, a multimodal survival model that represents genomic features as tokens and attends to compact histology context tokens derived from foundation-models, improving external C-index over baseline fusion methods across four cancer cohorts.
AI.motivation: External-cohort shift and computational complexity hinder effective fusion of histology and genomics in survival prediction; need a compact, robust fusion mechanism that leverages histology context.
AI.method: Genomic features are encoded as tokens that query histology context tokens derived from foundation-model histology representations. Fusion occurs via genomic-guided histology attention. Training combines discrete-time survival prediction with genomic feature masking, WSI dropout, and paired WSI-genomics contrastive alignment.
AI.result: In four external evaluations (colon, renal, lung, glioblastoma), MIST achieves higher external C-index than standard fusion baselines in primary comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Genomic-guided histology attention is a compact, effective strategy for multimodal oncology outcome prediction; code is available at the provided GitHub repository.

title: From Retrieval to Recognition:How Vision--Language Models Become OCR Specialists
summary: Does a general vision--language model acquire specialized OCR ability by developing a new reading circuit or by reusing an existing mechanism? We address this question in the setting of full-sequence OCR, rather than local-answer retrieval. Using an evidence-grounded protocol with held-out causal interventions, we identify sparse and stable OCR-head sets in GLM-OCR, MinerU2.5, and PaddleOCR-VL-1.6. We then investigate the mechanistic origin of these OCR heads by comparing them with independently identified textual retrieval/copy heads in general VLMs. Across two general VLMs, visual OCR heads strongly overlap independently identified textual retrieval/copy heads, yielding untuned top-20 intersections of 73.3% and all-head Spearman correlations of 0.677-0.886. The overlap and causal interventions suggest that full-sequence OCR operates as dense sequential multimodal copy-and-paste, repeatedly retrieving visual evidence and routing it to the current output position. Finally, we examine how this shared circuit changes as a general VLM becomes an OCR specialist. Matched base-to-specialized comparisons show that OCR specialization largely preserves head identity, retaining 17-20 of the top 20 heads per task with all-head rank correlations of 0.874-0.942, while redistributing their functional and causal strengths.

AI.tldr: OCR in general vision–language models appears to reuse existing textual retrieval/copy mechanisms, functioning as a dense sequential copy-and-paste process, with OCR specialization preserving most core heads but shifting their strengths.
AI.motivation: Resolve whether full-sequence OCR in general VLMs arises from a new specialized reading circuit or from reusing an existing mechanism for textual retrieval/copying, using rigorous causal interventions and cross-model comparisons.
AI.method: Identify sparse, stable OCR heads in three models (GLM-OCR, MinerU2.5, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6) via an evidence-grounded protocol with held-out causal interventions; compare these OCR heads with independently identified textual retrieval/copy heads in general VLMs; assess overlap (top-20 intersections) and all-head rank correlations (Spearman); examine head identity preservation during OCR specialization by base-to-specialized model comparisons.
AI.result: OCR heads strongly overlap with independently identified textual retrieval/copy heads across two general VLMs, with top-20 intersections of 73.3% and all-head Spearman correlations 0.677–0.886. This indicates a dense sequential multimodal copy-and-paste mechanism that retrieves visual evidence and routes it to the current output. Upon OCR specialization, head identity is largely preserved (17–20 of the top 20 heads retained), while the relative strengths and causal contributions redistribute (rank correlations 0.874–0.942).
AI.conclusion: Full-sequence OCR in general VLMs is largely embodied by reusing an existing copy-based mechanism rather than a distinct new OCR-reading circuit; OCR specialization preserves core head identities but reallocates functional/causal strengths, suggesting a shared, modular OCR-capable circuitry across tasks.

title: Optimal Randomized Proper Online Learning
summary: We prove that the optimal expected mistake bound of online learning a function class $\mathcal{H}$ by a randomized proper learning algorithm is $O(\mathtt{L}(\mathcal{H}) \log T)$, where $\mathtt{L}(\mathcal{H})$ is the Littlestone dimension of $\mathcal{H}$ and $T$ is the time horizon. Our result improves upon the previously best known bound of $O(\mathtt{L}(\mathcal{H}) \log^6 T)$ given by Daskalakis and Golowich (STOC 2022), and is optimal up to a universal constant for worst-case classes.

AI.tldr: An online learning result: randomized proper learner achieves an expected mistake bound of O(L(H) log T), tightening the horizon dependence from log^6 T to log T and improving on prior work; optimal up to a universal constant for worst-case hypothesis classes.
AI.motivation: Determine the tight horizon dependence of the worst-case expected mistake bound for online learning of a function class using a randomized proper algorithm, in terms of the Littlestone dimension L(H). The paper aims to close the gap with the previous O(L(H) log^6 T) bound and establish near-optimality.
AI.method: The abstract does not specify methodological details. The paper presumably introduces a new randomized proper learning algorithm for online prediction and provides a rigorous analysis showing the expected number of mistakes grows as O(L(H) log T), improving over the previous polylog factor. The approach likely leverages Littlestone dimension techniques and careful probabilistic analysis to achieve the logarithmic horizon dependence.
AI.result: Main result: The optimal expected mistake bound for online learning a function class H by a randomized proper learning algorithm is O(L(H) log T). This improves the previous O(L(H) log^6 T) bound and is optimal up to a universal constant for worst-case classes.
AI.conclusion: The work tightens the horizon dependence in the mistake bound for online learning with randomized proper learners, showing that the Littlestone dimension governs the bound with only a logarithmic dependence on the time horizon, and that this rate is essentially optimal for worst-case hypothesis classes.

title: LEMCA: LLM-Guided Synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures
summary: Physical control tasks in the natural world, such as driving or object manipulation, frequently exhibit dramatic variations in sensory and compute complexity over time. Correspondingly, a natural resource-efficient choice for robot control is to dynamically switch between control modes with varying resource allocations. However, such "mode-switching controllers" (MSCs) have historically required laborious, expert-driven design and synthesis for each new task. Driven by these design difficulties, modern robotic control architectures often fall back to a wasteful "monolithic" one-size-fits-all structure, where resource allocation is permanently anchored to the hardest, most resource-intensive task phases. To facilitate the design of performant yet efficient MSCs, we propose LLM-Guided synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures (LEMCA). LEMCA represents MSC designs as interpretable programs to be iteratively refined in an evolutionary loop. To evaluate design fitness, we propose MSC-compatible extensions of automated controller synthesis approaches, such as reinforcement learning in simulation. LEMCA then leverages the semantic priors, reasoning, and coding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively edit controller modes, their corresponding sensory-compute resource allocations, and mode transitions. Our experiments across diverse control benchmarks show that LEMCA consistently discovers strategies that surpass the Pareto frontier of monolithic designs by reclaiming wasted resources during "easy" task phases. LEMCA thus presents an automated, low-effort path to synthesize resource-efficient MSC designs.

AI.tldr: LEMCA is an LLM-guided, evolutionary synthesis framework that converts mode-switching controllers into interpretable programs, uses MSC-aware controller synthesis (e.g., RL in simulation) for evaluation, and leverages LLM priors to iteratively refine modes and transitions. It achieves Pareto-improvement over monolithic controllers by reclaiming resources in easy task phases.
AI.motivation: Modern robotics struggle with resource-inefficient MSC design; experts must hand-tune mode sets and resource allocations for each task, while monolithic designs waste resources during easy phases. LEMCA aims to automate and optimize MSC design to improve efficiency and performance.
AI.method: Represent MSC designs as interpretable programs and refine them in an evolutionary loop. Use MSC-compatible extensions of automated controller synthesis (e.g., RL in simulation) to evaluate design fitness. Leverage LLMs to edit modes, resource allocations, and mode transitions guided by semantic priors and reasoning.
AI.result: Across diverse control benchmarks, LEMCA discovers strategies that surpass the Pareto frontier of monolithic designs by reclaiming wasted resources during easy task phases, yielding efficient MSC designs without extensive manual engineering.
AI.conclusion: LEMCA provides an automated, low-effort pathway to synthesize resource-efficient MSC designs, with potential for broad application and integration with existing synthesis methods.

title: EnterpriseVal: Quantifying the Efficacy, Reliability and Value of Generative AI in the Enterprise
summary: Frontier language models now produce professional deliverables that expert graders judge to match human work on a substantial share of economically valuable tasks, yet most enterprise GenAI initiatives fail to show a measurable business effect and a large fraction of agentic projects are expected to be cancelled. We argue that this is substantially a measurement problem: public benchmarks answer "what can the model do?", whereas a deployment decision requires "is this workflow fit, reliable, safe and worth scaling - here, on our data, under our controls?". We present EnterpriseVal, a use-case-level evaluation system that closes this gap. It comprises (i) a formal specification of the use case and of the frozen socio-technical configuration under test, model, prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails and human oversight, with an autonomy level and consequence tier that jointly set the required evaluation intensity; (ii) a metric catalogue spanning fidelity, utility, efficiency, reliability, assurance and oversight; (iii) a grading protocol that scales blinded expert judgement with calibrated LLM-as-judge scoring through prediction-powered inference; (iv) a two-tier threshold gate, stated as an executable algorithm, that maps metric vectors with confidence bounds to REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE decisions; and (v) a value-and-risk model in which the reviewer catch rate is a measured parameter. We report a pilot across three workflows in a global bank. In credit-memo drafting, human-graded citation precision reached 88% and hallucination rate 1.6% for the best model against gates of 70% and 5%; in procedure transformation, analyst refinement effort fell from an estimated 27.4 to 2.9 hours per document. We separate established results, documented pilot evidence, the proposed system and open hypotheses, and specify the experiments required for full validation

AI.tldr: EnterpriseVal is a use-case‑level evaluation framework designed to close the deployment-readiness gap for enterprise GenAI, by formalizing use cases and socio-technical configs, supplying a comprehensive metric catalogue, a blinded expert + LLM judging protocol, an executable decision gate, and a value‑risk model; pilot results in a global bank show improved accuracy and efficiency (88% citation precision, 1.6% hallucination; 27.4→2.9 hours saved) while separating established results from hypotheses.
AI.motivation: Public benchmarks test model capabilities but do not measure fit, reliability, safety, or business value in real deployments. Enterprises require trustworthy evaluation that accounts for data, controls, and governance; without this, many GenAI initiatives fail to demonstrate measurable impact. EnterpriseVal aims to operationalize deployment readiness at the use-case level.
AI.method: (i) Formal specification of the use case and frozen socio-technical configuration (model, prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails, human oversight) with an explicit autonomy level and consequence tier; (ii) a metric catalogue spanning fidelity, utility, efficiency, reliability, assurance, and oversight; (iii) a grading protocol that blends blinded expert judgment with calibrated LLM-as-judge scoring via prediction-powered inference; (iv) a two-tier threshold gate (REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE) as an executable algorithm mapping metric vectors with confidence bounds to decisions; (v) a value-and-risk model incorporating a measured reviewer catch rate; pilot testing in three workflows within a global bank.
AI.result: Pilot evidence shows practical gains: in credit-memo drafting, best model achieved 88% citation precision and 1.6% hallucination rate against gate targets of 70% and 5%; in procedure transformation, analyst refinement time dropped from 27.4 to 2.9 hours per document. The authors delineate established results, pilot evidence, the proposed system, and open hypotheses, and specify the experiments needed for full validation.
AI.conclusion: EnterpriseVal presents a concrete, extensible framework to evaluate deployment viability of GenAI in enterprise settings. Its structured specs, multi-dimensional metrics, switching gate, and value-risk lens address the core gap between bench capabilities and deployment decisions. Future work should validate generalizability across domains, calibrate judgment components, and quantify long-term business impact.

title: GestureFAR: Streaming Co-Speech Gesture Generation with Flow Autoregression
summary: Generating natural co-speech gestures from streaming speech is essential for embodied conversational agents, where motion must be produced while a user is still speaking. Recent streaming gesture systems make online generation possible by autoregressing over discrete motion tokens, but this design compresses high-dimensional continuous motion into finite codebooks and can limit the realism and diversity of generated gestures. To preserve both causality and continuous expressiveness, we propose \textbf{GestureFAR}, a flow-autoregressive framework for streaming co-speech gesture generation. First, GestureFAR autoregresses over causal continuous motion latents, using a transformer to model streaming audio-motion context and a per-token flow-matching head to sample the next latent from a continuous distribution. Second, we introduce a head-only flow distillation strategy that freezes the causal backbone and distills the multi-step per-token flow head into a single network evaluation using consistency and distribution-matching objectives. This keeps the model token-causal while removing the main latency bottleneck for live interaction. Experiments on BEAT2 show that GestureFAR significantly improves the quality--latency trade-off among streaming-capable methods, preserving strong gesture quality while enabling real-time token-causal generation. Project Page: https://andypinxinliu.github.io/GestureFAR

AI.tldr: GestureFAR is a streaming co-speech gesture generator that uses a flow-based autoregressive model over continuous motion latents to achieve real-time, token-causal generation, augmented by a head-only flow distillation to reduce latency; shows improved quality-latency trade-off on BEAT2.
AI.motivation: Streaming co-speech gesture generation requires real-time, expressive motion. Discrete token-based approaches compress high-dimensional motion into finite codebooks, which can hurt realism and diversity. A method that preserves causality while enabling continuous expressiveness, with low latency, is needed.
AI.method: GestureFAR autoregresses over causal continuous motion latents using a transformer to model streaming audio-motion context. A per-token flow-matching head samples the next latent from a continuous distribution. A head-only flow distillation strategy freezes the causal backbone and distills the multi-step per-token flow head into a single network evaluation using consistency and distribution-matching objectives, maintaining token causality while reducing latency.
AI.result: Experiments on BEAT2 show GestureFAR significantly improves the quality–latency trade-off among streaming-capable methods, preserving gesture quality while enabling real-time token-causal generation.
AI.conclusion: GestureFAR provides a practical, real-time framework for streaming co-speech gesture generation by combining causal continuous motion latents with flow-based sampling and a distillation technique that minimizes latency without compromising quality.

title: Understanding LLM Quantization through Activation-Guided Compensation and Orthogonal Residuals
summary: Post-training weight-activation quantization reduces the memory and inference costs of large language models, but aggressive W4A4 quantization remains difficult because activation outliers degrade effective quantization resolution. Although weight optimization, channel-wise scaling, and orthogonal rotation mitigate this problem, the error components they address and their relationship remain unclear. Using an exact decomposition of local weight-activation quantization error into an activation-guided weight compensation term and an orthogonal residual, we bound the residual using persistent channel-wise outlier and regular activation quantities. This decomposition clarifies which error components can be addressed by weight compensation and which require transformation design. We then use the residual bounds to derive practical guidelines for applying randomized Hadamard rotation, sign selection, and channel scaling. In particular, the analysis explains how random signs suppress constructive interference among persistent outlier channels, how sampling multiple sign patterns can improve transformation selection, and how second-moment balancing leads to an $L_2$ scaling rule while a further relaxation recovers SmoothQuant-style $L_\infty$ scaling. We evaluate these guidelines through backpropagation-free configurations across eight Llama and Mistral models, obtaining performance competitive with gradient-trained SpinQuant.

AI.tldr: We present an exact decomposition of local weight-activation quantization error into an activation-guided weight compensation term and an orthogonal residual, with bounds on the residual that depend on persistent channel-outliers and activation statistics. This clarifies which error components can be mitigated by weight compensation versus transformation design, and yields practical guidelines (randomized Hadamard rotation, sign sampling, channel scaling) that enable aggressive W4A4 post-training quantization for large language models. Empirical results on eight Llama/Mistral models show competitive performance with gradient-trained SpinQuant in backpropagation-free settings.
AI.motivation: To enable effective post-training quantization of large language models at W4A4 by precisely characterizing and controlling the error components that arise from quantizing weights and activations, thereby enabling strong performance without gradient-based fine-tuning.
AI.method: Develop an exact decomposition of local weight-activation quantization error into two parts: an activation-guided weight compensation term and an orthogonal residual. Derive residual bounds using persistent channel-wise outliers and regular activation statistics. Use these bounds to justify and design practical transformation steps (randomized Hadamard rotation, sign selection patterns, and channel scaling). Analyze second-moment balancing (L2 scaling) and relaxations leading to an L-infinity (SmoothQuant-style) scaling. Validate through backpropagation-free experiments across multiple models.
AI.result: The residual bounds inform guidelines for applying Hadamard rotations, multiple sign patterns, and channel scaling. Random signs suppress constructive interference from persistent outlier channels; sampling multiple sign patterns improves transformation selection; second-moment balancing yields an L2 scaling, with relaxations achieving an L-infinity scaling. Across eight Llama and Mistral models, the proposed non-gradient configurations achieve performance competitive with gradient-trained SpinQuant.
AI.conclusion: The decomposition clarifies which error components are addressable by weight compensation versus by transformation design. It provides actionable guidelines for post-training quantization (Hadamard rotations, sign strategies, and channel scaling) that enable effective W4A4 quantization in large LMs, with empirical results approaching state-of-the-art gradient-based methods.

title: The EventCV Library for Event-Based Robotic Vision
summary: Event cameras detect per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously on microsecond timescales, with high dynamic range and low power draw. These are desirable properties for robots that move fast or work in difficult lighting conditions. However, integrating an event camera into a real-world robotic pipeline still requires substantial effort: plug-and-play drivers do not exist, event streams are recorded in a variety of incompatible file formats, and most projects rely on custom research-grade code. Here, we present EventCV, an open-source and extensible Rust library with OpenCV-style Python bindings that lowers the entry barrier to working with event cameras. EventCV provides a wide range of features: denoising filters and geometric transforms, augmentations, corner detection and unsupervised feature learning, contrast-maximization motion estimation, a video-to-events simulator, and Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) inference for deployment in robotic stacks. EventCV integrates the Neuromorphic Drivers package, allowing an event camera stream to be processed directly in real time. No existing toolkit covers this range of operations in one package, and EventCV builds representations and decodes files 1.1x to 3.7x faster than the currently available libraries. We deploy EventCV on a Jetson Orin AGX and present three robotics case studies spanning object detection, on-device model inference, and localization. Project webpage: https://eventcv.net.

AI.tldr: EventCV is an open-source Rust library with Python bindings that unifies diverse event-camera processing tools (denoising, transforms, detection, motion estimation, simulation, ONNX inference) and enables real-time robotic deployment; claims faster file decoding (1.1x–3.7x) and succeeds on Jetson Orin AGX across three robotics case studies.
AI.motivation: Researchers and practitioners face fragmentation: no plug-and-play drivers, diverse incompatible formats, and lack of a comprehensive toolkit for event cameras. EventCV aims to lower barriers and streamline integration into robotic pipelines.
AI.method: Developed EventCV in Rust with OpenCV-style Python bindings; integrates Neuromorphic Drivers for real-time streams; provides denoising, geometric transforms, augmentations, corner detection, unsupervised feature learning, contrast-maximization-based motion estimation, a video-to-events simulator, and ONNX inference; optimizes file decoding performance; deployed on a Jetson Orin AGX.
AI.result: Faster file decoding (1.1x–3.7x) vs existing libraries; supports real-time processing; demonstrated via three robotics case studies: object detection, on-device model inference, and localization.
AI.conclusion: EventCV fills a gap by offering a single, extensible toolkit that covers extensive event-camera processing and facilitates deployment in robotic stacks, accelerating development and experimentation.

title: AutoRecLab: Describe the Experiment, Get the Code!
comment: Accepted at the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys '26), Demo Track. 4 pages, 2 figures
summary: Empirical evaluation is central to recommender-systems (RecSys) research, but turning experimental designs into executable code remains a manual and error-prone task. We present AutoRecLab, a Python-based autonomous RecSys lab that automates RecSys experiments from natural-language prompts. Given a research idea, AutoRecLab derives explicit experiment requirements, builds and validates a prototype, and iteratively expands it into the requested full experiment. The workflow combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for documentation lookup, static type verification, and execution-steered tree search. In our demonstration, AutoRecLab autonomously implements an explicit-to-implicit feedback conversion study. In a baseline comparison across six algorithms and three datasets, 8 of 9 runs succeed at an average cost of approx- imately $1 per run with GPT-5.4-mini.

AI.tldr: AutoRecLab automates RecSys experiments from natural-language prompts using RAG, type verification, and execution-guided search; demonstrates 8/9 successful runs at ~1 USD per run in a six-algorithm, three-dataset study.
AI.motivation: Reduce manual, error-prone implementation of recommender-system experiments; improve reproducibility, efficiency, and accessibility of experimentation.
AI.method: Python-based autonomous lab that converts NL prompts into explicit experiment requirements, builds/validates prototypes, and iteratively expands to full experiments. Uses retrieval-augmented generation for documentation lookup, static type verification, and execution-steered tree search.
AI.result: Demonstration on explicit-to-implicit feedback conversion; baseline across six algorithms and three datasets yielded 8 of 9 successful runs; average cost ~ $1 per run with GPT-5.4-mini.
AI.conclusion: AutoRecLab shows feasibility of end-to-end autonomous experimentation in RecSys, offering potential efficiency gains and a basis for broader adoption, with room for robustness and scalability improvements.

title: A benchmark dataset and baseline methods for four-dimensional STEM diffraction patterns
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures. Data and trained model weights: https://doi.org/10.57760/sciencedb.nbsdc.00281. Code: https://github.com/Gaiya69-rgb/4D-ImageNet
summary: Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) records a two-dimensional diffraction pattern at each electron-probe position, yielding spatially resolved reciprocal-space information but large, heterogeneous data volumes. Here we describe 4D-ImageNet, a collection of 174,000 diffraction patterns comprising 145,000 experimental patterns selected from 29 acquisitions and 29,000 multislice simulations. The experimental data cover acquisition-level labels for Ag, Au, mixed Au-Ag, CoO, Pd and ZnO specimens across multiple fields of view, scan dimensions, camera lengths and exposure times. Each acquisition contributes 5,000 quality-ranked patterns with source scan coordinates and acquisition metadata. A set-prediction detector provides model-derived pseudo-labels for the direct-beam position and Bragg-disk centres, with a confidence score for each disk. The simulation data cover 13 crystal structures and include Euler rotations, reciprocal-space sampling and approximate low-index beam directions. A grouped mixed-domain masked-reconstruction benchmark is provided to assess leakage-resistant loading and evaluation across experimental and simulated data. The dataset is intended for representation learning, disk detection, diffraction-pattern retrieval, orientation analysis and simulation-to-experiment studies.

AI.tldr: 4D-ImageNet: a large-scale collection of 174k 4D-STEM diffraction patterns (experimental and simulated) with material labels, pseudo-labeled beam positions, and a mixed-domain, leakage-robust benchmark for representation learning and cross-domain analysis.
AI.motivation: To enable scalable, labeled 4D-STEM analysis and bridge simulation with experiment by providing a comprehensive, diverse dataset and a benchmark for robust loading and evaluation across domains.
AI.method: Assembled 174,000 diffraction patterns: 145,000 experimental patterns from 29 acquisitions (covering Ag, Au, mixed Au-Ag, CoO, Pd, ZnO across various FOVs, scan dims, camera lengths, and exposure times) with 5,000 patterns per acquisition including source coordinates and metadata. A set-prediction detector generated pseudo-labels for direct-beam and Bragg-disk centers with confidence scores. 29,000 multislice simulations spanning 13 crystal structures with Euler rotations, reciprocal-space sampling, and approximate low-index beam directions. Introduced a grouped mixed-domain masked-reconstruction benchmark to assess leakage-resistant loading/evaluation across experimental and simulated data.
AI.result: The work delivers a large, labeled 4D-STEM dataset (experimental and simulated) with per-disk pseudo-labels and acquisition metadata, plus a cross-domain benchmark: suitable for tasks such as representation learning, disk detection, diffraction-pattern retrieval, and orientation/structure analysis, as well as simulation-to-experiment studies.
AI.conclusion: 4D-ImageNet provides a versatile, cross-domain resource to advance machine learning for 4D-STEM, enabling robust representation learning, precise disk/orientation analysis, and improved integration of simulated and experimental diffraction data.

title: Efficient Architecture Search under Leave-One-Subject-Out Evaluation
summary: Deep neural architectures are widely used for signal processing in automated pain assessment systems. However, architecture design has remained largely a manual task despite the potential efficiency benefits of Neural Architecture Search (NAS). Embedding NAS in a Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) evaluation is computationally demanding because a fully nested implementation requires $N$ independent architecture searches and, assuming approximately linear training cost, scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$. We propose a block-based, leakage-controlled approach that shares NAS runs between subjects, reducing the number of searches from $N$ to $B$, where $B \ll N$, dubbed PainNAS. On the BioVid Heat Pain dataset, PainNAS yields comparable subject-level accuracy with substantially fewer parameters and FLOPs.

AI.tldr: A cross-subject NAS method (PainNAS) that uses block-based, leakage-controlled sharing to reduce LOSO NAS cost from N searches to B (B ≪ N) while achieving comparable accuracy and lower complexity on BioVid Heat Pain.
AI.motivation: Neural Architecture Search in Leave-One-Subject-Out evaluations is computationally expensive because it requires multiple independent searches; pain assessment from signals demands efficient NAS to enable subject-wise evaluation.
AI.method: A block-based, leakage-controlled NAS approach that shares NAS runs across subjects, reducing the number of searches from N to B (with B much smaller than N). This entails partitioning subjects into blocks and transferring architecture decisions across subjects within blocks while controlling for information leakage.
AI.result: PainNAS yields comparable subject-level accuracy on BioVid Heat Pain with substantially fewer parameters and FLOPs compared to full per-subject NAS.
AI.conclusion: PainNAS provides a computationally efficient NAS strategy for LOSO pain assessment, maintaining performance while reducing architecture search cost and resource usage.

title: FAN: Foresight Action Normalization for Continual Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models pre-trained on large-scale, closed datasets have demonstrated remarkable success across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. However, their long-term real-world deployment necessitates continuously acquiring new skills while retaining previously learned capabilities. While pioneering works have explored continual VLA adaptation using techniques such as experience replay and reinforcement fine-tuning, they overlook a foundational mechanism: action normalization, which determines the underlying coordinate system in which policies perceive and execute physical actions. To bridge this gap, we systematically evaluate five normalization strategies across four real-world task streams covering single-arm and bimanual manipulation. Our analysis reveals that existing protocols induce severe failure modes due to inter-task coordinate drift, limited motion coverage, or train-test coordinate mismatches. Motivated by these insights, we formulate three core design principles: consistency, coverage, and causality (3C), and introduce foresight action normalization (FAN). FAN estimates normalization statistics once from a small, task-independent calibration set prior to continual learning and freezes them throughout adaptation. Across all evaluated streams, FAN achieves the highest performance and demonstrates consistent robustness, providing insightful guidance for building stable action representations in achieving effective lifelong VLA adaptation.

AI.tldr: FAN ( foresight action normalization ) improves continual VLA adaptation by freezing a task-independent normalization learned from a small calibration set, addressing coordinate drift and coverage issues across real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Continual fine-tuning of VLA models can fail due to action-space misalignment and coordinate drift across tasks; robust, generalizable action normalization is needed to stabilize long-term learning in real-world robotic manipulation.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of five normalization strategies across four real-world task streams (single-arm and bimanual). Proposes three design principles—consistency, coverage, causality (3C)—and introduces FAN, which estimates normalization statistics from a small, task-independent calibration set and freezes them during continual adaptation.
AI.result: FAN achieves the highest performance and robust performance across all evaluated streams, outperforming other normalization strategies.
AI.conclusion: Stable, universal action normalization is essential for effective lifelong VLA adaptation; 3C principles provide practical guidance, and FAN offers a simple, robust solution that reduces coordination drift and test-train mismatch during continual learning.

title: What Should We Ask Next? Retrieval-Aware Question Learning under Partial Evidence
summary: Interactive retrieval under partial evidence is a sequential information-acquisition problem: an agent must decide which question will create the most useful evidence for the next retrieval update. Existing systems train this decision by imitating an offline ordering of candidate QA pairs, although question value is determined by the response it elicits and its downstream effect on retrieval. We establish that candidate discriminativeness and perceived usefulness provide weak supervision for this objective, then introduce RAVEL, a retrieval-aware online reinforcement learning framework for interactive person re-identification. RAVEL initializes from supervised question generation, observes the current Top-4 candidates directly, and optimizes the question policy with rank feedback from the full question-answer-retrieval loop. Experiments on Interactive-PEDES show that RAVEL delivers progressively stronger retrieval performance across five interaction rounds. Further analysis shows that RAVEL reallocates the questioning budget toward localized open-ended attributes, which provide more useful retrieval evidence and yield the largest gains on initially difficult queries.

AI.tldr: RAVEL is a retrieval-aware online reinforcement learning framework for interactive person re-identification that learns question policies from rank feedback and improves retrieval by focusing on localized open-ended attributes, outperforming offline ordering baselines over five interaction rounds on Interactive-PEDES.
AI.motivation: Interactive retrieval with partial evidence suffers from weak supervision when using offline candidate ordering; discriminativeness and usefulness of questions are insufficient proxies for the end-to-end retrieval objective; an online RL approach that optimizes the information-gathering process with feedback from the QA-retrieval loop is needed.
AI.method: Initialize from supervised question generation; observe the Top-4 candidates directly; optimize the questioning policy with rank feedback from the full QA-retrieval loop; perform online reinforcement learning to reallocate the questioning budget toward informative attributes; evaluate on Interactive-PEDES across five interaction rounds.
AI.result: RAVEL delivers progressively stronger retrieval performance across five interaction rounds; analysis shows that it reallocates questioning budget toward localized open-ended attributes, which provide more useful evidence and yield the largest gains on initially difficult queries.
AI.conclusion: RAVEL provides a viable online reinforcement learning approach for interactive person re-identification under partial evidence, outperforming offline candidate-ordering baselines by learning to gather more informative evidence through rank-based feedback.

title: HAT: Hypothesis-Anchored Tracking for Video Monocular Spacecraft Pose Estimation
summary: Monocular 6-DoF pose estimation of non-cooperative targets is important for on-orbit servicing and debris removal. A single-image estimator can confuse near-symmetric spacecraft orientations, and tracking can preserve an incorrect pose. We present Hypothesis-Anchored Tracking (HAT), a causal framework that uses inter-frame motion to select among competing CAD-based pose hypotheses before alignment and fusion. Rather than independently choosing the highest-scoring hypothesis in each image, HAT retains competing orientation histories and selects a pose to anchor the relative trajectory estimated by monocular SLAM. Sparse anchors and pose fusion provide per-frame estimates after initialization without revising past outputs. The method requires only a calibrated RGB sequence, a metric CAD model, and target image regions, which can be supplied by detection or segmentation. The pretrained pose and SLAM networks require no target-specific training or fine-tuning. We evaluate two versions, Mega-HAT and Pico-HAT, using MegaPose and PicoPose, on SPARK-2024, SwissCube and SHIRT, with YCB-Video assessing performance outside the space domain. Using one temporal configuration per method, the arithmetic means of the four dataset-wise comparisons show 9.4% lower mean pose error and 3.76 times the sustained input FPS for Mega-HAT relative to independent MegaPose, and 23.9% lower mean pose error and 2.42 times the FPS for Pico-HAT relative to independent PicoPose. Mega-HAT ablations on SPARK and an offline reference examine component contributions and the effect of revising past estimates.

AI.tldr: Hypothesis-Anchored Tracking (HAT) for monocular 6-DoF pose estimation uses inter-frame motion to select among CAD-based pose hypotheses, preserving orientation histories and anchoring SLAM trajectories; Mega-HAT and Pico-HAT improve accuracy and FPS without target-specific training.
AI.motivation: Ambiguity in single-image pose estimation due to near-symmetric spacecraft orientations; need temporal consistency to avoid incorrect poses and to provide per-frame updates without retroactive changes.
AI.method: Causal framework HAT retains competing hypotheses, anchors relative trajectory via monocular SLAM, uses sparse anchors and fusion; pretrained networks no target-specific training; outputs per-frame alignments after initialization.
AI.result: Mega-HAT reduces mean pose error by 9.4% and increases sustained FPS by 3.76x vs independent MegaPose; Pico-HAT reduces mean pose error by 23.9% and increases FPS by 2.42x vs PicoPose; ablations demonstrate component contributions; tested on SPARK-2024, SwissCube, SHIRT, YCB-Video; offline reference.
AI.conclusion: Temporal anchoring improves robustness and speed of monocular 6-DoF pose estimation for non-cooperative targets; compatible with various datasets and CAD models; no target-specific training required.

title: What Must Survive? Exact Task-Information--State Frontiers for Resource-Sufficient Learning
summary:
A system may be compressed before its downstream task is fully known. We ask how much retained state is then necessary and how much can be saved by limited advance task information.
  For a finite family of linear tasks, a task message is revealed before state formation and the exact task only afterwards. For an advice alphabet of size $K$, the exact frontier is \[ p^*(K)= \min_{\substack{\Pcal\text{ partition of }\U\\|\Pcal|\le K}} \max_{C\in\Pcal}\rank(T_C), \] with the $b$-bit frontier obtained by setting $K=\min(2^b,|\U|)$. Thus advance task information reduces state through partitions whose joint task operators have low rank.
  We also give an approximate singular-value frontier, a common-core lower bound and exact direct-sum law, and strong NP-hardness of finding an optimal advice partition. The hardness persists at every fixed positive approximation tolerance.
  Three examples illustrate the result. A well-conditioned softmax attention construction gives an exact $524{,}288\to1{,}024$ coordinate frontier when nine bits resolve one of $512$ continuations. A domain-decomposed digital twin yields an interface-plus-local-state law and a weighted partition problem for heterogeneous regions.
  A hierarchical multi-task model gives a two-stage frontier in which three bits reduce the required state from $3136$ to $448$ coordinates, with further task information approaching the irreducible $328$-coordinate single-task floor.

AI.tldr: Defines an exact/approximate frontier for state compression under partial task information, via task-advice partitions with bounded cardinality. Proves NP-hardness of finding the optimal partition, provides bounds (approximate singular-value frontier, common-core lower bound, direct-sum law) and illustrates with three constructions showing substantial state savings.
AI.motivation: Quantify how much system state must be retained when the downstream task is not fully known, and how much can be saved with limited advance task information.
AI.method: Consider a finite family of linear tasks. A task message is revealed before state formation; the exact task is revealed afterward. For an advice alphabet of size K, define the frontier p*(K) as the minimum over partitions P of the universe U with |P| ≤ K of the maximum rank(T_C) over C in P, where T_C is the joint task operator for region C. The b-bit frontier uses K = min(2^b, |U|). The paper also derives an approximate singular-value frontier, a common-core lower bound and an exact direct-sum law, and proves strong NP-hardness of finding an optimal advice partition (persistent at every fixed positive approximation tolerance). It includes three illustrative examples.
AI.result:
Exact frontier: p*(K)=min_{P:|\P|
le K} max_{C
in P} rank(T_C). For b bits, K=min(2^b,|U|). Demonstrates an approximate singular-value frontier, a common-core lower bound, and an exact direct-sum law. Proves strong NP-hardness of finding an optimal partition for advice, with hardness persisting under any fixed positive approximation. Three examples quantify the frontiers: (1) softmax attention: 524,288→1,024 coordinates when nine bits resolve one of 512 continuations; (2) domain-decomposed digital twin: interface-plus-local-state law with a weighted partition problem for heterogeneous regions; (3) hierarchical multi-task model: a two-stage frontier where 3 bits reduce state from 3,136 to 448 coordinates, approaching an irreducible 328-coordinate single-task floor.
AI.conclusion: Advancing task information can substantially reduce necessary state via low-rank joint task operators, but finding the optimal partition is strongly NP-hard. The results establish fundamental frontiers, provide practical constructions with significant state savings, and suggest applicability to attention mechanisms, modular systems, and hierarchical multitask designs.

title: MicroHookACT: Monocular Microscopic Vision Guided Visuomotor Policy for Flexible Microelectrode Hooking
summary: Automated needle-loop hooking is a critical step in flexible microelectrode (FME) implantation. This paper presents MicroHookACT, an imitation learning-based visuomotor policy for automated 3D hooking under monocular microscopic vision. First, a unidirectional hooking strategy exploits defocus cues and optical-axis guidance to enable palpation-free precise alignment and contact-rich threading. Second, an action-supervised object attention module built on a frozen ViT backbone learns to focus on the micro-needle tip and micro-loop directly from human demonstrations, without requiring manual visual annotations for training. Third, attention-centered global coarse and local fine features are dynamically weighted according to predicted action progress, enabling a single ACT policy to adapt to changing defocus blur and visual requirements throughout the operation. In the experiments, visuomotor policies were trained on 60 human demonstrations and evaluated under five setups with varying difficulties. Our MicroHookACT framework achieved the highest overall success rate of 96.7\% with an average execution time of 11.5 s. These results demonstrate the potential of visuomotor policy learning for micron-level control under varying operating conditions.

AI.tldr: Imitation-learning-based visuomotor policy MicroHookACT enables automated 3D hooking for flexible microelectrode implantation using monocular vision; achieves 96.7% success in 60 demos, 11.5 s per trial, via defocus-guided alignment and action-supervised ViT-based attention.
AI.motivation: The task requires precise, repeatable micron-scale threading under monocular microscopic vision, where palpation is undesirable or impractical. Automated solutions can improve accuracy, speed, and consistency across varying optical conditions.
AI.method: Unidirectional hooking strategy leveraging defocus cues and optical-axis guidance for alignment; an action-supervised object attention module on a frozen ViT backbone learns to localize the micro-needle tip and micro-loop from human demonstrations without manual visual annotations; attention-driven global and local features are dynamically weighted by predicted action progress to adapt to defocus blur and visual requirements; entire policy trained via imitation learning on 60 human demonstrations and evaluated in five setups.
AI.result: Achieved a 96.7% overall success rate with an average execution time of 11.5 seconds, demonstrating strong performance and efficiency; demonstrates potential for micron-level control under varying operating conditions.
