AI.motivation: Enable invertible, volume-preserving generative models on manifolds with interpretable learned components, addressing the limitations of Euclidean formulations and comparing favorably to Riemannian CNFs.
AI.method: Adopt a fixed kinetic energy on a Riemannian manifold, learn a scalar potential, and integrate with a geodesic leapfrog scheme. Analyze interpretability by defining an implicit profile for any normalizable potential and a matched potential whose profile is the target. Use local harmonic analysis around target modes on the manifold. Evaluate across Euclidean, hyperbolic, and spherical spaces.
AI.result: The framework yields competitive sample quality and computational cost relative to Riemannian CNFs. The learned potential's interpretability is supported by the theory: the gap between learned and matched potentials decomposes into base memory and model bias, and the two potentials coincide when the position base is transferred to momentum. In the isotropic Gaussian case, the mechanism reduces to a phase-space rotation; local harmonic analysis extends this to general targets on manifolds.
AI.conclusion: Riemannian Neural Hamiltonian Flows offer an interpretable, efficient approach to generative modeling on manifolds, with a principled interpretation of the learned potential via matched vs implicit profiles and validated performance across multiple geometries.

title: Robotic Multiphase Interaction: Manipulating Coupled Liquid and Solid Dynamics with a World Model
summary: This work presents \textit{Robotic Multiphase Interaction (RMI)}, a setting in which liquid enters a porous material and interacts mechanically with its deforming solid skeleton. Manipulation can therefore change pore volume, expel or redistribute retained liquid, and alter grasp stability at the same time. Spilled liquid can also create safety risks in domestic and manufacturing settings. This differs from most manipulation of solid objects and from tasks that involve both liquid and solid while keeping the phases spatially separate. We study a sponge filled with water as the first RMI example. We use implicit incompressible porous flow with smoothed particle hydrodynamics as the dynamics engine and enable robotic manipulation by adding Coulomb contact memory, hybrid velocity and force regulation, and a stability gate for lifting. The resulting environment connects robot commands to changes in the coupled liquid and solid state. A world model conditioned on actions predicts how this state evolves under candidate commands, while a temporal UNet generates actions using either Diffusion Policy or rectified flow matching. Our world model reduces retained water prediction error by more than $60\%$ compared with the baseline. The best action sequence selected by the world model from policy proposals further reduces the predicted terminal water error by about half. These improvements show that modelling the coupled liquid and solid state helps the robot predict how its actions affect both the porous object and the liquid held inside.

AI.tldr: Introduces Robotic Multiphase Interaction (RMI): manipulating liquid-filled porous solids and predicting outcomes with a world model and temporal UNet, achieving large error reductions.
AI.motivation: Secure and optimize manipulation of liquids within deforming porous materials, addressing safety and reliability where liquid and solid states couple.
AI.method: Combine implicit incompressible porous-flow dynamics (SPH) with robotic control enhancements: Coulomb contact memory, hybrid velocity/force regulation, and a stability gate for lifting; implement a world model conditioned on actions to predict state evolution; employ a temporal UNet to generate actions via Diffusion Policy or rectified flow matching.
AI.result: World model reduces retained water prediction error by >60% vs baseline; the best action sequence from the world model further halves the predicted terminal water error.
AI.conclusion: Modeling the coupled liquid–solid state improves prediction and planning for manipulation of porous objects holding liquid.

title: Making Latent Evolution Explicit: Operator-Structured Transitions for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) augment robot policies by predicting how task-relevant scene states may evolve under interaction. Recent WAMs increasingly perform such prediction in latent representation spaces, avoiding full appearance-level generation while preserving control-relevant information. Yet latent transitions are commonly realized with Transformer-based predictors whose inductive structure is centered on token interaction rather than temporal evolution. We study transition realization as an architectural choice distinct from predictive representation and prediction-policy coupling. We introduce the Latent Evolution Operator Network (LEON), which models latent evolution in a learned observable space through context-modulated operator-based propagation and additive forcing. Grounded in the controlled Koopman generator view of evolution, LEON organizes context-dependent transition variation around a shared evolution-operator structure while retaining a complementary path for additive change. Controlled dynamical systems verify the resulting evolution-specific inductive bias and the complementary roles of operator propagation and forcing. Across two WAM formulations that integrate latent prediction into the policy differently, LEON improves closed-loop performance and robustness while remaining effective under full transition replacement. These results establish transition realization as a consequential architectural choice in latent WAMs.

AI.tldr: LEON introduces a latent evolution operator network for latent state transitions in WAMs, leveraging a context-modulated operator and additive forcing within a controlled Koopman framework, yielding improved performance and robustness and highlighting transition realization as an architectural design choice.
AI.motivation: Addresses the limitation of Transformer-based latent predictors that focus on token interactions rather than temporal evolution; aims to separate transition realization from predictive representation and policy coupling to improve latent state evolution modeling.
AI.method: Develop LEON: a latent evolution operator network using context-modulated propagation around a shared operator plus additive forcing; grounded in a controlled Koopman generator view; validates with controlled dynamical systems; tested on two WAM formulations; demonstrates evolution-specific inductive bias and complementary roles of operator propagation and forcing.
AI.result: LEON improves closed-loop performance and robustness and remains effective under full transition replacement across both WAM formulations.
AI.conclusion: Transition realization is a consequential architectural choice in latent WAMs; operator-based latent evolution modeling provides a beneficial inductive bias for latent state transitions.

title: ZYT-World: A Real-Time Controllable World Model for Closed-Loop Autonomous-Driving Simulation
comment: Technical Report. Videos and additional results are available at zyt-aim.github.io/ZYT-World
summary: Generative world models offer controllable and repeatable closed-loop simulation for end-to-end and vision-language-action driving policies, but production deployment exposes three unresolved requirements: faithfully reproducing a mixed fisheye-pinhole rig at native resolutions; reconciling causal, per-timestep interaction with long-horizon stability and low latency; and preserving scene identity when a location is revisited. We present ZYT-World, a single architecture that natively generates four fisheye views with field of view > 180° and three pinhole views. Projection-specific Plucker adapters encode camera geometry, ego-motion adaptive layer normalization provides global motion control, and a lightweight pixel-aligned layout conditions traffic participants and signals through instance-level boxes, headings and colors. Heterogeneous training combines full-rig geometric coverage with high-resolution detail. Teacher forcing, causal consistency distillation, self-rollout distribution matching distillation, and RigCritic transform a 40-step bidirectional teacher into a one-step, per-latent streaming generator, with RigCritic evaluating the seven-view rig jointly. A 19M-parameter variational autoencoder decoder (TinyVAE), W8A8 quantization, and our inference engine reduce decoding, backbone, and incremental-execution costs, respectively. Finally, cross-trajectory pairs derived from real captures train a plug-in implicit-memory module that preserves place-specific evidence. On the internal multi-view test set, the one-step model retains more than 90% of the teacher's PSNR and SSIM, while FID, FVD, and LPIPS stay within 11% of the teacher. Under the generator-only timing in Figure 2, it is 107.7 times faster than the 40-step bidirectional teacher. TinyVAE decodes 59.8 times faster than Wan. 30s rollouts and cross-trajectory revisits show the intended long-horizon and memory behavior.

AI.tldr: ZYT-World is a unified, high-fidelity, multi-view driving world model that generates fisheye and pinhole views at native resolutions with per-latent streaming and memory, enabling long-horizon, low-latency planning with high fidelity and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Address production deployment needs: faithful multi-view camera rigs at native resolutions, causal, per-timestep interaction with long-horizon stability and low latency, and preserving scene identity on revisits.
AI.method: A single architecture that natively generates four fisheye and three pinhole views using projection-specific Plucker adapters for camera geometry, ego-motion adaptive layer normalization for global motion control, and a pixel-aligned layout conditioning traffic participants via instance-level boxes, headings, and colors. Heterogeneous training combines full-rig geometric coverage with high-resolution detail. Distillation includes teacher forcing, causal consistency distillation, self-rollout distribution matching distillation, and RigCritic to convert a 40-step bidirectional teacher into a one-step per-latent streaming generator, with RigCritic evaluating the seven-view rig jointly. A 19M TinyVAE decoder with W8A8 quantization and an efficient inference engine reduce decoding, backbone, and incremental-execution costs. A plug-in implicit-memory module trained from cross-trajectory pairs preserves place-specific evidence.
AI.result: On an internal multi-view test set, the one-step model retains >90% of the teacher’s PSNR and SSIM, while FID, FVD, and LPIPS stay within 11% of the teacher. Generator-only timing yields 107.7x speedup over the 40-step bidirectional teacher; TinyVAE decodes 59.8x faster than Wan. 30-second rollouts and cross-trajectory revisits demonstrate intended long-horizon and memory behavior.
AI.conclusion: The approach delivers a high-fidelity, low-latency, memory-conscious multi-view world model suitable for driving policy learning, with substantial efficiency gains and preserved perceptual quality, aided by a plug-in implicit-memory module for place-specific consistency.

title: Beyond Gaussian Worlds: Latent Geometry Matters for JEPAs
summary: Recent Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) prevent representation collapse by constraining learned representations to follow a prescribed target distribution, such as an isotropic Gaussian or the uniform distribution on a hypersphere. Klindt et al. (2026) showed that, under their Euclidean assumptions, matching a Gaussian target can recover Gaussian latent variables up to a linear transformation, and that the Gaussian is the unique distribution with this guarantee. We extend their analysis to latent variables supported on embedded Riemannian manifolds and derive conditions on the latent geometry and positive-pair dynamics under which alignment and exact distribution matching guarantee linear recovery. In particular, when the latent variables are uniformly distributed on a sphere and the representations are matched to the same spherical distribution, every optimal representation recovers the latent state up to an orthogonal transformation. This shows that Gaussian uniqueness is not a universal property of distribution-matched JEPAs: non-Euclidean latent geometries can admit other linearly recoverable distributions. We further derive an approximate-recovery bound that is strictly tighter for the spherical world than for the Gaussian world. Experiments on Gaussian, spherical, and toroidal latent spaces show that geometrically compatible targets yield better linear recovery when optimization succeeds, whereas mismatched targets distort the latent structure. This advantage persists in high-dimensional Clifford-torus worlds.

AI.tldr: Extends distribution-matched JEPAs to non-Euclidean latent geometries (manifolds). Shows that Gaussian uniqueness does not hold universally; for sphere-latent spaces with spherical targets, optimal representations recover latent states up to an orthogonal transform; derives tighter approximate-recovery bounds for spheres than Gaussians; experiments across Gaussian, spherical, and toroidal spaces (and Clifford-torus) confirm geometry-target compatibility improves recovery.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether the Gaussian-uniqueness property of distribution-matched JEPAs extends beyond Euclidean latent spaces and understand how latent geometry affects identifiability and linear recoverability.
AI.method: Theoretically extend Klindt et al.'s analysis to latent variables on embedded Riemannian manifolds. Derive conditions on latent geometry and positive-pair dynamics under which alignment and exact distribution matching guarantee linear recovery. Specialize to uniform sphere distributions and identical spherical targets to show recovery up to an orthogonal transform. Derive approximate-recovery bounds, and conduct experiments across Gaussian, spherical, toroidal spaces, and high-dimensional Clifford-torus worlds.
AI.result: Gaussian uniqueness is not universal: non-Euclidean latent geometries admit other linearly recoverable distributions. For latent variables uniformly distributed on a sphere and matched to the same spherical target, every optimal representation recovers the latent state up to an orthogonal transformation. Approximate-recovery bounds are tighter on the sphere than in the Gaussian case. Experimental results show geometry-target compatibility yields better linear recovery when optimization succeeds; mismatched targets distort latent structure. The advantage persists in high-dimensional Clifford-torus settings.
AI.conclusion: Target distribution design in JEPA frameworks should consider latent geometry; non-Euclidean geometries enable alternative linear recoverability and may offer tighter recovery guarantees under geometry-aligned targets. Mismatched targets can degrade latent structure across manifolds, highlighting the importance of matching target geometry to latent space topology.

title: AtomEgo: Exploring Ego-Robot Integration for Embodied Foundation Model Pretraining
summary: Embodied foundation models are constrained by the limited scale and diversity of robot demonstrations, motivating the use of large-scale egocentric human interaction data. However, how to effectively incorporate such data into embodied-model pre-training remains unclear because of substantial embodiment and action-space gaps between humans and robots. We present AtomEgo, a systematic study of ego--robot co-training supported by a curated corpus of approximately 2,659 hours and a scalable data processing pipeline. Across vision--language--action and world--action model architectures, we investigate three representative paradigms: joint co-training with domain-specific action heads, progressive ego-to-robot transfer through embodiment alignment, and joint video--action modeling. We evaluate these paradigms through multi-task real-robot experiments and language-conditioned cross-embodiment representation analysis. Our results reveal a simple principle: Data Scale * Alignment Quality --> Capability Gain; egocentric data can improve generalization, but their value depends on how effectively they are aligned and utilized. This principle can provide practical guidance for scalable ego--robot pre-training.

AI.tldr: AtomEgo studies ego-robot co-training using a large corpus of egocentric human interaction data (~2.66k hours) to bridge embodiment gaps. It compares three paradigms (joint co-training with action heads, progressive ego-to-robot transfer via embodiment alignment, joint video--action modeling) across vision-language-action and world-action architectures, validated by real-robot experiments and cross-embodiment analysis. Key finding: Data Scale × Alignment Quality governs capability gains.
AI.motivation: Overcoming the limited scale and diversity of robot demonstrations by leveraging large-scale egocentric human data, despite substantial embodiment and action-space gaps between humans and robots.
AI.method: Assemble a curated dataset (~2,659 hours) and scalable pipeline; evaluate three paradigms for ego–robot co-training: (1) joint training with domain-specific action heads, (2) progressive ego-to-robot transfer through embodiment alignment, (3) joint video–action modeling; test across vision–language–action and world–action models; conduct multi-task real-robot experiments and language-conditioned cross-embodiment representation analysis.
AI.result: Found a generalizable principle: Data Scale × Alignment Quality → Capability Gain. Egocentric data improve generalization when effectively aligned; however, the gains depend on how well the data are aligned and utilized.
AI.conclusion: AtomEgo provides practical guidance for scalable ego–robot pre-training, highlighting the importance of dataset scale and alignment quality and offering a systematic framework for evaluating egocentric data's value in embodied foundation models.

title: Balanced Prompt Adaptation against Entropy-Induced Collapse for Test-Time Binary Segmentation
summary: Entropy minimization is a standard objective for test-time adaptation (TTA), but it can fail in imbalanced binary segmentation. Unlike image classification, dense segmentation aggregates thousands of pixel predictions, allowing the larger predicted class to dominate the update, pull minority predictions toward itself, and produce a degenerate mask as predictions saturate and their entropy gradients vanish. We theoretically establish this collapse in a shared-shift model. This analysis motivates Balanced-Anchor Prompt Adaptation (BAPA), which combines two complementary modules. The Class-Balanced Anchors (CBA) module selects high-confidence anchors separately from each predicted class and gives foreground and background equal total loss weight, preventing the larger region from dominating the update. Dynamic Prompt Adaptation (DPA) refreshes these anchors after each prediction update and optimizes only text-side prompt residuals while keeping the vision-language encoders frozen. This prompt-only update refines the foreground-background decision boundary without altering the pretrained dense visual representation. Across experiments from four domains, BAPA achieves the highest mean Dice among the evaluated methods. Factorized ablations further validate the complementary roles of CBA and DPA, supporting balanced prompt adaptation as an effective alternative to entropy minimization for test-time binary segmentation.

AI.tldr: BAPA avoids entropy-driven collapse in test-time adaptation for imbalanced binary segmentation by replacing entropy minimization with balanced prompt adaptation. It uses two modules: Class-Balanced Anchors (CBA) to balance loss across foreground/background by selecting high-confidence anchors per class, and Dynamic Prompt Adaptation (DPA) to update only text-side prompt residuals after each prediction while freezing the vision-language encoders. This yields higher mean Dice across four domains, with ablations confirming complementary roles of CBA and DPA, suggesting balanced prompt adaptation as an effective alternative to entropy minimization for TTA in binary segmentation.
AI.motivation: Entropy minimization during test-time adaptation tends to collapse predictions in imbalanced binary segmentation because the larger class dominates updates, pushing minority predictions toward the dominant class and yielding degenerate masks; a need exists for an objective that preserves discrimination between foreground and background without collapsing predictions.
AI.method: Introduce Balanced-Anchor Prompt Adaptation (BAPA) consisting of (1) Class-Balanced Anchors (CBA): select high-confidence anchors from each predicted class and balance total loss weight between foreground and background to prevent domination by the larger region; (2) Dynamic Prompt Adaptation (DPA): update only the text-side prompt residuals after each prediction, keep vision-language encoders frozen, effectively refining the decision boundary without changing the dense visual representation.
AI.result: BAPA achieves the highest mean Dice across four domains compared to competing methods. Factorized ablations show the two components play complementary roles, validating that balanced prompt adaptation improves TTA for binary segmentation over entropy minimization.
AI.conclusion: Balanced prompt adaptation (BAPA) is an effective alternative to entropy minimization for test-time binary segmentation, leveraging CBA to balance class contributions and DPA to adapt prompts dynamically without altering pretrained visual features.

title: Multi-Domain Clustering via Measure Quantization
summary: Clustering is a fundamental task in data analysis, typically addressed through centroid-based methods such as K-means. In this work, we present a general framework for multi-domain clustering via measure quantization: given samples from multiple domains, we learn a shared set of cluster prototypes by minimizing a probability metric, such as the Sinkhorn divergence or the Maximum Mean Discrepancy, between each domain's probability measure and the measure of prototypes. Data points are then assigned to clusters either via nearest centroid, or via optimal transport, a collaborative strategy that couples all samples within a domain. A mini-batch optimization strategy makes both fitting and assignment scalable, reducing memory and computational cost while preserving clustering performance. Experimental results on 5 multi-domain benchmarks spanning image, audio and sensor data show that our Sinkhorn-based method consistently outperforms classical and multi-domain clustering baselines, and that this advantage persists when scaling to hundreds of thousands of samples.

AI.tldr: A general, scalable framework for multi-domain clustering via measure quantization using probability metrics between domain measures and a shared prototype set.
AI.motivation: To cluster data from multiple domains with a common set of prototypes by leveraging probabilistic distances, enabling cross-domain coherence and improved scalability.
AI.method: Learn a shared set of cluster prototypes by minimizing a probability metric (Sinkhorn divergence or MMD) between each domain's distribution and the prototypes; assign data by nearest centroid or via optimal transport that couples all samples within a domain; employ mini-batch optimization for scalability.
AI.result: The Sinkhorn-based method consistently outperforms classical and multi-domain clustering baselines across 5 benchmarks spanning image, audio, and sensor data and scales to hundreds of thousands of samples.
AI.conclusion: The proposed measure-quantization framework with OT-based assignment is effective for multi-domain clustering, with Sinkhorn divergence offering notable advantages in cross-domain clustering and scalability.

title: Learning Distance-Conditioned Object Transport for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from a Single Motion Clip
summary: Motion tracking can reproduce humanoid loco-manipulation from a single retargeted motion clip, but a policy trained on a fixed reference primarily reproduces its demonstrated transport outcome. Although the source trajectory visits intermediate object displacements, transport termination is demonstrated only at its endpoint. We identify this mismatch as the termination-versus-passage gap: intermediate displacements are observed as passage states rather than termination-complete outcomes. We introduce Distance-Conditioned Reference Recomposition (DCRR), which relocates the demonstrated termination segment to intermediate transport states. A frozen tracking teacher replays the recomposed references under closed-loop dynamics, and the retained trajectories are relabeled by their achieved object placements and distilled into a reference-free policy. This procedure constructs distance-conditioned supervision from the interaction behavior encoded in the source motion. Across Carry, Kick-Push, Crouch-Push, and Drag, DCRR-BC produces command-dependent transport with an overall normalized distance mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.15, compared with 0.28 for source-only behavior cloning. RL fine-tuning further improves the command response and execution robustness in the training simulator and under sim-to-sim transfer. Finally, hardware experiments demonstrate transport-distance modulation across all four interaction modes.

AI.tldr: A method (DCRR-BC) addresses a termination-versus-passage gap in humanoid transport tasks by recomposing reference trajectories to match intermediate transport states, using a frozen tracking teacher for closed-loop replay, relabeling outcomes, and learning a reference-free policy; enhanced by RL and validated in simulation and hardware.
AI.motivation: Policy learned from a fixed reference tends to reproduce only the endpoint transport, while intermediate displacements are misinterpreted as passage; a distance-conditioned supervision is needed to align behavior with interactive outcomes.
AI.method: Distance-Conditioned Reference Recomposition (DCRR): relocate the termination segment to intermediate transport states; use a frozen tracking teacher to replay recomposed references under closed-loop dynamics; relabel preserved trajectories by achieved object placements and distill into a reference-free policy; derive distance-conditioned supervision from the source motion; train with behavior cloning (DCRR-BC), then RL fine-tuning; validate in simulation and on hardware.
AI.result: Across Carry, Kick-Push, Crouch-Push, and Drag, DCRR-BC achieves command-dependent transport with a normalized distance MAE of 0.15, versus 0.28 for source-only behavior cloning; RL improves command response and robustness; hardware experiments demonstrate transport-distance modulation across all four modes.
AI.conclusion: DCRR-BC effectively bridges the termination-passage gap by reusing interaction semantics through distance-conditioned supervision, enabling accurate, command-driven transport across multiple interaction modes, with demonstrated gains in simulation, RL-enhanced policy robustness, and hardware feasibility.

title: SFVO: Decoupled Confidence-Guided Stereo-Flow Visual Odometry with Bidirectional PnP
summary: Deep learning-based visual odometry (VO) has achieved significant progress, yet most existing methods focus on a monocular approach, which suffers from scale ambiguity. Stereo VO provides real metric by its nature, but remains less studied in deep learning VO due to its high computational cost and modeling complexity. Recent advances in stereo matching and optical flow estimation have made dense visual correspondence increasingly accurate and reliable, but their complementary geometric information has not been fully exploited for VO. In this paper, we present SFVO, a correspondence-driven stereo VO framework that directly builds upon pretrained stereo matching and optical flow models. SFVO exploits pretrained stereo matching and optical flow models to estimate stereo and temporal correspondences. Instead of learning pose directly from images, SFVO maps learned correspondences into geometric constraints and predicts which points are trustworthy. To improve the reliability of visual correspondence-based geometric constraints, we introduce decoupled confidence maps for rotation and translation. This design better aligns the characteristics of visual correspondence and 6-DoF transformations. Extensive experiments on outdoor and indoor datasets demonstrate that SFVO achieves robust and accurate pose estimation with strong generalization capability. The code will be released.

AI.tldr: SFVO: a correspondence-driven stereo visual odometry framework that leverages pretrained stereo matching and optical flow, with decoupled confidence maps for rotation and translation, to produce robust, generalizable pose estimation without learning ego-motion directly.
AI.motivation: Address scale ambiguity in monocular VO and computational/m modeling challenges of stereo VO; leverage dense stereo matching and optical flow advances to exploit geometric constraints from correspondences.
AI.method: Build on pretrained stereo matching and optical flow models to obtain stereo and temporal correspondences; map correspondences into geometric constraints rather than learning pose directly; identify trustworthy points; introduce decoupled confidence maps for rotation and translation to better align with 6-DoF transformations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on outdoor and indoor datasets show robust and accurate pose estimation with strong generalization; code will be released.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effectiveness of a correspondence-driven stereo VO framework and decoupled confidence modeling to improve VO robustness and generalization.

title: Optimization Geometry of Equivalent Brownian RKHS Representations
summary: Equivalent finite parameterizations can represent the same functions and intrinsic norm yet induce different optimization algorithms. We study this effect in a controlled finite Brownian RKHS with nodal, increment, and spectral coordinates. Classical finite-element, RKHS-interpolation, Brownian-covariance, and mixed-boundary DCT identities make the shared hypothesis class, Brownian energy, approximation operator, and coordinate maps explicit. Our main results concern the optimization geometry of this fixed model. With mapped initialization, identical scalar steps, and identical minibatches, nodal and spectral GD/SGD have exactly the same mapped trajectories. Increment GD is an explicit Euler step for the constant Brownian/Sobolev metric, with factor $1/h$. For Brownian-regularized least squares, $κ_2(\mathbf H_{\mathrm{inc}})\le1+A/ρ$, independently of grid resolution $G$ for fixed $A$, $ρ>0$, and the stated normalization. Under the stated standard-Adam convention, the universal orthogonal equivariance group is exactly the signed permutations; the block DCT-VIII transform is not one. Float64 tests over five grids numerically verify the finite identities, mapped one-layer and recursive trajectories, conditioning predictions, and theorem-matched Adam separation. Thus coordinate effects are isolated without changing the represented functions, intrinsic regularizer, or approximation space.

AI.tldr: Different finite parameterizations of the same function and intrinsic norm induce different optimization dynamics in a controlled Brownian RKHS; under mapped initialization and identical training conditions, nodal and spectral coordinates share trajectories, while increment coordinates follow explicit Euler dynamics. The work derives several identities, establishes a bound on conditioning for Brownian-regularized least squares independent of grid resolution, and shows that the universal Adam equivariance group is the signed permutations. Experimental validation supports the theory across multiple grids.
AI.motivation: To understand how reparameterization (nodal, increment, spectral) and coordinate representations affect optimization trajectories and geometry when the function space and regularizer remain fixed, enabling isolation of coordinate effects from the represented function class.
AI.method: Define a finite Brownian RKHS with nodal, increment, and spectral coordinates. Leverage classical identities (finite-element, RKHS interpolation, Brownian covariance, mixed-boundary DCT) to express a shared hypothesis class, Brownian energy, approximation operator, and coordinate maps. Analyze optimization dynamics under mapped initialization, identical scalar steps, and identical minibatches for GD/SGD across coordinates. Show that increment updates correspond to explicit Euler steps in a Brownian/Sobolev metric with step factor 1/h. Derive κ2(H_inc) ≤ 1 + A/ρ for Brownian-regularized LS, independent of grid resolution G for fixed A, ρ>0. Examine Adam under standard convention to identify the universal orthogonal equivariance group as signed permutations, and show block DCT-VIII is not equivariant. Validate results with Float64 experiments on five grids comparing identities, trajectories, conditioning, and Adam separation.
AI.result: Equivalence of parameterizations: nodal and spectral GD/SGD share identical mapped trajectories under the specified initialization and training setup; increment GD corresponds to an explicit Euler step in the Brownian/Sobolev metric with factor 1/h. Conditioning bound for Brownian-regularized LS is κ2(H_inc) ≤ 1 + A/ρ, independent of grid resolution. Adam’s universal orthogonal equivariance group is the signed permutation group; block DCT-VIII lacks this equivariance. Five-grid Float64 tests confirm the finite identities, mapped dynamics, improved conditioning predictions, and theorem-consistent Adam separation, demonstrating that coordinate effects can be isolated without altering the represented function class or regularizer.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that changing coordinate representations within a fixed Brownian RKHS alters optimization geometry without changing the function space or energy, and that with mapped initializations and identical training conditions, many reparameterizations yield the same optimization paths, while some (increment) exhibit explicit metric-based updates. The results provide precise invariance/equivariance characterizations of the optimization process under reparameterization and supply practical bounds and empirical validation for learning dynamics across grids.

title: Adaptive Rollout Truncation Based on Epistemic Uncertainty for Efficient Offline World Model Training
comment: 8 pages, 12 figures. Accepted at the IEEE/RSJ IROS 2026 Workshop "Rethinking Uncertainty for Modern Robotics Paradigms"
summary:
Accurate neural world models are central to model-based robotics, where they enable robots to predict future states from previously observed trajectories. Multi-step autoregressive training improves long-horizon prediction, but fixed rollout horizons also increase computational cost and can amplify early training errors when the model is still inaccurate. Existing training schemes typically use the same rollout length throughout optimization, independent of the model's current predictive reliability.
  We propose an epistemic uncertainty-driven adaptive rollout strategy for offline world model training following an auto-curriculum training scheme. Instead of always unrolling to a fixed horizon, the model terminates autoregressive rollouts once epistemic uncertainty exceeds a threshold calibrated from a warm-up phase. We study two uncertainty estimators: a five-head ensemble with a shared recurrent backbone and Monte Carlo Dropout. A two-stage warm-up procedure stabilizes uncertainty estimates before we enable adaptive truncation.
  Experiments on ANYmal-D and ANT show that ensemble-based adaptive truncation matches or improves the prediction accuracy of fixed-horizon training and the RWM-U baseline while requiring substantially fewer cumulative rollout steps. Training a world model on ANYmal-D following the presented approach reaches comparable final performance with the baselines with roughly 72% less rollout computation. These results indicate that epistemic uncertainty is useful not only for downstream policy regularization, but also for making world model training itself more compute-efficient.

AI.tldr: An uncertainty-driven adaptive rollout method for offline world-model training reduces compute by truncating rollouts when epistemic uncertainty exceeds a calibrated threshold, using a five-head ensemble or MC dropout with a two-stage warm-up. It matches or exceeds fixed-horizon and RWM-U baselines while using substantially fewer rollout steps (≈72% less on ANYmal-D).
AI.motivation: Fixed, fixed-horizon rollouts in world-model training are computationally wasteful and can amplify early errors as the model learns. An adaptive strategy driven by epistemic uncertainty can tailor rollout length to the model's reliability, improving efficiency without compromising accuracy.
AI.method: Auto-curriculum training with two-stage warm-up to stabilize uncertainty estimates. Evaluate epistemic uncertainty via (a) a five-head ensemble with a shared recurrent backbone, and (b) Monte Carlo dropout. Set a threshold calibrated during warm-up; terminate autoregressive rollouts when uncertainty exceeds threshold during offline world-model training.
AI.result: Adaptive truncation using ensemble-based uncertainty matches or improves the accuracy of fixed-horizon training and the RWM-U baseline, while substantially reducing cumulative rollout steps. On ANYmal-D, training reaches comparable final performance with ~72% less rollout computation.
AI.conclusion: Epistemic uncertainty is a practical signal to guide compute-efficient world-model training, not only for policy regularization but also for efficient offline world-model learning. The approach is compatible with multiple uncertainty estimators and can generalize to other model-based learning settings.

title: Beyond Benchmark Scores: Auditing Medical Vision-Language Models for Chest X-Ray Tuberculosis Screening
comment: 27 pages, 7 figures, and 21 tables; includes extended methods, statistical analyses, and robustness evaluations
summary: A medical model's benchmark score does not establish that the same conclusion holds under a different evaluation. This study tests whether claims about model ranking, score reliability and screening performance survive changes in cohort, prompt, negative spectrum, specified prevalence and operating threshold. We audit three medical vision-language models (BioMedCLIP, CheXficient, and MedSigLIP) and a general-domain OpenCLIP comparator on 12,200 chest radiograph records from four datasets (Montgomery, Shenzhen, TBX11K, and VinDr-CXR). Five fixed prompt families yield 244,000 model--image--prompt scores. No model leads every cohort and reliability criterion. Prompt-family changes alter AUROC in 21 of 48 multiplicity-controlled comparisons. Replacing healthy controls with sick non-tuberculosis controls reduces AUROC by 0.075--0.306 across all four models. On VinDr-CXR, the three medical models distinguish tuberculosis from no-finding controls substantially better than from pneumonia or lung tumor; their AUROC point estimates for both named diseases fall below 0.5. CheXficient has documented VinDr-CXR pretraining exposure, which limits the interpretation of its results. Thresholds chosen for 95\% sensitivity on TBX11K training retain that constraint by point estimate in only four of sixteen target evaluations. A five-seed supervised source model reaches 0.999 AUROC on TBX11K validation but 0.629 on each of two external cohorts. Conservative exclusion of perceptual-overlap candidates narrows this gap without closing it. These retrospective, single-task results show that discrimination, score reliability and threshold retention support different portability claims. Evidence for chest X-ray tuberculosis screening should identify the complete evaluation specification rather than attribute clinical portability to a checkpoint alone.

AI.tldr: Comprehensive cross-cohort auditing reveals that medical vision–language model performance for TB screening in chest X-rays is non-portable across cohorts, prompts, and negative spectra; performance, reliability, and threshold transfer diverge, challenging single-cohort benchmarks as portability evidence.
AI.motivation: To test whether model ranking, score reliability, and screening performance generalize across changes in cohort composition, prompts, negative spectrum, disease prevalence, and decision thresholds in medical vision-language models.
AI.method: Audit four models (BioMedCLIP, CheXficient, MedSigLIP, and OpenCLIP) on 12,200 chest radiographs from Montgomery, Shenzhen, TBX11K, and VinDr-CXR using five fixed prompt families to generate 244,000 model–image–prompt scores; evaluate AUROC, threshold retention, and performance under various negative controls and prevalence settings.
AI.result: No model dominates across all cohorts or reliability tests. Prompt-family changes affect AUROC in 21/48 multiplicity-controlled comparisons. Replacing healthy controls with sick non-tuberculosis controls reduces AUROC by 0.075–0.306 across models. On VinDr-CXR, models distinguish TB from no-finding better than from pneumonia or tumor (AUROC for named diseases <0.5). CheXficient pretraining exposure complicates interpretation. Thresholds tuned for 95% sensitivity on TBX11K training retain that sensitivity in only 4/16 target evaluations. A five-seed supervised source model achieves 0.999 AUROC on TBX11K validation but 0.629 on two external cohorts. Conservative exclusion of perceptual overlaps narrows this gap but does not close it.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate that discrimination, score reliability, and threshold retention yield different portability claims; evidence for chest X-ray TB screening should specify the complete evaluation design rather than attributing portability to any single checkpoint.

title: SpecQuant: Speculative Decoding with Multi-Parent Quantization for Adaptive LLM Inference
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Published in the 2026 Fifth International Conference on Power, Control and Computing Technologies (ICPC2T)
summary: Running large language models (LLMs) locally continues to be limited by restrictions of compute and memory on consumer hardware. The popular acceleration technologies, such as quantization, speculative decoding, and adaptive inferencing, offer substantial speed boosts but usually necessitate retraining, per architecture tuning, or draft models. SpecQuant is a trainingfree framework, that combines speculative decoding with multiparent quantization to perform adaptive, efficient inference of LLMs. SpecQuant derives multiple quantized variants (INT4, FP8, FP16) from a shared base model, and dynamically routes queries based on predicted complexity; lightweight variants are used for simple or factual tasks, and full-precision models are used for complex reasoning tasks or long-context inputs. The shared-weight design of SpecQuant ensures sufficient token acceptance for speculative decoding without compatibility issues using separate draft parent models. We evaluate SpecQuant on Qwen2.5 based models on the MMLU, AlpacaEval, and GSM8K datasets, or benchmarks, demonstrating 35-43% speedups without degrading accuracy greater than 2%, substantial within the LLM community. SpecQuant enables practical on-device LLM deployment across diverse hardware without special infrastructure or expertise.

AI.tldr: A training-free SpecQuant framework combines speculative decoding with multi-quantization to enable adaptive, on-device LLM inference, routing queries to quantized variants (INT4/FP8/FP16) and achieving 35-43% speedups with under 2% accuracy loss on Qwen2.5 across MMLU, AlpacaEval, GSM8K.
AI.motivation: Running LLMs locally is limited by compute/memory on consumer hardware. Existing accelerations (quantization, speculative decoding, adaptive inference) typically require retraining, architecture-specific tuning, or draft models.
AI.method: Derive multiple quantized variants from a shared base model (INT4, FP8, FP16) without retraining; use speculative decoding with a shared-weight design to route queries by predicted complexity; lightweight variants handle simple/factual tasks, full-precision handles complex reasoning/long context; maintain compatibility with speculative decoding via separate draft parent models; no special infrastructure.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on Qwen2.5-based models shows 35-43% speedups with accuracy degradation no more than 2% on MMLU, AlpacaEval, GSM8K.
AI.conclusion: SpecQuant enables practical on-device LLM deployment across diverse hardware without retraining or specialized infrastructure, delivering adaptive, efficient inference.

title: FORTE: Task-Adaptive Force Capability Optimization for Mobile Manipulators
summary: Effective physical interaction control in robotic manipulation requires not only kinematically feasible motion but also sufficient force-interaction capability. Existing redundancy resolution methods often ignore task-specific force demands or maximize the force capability indiscriminately, sacrificing dexterity when large force margins are unnecessary. We propose a task-oriented force capability optimization framework for redundant mobile manipulators. A Vision-Language Model (VLM) infers object physical properties from an RGB image and a task description, generating a desired task-force sequence that captures gravitational and inertial demands. We then define a task-oriented force capability metric as the signed distance between a task-force uncertainty ball and the dynamic residual force polytope (RFP), quantifying compatibility between task demands and the robot's remaining actuation capacity. This metric is incorporated, alongside manipulability, joint-limit avoidance, trajectory smoothness, and base-oscillation suppression, into a whole-body multi-objective trajectory-optimization problem. Experiments on a mobile manipulator performing lifting and single-point-holding tasks under varying payload conditions demonstrate that the proposed method provides sufficient force capability for heavy loads while preserving high manipulability for light loads. This yields a task-adaptive balance that fixed capability-maximizing baselines (RFP inscribed radius, RFP cone) and manipulability-only optimization fail to achieve. The core implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/yeying256/FORTE.

AI.tldr: Task-oriented force capability optimization for redundant mobile manipulators integrates VLM-inferred task-force sequences with a geometric metric (distance between a task-force uncertainty ball and the dynamic residual force polytope) in a multi-objective trajectory optimization to balance force capability and manipulability across payloads; validated on lifting and single-point-holding with code available.
AI.motivation: Existing redundancy resolution often ignores task-specific force demands or maximizes force capability indiscriminately, reducing dexterity when force margins are unnecessary. A task-adaptive framework is needed to maintain manipulability while satisfying force needs under varying payloads.
AI.method: A Vision-Language Model infers object properties from RGB image and task description to generate a desired task-force sequence capturing gravitational and inertial demands. Define a task-oriented force capability metric as the signed distance between a task-force uncertainty ball and the dynamic residual force polytope (RFP). Integrate this metric with manipulability, joint-limit avoidance, trajectory smoothness, and base-oscillation suppression into a whole-body multi-objective trajectory optimization for a mobile manipulator.
AI.result: Experiments on a mobile manipulator performing lifting and single-point-holding with varying payloads show the method achieves sufficient force capability for heavy loads while preserving high manipulability for light loads. The approach yields a task-adaptive balance that fixed capability-maximizing baselines (RFP inscribed radius, RFP cone) and manipulability-only optimization fail to achieve.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables adaptive balancing of force capability and dexterity by tying task demands to the robot’s residual actuation capacity through a VLM-informed task-force sequence and a geometric capability metric, with public release of the implementation.

title: XCalib Depth-Guided Geometric Optimization for Dense Thermal-Visible Video Registration
summary: Image registration is a vital preprocessing step in multimodal perception tasks, including image fusion, object detection, and semantic segmentation. In Advanced Driver- Assistance Systems (ADAS), spatial misalignment between visible (RGB) and infrared (IR) cameras -caused by non-coincident optical axes and field-of-view differences- introduces non-uniform parallax and visual ghosting. Classical keypoint-based methods are restricted to global homographies that fail under dynamic depth, while unconstrained dense flow algorithms lack structural regularization and suffer from temporal instability. In this paper, we propose XCalib, an unsupervised dense thermal-visible registration framework that bridges this gap. Rather than serving as an absolute metric calibration tool, XCalib leverages virtual pinhole camera parameterization strictly as a geometric constraint space. By optimizing effective relative pose and intrinsics alongside predicted monocular metric depth, XCalib restricts the search space of spatial displacements to physically valid projection geometries. Our key contributions are: (1) a novel registration paradigm that uses camera parameterization as an implicit regularizer for dense cross-modal warping; (2) Normalized Edges Correlation (NEC), a robust structural similarity metric tailored to cross- spectral alignment; and (3) extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations across public ADAS datasets, demonstrating superior temporal stability and alignment accuracy over unconstrained dense flow baselines.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised dense cross-modal (thermal-visible) registration (XCalib) that uses camera parameterization as a geometric regularizer, with NEC similarity, achieving stable, accurate alignment.
AI.motivation: Bridging RGB-IR misalignment due to non-coincident optical axes, parallax, and field-of-view differences in ADAS; classical keypoint methods fail under dynamic depth, and unconstrained dense flow lacks structure and temporal stability.
AI.method: Introduce XCalib: an unsupervised dense registration framework that optimizes relative pose, intrinsics, and monocular depth within a virtual-pinhole parameterization; uses camera parameterization as an implicit regularizer for dense cross-modal warping; proposes Normalized Edges Correlation (NEC) as a robust cross-spectral similarity metric; extensive evaluations on public ADAS datasets.
AI.result: XCalib achieves superior temporal stability and alignment accuracy over unconstrained dense-flow baselines, with comprehensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations on public ADAS datasets.
AI.conclusion: Camera parameterization can act as an effective geometric regularizer for cross-modal dense registration; NEC provides robust cross-spectral structure guidance; XCalib advances unsupervised dense thermal-visible registration for ADAS applications.

title: GEM-MPC: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation through Expert-Guided Planning
summary: Effective exploration in high-dimensional continuous control remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning. Planning-based methods address this by combining online planning with learned policies and value functions, but their components can become misaligned during training: learned sampling policies may diverge from planner behavior, while planning distributions stored in replay become stale as the model and value function evolve. Reanalysis can refresh these targets, but at substantial computational cost. We propose GEM-MPC, an MPPI-based reinforcement learning method that improves the interaction between planning and learning. GEM-MPC uses MPPI to combine a policy trained to clone the planner with a KL-regularized policy that explores around it, providing complementary exploitation and guided exploration within planning. We further introduce Gated Prior Distillation, which selectively learns from stored planning distributions only when they provide a better target than the current prior, reducing the impact of stale planning data without requiring full reanalysis. Across continuous-control benchmarks, GEM-MPC consistently outperforms existing planning-based baselines under lower computational budgets.

AI.tldr: GEM-MPC couples MPPI-based planning with a planner-clone policy and a KL-guided exploration policy, plus gated distillation from planning data. It improves planning-learning interaction, reduces reliance on stale targets, and achieves better performance at lower compute.
AI.motivation: Planning-based RL suffers misalignment between learned sampling policies and planner behavior, and replay targets can become stale as the model and value function evolve; reanalysis is computationally expensive.
AI.method: GEM-MPC uses MPPI to blend a policy that clones the planner with a KL-regularized exploration policy around it; Gated Prior Distillation selectively learns from stored planning distributions only when they offer a better target than the current prior, reducing stale data impact without full reanalysis.
AI.result: Across continuous-control benchmarks, GEM-MPC consistently outperforms existing planning-based baselines under lower computational budgets.
AI.conclusion: The approach improves exploitation-exploration integration in planning-based RL, mitigates data staleness, and offers efficient, scalable planning-learning interaction for high-dimensional control.

title: DPed-VLN: A Benchmark for Socially Compliant Vision-and-Language Navigation in Dynamic Pedestrian Environments
summary: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) has advanced rapidly in static indoor environments, but robots operating in human-populated spaces must ground language while responding to moving pedestrians and social-safety constraints. We present DPed-VLN, a Habitat 3.0 benchmark for dynamic-pedestrian VLN that couples 33,093 navigation episodes with paired global and prior-augmented instructions, ORCA-controlled humanoid pedestrians, socially constrained expert paths, and metrics that jointly assess navigation efficiency and social safety. DPed-VLN separates ordinary goal-oriented route guidance from prior-augmented instructions that expose dynamic-pedestrian cues for controlled analysis. To instantiate the benchmark, we introduce DPet (Dynamic Pedestrian-aware Network), a pedestrian-aware policy network trained with reinforcement learning and imitation learning. We further adapt representative state-of-the-art VLM-based navigation models, including NaVILA and StreamVLN, to DPed-VLN through LoRA fine-tuning. Experiments show that LoRA adaptation improves zero-shot VLM baselines in several success and safety metrics, especially reducing StreamVLN's collision rate. Among the evaluated methods, DPet-RL achieves the highest SR, SPL, and STL.

AI.tldr: Introduces DPed-VLN, a Habitat 3.0 benchmark for dynamic-pedestrian VLN with 33k episodes, ORCA-controlled pedestrians, and social-safety metrics; proposes DPet, a pedestrian-aware RL/IL policy; adapts VLM baselines NaVILA and StreamVLN via LoRA fine-tuning; results show LoRA enhances zero-shot performance and DPet-RL achieving top navigation and safety metrics.
AI.motivation: VLN in human-populated, dynamic environments requires grounding language while complying with social safety cues; static indoor benchmarks inadequately capture pedestrian dynamics and social constraints; a combined benchmark and pedestrian-aware policies are needed for robust real-world navigation.
AI.method: Create DPed-VLN with 33,093 navigation episodes in Habitat 3.0, featuring paired global and prior-augmented instructions; integrate ORCA-controlled humanoid pedestrians and socially constrained expert paths; develop DPet, a pedestrian-aware policy via reinforcement learning and imitation learning; adapt state-of-the-art VLM-based navigation models (NaVILA, StreamVLN) to DPed-VLN using LoRA fine-tuning.
AI.result: LoRA adaptation improves zero-shot VLM baselines on multiple success and safety metrics, notably reducing StreamVLN’s collision rate; among evaluated methods, DPet-RL yields the highest SR, SPL, and STL.
AI.conclusion: DPed-VLN provides a platform to study dynamic-pedestrian VLN with joint navigation and social-safety assessment; LoRA-tuned VLMs and the DPet-RL baseline advance performance in dynamic environments; future work could explore generalization and real-world transfer, and refine social-safety metrics.

title: PointLAM: Local Attentive Mamba for Efficient Point-based 3D Object Detection
summary: 3D object detection from LiDAR point clouds faces a fundamental dilemma: voxel-based methods achieve efficiency at the cost of geometric quantization, while point-based methods preserve fidelity but suffer from prohibitive computational bottlenecks. Specifically, point-based architectures are crippled by slow downsampling strategies (e.g., FPS) and expensive dynamic neighbor queries (e.g., k-NN) coupled with costly continuous interactions. To tackle these systemic inefficiencies, we propose PointLAM, a highly efficient and powerful point-based architecture driven by two synergistic innovations. First, to resolve the downsampling bottleneck, we develop the Laplacian Point Sampler (LPS). LPS employs an implicit discrete Laplacian high-pass filter and Doubly Sorted Sampling to achieve fast, structure-aware foreground preservation. Second, to overcome local modeling latency, we design the Local Hadamard Aggregator (LHA). LHA decouples spatial indexing from feature representation using transient grids, and replaces complex continuous interactions with a Hadamard Gating mechanism for topology-aware, attentive modulation. By coupling this local gating with Bi-Directional Mamba (BDM) layers for global sequence modeling, we formulate the Local Attentive Mamba (LAM) block. Powered by this architecture, PointLAM achieves competitive performance on nuScenes and Waymo for point-based detectors. It rivals highly optimized voxel competitors while requiring a fraction of the computational footprint, demonstrating marked superiority in detecting small instances and handling extreme sparsity. Project page: https://pointlam.github.io/.

AI.tldr: PointLAM introduces two novel point-based modules—Laplacian Point Sampler (LPS) and Local Hadamard Aggregator (LHA)—to deliver an efficient 3D detector that matches voxel-based performance with lower compute and better sparsity handling.
AI.motivation: Voxel-based 3D detectors are efficient due to quantization but lose geometric fidelity, while point-based detectors preserve detail but suffer from slow sampling and expensive neighbor queries, hindering real-time performance.
AI.method: LPS employs an implicit discrete Laplacian high-pass filter with Doubly Sorted Sampling for fast, structure-aware foreground preservation. LHA decouples spatial indexing from features using transient grids and uses a Hadamard gating mechanism to enable topology-aware, attentive modulation. These are combined in the Local Attentive Mamba (LAM) block with Bi-Directional Mamba layers for global modeling.
AI.result: PointLAM achieves competitive results on nuScenes and Waymo, rivalling optimized voxel detectors while using a fraction of the compute; shows clear advantages in detecting small objects and handling extreme sparsity.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a highly efficient, accurate point-based architecture for 3D detection that narrows the gap with voxel methods while reducing computational overhead, validated on standard benchmarks and provided with a project page.

title: GraphSkillEvo: Evolutionary Optimization of Graph-Structured Agent Skills
summary: Skills can improve the performance of Large Language Model (LLM) agents by providing task-specific procedural guidance, while skill optimization further improves their effectiveness through iterative refinement. However, existing skill optimization methods typically represent skills as unstructured natural-language instructions, creating two key challenges: 1) Unstructured skills often lack explicit workflow-level guidance and contain substantial redundancy, making them difficult for LLMs to execute; 2) the vast search space of unconstrained natural-language skills makes skill optimization ineffective. To address these challenges, we propose representing skills as graph-structured natural-language artifacts. In graph-structured skills, each node represents an execution step together with its operational guidance, while directed edges encode context-dependent transitions between steps. Compared to unstructured skills, graph-structured skills can provide clear workflow-level guidance. Moreover, the proposed graph-structured skill can also facilitate skill optimization. Building on this structured representation, we introduce GraphSkillEvo, a population-based evolutionary optimization framework with mutation and crossover operators for graph-structured skills. By maintaining multiple candidate skills and combining effective components, GraphSkillEvo enables broader and more comprehensive exploration of the structured skill space than purely LLM-based iterative self-refinement. Extensive experiments across five agent benchmarks demonstrate that GraphSkillEvo consistently outperforms the strong skill optimization baseline SkillOpt, improving average accuracy by 4.01% on GPT-5.4-nano and 1.76% on GPT-5.4. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruisun7/GraphSkillEvo.

AI.tldr: Represent skills as graph-structured natural-language artifacts and optimize them with GraphSkillEvo, a population-based evolutionary framework, yielding consistent gains over SkillOpt.
AI.motivation: Unstructured, natural-language skills suffer from lack of explicit workflow guidance and a prohibitively large search space, hindering execution and optimization.
AI.method: Model skills as graph-structured artifacts where nodes are steps with guidance and directed edges encode context-dependent transitions; apply GraphSkillEvo, a population-based evolutionary algorithm with mutation and crossover to explore and evolve graph skills.
AI.result: GraphSkillEvo consistently outperforms SkillOpt across five agent benchmarks, improving average accuracy by 4.01% on GPT-5.4-nano and 1.76% on GPT-5.4; code is released at the provided repository.
AI.conclusion: Graph-structured skills provide clearer workflow guidance and enable more effective optimization; the evolutionary framework expands exploration of structured skill space and yields practical performance gains.

title: 2nd Place Solution to the HANDS 2026 Workshop Challenge-Dexterous Grasp Motion Track: Single-Shot Trajectory Warping for Grasp Motion Generation
summary: This report describes our 2nd place solution to the HANDS 2026 workshop challenge (Dexterous Grasp Motion track) in conjunction with ECCV 2026. In this challenge, we address grasp motion generation for the 12-DoF LinkerHand O6, aiming to produce physically plausible reach-and-lift trajectories for unseen objects from randomized initial hand poses in simulation. This task is particularly challenging because each grasp requires a per-step policy to make approximately $70$ twelve-dimensional decisions, with errors accumulating over time, while test objects and physical dynamics may differ from those encountered during training. To address these challenges, we propose editing a single successful GraspM3 demonstration instead of generating the motion step by step: a policy observes the object once and outputs a 12-D warp of the demonstration, which is then replayed open-loop. Moreover, we train the warp policy with one-step PPO over all $4{,}824$ training objects in parallel. As a result, our method achieved success rates of $94.61\%$ on the easy track, the highest of all submissions, and $57.18\%$ on the hard track of the private test set.

AI.tldr: A warp-based imitation approach for 12-DoF dexterous grasp motion: modify a single GraspM3 demonstration via a predicted 12-D warp, trained with one-step PPO over 4,824 training objects, achieving 94.61% easy-track and 57.18% hard-track success.
AI.motivation: Overcome long-horizon, high-dimensional decision-making in dexterous grasp motion with generalization to unseen objects and dynamics mismatch by avoiding per-step policy rollout and reducing error accumulation.
AI.method: Observe an object once, output a 12-D warp of a successful GraspM3 demonstration, then replay the warped trajectory open-loop. Train the warp policy with one-step PPO in parallel across 4,824 training objects.
AI.result: On the HANDS 2026 benchmark: 94.61% success on the easy track (highest among submissions) and 57.18% on the hard track in the private test set.
AI.conclusion: Warp-based adaptation of a single demonstration can achieve strong performance and robustness to object variation by avoiding cumulative step-wise errors; relies on a high-quality demonstration and may be sensitive to dynamics changes beyond the warp; parallel one-step PPO enables scalable training.

title: A Principled Approach to Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
summary: Traditional unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) methods are designed to flag or localise deviations from a normative distribution, ignoring the underlying generative mechanisms of the anomalies. Yet the nature of an anomaly is often as important as its presence. We reformulate UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem, in which the objective is to infer the most probable corruption responsible for each observation. Our framework yields a probabilistic anomaly score as the energy of the inferred corruption parameters, and serves as a principled recipe for developing new UAD algorithms. We derive several existing methods as instances of the general framework, each corresponding to the same energy score under different modelling choices. Experimentally, we study the framework's components in a controlled setting, and improve object-class AUROC on the MVTec AD dataset by 2.3% by adapting the underlying corruption model. Finally, we validate the framework on a brain MRI benchmark, achieving strong detection performance while producing estimates of pathology intensity, bias, and geometry. Code is available at https://github.com/jgmyles/inverse-uad.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian inverse-problem formulation for unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) is proposed, unifying existing methods via a probabilistic corruption model; the anomaly score is the energy of inferred corruption. Demonstrates improvements on MVTec AD and brain MRI with interpretable pathology estimates, and provides code for reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Traditional UAD methods flag deviations from a normative distribution but ignore how anomalies arise. A principled approach that models the generative corruption behind observations can yield interpretable, probabilistic anomaly scores and unify disparate methods.
AI.method: Formulate UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem to infer the most probable corruption for each observation. Use the energy of the inferred corruption as the anomaly score. Show that several existing UAD methods are special cases corresponding to the same energy under different modelling choices. Test components in controlled settings, adapt corruption models to improve AUROC on MVTec AD by 2.3%, and validate on brain MRI to obtain pathology-related estimates. Code is provided.
AI.result: Probabilistic anomaly scores derived from inferred corruption parameters; improved object-class AUROC on MVTec AD by 2.3% via corruption-model adaptation; strong brain MRI detection performance with estimates of pathology intensity, bias, and geometry; code available at the provided repository.
AI.conclusion: A general, principled Bayesian inverse UAD framework that can reproduce existing methods as instances, yields interpretable anomaly signals via corruption energy, and demonstrates practical performance gains on standard and medical imaging benchmarks.

title: Bilevel Optimization of Topology and Hyperparameters (BOTH)
comment: Currently under submission to SMO journal
summary: Topology optimization (TO) represents a significant step towards automating the design process: given a working simulation, TO can produce a viable prototype at the press of a button by differentiating the simulation and iteratively improving the design. In practice, however, TO is riddled with ``magic numbers''---hyperparameters whose tuning significantly affects the outcome. Finding the right values typically requires not only deep problem-specific knowledge but also extensive trial-and-error. While practitioners can use surrogate-assisted hyperparameter optimization as an alternative, this approach requires strictly limiting the number of hyperparameters through careful problem formulation. Here, we propose differentiating TO itself using automatic differentiation. This yields ``hypergradients'' that allow us to tune these hyperparameters in tandem with the primary optimization. We show that evaluating just one or two steps of TO is sufficiently informative and that the method scales favorably to thousands of hyperparameters at an expense comparable to only a few standard TO runs. We demonstrate this approach on stress-constrained and compliance problems, with the latter utilizing a neural parameterization of the density field.

AI.tldr: Differentiating topology optimization with automatic differentiation yields hypergradients to tune hyperparameters in tandem with the TO process, scalable to thousands of hyperparameters with cost similar to just a few TO runs; demonstrated on stress-constrained and compliance problems (the latter with a neural density-field parameterization).
AI.motivation: TO designs are highly sensitive to hyperparameters, and surrogate-based hyperparameter optimization becomes impractical when many hyperparameters exist. An approach that can tune hyperparameters on the fly during optimization could greatly improve robustness and efficiency.
AI.method: Apply automatic differentiation through the TO pipeline to obtain hypergradients with respect to hyperparameters. Use a very short unrolling (1–2 TO steps) to compute informative gradients, enabling scalability to thousands of hyperparameters. Validate on stress-constrained and compliance problems; in the compliance case, use a neural network to parameterize the density field.
AI.result: Hypergradients enable joint tuning of a large number of hyperparameters with computational cost comparable to performing only a few TO runs. Demonstrations show successful tuning for both stress-constrained and compliance-based TO, the latter employing a neural density-field parameterization.
AI.conclusion: Differentiating TO via automatic differentiation is a feasible, scalable strategy for hyperparameter optimization, reducing manual tuning burden and enabling efficient exploration across many hyperparameters.

title: Skel-WAM: A Hand-Skeleton-Conditioned World Action Model for Human-to-Robot Manipulation Transfer
summary: Robot demonstrations are expensive to collect and often provide limited distributional coverage of task variations. Human videos offer a low-cost source of complementary manipulation experience, but learning from them requires bridging embodiment gaps in visual appearance and action spaces. We introduce Skel-WAM, a world action model that bridges these differences through a unified hand-skeleton motion interface. The key insight is to align human and robot motion through a common hand topology, combining skeleton overlays that ground motion in the scene with structured 2.5-D keypoints that encode explicit hand kinematics. Video and Keypoint Experts jointly learn visual and skeletal dynamics through a Mixture-of-Transformers, while a separate robot-trained Action Expert maps these predictions to executable controls. This separation enables human and robot demonstrations to directly supervise shared dynamics without requiring robot action labels for human videos. Across four real-world bimanual tasks and seven simulated tasks, Skel-WAM achieves average success rates of 79.86% and 63.29%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 22.22 and 8.28 percentage points, respectively. Human-robot cotraining more than doubles real-world success on task variations absent from robot training data, from 38.89% to 86.11%. These results demonstrate that a shared skeletal interface enables joint learning across human and robot data and expands robot task coverage through complementary human demonstrations.

AI.tldr: Skel-WAM introduces a unified hand-skeleton motion interface to bridge human and robot demonstrations, enabling joint learning via Video/Keypoint Experts with a Mixture-of-Transformers and a separate Action Expert for robot control, achieving improved task coverage and robustness through cotraining.
AI.motivation: Robot demonstrations are expensive and offer limited variation; human videos provide complementary data but differ in embodiment and action spaces. A common skeletal representation can bridge visual and action gaps, enabling joint supervision without robot action labels.
AI.method: Ground motion through a common hand topology using skeleton overlays and 2.5-D keypoints to encode explicit hand kinematics. Video and Keypoint Experts jointly learn visual and skeletal dynamics via a Mixture-of-Transformers; a separate robot-trained Action Expert maps predictions to executable robot controls. This design allows human and robot demonstrations to supervise shared dynamics without robot action labels for human videos, and enables cotraining across domains across four real-world bimanual tasks and seven simulated tasks.
AI.result: Skel-WAM achieves average success rates of 79.86% (real-world) and 63.29% (simulated), surpassing the strongest baseline by 22.22 and 8.28 percentage points, respectively. Human-robot cotraining more than doubles real-world success on task variations absent from robot training data (38.89% to 86.11%).
AI.conclusion: A shared skeletal interface enables joint learning across human and robot data and expands robot task coverage through complementary human demonstrations.

title: VideoReloc: Long-Term Indoor Video Relocalization against a Kilobyte-Scale Semantic Scene Graph
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://videoreloc.github.io
summary: Given a compact semantic scene graph, long-term indoor video relocalization estimates a map-frame trajectory after lighting and furniture changes. Visual methods rely on appearance and become unreliable under these changes; localizing one frame at a time from object classes and geometry instead leaves sparse, ambiguous evidence. We introduce VideoReloc, whose adaptive clips use odometry to gather spatial evidence until object and motion criteria are met, adapting query length to the observed scene. Its run-level decision rechecks conflicting placements using evidence accumulated across connected clips, stabilizing the trajectory beyond adjacent-clip tracking. Hypothesis-first registration proposes poses from object triplets and verifies each using clip-wide object centers and box surfaces. Orientation-aware refinement uses box faces, gravity and wall directions to resolve ambiguity in camera orientation and refine the full pose. This reframes sparse-map relocalization as verification of spatially extended video queries, moving discriminative support from stored appearance to temporal context and permitting a 100 kB map of class-labelled boxes. On RIO10 and ReplicaCAD, the all-frame localization success rate at 1 m/10$^\circ$ is 73.5% and 61.1% under causal evaluation, rising to 90.6% and 74.8% with clip closure. The evaluated per-frame scene coordinate regressors reach up to 47.6% and 49.8%, respectively, with maps of 12.6-42 MB. Project page: https://videoreloc.github.io

AI.tldr: VideoReloc uses adaptive, odometry-guided clips and object-geometry verification to perform long-term indoor relocalization with compact, box-based maps.
AI.motivation: Visual relocalization based on appearance fails under lighting and furniture changes; need robust, temporally contextual methods that leverage objects and geometry while keeping memory-efficient maps.
AI.method: Adaptive clips gathered via odometry accumulate spatial evidence until object/motion criteria are met; run-level rechecks across connected clips to stabilize trajectories; hypothesis-first registration derives poses from object triplets and verifies with clip-wide object centers and box surfaces; orientation-aware refinement uses box faces, gravity, and wall directions to resolve yaw ambiguities; maps store class-labelled boxes (~100 kB).
AI.result: All-frame localization rates at 1 m/10°: 73.5% (RIO10) and 61.1% (ReplicaCAD) under causal eval; rise to 90.6% and 74.8% with clip closure; per-frame scene-coordinate regressors reach up to 47.6% and 49.8% with maps sized 12.6–42 MB.
AI.conclusion: Reframes sparse-map relocalization as verification of spatially extended video queries, enabling robust, temporally contextual localization with compact maps and improved stability through clip-based verification and orientation-aware refinement.

title: RegKT: Interpretable and Robust Deep Knowledge Tracing With IRT-Regularizer
summary: As deep learning models continue to advance, knowledge tracing models have achieved higher accuracy. However, these gains come at the cost of reduced interpretability, which is crucial for practitioners in educational settings to adopt new methodologies. Additionally, deep learning models are prone to overfitting, particularly when dealing with the small datasets that are common in educational applications. In this paper, we propose a novel regularization technique designed to enhance the robustness of deep-learning-based knowledge tracing models, while simultaneously improving their interpretability. Our method addresses both the interpretability and overfitting challenges, making it more feasible for real-world educational applications.

AI.tldr: A new regularization technique to boost robustness and interpretability of deep-learning-based knowledge tracing, addressing overfitting on small educational datasets.
AI.motivation: Deep learning improves accuracy in knowledge tracing but often hurts interpretability. Small educational datasets exacerbate overfitting, hindering practical deployment; a method that improves robustness while preserving interpretability is needed.
AI.method: Proposes a novel regularization scheme integrated into deep knowledge tracing models that enforces interpretability and robustness, likely via constraints on latent representations, sparsity, and compatibility with domain priors, balancing predictive loss with interpretability penalties.
AI.result: The abstract claims improved robustness and interpretability and reduced overfitting, making deep-learning-based knowledge tracing more viable for real-world educational applications.
