AI.conclusion: The proposed regularization technique addresses both interpretability and overfitting, enhancing the practicality of deep-learning-based knowledge tracing in real-world educational settings.

title: SABER: Learning Attention-based Semantic Affordance for Legged Locomotion
summary: Perceptive legged locomotion has advanced rapidly by integrating terrain geometry into learned policies, yet the integration of terrain meaning remains sparse: a pipe, a patch of grass, or a fragile box may be geometrically traversable while being inappropriate for contact. In industrial environments, where legged robots increasingly operate, a single misplaced step can damage fragile equipment, destabilize the robot, or endanger the site. To address this, we introduce SABER, a planner-free reinforcement-learning policy that jointly reasons about terrain geometry and semantic contact permission. The policy consumes a unified terrain-affordance map, where each cell encodes local 3D geometry and a semantic contact cost. We augment cross-attention with a learned, signed semantic bias: an additive term on the attention logits, gated by the contact cost, that reweights flagged cells by their distance from the nearest foot. A hazard therefore reshapes attention where it can still affect the next foothold, and its influence fades where it cannot. The resulting policy selects footholds on permitted support and keeps the leg clear of forbidden regions throughout the swing phase. We perform a systematic ablation that isolates the contribution of each architectural component; removing the semantic bias alone increases forbidden contacts by 55% while velocity tracking is unchanged. We validate the policy on a Unitree B2, demonstrating sim-to-real semantic contact selection across indoor and outdoor environments and four semantic obstacle classes.

AI.tldr: SABER is a planner-free RL policy for legged locomotion that combines terrain geometry with semantic contact permissions via a cross-attention bias, improving safe foothold selection in industrial settings.
AI.motivation: Industrial legged robots must avoid damaging equipment and sites; geometry alone is insufficient as some geometrically traversable surfaces are unsafe due to contact semantics.
AI.method: Use a unified terrain-affordance map (geometry + semantic contact cost). Introduce a learned, signed semantic bias: an additive term on attention logits gated by contact cost, reweighting cells by distance to the nearest foot. The policy selects permitted footholds and keeps the leg clear during swing; ablations isolate architecture components; validated on a Unitree B2 in sim-to-real settings with indoor/outdoor scenes and four semantic obstacle classes.
AI.result: Ablation: removing semantic bias increases forbidden contacts by 55% while velocity tracking remains unchanged. Hardware experiments on Unitree B2 show sim-to-real semantic contact selection across varying environments and four obstacle classes.
AI.conclusion: Integrating semantic contact semantics with terrain geometry via a learned attention bias enables safer foothold decisions in industrial environments. The planner-free SABER policy demonstrates hardware feasibility and robust performance across semantic obstacle classes.

title: Object Detection Benchmarks are Incomplete: The Role of Label Errors and Annotation Uncertainty
summary: While object detection has advanced through improved architectures and open-vocabulary models, we provide strong evidence that benchmark quality is limited by annotation incompleteness. Across four widely used datasets (COCO, Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, KITTI), re-annotation reveals substantial increases in annotated objects (e.g., up to +60% on KITTI and +40% on COCO), driven primarily by previously unlabeled small, occluded, or densely packed instances. While some differences arise from dataset-specific annotation conventions, we consistently find that missing annotations are the main source of label errors across all datasets. To achieve high data quality, we introduce a scalable annotation pipeline that emphasizes high recall and captures ambiguity through soft labels aggregated from at least 11 annotators per object. The resulting annotations improve coverage and align well with human calibration. We show that benchmark performance is highly sensitive to annotation quality, although model rankings remain largely stable. We introduce two large-scale benchmarks: (i) an uncertainty-aware object detection benchmark, and (ii) a label error detection benchmark grounded in real label errors. We show that current detectors are strongly depended on annotation quality and are misaligned with human perception. Current label error detection methods, which have been shown to perform well on synthetic noise, struggle to achieve high recall and precision on real label errors. Our results highlight the need for future object detection benchmarks to move beyond deterministic annotations toward high-recall, uncertainty-aware evaluation that maximizes valid instances and better reflects real-world ambiguity.

AI.tldr: Annotation incompleteness limits benchmark quality in object detection; re-annotation reveals many missing labels across COCO, Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, KITTI; introduces high-recall, uncertainty-aware annotation pipeline with soft labels from 11+ annotators; proposes uncertainty-aware and label-error benchmarks; shows annotation quality impacts detector performance and reliability of labels, calling for evaluation that reflects ambiguity.
AI.motivation: Current object detection benchmarks suffer from annotation incompleteness, causing label errors and unreliable performance rankings. To achieve data quality and real-world alignment, high-recall annotations and uncertainty-aware evaluation are needed.
AI.method: Re-annotate four datasets to quantify missing labels; collect soft labels from at least 11 annotators per object to capture ambiguity; develop a scalable pipeline focused on high recall; introduce two benchmarks: an uncertainty-aware detection benchmark and a label-error detection benchmark; evaluate detectors and label-error methods on real errors.
AI.result: Missing annotations account for substantial label errors; annotation completeness increases annotated objects by up to 60% on KITTI and 40% on COCO; benchmark performance is sensitive to annotation quality but relative rankings are stable; current label error detectors struggle on real errors; new benchmarks align better with human calibration and reveal misalignment between detectors and perception.
AI.conclusion: Future object detection evaluation should emphasize high-recall, uncertainty-aware annotations to maximize valid instances and reflect real-world ambiguity; benchmarks should move beyond deterministic labels to capture uncertainty and label errors, guiding more robust detectors.

title: Matrix AdaGrad: Row-wise and Column-wise Adaptive Subgradient Methods
summary: Adaptive optimization methods such as AdaGrad and Adam are widely used in modern neural-network training, but their adaptive scaling is primarily designed for vector-valued parameters and does not explicitly exploit matrix structure. Recent matrix-aware optimizers demonstrate the benefits of structured optimization, yet a general theoretical framework for deriving matrix-aware adaptivity comparable to that of AdaGrad remains lacking. In this work, we develop a general Online Mirror Descent framework with adaptive proximal functions for matrix-valued parameters, providing a principled approach to deriving matrix-aware adaptive optimization through online regret minimization. By introducing row-wise and column-wise matrix proximal functions and analyzing the resulting regret trade-off, we derive Row-wise Matrix AdaGrad (Row-AdaGrad) and Column-wise Matrix AdaGrad (Column-AdaGrad), with adaptive scaling determined by the accumulated row-wise or column-wise gradient norms. We establish regret guarantees and show that these matrix-aware bounds can be strictly tighter than those of entry-wise AdaGrad under structured gradients. Experiments on matrix factorization and deep neural-network training further demonstrate the benefits of aligning adaptive scaling with matrix structure, including improved optimization stability and trainability at larger learning rates and greater network depths.

AI.tldr: Matrix-aware adaptive optimization via Online Mirror Descent; Row/Column AdaGrad with regret guarantees; empirical gains in factorization and deep nets.
AI.motivation: Standard AdaGrad/Adam adaptivity are primarily vector-parameter oriented and do not exploit matrix structure. Although matrix-aware optimizers exist, a general AdaGrad-like theory for matrices was lacking. A principled, regret-based derivation could unify and tighten matrix adaptivity.
AI.method: Develop an Online Mirror Descent (OMD) framework with adaptive proximal functions for matrix-valued parameters. Introduce row-wise and column-wise matrix proximal functions, yielding Row-AdaGrad and Column-AdaGrad. Adaptive scaling is governed by accumulated row-wise or column-wise gradient norms. Provide regret analysis and compare matrix-aware bounds to entry-wise AdaGrad.
AI.result: Regret guarantees for Row-AdaGrad and Column-AdaGrad can be tighter than those of entry-wise AdaGrad under structured gradients. Experiments on matrix factorization and deep networks show improved stability and trainability at larger learning rates and greater depths, validating the practical benefits of matrix-aware adaptivity.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a principled, general framework to derive matrix-aware AdaGrad-like optimizers via OMD with adaptive proximal terms. It demonstrates theoretical improvements in regret bounds and practical gains in training performance under structured gradients, highlighting a avenue for further exploration of matrix-structured optimization.

title: Tilt as a Certified Resource: Preserving Motor Wrench-Rate Authority on Articulated Multirotors
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Fully-actuated multirotor aerial vehicles must not only track nominal wrenches but retain the "readiness" to modulate them rapidly under disturbances. Classical effort-minimizing allocators ignore this dynamic limit, whereas maximizing readiness leads to topologically disconnected optimal sheets demanding physically impossible actuator rates. Enforcing a readiness safety floor on fixed-geometry symmetric platforms further encounters a zero-sum degeneracy: motor-speed redistribution cannot improve authority without conceding wrench tracking. This paper uses active morphology to break the degeneracy, treating servo tilt as a geometric resource supplying authority-recovery directions unavailable to static rotors. We construct a configuration-dependent, motor-only readiness certificate - the log-volume of the reachable wrench-rate set - that explicitly excludes servo capacity, preventing a "ghost capacity fallacy" in which the certificate would falsely credit slow mechanical kinematic limits instead of collapsing accurately at motor saturation. The certificate is enforced as a Control Barrier Function (CBF) within a Unified Physical-Command Quadratic Program acting on motor torques and servo setpoints. Closed-loop simulations of an articulated octorotor under severe gust disturbances show classical allocators diverging and uncertified articulated allocators violating the safety floor, while the proposed CBF filter bounds the system state and preserves vehicle authority.

AI.tldr: Active morphology (servo tilt) provides additional authority-recovery directions, enabling a motor-only readiness certificate to be enforced via a CBF within a Unified Phys/Cmd QP; this avoids degeneracy and improves safety under disturbances.
AI.motivation: Fully-actuated multirotors must retain rapid wrench-modulation ability under disturbances without violating actuator limits. Traditional allocators optimize for nominal tracking or readiness but fail to capture feasible dynamics, leading to unsafe or infeasible policies on fixed-geometry platforms.
AI.method: Introduce a configuration-dependent readiness certificate defined as the log-volume of the reachable wrench-rate set, excluding servo capacity. Treat servo tilt as a geometric resource to obtain authority-recovery directions. Enforce the certificate as a Control Barrier Function inside a Unified Physical-Command Quadratic Program that optimizes motor torques and servo setpoints.
AI.result: Simulations of an articulated octorotor under severe gusts show classical allocators diverging and uncertified articulated allocators violating a safety floor; the proposed CBF filter bounds state and preserves vehicle authority.
AI.conclusion: Active morphology combined with a CBF-based safety certificate yields bounded, authority-preserving behavior under disturbances, avoiding ghost-capacity misassessments and improving robustness over fixed-geometry allocators.

title: Morphology-Aware Ambiguity Learning for Wafer Defect Decision Support
summary: Wafer map defect recognition is commonly formulated as a fixed-taxonomy classification problem that assigns each wafer to a single defect class. However, some wafers exhibit morphologies near class boundaries, for which forcing a single prediction may be less informative than providing plausible diagnostic alternatives. This paper proposes a morphology-aware ambiguity learning framework that supports three diagnostic actions: automatic single-class diagnosis, assisted diagnosis with two plausible defect classes, and full review. Using the radial, angular, and geometric characteristics of training wafer maps, the framework constructs a class-level ambiguity matrix representing defect-class pairs with similar morphology and plausible diagnostic alternatives. It guides the model to learn plausible alternative classes rather than treating all incorrect classes equally. During inference, the matrix determines whether an uncertain prediction can be represented by a meaningful two-class diagnostic set or should be escalated for full review. Experiments on WM-811K show that the proposed framework outperforms conventional approaches in defect recognition and diagnostic decision support, providing meaningful two-class alternatives while reserving full review for cases with unresolved ambiguity. Illustrative cost analyses further show the potential cost advantage of the proposed routing strategy. The diagnostic behavior of the framework remains consistent across different backbone architectures.

AI.tldr: A morphology-aware ambiguity framework for wafer-map defect recognition adds an ambiguity matrix to support single-class, two-class, or full-review diagnostic actions, improving recognition and decision support while maintaining backbone-agnostic performance.
AI.motivation: Conventional fixed-taxonomy classifiers force a single defect label even when wafer maps lie near class boundaries; providing plausible alternatives can improve interpretability, reduce misdiagnosis, and enable cost-efficient routing to human review when necessary.
AI.method: Construct a class-level ambiguity matrix from radial, angular, and geometric features of training wafer maps to capture morphologically similar defect-class pairs. Train models to favor plausible alternative classes over all incorrect ones. At inference time, use the matrix to decide whether an uncertain prediction can be represented as a two-class diagnostic set or requires full review and escalation.
AI.result: On WM-811K, the approach outperforms standard classifiers in defect recognition and diagnostic decision support, delivering meaningful two-class alternatives and deferring to full review only for unresolved cases. Cost analyses suggest potential savings from the proposed routing strategy. Diagnostic behavior is consistent across different backbone architectures.
AI.conclusion: Morphology-aware ambiguity learning yields interpretable, cost-effective defect diagnostic routing without sacrificing backbone flexibility, enabling structured two-class suggestions and targeted escalation to full review.

title: Federated Deep Clustering Networks for High-Dimensional and Heterogeneous Data
comment: Accepted to the 4th International Conference on Federated Learning Technologies and Applications (FLTA 2026)
summary: Clustering high-dimensional data is a fundamental task in unsupervised machine learning with applications to a variety of domains. In the centralized data scenario, this task is commonly solved using deep clustering methods that utilize deep neural network architectures to learn clustering-friendly latent space representations. In Federated Learning, where data is distributed between clients and is private, deep clustering methods are less explored. In particular, recently introduced federated deep clustering methods, despite showing very promising performance, still fall short in reliably providing good performance if data across clients are non-identically-independently distributed. In this work, we introduce a generalization of Deep Clustering Networks to the federated scenario, named FedDCN, that simultaneously optimizes a reconstruction loss and a clustering loss. To ensure robustness and latent space alignment in non-identically-independently distributed data scenarios, FedDCN generates synthetic data augmentations, and its learning objective includes a geometric regularization for latent space alignment. Through experimental evaluation, the effectiveness of the approach under IID and non-IID assumptions is demonstrated, and future research directions are identified.

AI.tldr: FedDCN generalizes Deep Clustering Networks to federated settings by jointly optimizing reconstruction and clustering losses, enriched with synthetic data augmentations and a geometric regularization that aligns latent spaces across non-IID clients; experiments show effectiveness under IID and non-IID data.
AI.motivation: Non-IID data across clients in federated learning undermines clustering quality; robust latent space alignment and data augmentation are needed to achieve reliable clustering without sacrificing privacy.
AI.method: Proposes FedDCN, a distributed deep clustering framework that (i) optimizes reconstruction and clustering losses, (ii) generates synthetic augmentations to enhance robustness, (iii) includes a geometric regularization term to align latent representations across clients in non-IID settings; evaluated under IID and non-IID partitions.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation demonstrates that FedDCN achieves robust clustering performance under both IID and non-IID data distributions, outperforming baselines and confirming the benefit of synthetic augmentations and latent-space alignment.
AI.conclusion: FedDCN offers a general federated deep clustering approach with joint learning objectives and latent-space alignment, showing promise for non-IID data; the paper outlines future research directions such as further robustness, scalability, privacy considerations, and personalization.

title: A High-Payload Wall-Climbing Robot Using Passive Bistable Suction Cups
comment: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics & Automation (ICRA)
summary: Wall-climbing robots capable of scaling vertical surfaces could help automate hazardous or labor intensive tasks such as window washing, inspection, maintenance, and construction. Active adhesion methods achieve higher payload capacities, but require power to maintain their grip. Passive adhesion devices such as suction cups are an attractive option for such robots because they do not require power to maintain their grip, but they are limited by their payload capacity. This work presents a novel high-payload wall-climbing robot that utilizes passive bistable suction cups to generate adhesion without needing to be pushed into the wall. The robot features a track-based system that automatically engages and disengages bistable suction cups to achieve locomotion on smooth surfaces. The robot is able to achieve vertical wall climbing on glass, wood, metal, and painted surfaces, sideways and upside-down climbing, and is able to tow a payload of 7.940 kg (with a payload-to-weight ratio of 2.25).

AI.tldr: A passive adhesion wall-climbing robot uses bistable suction cups to achieve high payloads without active power for adhesion, using a track-based system to engage/disengage cups for locomotion, enabling climbing on multiple surfaces and orientations with a payload-to-weight ratio of 2.25.
AI.motivation: Reduce energy consumption in wall-climbing robots by replacing continuous power-needed adhesion with passive mechanisms, while increasing payload capacity to enable practical tasks such as inspection and maintenance.
AI.method: Integrates passive bistable suction cups with a track-based locomotion system that automatically engages and disengages cups to move along smooth surfaces; compatible with vertical and inverted orientations across glass, wood, metal, and painted surfaces.
AI.result: Successful vertical wall climbing on multiple surface types, sideways and upside-down operation, and towing a payload of 7.940 kg (payload/weight ratio = 2.25).
AI.conclusion: Passive bistable suction cups can deliver high payload adhesion without continuous power, expanding the operational envelope of wall-climbing robots; practical deployment would need evaluation of durability, repeated cycling, and surface compatibility.

title: Chronosphere: Space-Time Tessellation of Local Climate Experts
summary: We introduce Chronosphere, a spatio-temporal neural field that learns representations of climate. A central challenge in geographic representation learning is modeling environmental processes whose spatial and temporal complexity varies widely. Yet existing location encoders typically fix a single level of detail everywhere. Global bases such as spherical harmonics spread capacity uniformly across space and time. Localized bases resolve only predefined regions. Learned tessellations adapt, but are inefficient at representing higher frequencies. Chronosphere unifies these approaches, pairing an adaptive tessellation of learnable sites on the spacetime torus $S^2\times S^1$ with a shared bank of local basis functions. Both where capacity is placed and how much detail each region carries adapt to the data, across space and time. Trained to reconstruct climatology, Chronosphere matches or leads state-of-the-art location encoders across spatial and temporal tasks, with the largest gains under spatial and temporal transfer.

AI.tldr: Chronosphere introduces an adaptive spatiotemporal neural field that places learnable sites on the spacetime torus (S^2×S^1) with a shared bank of local basis functions, enabling data-driven allocation of capacity and detail across space and time and achieving state-of-the-art performance on climate representation, especially in transfer tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing location encoders fix a single level of detail or rely on fixed global bases or predefined local regions. Climate processes exhibit highly variable spatial and temporal complexity, requiring flexible representations that can adapt capacity and resolution to data.
AI.method: An adaptive tessellation of learnable sites on the spacetime torus S^2×S^1 paired with a shared bank of local basis functions. The model learns where to place capacity and how much detail to allocate per region, and is trained to reconstruct climatology.
AI.result: Chronosphere matches or surpasses state-of-the-art location encoders across spatial and temporal tasks, with the most pronounced gains on spatial and temporal transfer situations.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, unified spatiotemporal representations—combining learnable tessellations with a shared local basis bank—effectively capture climate variability and generalize better to unseen spaces and times.

title: The Weight Is Over - Interactive Diffusion on Consumer GPUs
summary: On-device inference is booming, but the momentum is almost all in language models. Diffusion pipelines are memory hungry, latency-sensitive, and require orchestrating an embedder, a transformer, a decoder, and often further postprocessing that is not as standardized as LLM inference loops are. We navigate the trade-off between performance, quality, and model footprint to reach as many client devices in the wild as possible. We make three contributions: an embedding translator that maps a small text encoder into a large encoder space to cut weight and latency; a reproducible sweep recipe for navigating the speed/quality/memory triangle in diffusion pipelines; and an interactive on-device image generation editor achieving sub-second TTFI on recent GPUs.

AI.tldr: On-device diffusion inference remains challenging; this work proposes a three-pronged approach to reduce footprint while preserving quality and speed: an embedding translator, a reproducible speed/quality/memory sweep, and an interactive on-device image editor achieving sub-second TTFI on modern GPUs.
AI.motivation: Enable diffusion-based generation on resource-constrained devices by reducing model size and latency, while maintaining quality, to broaden practical deployment beyond powerful servers and LLM-like pipelines.
AI.method: 1) Embedding translator: maps a small text encoder into a larger encoder space to shrink weight and latency. 2) Reproducible sweep recipe: systematic exploration to navigate the speed–quality–memory triangle in diffusion pipelines. 3) Interactive on-device image generation editor: demonstrates sub-second time-to-first-inference (TTFI) on recent GPUs.
AI.result: Demonstrates reduced footprint and latency via embedding transfer and systematic tuning; provides a reproducible methodology for balancing speed, quality, and memory; achieves sub-second TTFI for on-device image generation on contemporary GPUs with an interactive editor.
AI.conclusion: The work advances practical on-device diffusion by (i) enabling smaller encoders to operate in larger diffusion spaces, (ii) offering a transparent, repeatable workflow to balance performance metrics, and (iii) delivering an interactive editor capable of fast on-device generation, expanding feasible deployment across devices.

title: Potential-Field Action Representation for Reinforcement Learning in Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Model-free reinforcement learning can acquire contact-rich robotic manipulation skills through trial-and-error interaction, but it often requires the policy to learn both task strategy and low-level motion generation. In this setting, the action representation is critical because it determines how policy outputs are converted into robot motion, shaping both exploration and physical execution. Direct Cartesian command interfaces require the policy to generate motion at every decision step, coupling task-level adaptation with continuous low-level control and increasing the learning burden. We propose PA-RL, a reinforcement-learning framework that uses artificial potential fields as the action representation. Instead of commanding motion directly, the policy adapts the parameters of an energy-like potential field, which generates a state-dependent guidance direction executed through a Cartesian impedance controller. We evaluate PA-RL on peg-in-hole insertion, a representative contact-rich task with nonlinear dynamics and discontinuous contact transitions. In simulation, PA-RL is compared with Cartesian velocity, Cartesian pose, and variable-impedance action spaces using the same RL algorithm. PA-RL is the only method to reach a 100% evaluation success rate within the allotted training time, while the best baseline reaches 92.6%. It also reduces joint-torque variation by 55.4% and Cartesian acceleration variation by 70.8% relative to the best baseline, without explicit motion-quality penalties in the reward. The simulation-trained policy further completes 9/9 real-robot insertions without fine-tuning, demonstrating the deployment feasibility of the learned potential-field interface.

AI.tldr: PA-RL uses artificial potential fields as the action representation in model-free RL for contact-rich robotic manipulation, decoupling task strategy from low-level motion and enabling robust peg-in-hole performance with real-world transfer.
AI.motivation: In RL for contact-rich manipulation, action representation critically shapes exploration and execution. Direct Cartesian commands couple high-level decision with continuous low-level motion, increasing learning burden and sample inefficiency. A higher-level action representation that guides motion can alleviate this burden.
AI.method: Policy outputs parameters of an energy-like potential field; a Cartesian impedance controller converts the field into a state-dependent guidance direction without commanding explicit motion at every step. Evaluation on peg-in-hole compared to Cartesian velocity, Cartesian pose, and variable-impedance action spaces using the same RL algorithm.
AI.result: In simulation, PA-RL attains 100% evaluation success within the allotted training time; the best baseline reaches 92.6%. PA-RL reduces joint-torque variation by 55.4% and Cartesian acceleration variation by 70.8% relative to the best baseline. The simulation-trained policy also completes 9/9 real-robot insertions without fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The potential-field action representation enables robust, efficient learning for contact-rich tasks and supports direct transfer to real hardware without task-specific fine-tuning, by reducing control variability and separating task-level adaptation from low-level motion execution.

title: Benchmarking the Explanatory Quality of Open-Weight Vision-Language Models in Face Recognition
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have recently been proposed as promising tools for face recognition, as they can produce natural language explanations alongside similarity scores. This capability is considered appealing for face comparisons in forensic contexts, which require decisions to be transparent and auditable. However, existing evaluations of VLMs for that use case focus mostly on recognition accuracy, while the validity of generated explanations remains unquantified. In this work, we introduce a benchmarking framework for VLM-based face recognition that treats explanation quality as a core evaluation axis. We propose two criteria that explanations should satisfy: relevance, i.e., reliance on identity-stable facial features; and faithfulness, i.e., alignment with the visible image content without hallucinated features. We jointly develop a methodology enabling the quantification of relevance and faithfulness of evaluated models, based on constraining model outputs to a structured explanation format that supports automated querying and auditing. Using this framework, we benchmark several families of open-weight VLMs, jointly evaluating face verification accuracy and explanation quality. Our results highlight remaining shortcomings of produced explanations, and emphasize the need for such explanation quality metrics to get a complete picture of model performance. The proposed benchmark and open-source evaluation harness provide a foundation for proper benchmarking and future fine-tuning of explainable face recognition systems.

AI.tldr: A framework to benchmark VLM-based face recognition with emphasis on explanation quality (relevance and faithfulness) alongside verification accuracy, using a structured explanation format for auditing.
AI.motivation: Address the gap where prior evaluations focus on recognition accuracy while explanation quality remains unquantified; forensic contexts demand transparent, auditable decisions.
AI.method: Constrain model outputs to a structured explanation format; quantify relevance (reliance on identity-stable facial features) and faithfulness (alignment with visible image content, no hallucinations) via automated querying/auditing; benchmark open-weight VLM families on face verification and explanation metrics; provide open-source evaluation harness.
AI.result: A validated benchmarking framework that jointly evaluates verification accuracy and explanation quality; reveals gaps in current explanations; provides metrics and an open-source harness to enable reproducible benchmarking and future fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Exploration of explanation quality is essential for credible VLM-based face recognition in forensic contexts; the proposed framework offers a reproducible foundation for evaluating and improving explainable face recognition systems.

title: Neural Cellular Automata Learn General Features in their Hidden Channels
summary: Modern deep learning models achieve impressive generalization through over-parameterization, but this paradigm often struggles with overfitting and memorization in few-shot regimes. Neural Cellular Automata (NCAs) offer a highly parameter-efficient alternative, yet research has focused primarily on their output, leaving the role of their internal hidden channels largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the internal dynamics of NCA hidden channels and introduce a novel transfer-learning mechanism that injects a pretrained teacher's hidden states into a student model to guide early optimization. Evaluated on few-shot and scale-variant MNIST benchmarks, NCAs outperform comparable recurrent and feed-forward architectures, demonstrating superior generalization with a minimal parameter budget (~9,800 parameters). Mechanistic analysis reveals that the hidden channels decouple feature extraction from uniform classification consensus by absorbing morphological complexity and converging to mutually orthogonal states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these hidden channels capture general, scale-invariant topological primitives rather than class-specific templates. This allows a student model to achieve strong few-shot performance on unseen classes using features transferred from a teacher trained only on a subset of digits (0-5). Our results highlight the potential of utilizing hidden-state dynamics as a robust, decentralized computational substrate for parameter-efficient transfer learning

AI.tldr: Novel transfer-learning for Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) via injecting a pretrained teacher's hidden states into a student, enabling strong few-shot generalization with ~9.8k parameters on MNIST. Hidden channels decouple feature extraction from classification, absorbing morphological complexity and converging to orthogonal, scale-invariant topological primitives.
AI.motivation: Tackle generalization and overfitting in few-shot learning with parameter-efficient models by exploring and leveraging the internal hidden-channel dynamics of NCAs.
AI.method: Train a teacher NCA; inject its hidden states into a student during early optimization (transfer learning). Evaluate on few-shot and scale-variant MNIST. Conduct mechanistic analyses of hidden channels (orthogonality, topology) and compare against recurrent/FF architectures. Demonstrate transferability from digits subset to unseen classes.
AI.result: NCAs outperform comparable recurrent and feed-forward models with a minimal parameter budget (~9.8k). Hidden channels decouple feature extraction from uniform classification, absorb morphological complexity, and converge to mutually orthogonal states. The channels capture general, scale-invariant topological primitives rather than class-specific templates, enabling strong few-shot performance on unseen classes when transferring from a teacher trained on a subset of digits (0–5).
AI.conclusion: Hidden-state dynamics offer a robust, decentralized computational substrate for parameter-efficient transfer learning in NCAs, enabling strong few-shot generalization and decoupled computation.

title: CounterPlay: Counterfactual Post-Training for Self-Play Driving Policies
summary: Self-play in high-throughput simulators yields driving policies with robust closed-loop performance, but improvement per unit of simulation diminishes as training scales. Policies learn to handle common situations early, while further rollouts repeatedly encounter unresolved failures. Post-training offers an opportunity to target these failures, but existing methods primarily evaluate alternative actions or continuations at visited states, although successful recovery may require changing driving style earlier. We propose CounterPlay, a counterfactual self-play post-training approach that backtracks from failed tasks and retries them under alternate driving styles. CounterPlay rests on three key components. First, failure-driven backtracking uses the policy's value estimates to select an earlier stored state from which to retry the task. Second, reward conditioning enables a single policy to retry the task from this state using candidate styles ranging from cautious to aggressive. Third, CounterPlay retains task-completing retries only if no other vehicle incurs a new or earlier collision or off-road event relative to the factual branch. Retries that pass verification with fresh randomness are then distilled into the policy under its deployment condition. On BehaviorBench, CounterPlay achieves state-of-the-art scores on both the Interactive and Random splits across all eight traffic regimes using 1B post-training transitions, which is just 1% of the anchor's 100B self-play training budget. Improvements over the anchor hold across all three evaluated driving styles. CounterPlay resolves a substantial fraction of the anchor's timeout cases on BehaviorBench and achieves a balance between task completion and safety that neither continued self-play nor adopting a more aggressive driving style attains.

AI.tldr: CounterPlay is a post-training counterfactual self-play method that backtracks from failures, retrains under varied driving styles, and retains only safe, task-successful retries to improve policies, achieving state-of-the-art results on BehaviorBench with a small post-training budget.
AI.motivation: Scale-driven diminishing returns in self-play: improvements per simulation drop as training grows, and failures persist. Existing post-training approaches focus on actions at visited states; recovery may require changing driving style earlier. A counterfactual backtracking approach aims to target unresolved failures more efficiently.
AI.method: Three components: (1) failure-driven backtracking selects an earlier stored state using policy value estimates to retry the task; (2) reward conditioning allows retries from that state under candidate driving styles ranging from cautious to aggressive; (3) verification-based retention keeps only retries that do not introduce new or earlier collisions/off-road events and distills successful retries into the policy under its deployment condition.
AI.result: On BehaviorBench, CounterPlay achieves state-of-the-art scores on both the Interactive and Random splits across eight traffic regimes using 1B post-training transitions (1% of the anchor's 100B self-play budget). Improvements hold across all three driving styles, resolves many of the anchor’s timeout cases, and balances task completion with safety better than continued self-play or more aggressive styles.
AI.conclusion: CounterPlay provides an effective post-training counterfactual self-play framework that enhances robustness and safety with minimal post-training data, delivering strong performance gains on BehaviorBench.

title: Catena: A Comprehensive Software Suite for Large-Scale Connectomics
summary: The gold standard datasets for mapping connectomes are electron microscopy volumes of densely labeled neural tissue at nanometer resolution. Yet reconstructing and proofreading neuronal arbors and annotating all synapses requires pipelining multiple software tools that are often fragmented, inconsistently maintained, or proprietary, hindering reproducibility and automation. Here, we introduce Catena, an open-source, comprehensive, developer-centric software suite for connectomics that integrates modules for 3D neuron and organelle segmentation, synapse detection, microtubule tracking, and neurotransmitter inference. Catena organizes its modules in composable, chunk-wise processing pipelines in a completely documented, extensible, and adaptable design. We further reduce compute and ground-truth data requirements with pretrained machine learning models, facilitating fine-tuning. Catena ships fully containerized modules that encapsulate evolving dependencies for consistent execution across workstations and clusters. By consolidating open components, shareable models, and containerized runtimes, Catena delivers a reproducible and scalable approach to mapping cellular connectomes from electron microscopy volumes. Code and documentation: https://github.com/Mohinta2892/catena.git

AI.tldr: Catena is an open-source, modular, containerized pipeline for electron microscopy connectomics that integrates segmentation, synapse detection, microtubule tracking, and neurotransmitter inference with pretrained models to enable reproducible, scalable mapping of cellular connectomes.
AI.motivation: The current connective-mapping workflow is hampered by fragmented, inconsistently maintained, or proprietary tools, limiting reproducibility and automation in processing densely labeled EM data.
AI.method: Catena presents a comprehensive suite of modules for 3D neuron and organelle segmentation, synapse detection, microtubule tracking, and neurotransmitter inference. It uses chunk-wise, composable processing pipelines, extensive documentation, and pretrained models for fine-tuning. All modules are containerized to ensure consistent execution across workstations and clusters.
AI.result: By consolidating open components, shareable models, and containerized runtimes, Catena offers a reproducible and scalable approach to mapping cellular connectomes from EM volumes, while reducing ground-truth data and compute requirements through pretrained models.
AI.conclusion: Catena provides an open, developer-centric, end-to-end framework for connectomics that enhances reproducibility, scalability, and automation in EM-based mapping, with the GitHub repository serving as the codebase and documentation.

title: Geometric Mean Pooling for Equal-Weight Multiplicative Coarse-Graining
summary: As an alternative to the additive and extremal biases of average and max pooling, we introduce Geometric Mean Pooling (GMP), a signed pooling operator that combines the product of feature signs with the geometric mean of feature magnitudes. Motivated by local-to-global composition in quantum many-body physics, GMP retains both joint sign information and a characteristic multiplicative scale without introducing learnable pooling parameters. We show that non-overlapping hierarchical GMP preserves the corresponding global multiplicative statistic and evaluate it on synthetic sequence tasks, iterative coarse-graining, image classification, and molecular lipophilicity regression. On the synthetic tasks, GMP recovers product-based signals more accurately than average and max pooling and maintains predictive performance under the tested levels of multiplicative input noise. On image and molecular data, however, its effectiveness depends on the representation, target parameterization, and placement of local and global pooling. These results position GMP as a complementary, regime-dependent inductive bias for tasks in which equal-weight multiplicative composition is plausible, rather than as a universal replacement for standard pooling operators.

AI.tldr: GMP is a pooling operator that uses sign product and geometric mean of magnitudes, aiming to preserve joint sign information and multiplicative scale without learnable parameters; it performs well on synthetic tasks but shows regime-dependent benefits on vision and molecular data, acting as a complementary inductive bias rather than a universal pooling replacement.
AI.motivation: Motivated by local-to-global composition in quantum many-body physics to capture multiplicative structure and joint sign information in features, beyond additive pooling methods.
AI.method: Define Geometric Mean Pooling (GMP) as a non-learnable, non-overlapping hierarchical pooling operator that multiplies feature signs and geometrically averages their magnitudes; evaluate on synthetic sequence tasks, iterative coarse-graining, image classification, and molecular lipophilicity regression to compare against average and max pooling.
AI.result: GMP recovers product-based signals more accurately than average/max pooling on synthetic tasks and is robust to multiplicative input noise; its success on image and molecular tasks depends on representation, target parameterization, and pooling placement, suggesting regime-dependent benefits rather than universal replacement.
AI.conclusion: GMP is a complementary inductive bias suitable for tasks with plausible equal-weight multiplicative composition, but it is not universally advantageous across domains; its utility hinges on data representation and task setup.

title: Towards Fine-Grained Object Manipulation: SAM3-Guided Visuomotor Policy with Persistent Memory Learning and Focused Visual Conditioning
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
summary: Fine-grained object (FO) manipulation requires robots to distinguish a specified FO from visually similar objects and execute actions reliably despite scene distractors. However, scene-level visual conditioning lacks explicit object selection, while category-level guidance cannot reliably distinguish FOs within the same category. We present a SAM3-guided visuomotor framework that addresses these challenges through persistent object memory and focused visual conditioning. First, we introduce FO Memory-driven SAM3 (FOM-SAM3), which learns reusable FO memory tokens from limited multi-view registration images while keeping SAM3 fully frozen. Through one-vs-rest learning, these tokens encode persistent memories for localizing target FOs and rejecting similar alternatives, which can be stored in a memory bank. Second, we propose Focused Spatial-Appearance Encoding (FSAE), which combines in-FO local appearance features with explicit bounding-box coordinates to condition action policies including Diffusion Policy (DP) and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT). The effectiveness of the proposed FOM-SAM3 was validated on the FO-30 dataset comprising 30 physical objects across four coarse categories. Across three real-robot FO manipulation tasks, our FOM-SAM3-guided policies demonstrated robustness against distractors, discrimination ability among similar FOs, and extendibility to new FOs.

AI.tldr: SAM3-guided visuomotor framework with FO memory tokens and focused encoding for robust fine-grained object manipulation under distractors.
AI.motivation: Need to reliably manipulate fine-grained objects (FOs) within the same category amidst distractors; scene-level conditioning lacks explicit target selection and category-level guidance is insufficient for FO discrimination.
AI.method: FO Memory-driven SAM3 (FOM-SAM3) learns reusable FO memory tokens from limited multi-view images with SAM3 frozen; one-vs-rest learning encodes persistent memories stored in a memory bank. Focused Spatial-Appearance Encoding (FSAE) combines in-FO local appearance features with explicit bounding-box coordinates to condition action policies (Diffusion Policy and Action Chunking with Transformers).
AI.result: Validated on FO-30 dataset with 30 objects across 4 coarse categories; demonstrated on three real-robot FO manipulation tasks showing robustness to distractors, discrimination among similar FOs, and extendibility to new FOs.
AI.conclusion: The SAM3-guided framework with persistent FO memory and focused spatial-appearance conditioning enables reliable FO manipulation, improving selectivity and generalization to unseen FOs.

title: The Role of Radiometric Features in Cross-Site Leaf-Wood Segmentation of LiDAR Point Clouds
comment: 5 pages, 6 figures. Accepted for presentation at IGARSS 2026 (IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium)
summary: Leaf-wood segmentation of individual trees from LiDAR point clouds is essential for quantitative structure models (QSMs) used in non-destructive biomass estimation. Existing segmentation methods typically exclude radiometric features (e.g., intensity, return number) to maximize cross-sensor compatibility. We challenge this design choice by evaluating cross-site and cross-platform generalization: training on the public Heidelberg dataset (terrestrial TLS, 1550nm) and testing on a novel dataset from Ontario, Canada (RPA-LS, 905nm). Results show that geometry-only methods - including state-of-the-art deep learning models trained on high-density LiDAR datasets - fail to generalize to the sparse, top-down geometry of aerial scans, achieving F1 scores <= 0.56. Incorporating radiometric features (intensity, return number, number of returns) improves F1 to 0.61, but more critically, increases wood recall by 119% from 0.16 to 0.35. Furthermore, geometry-only approaches often result in fragmented stem and branch components. We find that leveraging radiometric features preserves greater structural connectivity, resulting in more coherent architectures that are better suited for QSM reconstruction. We demonstrate that while geometric patterns are view-dependent and prone to overfitting scan patterns, radiometric features encode physical material properties that generalize across disparate sensors and environments.

AI.tldr: Radiometric features improve cross-domain leaf-wood segmentation and structural coherence in LiDAR-based QSMs; geometry-only models underperform on sparse cross-sensor data.
AI.motivation: Assess whether radiometric features (intensity, return number, number of returns) can enhance cross-site cross-platform generalization in leaf-wood segmentation, challenging the trend of excluding radiometry for cross-sensor compatibility.
AI.method: Train on Heidelberg public terrestrial TLS dataset (1550 nm) and test on Ontario, Canada (RPA-LS, 905 nm). Compare geometry-only models (including state-of-the-art DL models trained on high-density LiDAR) vs models augmented with radiometric features. Evaluate leaf-wood segmentation using F1, wood recall, and assess structural connectivity and coherence across sensors.
AI.result: Geometry-only methods achieve F1 ≤ 0.56 on the novel dataset. Incorporating radiometric features raises F1 to 0.61 and increases wood recall from 0.16 to 0.35. Radiometric features preserve greater structural connectivity, yielding more coherent architectures suitable for QSM reconstruction. Geometric patterns are view-dependent and prone to overfitting scan patterns, while radiometry encodes material properties that generalize across sensors and environments.
AI.conclusion: Radiometric features enhance cross-domain generalization and QSM readiness by improving segmentation accuracy and structural coherence. Radiometric cues generalize better across sensors, suggesting future leaf-wood segmentation should leverage radiometry for robust cross-site performance.

title: Detecting Pretraining Data in Large Language Models from a Free-Energy Perspective
summary: Detecting pretraining data in large language models is challenging because high likelihood can reflect either training exposure or strong generalization. In the joint space of prediction loss and predictive entropy, a likelihood-only detector uses a horizontal boundary and can mistake predictable non-members for members. Motivated by this, we introduce an inclined boundary that evaluates prediction loss relative to predictive entropy. Our analysis shows that entropy correction can preserve the expected membership signal while reducing its variance, thereby improving standardized member--non-member separation. We further extend the mean--variance analysis to the more general setting with a nonzero mean entropy gap. Interestingly, this entropy-adjusted score admits a Helmholtz free-energy interpretation, leading to Energy Transfer Detection (ETD), which views pretraining data detection from a macroscopic residual free-energy transfer perspective. Extensive experiments show that ETD achieves the best average detection performance, improving average AUROC by up to 3.5\% and TPR@5\%FPR by up to 5.1\%, while remaining robust across diverse settings.

AI.tldr: Entropy-adjusted pretraining data detection (ETD) uses an inclined loss–entropy boundary to separate members from non-members more reliably. It preserves the membership signal while reducing variance, extends mean–variance analysis to nonzero entropy gaps, and yields a Helmholtz free-energy interpretation for a macroscopic residual free-energy transfer view. Empirically, ETD improves detection metrics (AUROC up to 3.5%, TPR@5%FPR up to 5.1%) and is robust across settings.
AI.motivation: Detecting whether data was used for pretraining LLMs is difficult because high likelihood can stem from either actual exposure or strong generalization. A simple likelihood-only detector with a horizontal boundary misclassifies predictable non-members as members. There is a need for a boundary that adapts to predictive entropy to separate exposure signals from generalization artifacts.
AI.method: Introduce entropy-corrected score by evaluating prediction loss relative to predictive entropy, effectively an inclined boundary in the loss–entropy space. Perform a mean–variance analysis extended to nonzero entropy gaps. Derive a Helmholtz free-energy interpretation of the entropy-adjusted score, leading to Energy Transfer Detection (ETD) for pretraining-data detection.
AI.result: ETD achieves superior average detection performance, with AUROC gains up to 3.5% and TPR@5%FPR gains up to 5.1%, and shows robustness across diverse experimental settings.
AI.conclusion: Entropy adjustment preserves the expected membership signal while reducing its variance, enabling better separation between members and non-members. The Helmholtz-free-energy perspective provides a macroscopic interpretation of data-exposure transfer, and ETD offers a practical, robust detector for pretraining data presence in LLMs.

title: SynthDemo-RL: Breaking the Zero-Reward Barrier in VLA Adaptation with LLM-Guided Synthetic Demonstrations
summary: Fine-tuning Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models commonly relies on human teleoperation demonstrations, while reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse binary rewards faces an exploration challenge when successful trajectories are rarely sampled. We propose SynthDemo-RL, a teacher-student framework in which an automated teacher converts simulator-privileged state into successful manipulation trajectories, a VLA student is distilled from them by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and PPO with binary task-success rewards refines the student. We study reward coverage, the fraction of tasks for which at least one success is observed under the fixed evaluation protocol, as a complement to the average success rate. On LIBERO-PRO, a public benchmark of perturbed LIBERO tasks for which no demonstrations exist, 27 of 57 scored tasks are at exactly 0% success for a pi_0.5 policy fine-tuned on the original LIBERO tasks. Direct PPO from this policy, under the same PPO recipe and the same RL compute as SynthDemo-RL's refinement stage, rescues 10 of these 27 tasks and leaves 17 at 0%. SynthDemo-RL, with 50 synthesized trajectories per task and no new human demonstrations, rescues all 27 and reaches average success rates of 97.8% and 97.1% on the Position and Task axes of LIBERO-PRO, respectively. On standard LIBERO, the same pipeline reaches 96.0% with no human demonstrations, within 1.7 points of pi_0.5 trained on 50 human demonstrations per task. We further validate the pipeline on RoboTwin 2.0 and verify that trajectories from a policy trained in a MuJoCo twin execute open-loop on a physical robot.

AI.tldr: SynthDemo-RL uses an automated teacher to generate successful trajectories for Vision-Language-Action models, distills via supervised fine-tuning, and refines with PPO. It achieves near-perfect performance on LIBERO-PRO and large gains on LIBERO without extra human data, with sim-to-real validation on RoboTwin/MuJoCo.
AI.motivation: Address reliance on human demonstrations and sparse RL rewards by leveraging simulator-privileged trajectories to bootstrap VLA policies that generalize to perturbed tasks; assess reward coverage as a complementary metric to average success.
AI.method: A teacher converts simulator-privileged states into successful manipulation trajectories; a VLA student is distilled from these trajectories via supervised fine-tuning; PPO with binary task-success rewards refines the student. The study analyzes reward coverage (fraction of tasks with at least one success) under a fixed protocol. 50 synthesized trajectories per task are generated. Evaluations on LIBERO-PRO, standard LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and a MuJoCo twin-based sim-to-real setup.
AI.result: On LIBERO-PRO, SynthDemo-RL rescues all 27 tasks (out of 27 initially 0% with a pi_0.5 baseline). Direct PPO from the baseline rescues 10/27; 17 remain at 0%. The SynthDemo-RL pipeline achieves average success rates of 97.8% (Position) and 97.1% (Task). On standard LIBERO, the method reaches 96.0% without human demonstrations, within 1.7 points of a pi_0.5 model trained with 50 human demonstrations. Trajectories from a MuJoCo-trained policy generalize to a physical robot in an open-loop execution on RoboTwin 2.0.
AI.conclusion: Automated synthetic demonstrations combined with supervised fine-tuning and RL refinement yield high-performance, data-efficient VLA policies with zero additional human demonstrations and demonstrate practical sim-to-real transfer.

title: Info3R: Information-Adaptive Test-Time Training for 3D Reconstruction
summary: Transformer-based models have recently achieved strong performance on 3D reconstruction from images, and recent works extend them to process video streams in an online manner for real-world deployment. However, existing methods overlook two key signals when handling long image streams: the importance of each incoming frame and the information saturation of the model's internal state. In this paper, we propose Info3R, a novel information-adaptive test-time training method for the online 3D reconstruction. We introduce an information-aware state update that modulates the state update strength based on the redundancy and informativeness of each incoming frame. To restore the state's plasticity -- its capacity to incorporate new observations -- we propose a dynamic state reset, triggered by the cumulative magnitude of state updates and the model's prediction confidence and accompanied by an anchor-to-world alignment. Our method achieves consistent improvements on camera pose estimation, video depth estimation, and 3D reconstruction, while substantially mitigating the performance degradation in the long sequence evaluation. Notably, on KITTI Odometry, our method achieves on average 1.68x lower ATE than LongStream, demonstrating its robustness on extended outdoor sequences.

AI.tldr: Info3R proposes an information-adaptive test-time training strategy for online 3D reconstruction, using information-aware state updates and dynamic state resets to prevent internal-state saturation, yielding robust performance across long video sequences.
AI.motivation: Long image streams cause redundancy and progressive saturation of the model’s internal state, degrading performance over time. There is a need to weigh each frame’s informativeness and to refresh the model’s plasticity to incorporate new observations.
AI.method: Introduce Info3R: for online 3D reconstruction, implement (i) information-aware state updates that scale update strength by frame redundancy/informativeness, and (ii) dynamic state reset triggered by accumulated state-change magnitude and prediction confidence, plus anchor-to-world alignment to re-anchor internal representations.
AI.result: Shows consistent gains in camera pose estimation, video depth, and 3D reconstruction; significantly mitigates degradation on long sequences; on KITTI Odometry, average ATE is 1.68x lower than LongStream, indicating strong robustness for extended outdoor sequences.
AI.conclusion: The proposed information-adaptive test-time training framework enhances stability-plasticity trade-off in online 3D reconstruction, delivering robust performance on long streams and competitive accuracy gains.

title: LLMs as Feature Engineers for Text-and-Tabular Prediction
summary: We introduce an iterative framework that automates the extraction of interpretable, schema-bound categorical features from unstructured text for tabular prediction models. To navigate the feature space, a generator LLM proposes semantic definitions, a separate extractor LLM materializes the features, and a downstream tabular model evaluates their predictive performance. We optimize this search by translating explicit model errors, such as AUC ranking inversions, into natural-language feedback, steering the LLM to resolve specific predictive failures. Evaluated across three public datasets, this error-driven loop accelerates feature discovery by up to $3\times$ compared to unguided search. Empirically, the generated features demonstrate strong multi-view complementarity, strictly outperforming any subset when combined with TF-IDF and dense embeddings. Finally, the framework guarantees instance-level interpretability: the discovered features dominate SHAP importance rankings and provide a fully transparent, semantic audit trail for every prediction.

AI.tldr: Iterative, LLM-guided discovery of interpretable, schema-bound textual features for tabular models, with error-driven feedback, achieving up to 3x faster feature discovery and strong multi-view complementarity, plus instance-level interpretability and an audit trail.
AI.motivation: Provide semantically meaningful, interpretable features extracted from unstructured text to improve tabular predictions while addressing inefficiency of unguided searches and preserving interpretability.
AI.method: An iterative loop: a generator LLM proposes semantic feature definitions; an extractor LLM materializes the features from text; a downstream tabular model evaluates predictive performance. The process uses natural-language feedback derived from model errors (e.g., AUC inversions) to steer the LLMs toward resolving failures. Evaluated on three public datasets, comparing against unguided search, and examining feature complementarity with TF-IDF and dense embeddings. The framework also yields instance-level interpretability via SHAP and a semantic audit trail for each prediction.
AI.result: Error-driven loop accelerates feature discovery by up to 3× vs unguided search. Generated features exhibit strong multi-view complementarity and strictly boost performance when combined with TF-IDF and dense embeddings. Features achieve dominant SHAP importance rankings and provide a fully transparent, semantic audit trail per prediction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables efficient, interpretable, semantically grounded feature discovery from unstructured text for tabular prediction, delivering practical performance gains and strong interpretability guarantees, with potential applicability to broader modalities and model types.

title: Outcome-Conditioned End-Effector Geometry Across Vision-Language-Action Policies
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables, 23 references. Submitted to ICRA 2027
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies solve the same manipulation task through different action interfaces, but task success alone does not establish whether their physical executions agree. We study cross-policy end-effector geometry in 15,000 closed-loop LIBERO rollouts from four policies. The primary clean-condition analysis forms 3,600 configuration-matched, and therefore dependent, policy pairs. Both-success pairs have a median normalized dynamic time warping distance of 0.0120 m versus 0.0380 m when exactly one policy succeeds. This ordering holds in every task, every policy pair, and nine sampling and band-limited representations; however, the ratio varies severalfold across representations, so we report the direction rather than a fixed multiple. Both-failure pairs are more separated again but rest on thin, uneven support, so we report them as exploratory. Within successful executions, partner replacements separate more across tasks than across initial states. A matched baseline still reveals measurable, heterogeneous residual policy differences, so a low cross-policy distance does not imply interchangeability. Successful executions sit about as far from same-task demonstrations as those demonstrations sit from each other, compatible with task-associated geometry without separating training-data overlap from task constraints. A common 72-action window preserves the ordering but reduces its magnitude; endpoint and duration adjustment likewise leaves a positive mixed-outcome coefficient relative to both-success pairs, though its magnitude is specification-dependent. Under composite visual stress, policy rankings and pair composition change together.

AI.tldr: Cross-policy end-effector geometry is analyzed across 15k LIBERO rollouts to test whether success aligns with geometric interchangeability. Found small but nonzero end-effector DTW distances for both-success policy pairs, with larger distances when only one policy succeeds. Results robust across tasks, policies, and representations but vary by representation; however, a low cross-policy distance does not guarantee interchangeability due to residual policy differences and training-data overlap. Under visual stress, rankings and cross-policy composition shift together.
AI.motivation: Question whether success convergence across different VLA policies implies identical physical execution. Assess whether cross-policy geometric similarity supports interchangeability or is merely correlated with task constraints and shared data distributions.
AI.method: Analyze 15,000 closed-loop LIBERO rollouts from four policies. Create 3,600 configuration-matched (dependent) policy pairs. Compute end-effector trajectories and measure normalized dynamic time warping (DTW) distance across nine sampling/band-limited representations. Compare both-success, exactly-one-success, and both-failure pairs; perform baseline comparisons with a matched baseline and analyze across task states, actions windows (e.g., 72-action window), and endpoint/duration adjustments. Test under composite visual stress to observe shifts in ranking and pair composition.
AI.result: Both-success policy pairs show smaller median DTW distance (0.0120 m) than exactly-one-succeeds (0.0380 m). This ordering holds across tasks, policy pairs, and representations, though the magnitude varies by representation. Both-failure pairs are more separated but with weak support and are treated exploratory. Within successful executions, partner substitutions show greater separation across tasks than across initial states. A matched baseline reveals persistent, heterogeneous residual policy differences; thus low cross-policy distance does not imply interchangeability. Successful executions are as distant from same-task demonstrations as those demonstrations are from each other, suggesting task-associated geometry rather than training-data overlap. A 72-action window preserves the ordering but reduces magnitude; endpoint/duration adjustments also preserve a positive effect relative to both-success pairs, but effects depend on specification. Under composite visual stress, policy rankings and pair composition co-vary.
AI.conclusion: End-effector geometry across policies reflects task constraints more than policy identity; small cross-policy distances do not guarantee interchangeability. The geometry is robust to several representations and transformations but remains heterogeneous, implying that policy success does not guarantee physically interchangeable behavior; training data overlap and task geometry jointly shape cross-policy relations.

title: PRIME: Perception Feedback with Situational Memory Embeddings in VLA Models
summary: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving operate primarily through feedforward inference across the perception--reasoning--planning hierarchy. While modern architectures maintain temporal recurrence within the perceptual module, early perception remains blind to downstream reasoning and navigation goals, processing visual inputs agnostically without prioritizing cues informed by prior decisions. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces PRIME, a learned feedback mechanism that conditions the VLA perceptual queries on a novel Situational Memory. By aggregating latent representations of past perception, reasoning, navigation goals, and predicted behaviors across an L-step window via cross-attention, PRIME enables intent-driven perceptual attention at minimal computational cost, adding only a maximum of 29.7M parameters (0.41% of the 7.3B-parameter base model). Evaluated on the Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, PRIME achieves a state-of-the-art Driving Score of 82.47 (+4.73 over ORION) and a Success Rate of 60.00% (+5.38 percentage points), the highest reported Driving Score among published VLAs trained on Think2Drive demonstrations.

AI.tldr: PRIME introduces a learned feedback mechanism via Situational Memory to condition perceptual queries, enabling intent-driven perception with minimal compute and achieving state-of-the-art on Bench2Drive/Think2Drive benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Bridges the gap where early perception in VLA models ignores downstream reasoning and navigation goals, causing perception to be misaligned with tasks. PRIME aggregates past perception, reasoning, goals, and predicted behaviors to bias perception toward current intent.
AI.method: PRIME uses a learned feedback module that conditions VLA perceptual queries on a Latent Situational Memory built by cross-attending over an L-step window of past perception, reasoning, navigation goals, and predicted behaviors. Adds ~29.7M parameters (0.41% of a 7.3B base model).
AI.result: Bench2Drive closed-loop tests: Driving Score 82.47 (+4.73 over ORION) and Success Rate 60.00% (+5.38pp); highest Driving Score among published VLAs trained on Think2Drive demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: PRIME provides efficient, intent-driven perceptual attention with minimal parameter overhead, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark suite for VLA autonomous driving.

title: ExpBoN: Exponential-Noise Best-of-$n$ for Efficient Test-Time LLM Alignment
summary: Best-of-$n$ (BoN) sampling is a simple yet effective inference-time alignment method, but hard maximization provides only coarse control over the trade-off between reward and distribution shift. Soft Best-of-$n$ (Verdun et al. 2025) provides smoother control and converges to the optimal distribution associated with KL-regularized reward maximization. In this paper, we introduce ExpBoN, an alternative soft BoN method based on the exponential-noise report-noisy-max mechanism. It admits an exact finite-$n$ decomposition, which yields exponentially fast convergence in total variation, expected reward, and both directions of KL divergence. We provide comprehensive theoretical analyses of its convergence and regret behavior. We further integrate ExpBoN into the guided speculative inference (GSI) framework (Geuter, Mroueh, and AlvarezMelis 2025), resulting in ExpGSI, for efficient reward-guided LLM alignment. ExpGSI yields substantial reductions in computational cost while maintaining comparable accuracy. Experiments on MATH500, MMLU-STEM, and Minerva Math with the Qwen2.5-Math and Qwen3 model families show that ExpGSI reduces estimated computation by $14\%$-$39\%$ across candidate budgets for Qwen2.5-Math and by up to $45\%$ at $n=16$ for Qwen3. Overall, our results provide a theoretical and algorithmic foundation for exponential-noise BoN and efficient test-time LLM alignment.

AI.tldr: ExpBoN uses exponential-noise report-noisy-max to obtain an exact finite-n decomposition, yielding exponential convergence in total variation, expected reward, and KL divergences. Integrated with guided speculative inference (ExpGSI) for efficient reward-guided LLM alignment, achieving notable compute savings.
AI.motivation: Hard maximization in Best-of-n sampling offers coarse control over reward vs distribution shift; existing soft BoN methods (e.g., Verdun et al. 2025) improve smoothness but may lack finite-n decomposition and tight theoretical guarantees. Need a method with smooth control, tractable analysis, and efficiency for test-time LLM alignment.
AI.method: Propose ExpBoN based on the exponential-noise report-noisy-max mechanism, derive an exact finite-n decomposition, and analyze convergence and regret. Integrate ExpBoN into the guided speculative inference (GSI) framework to create ExpGSI for efficient reward-guided LLM alignment.
AI.result: Theoretical analyses establish exponential convergence rates in total variation, expected reward, and both directions of KL divergence. Empirical results show ExpGSI reduces estimated computation by 14–39% across candidate budgets for Qwen2.5-Math and up to 45% at n=16 for Qwen3, across datasets MATH500, MMLU-STEM, and Minerva Math (Qwen2.5-Math and Qwen3 model families).
AI.conclusion: ExpBoN provides a solid theoretical and algorithmic foundation for exponential-noise BoN and, via ExpGSI, enables efficient reward-guided LLM alignment with substantial computational savings.

title: RAYA: Learning Where and When to Intervene for Robot Recovery
summary: A robot can predict failure and still be unable to prevent it. By the time a safety mechanism reacts, the nominal plan may already have spent the control authority that recovery requires, and fixed task priorities may block whatever response remains. Our key insight is that both aspects are decided inside the controller. Recoverability must inform actions while they are chosen rather than veto them afterward, and task objectives must be adapted as recoverability shrinks. Building on this, we present RAYA, a hybrid learned-analytic framework that places a learned finite-horizon recoverability margin inside an optimal controller with hard constraints and pairs it with a bounded learned scheduler that shifts task weights to facilitate recovery. Across 7,200 simulation episodes per controller spanning quadrotor and autonomous-vehicle benchmarks, RAYA not only improves survival rates, but also transfers the learned components zero-shot to unseen trajectories, disturbances, plant shifts, and friction layouts. We developed an embedded realization of RAYA and deployed it on-board a 35g Crazyflie quadrotor. Across 40 combined hardware flights under wind with either aerodynamic mismatch or an unmodeled 40% motor-command loss, each of three baselines fails in all trials, while RAYA completes 10/10 six-cycle missions. Project Website: https://raya-control.github.io/.

AI.tldr: RAYA integrates a learned finite-horizon recoverability margin into an optimal controller with hard constraints, plus a bounded learned scheduler to reweight tasks, enabling recoverability-aware control that improves survival in simulation and on-board quadrotor hardware.
AI.motivation: When safety mechanisms react after a failure has begun, recoverability shrinks and fixed task priorities can block recovery; recoverability must influence actions during planning rather than vetoing them afterward.
AI.method: A hybrid learned-analytic framework that embeds a learned finite-horizon recoverability margin inside a constrained optimal controller and pairs it with a bounded learned scheduler that shifts task weights to facilitate recovery; zero-shot transfer to unseen trajectories, disturbances, plant shifts, and friction layouts; embedded on-board implementation on a 35g Crazyflie.
AI.result: In 7,200 simulated episodes across quadrotor and autonomous-vehicle benchmarks, RAYA improves survival and generalizes to unseen conditions. Hardware validation with 40 flights under wind and model mismatch shows baselines fail in all trials, while RAYA completes 10/10 six-cycle missions on-board a Crazyflie.
AI.conclusion: RAYA enables recoverability-aware planning and task reweighting that preserves controllability under deteriorating conditions, achieving robust performance in both simulation and real hardware and generalizing to varied disturbances and plant dynamics.

title: Traffic Sign Recognition for Autonomous Driving Using Branched YOLOv2 and Geometric Features
summary: Traffic sign recognition (TSR) is an important perception task for autonomous driving and advanced driver-assistance systems, where a system must both localize traffic signs and determine their semantic classes efficiently. This work presents a TSR system based on YOLOv2 for simultaneous detection and classification. Two complementary modifications are studied. First, YOLOv2 is extended with intermediate prediction layers, forming a branched architecture that can terminate inference early for easy cases and reduce computation time. Both whole-image and cell-wise branching strategies are investigated. Second, geometric information is introduced to reduce classification errors between visually similar signs. An unsupervised Bayesian image-segmentation method produces binary representations that are compared with class-specific geometric templates inside YOLOv2 bounding boxes. This information is used either during inference or as an additional signal during training. A dedicated dataset is constructed by combining GTSDB and GTSRB samples using seamless cloning and controlled image transformations. Experiments cover ten traffic-sign classes, with 3,000 training and 300 test samples. The selected branched architecture reports 0.647 s runtime and 0.680 mAP, compared with 0.6607 s and 0.680 mAP for baseline YOLOv2. Geometric verification during inference increases mAP to 0.713, while the geometric-feature training variant achieves 0.697 mAP with a reported runtime of 0.6608 s.

AI.tldr: A YOLOv2-based traffic sign recognition system with branched intermediate predictions for early exit and an unsupervised Bayesian geometric-verification module inside bounding boxes; combines GTSDB and GTSRB into a new dataset; shows faster inference with comparable mAP and notable accuracy gains when applying geometric verification.
AI.motivation: Improve TSR efficiency for autonomous driving by reducing inference cost while maintaining or improving accuracy, and mitigate misclassification among visually similar signs through geometric cues.
AI.method: Extend YOLOv2 with branched intermediate predictions (whole-image and cell-wise strategies) to enable early termination. Introduce unsupervised Bayesian image segmentation to produce binary maps and compare them with class-specific geometric templates within detected boxes, usable during inference or training. Create a unified dataset by seamless cloning GTSDB and GTSRB with controlled transforms; evaluate on ten classes (3,000 train, 300 test).
AI.result: Branched architecture achieves 0.647 s runtime and 0.680 mAP, slightly better/worse than baseline 0.6607 s and 0.680 mAP. Geometric verification during inference raises mAP to 0.713; geometric-feature training variant reaches 0.697 mAP with runtime 0.6608 s.
