AI.conclusion: The branched YOLOv2 approach reduces computation without sacrificing accuracy and is further strengthened by geometric verification. Using geometry either at inference or training offers improved discrimination among visually similar signs; dataset construction demonstrates the method for controlled TSR evaluation.

title: Intervention Granularity Matters: Coherent Treatment Bundles in Counterfactual Simulation with Clinical World Models
summary: Counterfactual simulation with a clinical world model means fixing a patient's history, changing the treatment, and reading off the predicted response. Doing so requires deciding what counts as one intervention. In clinical settings, interventions are documented as bundles: a co-occurrence audit of 945,707 patient-hours from MIMIC-IV shows groups of components, such as every parameter of a dialysis circuit, that never appear apart, so an edit that changes one component on its own describes an hour that never occurs in the data. We hypothesize that the granularity at which an intervention is edited changes how a world model responds, and test this with Clin-JEPA, a latent world model of patient trajectories conditioned on hourly treatment text. At 1,019 documented onsets of invasive ventilation, we keep the patient's history and other treatments fixed and compare editing one ventilator setting with editing the complete configuration recorded for a real patient with the most similar recent trajectory. The complete bundle moves the predicted next state further than any single setting, consistently across all five settings, and the difference remains after accounting for how much each edit changes the model's input. Intervention granularity therefore materially affects the response of a clinical world model: single-component edits may understate treatment sensitivity, and bundle-aware editing may offer a better-supported basis for counterfactual treatment simulation.

AI.tldr: Shows that in clinical counterfactuals, the granularity of intervention edits matters: editing a complete treatment bundle yields larger changes in predicted next states than editing a single component, suggesting bundle-aware editing provides more reliable counterfactual simulations.
AI.motivation: Clinical world models must simulate counterfactual treatments. In practice, interventions are bundled components that co-occur; ignoring bundle structure may understate treatment sensitivity. The study tests how edit granularity (single-component vs bundle) affects model predictions.
AI.method: They introduce Clin-JEPA, a latent world model of patient trajectories conditioned on hourly treatment text, trained on MIMIC-IV data. They identify co-occurring intervention bundles (e.g., all dialysis parameters) and compare two editing strategies on invasive ventilation events: (1) fix history and other treatments, edit a single ventilator setting; (2) edit the complete recorded bundle for a similar recent trajectory. They evaluate on 1,019 onsets of invasive ventilation across five settings, measuring changes in predicted next state while accounting for input changes.
AI.result: The complete intervention bundle shifts the predicted next state more than any single ventilator setting across all five settings. This effect persists after adjusting for how much the edit changes model inputs, indicating that intervention granularity materially affects the world model’s response.
AI.conclusion: Intervention granularity significantly influences clinical world-model predictions. Single-component edits may understate treatment sensitivity, while bundle-aware edits offer a more supported basis for counterfactual treatment simulation and clinical decision-making.

title: NeuRIO: A Streaming Neural Estimator for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Multi-Robot Relative Inertial Odometry
summary: We present NeuRIO, a streaming neural estimator for anchor-free 6-DoF relative inertial odometry using only identified inter-robot bearings, ranges, and IMU measurements. NeuRIO canonicalizes measurements into gravity-aligned coordinates, represents robots as nodes and mutual observations as factors, and uses attention for spatial reasoning and GRUs for temporal modeling. As a graph network, NeuRIO applies shared node-wise and factor-wise operators throughout the network, enabling it to handle different team sizes and time-varying observation graphs. NeuRIO is trained on a simulator that couples various motion patterns, device-level sensor characteristics, and diverse, realistic modeled, and temporally persistent sensor corruptions. In this way, NeuRIO achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. Across $24$ real-world sequences, NeuRIO achieves $14.1\,\mathrm{cm}$ position RMSE and $3.9^\circ$ rotation RMSE. More importantly, NeuRIO demonstrates strong computational scalability, maintaining an update cost below $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ with up to $400$ robots in simulation, while optimization-based methods exceed $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ at only $24$ robots. Moreover, even trained on limited team sizes, NeuRIO transfers directly to unseen larger teams without architectural or parameter changes.

AI.tldr: NeuRIO is a scalable streaming neural estimator for anchor-free 6-DoF relative inertial odometry using inter-robot bearings, ranges, and IMU, achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and real-time performance on large teams.
AI.motivation: To enable accurate, real-time relative pose estimation in multi-robot systems with limited sensing, while supporting variable team sizes and robust sim-to-real transfer.
AI.method: Graph-based neural estimator: nodes for robots, factors for observations; gravity-aligned measurement canonicalization; attention for spatial reasoning; GRUs for temporal modeling; shared node- and factor-wise operators to support variable team sizes; trained in a simulator with diverse motion patterns and sensor corruptions to enable zero-shot transfer.
AI.result: Achieves 14.1 cm position RMSE and 3.9° rotation RMSE across 24 real sequences; update latency under 20 ms with up to 400 robots in simulation; optimization-based methods fail to sustain sub-20 ms beyond 24 robots; transfer to unseen larger teams without architecture changes.
AI.conclusion: NeuRIO demonstrates scalable, accurate, and transferable relative inertial odometry for multi-robot teams, combining real-time performance with robust sim-to-real transfer and graceful scaling to large teams.

title: OmniVBench: A Benchmark and Large-Scale Dataset for Omni Reference-to-Video Generation
summary: Reference-to-video (R2V) generation is evolving toward increasingly general and versatile reference control, giving rise to the emerging paradigm of omni R2V generation. However, existing benchmarks fall short of these emerging capabilities: their test cases cover limited reference types and compositions, and their evaluation protocols largely assess holistic reference consistency, overlooking whether reference factors are properly preserved, disentangled, and routed. Meanwhile, the high cost of constructing omni R2V training data makes suitable training resources scarce. To address these gaps, we introduce OmniVBench and the Omni-R2V Dataset for evaluating and training omni R2V models. OmniVBench expands R2V evaluation across broader reference types, fine-grained control tasks, and richer reference compositions, covering 7 task families and 18 fine-grained tasks spanning content, motion, style, structure, narrative, and multi-reference settings. We introduce factor-grounded evaluation with 12,172 case-specific checklist items, assessing whether intended reference factors are faithfully preserved, correctly disentangled and bound to their targets, and properly realized according to the instruction. We further introduce the Omni-R2V Dataset, bringing industrial-grade training resources for diverse R2V tasks to the broader research community. Drawing primarily on a large-scale corpus of professional video footage, it comprises 340K processed training samples spanning diverse reference types and multi-reference compositions. We develop task-specific pipelines for reference-target pair construction, offering a practical and scalable recipe for omni R2V data construction. Extensive evaluation of advanced open- and closed-source R2V models reveals clear performance gaps across task families and evaluation dimensions on OmniVBench, highlighting remaining limitations of current R2V models.

AI.tldr: Proposes OmniVBench and the Omni-R2V Dataset to enable comprehensive evaluation and training for omni reference-to-video generation, including factor-grounded evaluation; reveals gaps in current models.
AI.motivation: Current R2V benchmarks are too narrow in reference types and evaluation protocols; training data for omni R2V is costly, hindering progress. A broad, factor-aware benchmark and large-scale training dataset are needed to advance omni R2V capabilities.
AI.method: Introduce OmniVBench with 7 task families and 18 fine-grained tasks across content, motion, style, structure, narrative, and multi-reference settings; implement factor-grounded evaluation with 12,172 case-specific checklist items to assess preservation, disentanglement, binding, and instruction-alignment of reference factors; release Omni-R2V Dataset with 340k training samples and task-specific pipelines for reference-target pair construction.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation of open- and closed-source R2V models reveals clear performance gaps across task families and evaluation dimensions, highlighting limitations of current models and the need for richer benchmarks and data.
AI.conclusion: OmniVBench and the Omni-R2V Dataset fill critical gaps in evaluation and training resources for omni R2V, enabling systematic progress and benchmarking of future models.

title: Beyond Kinematics: Benchmarking Simulation Fidelity for Muscle-Driven Imitation Learning
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables, submitted to ICRA 2027
summary: In this work, we conduct a systematic comparison of two state-of-the-art motion-imitation reinforcement learning (MIRL) pipelines, one built on SCONE/HyFyDy and one built on MuJoCo/MyoSim. HyFyDy emphasizes physiological realism through detailed musculotendon modeling, while MuJoCo prioritizes computational efficiency and scalable policy learning. While recent work has demonstrated that both pipelines reproduce human kinematics with high fidelity, it remains unclear if they accurately capture the underlying neuromuscular behavior that produced the movement. This limitation is particularly important for robotic assistive-device design and control, where outcome measures such as muscle activation patterns and metabolic cost are often used as optimization targets. To conduct a systematic comparison, our work compares both pipelines using a common set of human motion-capture and electromyography (EMG) measurements. The results find that while both pipelines produce similar kinematics with relative accuracy, the muscle activations from HyFyDy are more aligned with the experimental EMG, as supported by the average pooled (RMSE, r) values for muscle activations from HyFyDy and MuJoCo: (0.164, 0.4) and (0.344, 0.11), respectively. While we conclude that the more advanced physiological realism of HyFyDy currently makes it more suitable for musculoskeletal modeling, both require further development to bring physiological realism to GPU-parallelizable simulation environments and advance robotic assistive device design.

AI.tldr: Systematic comparison of two MIRL pipelines (SCONE/HyFyDy vs MuJoCo/MyoSim) shows similar kinematics; HyFyDy's activations align better with EMG, though both lack GPU-accelerated physiological realism for broader robotic use.
AI.motivation: To determine whether high-fidelity musculotendon models (HyFyDy) or computationally efficient musculoskeletal simulators (MuJoCo/MyoSim) yield neuromuscular patterns consistent with human data, informing design of assistive devices and optimization targets.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation using a common set of human motion-capture and EMG measurements. Compare kinematics and muscle activations from both MIRL pipelines; report average-pooled RMSE and correlation (RMSE, r) for muscle activations.
AI.result: Both pipelines reproduce similar kinematics with high relative accuracy. HyFyDy activations align more closely with EMG (HyFyDy: RMSE=0.164, r=0.4; MuJoCo/MyoSim: RMSE=0.344, r=0.11).
AI.conclusion: HyFyDy’s advanced physiological realism is more suitable for musculoskeletal modeling, though both pipelines require further development to achieve GPU-parallelizable physiological realism and enhance robotic assistive-device design.

title: AgenticSwarm: Semantic Perception and Adaptive Task Allocation for Heterogeneous Multi-UAV Missions
summary: Multi UAV missions in complex environments require the system to understand both the surrounding scene and the intent of a human operator while maintaining feasible task allocation as mission conditions change. This paper presents AgenticSwarm, an agentic framework for semantic perception and adaptive task allocation in heterogeneous multi UAV missions. An agent interprets aerial imagery and natural language instructions to construct a grounded mission representation that links perceived objects and regions with task requirements, capability constraints, and mission dependencies. This information augments a constrained task allocation process in which obstacle aware path feasibility, energy consumption, and protected return home requirements are incorporated before assignment. During execution, changes such as UAV failure, battery degradation, or task modification trigger residual mission reconstruction from the current system state, while completed work and reconnaissance progress are retained. AgenticSwarm is evaluated across five diverse Gazebo environments and an indoor real test environment, demonstrating its ability to connect semantic reasoning with constrained allocation and adaptive multi UAV mission execution. Compared with a Grounding DINO+SAM~2.1 perception baseline, the SAM3-based pipeline improves class-aware recall by 25.2 percentage points (pp) and semantic label accuracy by 29.5 pp. Ablating residual mission replanning increases mean repeated work from 0% to 61.7% and post-event recovery time by 58.6%, highlighting the contribution of adaptive replanning to mission execution.

AI.tldr: AgenticSwarm combines semantic perception with adaptive task allocation for heterogeneous multi-UAV missions, achieving improved semantic understanding and resilient replanning.
AI.motivation: To enable autonomous, semantically-aware decision-making in multi-UAV missions in complex environments, integrating human intent, scene understanding, and constraint-aware task allocation to maintain feasible operations as mission conditions change.
AI.method: An agent interprets aerial imagery and natural language to build a grounded mission representation linking objects/regions to tasks, requirements, constraints, and dependencies; it uses constrained task allocation with obstacle-aware path feasibility, energy consumption, and protected return home; during execution, residual mission reconstruction preserves progress when failures or changes occur.
AI.result: SAM3-based perception pipeline improves class-aware recall by 25.2 percentage points and semantic label accuracy by 29.5 percentage points over a Grounding DINO+SAM~2.1 baseline; ablation of residual replanning increases mean repeated work from 0% to 61.7% and post-event recovery time by 58.6% (worse without replanning).
AI.conclusion: Integrating semantic reasoning with constrained, adaptive task allocation enhances multi-UAV mission execution and resilience, with substantial gains in perception quality and reduced rework through residual replanning.

title: MintAct: A Unified Visual Agent for Digital Environments
summary: We present MintAct, a family of vision-language models that unifies UI grounding, multi-step navigation across mobile, desktop, and web, and visual tool use, trained at 2B, 4B, and 8B scales. Through careful design of our environments, data, and training recipes, MintAct models match the performance of per-domain specialists across all of these capabilities. To enable this, we develop a scalable environment and reinforcement learning (RL) infrastructure. On the environment side, we host hundreds of concurrent instances across heterogeneous per-domain backends, serving both trajectory data collection and online RL. To enable efficient and scalable RL training, an asynchronous framework keeps explicit control over the cross-domain training distribution and remains stable under noisy environment feedback and off-policy drift. Experimental results show that MintAct achieves state-of-the-art performance (48.9 on OSWorld-Verified) across a wide range of benchmarks at comparable model sizes.

AI.tldr: MintAct is a scalable family of vision-language models that unify UI grounding, multi-step navigation across mobile/desktop/web, and visual tool use, achieving state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks with cross-domain RL infrastructure.
AI.motivation: To create a single generalist model that can handle UI grounding, navigation, and tool use across multiple domains, reducing reliance on domain-specific specialists, and to enable scalable, stable training via asynchronous RL over a diverse, multi-backend environment.
AI.method: Develop diverse, concurrent environments across heterogeneous per-domain backends; scale pretraining to 2B/4B/8B parameters; implement an asynchronous RL framework with cross-domain data collection and online RL, designed to be robust to noisy feedback and off-policy drift.
AI.result: MintAct matches per-domain specialists across UI grounding, multi-step navigation, and tool use; achieves 48.9 on OSWorld-Verified; state-of-the-art across benchmarks at comparable model sizes.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that a unified vision-language model can achieve multi-domain UI capabilities with scalable RL infrastructure, suggesting a path toward generalist models in UI tasks.

title: Kinks vs. Smoothness: Identifiability of Real Analytic nICA for Laplace-like Sources
summary: Many machine learning systems try to explain complex data - like images or financial time series - in terms of hidden, independent factors that generated them. Recovering the true underlying factors, rather than some scrambled version of them, is the central challenge of nonlinear Independent Component Analysis (nICA). We prove identifiability (exact recovery) up to trivial ambiguities for real analytic generating functions when source probability density functions have a finite number of discontinuities in the first derivative. The Laplace distribution is the most prominent example satisfying this assumption. Our proof relies on the contrast between kinks in the source distribution and the smoothness of real analytic functions. Real analytic functions comprise a broad class of generating mechanisms, and can be approximated with Normalizing Flows or Variational Autoencoders with standard activation functions (e.g., tanh, softplus, GELU), so our result applies with minimal changes to existing training pipelines. We perform experiments on real and synthetic data with both Normalizing Flows and Variational Auto-Encoders demonstrating their identifiability properties. In experiments on CelebA data we recover several interpretable latent factors controlling unique attributes across the dataset.

AI.tldr: Identifiability in nonlinear ICA with real-analytic generators for sources having a finite number of first-derivative discontinuities; proves exact recovery up to trivial ambiguities; connects theory to practical NF/VAE pipelines and validates on synthetic data and CelebA.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear ICA suffers from inherent indeterminacies; by leveraging the contrast between kinks in source distributions and the smoothness of real-analytic generators, the authors aim to establish identifiability under plausible conditions and show compatibility with common deep generative models.
AI.method: Prove identifiability (up to trivial ambiguities) for real-analytic generating functions when source PDFs have a finite number of first-derivative discontinuities (e.g., Laplace). Use the contrast between distributional kinks and analytic smoothness. Argue that real-analytic generators are compatible with Normalizing Flows and VAEs with standard activations, enabling practical training.
AI.result: Theoretical identifiability result up to trivial ambiguities; Laplace distribution as a key example; empirical demonstrations with Normalizing Flows and VAEs showing recovery of latent factors in synthetic and real data; CelebA experiments recover interpretable latent factors controlling attributes.
AI.conclusion: Identifiability for nonlinear ICA extends to common deep generative pipelines by exploiting density discontinuities and analytic generation; supports practical latent-factor recovery with existing architectures, while highlighting conditions and potential limitations for real-world data.

title: A Novel Path-Tracking Algorithm for Automated Tractor-Trailer Forward and Backward Maneuvers
summary: Fully autonomous tractor--trailer systems are increasingly deployed in logistics, agriculture, and industrial environments, where precise and robust path-tracking capabilities are essential. However, the articulation between the tractor and the trailer introduces additional nonlinearities and significantly complicates lateral and longitudinal control, particularly during reversing maneuvers. This paper introduces a novel path-tracking algorithm specifically designed for articulated vehicles with a single trailer. The proposed method combines a lateral control law applied at the trailer level with a short-horizon predictive adjustment of the tractor steering angle, ensuring stable convergence toward the desired path in both forward and backward motion. The approach is geometry-based and requires no per-vehicle calibration or training. Simulation studies in a high-fidelity physics simulator demonstrate the ability of the controller to match or outperform classical and state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, stability, and robustness to disturbances.

AI.tldr: A geometry-based path-tracking controller for single-trailer articulated vehicles that combines trailer-level lateral control with a short-horizon predictive adjustment of the tractor steering. It operates without per-vehicle calibration or training and is effective in both forward and reverse maneuvers, validated by high-fidelity simulations.
AI.motivation: articulated tractor-trailer systems introduce nonlinear coupling between steering and trailer dynamics, especially during reversing, making robust, accurate path tracking challenging. A calibration-free, geometry-based solution that works in forward and backward motion is desirable for autonomous logistics, agriculture, and industry.
AI.method: A two-layer control scheme: (1) a lateral control law applied at the trailer level to enforce path-following relationships, and (2) a short-horizon predictive adjustment of the tractor steering angle to align with the desired path. The method is geometry-based, requires no per-vehicle calibration or training, and handles both forward and backward motion.
AI.result: Simulation studies in a high-fidelity physics simulator show that the controller matches or outperforms classical and state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, stability, and disturbance robustness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed geometry-based, calibration-free approach provides stable convergence toward the desired path for articulated vehicles with a single trailer in both forward and reversing maneuvers, performing competitively against established methods in simulation.

title: Joint Remaining Useful Life Prediction and Capacity Estimation of Lithium-Ion Batteries Using Partial-Charging Data
summary: Joint remaining useful life (RUL) prediction and capacity estimation require representations of both gradual degradation and recent battery behavior. This paper presents a cross-expert framework using partial-charging measurements without measured historical full-cycle capacity as an input. The RUL Expert encodes nominal 10-min segments from ten cycles sampled within a 30-cycle history using a pretrained gated recurrent unit (GRU) encoder, a two-dimensional convolutional neural network (2D-CNN), and a temporal GRU. The Capacity Expert processes statistical descriptors of nominal 40-min segments from ten consecutive cycles using a 2D-CNN and a Transformer. A feature-wise linear modulation module uses the short-term representation to condition the long-term representation for joint prediction. Training comprises supervised autoencoder pretraining, independent expert pretraining, and fusion training with frozen experts. On two public battery-aging datasets, the reference configuration achieves mean RUL root-mean-square errors of 143.69 and 161.10 cycles and capacity errors of 12.36 and 7.28mAh, respectively. On Dataset I, fusion reduces both mean errors relative to either standalone expert. The results demonstrate a trade-off between RUL and capacity accuracy: the proposed method attains the lowest reported RUL RMSE among the compared methods on both datasets, whereas several baselines yield lower capacity errors.

AI.tldr: A cross-expert framework jointly predicting RUL and battery capacity from partial charging data, achieving state-of-the-art RUL RMSE on two public datasets; capacity error is competitive but not the best.
AI.motivation: To capture both long-term degradation and short-term battery behavior using partial charging measurements without full historical capacity, enabling joint RUL and capacity estimation.
AI.method: Two specialized experts: RUL Expert (10-minute segments over 30-cycle history) using a pretrained GRU encoder, 2D-CNN, and a temporal GRU; Capacity Expert (40-minute segments over ten cycles) using a 2D-CNN and a Transformer. A feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) fuses short-term and long-term representations for joint prediction. Training involves supervised autoencoder pretraining, independent expert pretraining, and fusion with frozen experts.
AI.result: On two public datasets, the reference configuration achieves mean RUL RMSE of 143.69 and 161.10 cycles, and capacity errors of 12.36 and 7.28 mAh, respectively. Fusion improves both errors over standalone experts on Dataset I; the method delivers the lowest reported RUL RMSE among compared methods on both datasets, though several baselines yield lower capacity errors.
AI.conclusion: The cross-expert fusion approach with partial measurements effectively improves RUL predictions while maintaining reasonable capacity estimates, highlighting a trade-off between RUL and capacity accuracy and demonstrating strong performance for joint estimation under limited input data.

title: ZeroTouch: Tactile-Supervised Visual Contact Estimation for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Reliable robotic grasping benefits from estimating the evolving physical interaction and selecting a grasp-dependent compression target. Tactile sensors provide direct interaction measurements but require dedicated hardware at deployment. We introduce ZeroTouch, a tactile-supervised framework that predicts dense contact deformation, the instantaneous six-axis wrench, and a grasp-dependent desired compression target from wrist RGB observations, gripper state, and local gravity direction. Tactile measurements are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at deployment. On the full validation set, the complete architecture reduces normal-force MAE from 2.017 N for a state-only baseline to 0.531 N. In physical evaluation with 20 trials per condition, ZeroTouch achieves 95% success on an unseen object, 80% in a seen-object/unseen-grasp condition, and 90% under a content/load shift. Under the same evaluation protocol, OpenVLA achieves 25%, 40%, and 55%, while SmolVLA achieves 10%, 25%, and 35%, respectively.

AI.tldr: ZeroTouch is a tactile-supervised training framework that predicts dense contact deformation, six-axis wrench, and a grasp-dependent compression target from wrist RGB, gripper state, and gravity direction; tactile data are used only during training, enabling deployment without tactile sensors and achieving strong grasping performance and lower normal-force error.
AI.motivation: Improve reliable robotic grasping by leveraging tactile information during training to infer contact state and interaction forces, while avoiding the need for tactile hardware at deployment.
AI.method: ZeroTouch trains a model that outputs dense contact deformation, instantaneous six-axis wrench, and a grasp-dependent compression target using wrist RGB observations, gripper state, and local gravity as inputs. Tactile measurements are used as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference.
AI.result: Normal-force MAE reduced from 2.017 N (state-only baseline) to 0.531 N. Physical evaluation (20 trials per condition): 95% success on unseen objects, 80% on seen-object/unseen-grasp, 90% under content/load shift. Baselines: OpenVLA 25%, 40%, 55%; SmolVLA 10%, 25%, 35%.
AI.conclusion: ZeroTouch demonstrates strong performance gains over baselines and enables tactile-supervised learning without tactile sensors at deployment, improving grasp reliability and contact-state estimation.

title: Learning to Move Cities: Deep Meta-Models and Reinforcement Policies for Calibration and Control in Urban Networks
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE 29th International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC), Naples, Italy. (c) 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted; permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses
summary: Urban transportation networks present complex optimization challenges spanning calibration of high-fidelity simulators and real-time operational control. This paper presents a shared latent-space framework that connects simulator calibration and reinforcement learning control through a common learned representation of urban traffic dynamics. First, we develop a combinatorial MLP-autoencoder architecture that learns low-dimensional manifolds linking simulator inputs (origin-destination demand, network parameters) to outputs (travel times, congestion patterns), enabling efficient Bayesian optimization for calibration. This approach demonstrates superior sample efficiency compared to traditional dimension reduction methods, achieving better fit to observational data within fixed computational budgets. Second, we implement a deep Q-learning agent with experience replay and target networks to optimize dynamic traffic assignment through scheduling and routing adjustments. In empirical evaluations on benchmark networks, our approach reduces system-wide travel times by up to 51% compared to baseline operations. The learned latent representation is not only used to reduce the dimensionality of Bayesian calibration, but is also incorporated into the reinforcement learning state representation, allowing the control policy to operate on compressed and calibrated traffic dynamics. This shared latent-space formulation provides a unified pathway from simulator calibration to adaptive operational control within intelligent transportation systems. Our results highlight the transformative potential of deep learning methods in urban mobility planning and management, particularly for large-scale networks where traditional optimization approaches face computational bottlenecks.

AI.tldr: A unified latent-space framework links simulator calibration and deep RL for urban traffic, improving calibration efficiency and achieving substantial travel-time reductions (up to 51%).
AI.motivation: Calibrating high-fidelity traffic simulators and enabling real-time, scalable control in large urban networks is computationally expensive; a shared representation could improve sample efficiency and unify calibration with control.
AI.method: Develop a combinatorial MLP-autoencoder to learn low-dimensional manifolds linking simulator inputs (OD demand, network parameters) to outputs (travel times, congestion). Use Bayesian optimization for calibration on the latent space. Implement a deep Q-learning agent with experience replay and target networks to optimize dynamic traffic assignment, using the latent representation as part of the RL state.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on benchmark networks shows up to 51% reduction in system-wide travel times compared with baselines. The latent space improves calibration efficiency and enhances RL performance by operating on compressed, calibrated dynamics.
AI.conclusion: A shared latent-space formulation provides a unified path from simulator calibration to adaptive, data-driven traffic control in intelligent transportation systems, with strong potential for scaling to large networks.

title: Visual Proactivity: Enhancing Human-Robot Collaboration Through Intent Communication
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
summary: As robots transition from performing repetitive tasks to collaborating with humans, understanding human intent becomes crucial to effective interaction. Anticipation enables robots to predict human actions, while proactivity allows them to take initiative and guide human behavior toward optimal outcomes. Although research has largely focused on how robots infer and respond to human intentions, less attention has been paid to how robots communicate their own intent. This paper introduces visual proactivity, a novel, simple yet effective approach that enables robots to communicate their intentions through visual feedback, influencing human behavior and enhancing transparency and fluency. We develop and evaluate proactive robotic behaviors in a human-to-robot handover scenario, where a user study validates human perception of reactive, anticipatory, and proactive behaviors. The results demonstrate that effective visual proactivity fosters better alignment and coordination, paving the way for more intuitive human-robot collaboration.

AI.tldr: Proposes visual proactivity: robots communicate intent via visual feedback to improve transparency and collaboration, validated in a human-to-robot handover task where reactive, anticipatory, and proactive behaviors are compared.
AI.motivation: To address the gap in human-robot interaction where humans understand and align with robot behavior; while much work focuses on inferring human intent, there is less emphasis on making robot intent visible to humans to enhance transparency and fluency.
AI.method: Developed proactive robotic behaviors using visual cues to convey intent in a human-to-robot handover scenario; conducted a user study comparing reactive, anticipatory, and proactive behaviors to assess perceptions of intent communication and coordination.
AI.result: Effective visual proactivity improved alignment and coordination between human and robot; users perceived proactive behavior as clearer and more coordinated, supporting enhanced collaboration.
AI.conclusion: Visual proactivity is a simple, effective approach to communicating robot intent, improving transparency and fluency in human-robot collaboration, with potential applicability beyond handover tasks.

title: RACER: Role-Aligned Competence Estimation for Human-AI Routing
summary: Learning to defer asks a predictive system when to act autonomously and when to defer to a human expert. Population-adaptive deferral extends this problem to unseen experts using a small context set of expert behavior. Neural context encoders such as L2D-Pop can be query-dependent, but may learn routing shortcuts tied to absolute class coordinates. Identity-Free Deferral (IFD) removes such shortcuts through role-indexed classwise competence profiles, but its estimates are constant within each class and cannot capture instance-level expert specialization. We propose RACER---Role-Aligned Competence Estimation for Routing---a role-relative framework for estimating an unseen expert's competence from context. RACER estimates the posterior-predictive probability that the expert is correct on a query under each candidate class role, then combines these estimates with the model posterior to obtain the Bayes-relevant expert-correctness probability. Nonparametric and neural kernel-pooling estimators use candidate-role relations, shared aggregation, and symmetric summaries, excluding absolute class-identity channels. We prove coherent class-relabelling invariance, derive a Bayes-aligned deferral surrogate, and give a plug-in regret bound relating routing regret to classifier and competence-estimation error. On controlled synthetic benchmarks, including a PathMNIST histopathology context-scaling study with simulated experts, RACER benefits from additional context under hidden subtype dependence and gives the strongest aggregate performance on a separately sampled unseen-expert split in the CIFAR-100 synthetic experiments. On the radiologist and human--AI chest-radiography benchmarks (VinDr-CXR and CheXpert), the RACER family is competitive or best in budget-swept deferral, with calibration results varying across metrics and datasets.

AI.tldr: RACER introduces Role-Aligned Competence Estimation for Routing to improve deferral with unseen experts; it models context-specific expert competence per role and uses Bayes-aligned decisions, achieving strong results on synthetic and medical benchmarks by avoiding absolute class identity shortcuts.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable deferral when expert availability is unseen or variable. Prior methods suffer from routing shortcuts tied to absolute class coordinates (L2D-Pop) or cannot capture instance-level specialization (IFD). RACER aims to capture role-relative competence from context for better routing decisions and calibration.
AI.method: RACER estimates the posterior-predictive probability that an unseen expert is correct on a query for each candidate class role. These estimates are combined with the model posterior to yield a Bayes-relevant expert-correctness probability. The framework uses nonparametric and neural kernel-pooling estimators with candidate-role relations, shared aggregation, and symmetric summaries that exclude absolute class-identity channels. It proves class-relabelling invariance, derives a Bayes-aligned deferral surrogate, and provides a plug-in regret bound linking routing regret to classifier and competence-estimation error.
AI.result: On controlled synthetic benchmarks (including PathMNIST with simulated experts) RACER benefits from additional context under subtype dependence and shows the strongest aggregate performance on an unseen-expert split in CIFAR-100 synthetic experiments. On radiology benchmarks (VinDr-CXR and CheXpert), RACER is competitive or best in budget-swept deferral, with calibration results varying by metric and dataset.
AI.conclusion: RACER provides a principled role-relative competence estimation framework for routing deferrals to unseen experts. It achieves Bayes-aligned deferral decisions, enjoys theoretical guarantees (invariance, surrogate, regret bound), and demonstrates empirical gains across synthetic and real-world datasets, particularly when context reveals expert-subtype variation.

title: When Should Robots Intervene? Balancing Engagement and Intrusiveness in Human-Robot Interaction
comment: Accepted for publication at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026)
summary: Designing effective Human-Robot Interaction in task-oriented settings requires carefully balancing user engagement with socially acceptable levels of robot intrusiveness. In this paper, we examine how different robot intervention strategies shape user experience, interaction dynamics, perceived intrusiveness, and sense of support. We compare two approaches: a continuous engagement-seeking robot strategy, and a context-aware strategy that selectively intervenes based on the user's state and task context. Both approaches rely on multimodal behavioral cues, including body orientation and attentional signals, to guide robot actions. We evaluate these strategies in a user study with 32 participants performing a task in a simulated hospital environment. Our findings show that higher interaction frequency does not necessarily lead to better engagement. Instead, we observe a systematic trade-off between perceived support and intrusiveness, influenced by factors such as physical proximity and user effort. These results provide empirical evidence that effective engagement in HRI depends on adaptive, context-sensitive intervention policies.

AI.tldr: Context-aware, selectively intervening robot policies outperform continuous engagement; higher frequency does not necessarily boost engagement, with a trade-off between support and intrusiveness influenced by proximity and user effort.
AI.motivation: To understand how robot intervention strategies shape user experience and interaction dynamics in task-oriented HRI, focusing on engagement versus intrusiveness and the role of multimodal cues.
AI.method: Experimental comparison of two strategies (continuous engagement-seeking vs context-aware selective) using multimodal cues (body orientation, attentional signals) to guide actions; 32 participants performing a task in a simulated hospital setting; measures included engagement, interaction dynamics, perceived intrusiveness, and perceived support.
AI.result: Higher interaction frequency did not improve engagement; a systematic trade-off between perceived support and intrusiveness emerges, influenced by physical proximity and user effort; results support adaptive, context-sensitive intervention policies for effective engagement in HRI.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, context-aware intervention policies are essential for effective engagement in task-oriented HRI; designers should balance proximity, user effort, and intrusiveness rather than maximizing interaction frequency.

title: Time series generation with spectrally aligned latent flow matching
summary: Latent flow models have proven to be a reliable and cost-effective method for time series generation. However, the latent compression induces unwanted artefacts, such as a spectral mismatch with respect to the underlying dataset, thus hindering their use as training surrogates. In this article, we propose a spectrally-aligned latent-flow time series generator, where the latent space for flow matching is trained to preserve dynamical properties that are relevant for the suitability of synthetic samples. We find that incorporating fine-tuning losses based on canonical signal representations such as the Fourier, wavelet and signature transforms helps overcome these issues. The interpretability of these transformations allows us to ensure that the synthetic signals are aligned with the true ones in terms of relevant features, such as smoothness or targeted spectral content, as opposed to relying on pointwise reconstruction losses only. We compare the proposed aligned models against a base latent-flow model and the state of the art over real-world long-range univariate and multivariate benchmark datasets. Our quantitative results validate the superiority of the proposed method in terms of its performance on metrics reflecting signal realness and computational efficiency, while being aligned to the training set with respect to its local structure.

AI.tldr: Spectrally-aligned latent-flow generator with losses from Fourier, wavelet, and signature transforms to preserve spectral/dynamical properties in time-series generation; improves realism and efficiency against base latent-flow models on long-range univariate/multivariate data.
AI.motivation: Address spectral artefacts and limited realism caused by latent compression in latent-flow models; need to preserve dynamical and spectral properties relevant for training surrogates.
AI.method: Introduce spectrally-aligned latent-flow; train latent space with flow matching plus fine-tuning losses derived from canonical representations (Fourier, Wavelet, Signature) to enforce spectral and smoothness properties; interpretability of transforms.
AI.result: Outperforms base latent-flow and state of the art on real-world long-range datasets in metrics of signal realness and computational efficiency; better local structure alignment with training data.
AI.conclusion: Spectrally-aligned latent-flow generation yields more realistic and computationally efficient synthetic time series by embedding spectral/dynamical priors via interpretable transforms.

title: Sandwich-Residuals: Parameter-Efficient Test-time Adaptation of World Models
summary: Latent world models enable planning by predicting the effects of actions in a learned representation space, but their predictions can become unreliable when test-time conditions differ from training. Existing test-time adaptation methods address this by updating parts of the pretrained model, often modifying millions of parameters and requiring a choice of which internal components to adapt. We introduce Sandwich-Residuals, a lightweight alternative that keeps the pretrained world model frozen and learns only small residual corrections around the predictor. The residuals are optimized online using the model's self-supervised prediction error and require no rewards, labels, or source-domain data. Across 21 conditions on the AdaJEPA benchmark, our method achieves $1.3\times$ the success rate of the frozen model while retaining 95% of the performance of the strongest AdaJEPA variant and adapting 97-99% fewer parameters. Under compound shifts, this advantage increases to $1.9\times$ the success rate of the frozen model, while remaining comparable to internal block adaptation. We further demonstrate the same adaptation principle on a DINO-WM model for 3-D manipulation. These results suggest that effective test-time adaptation of world models does not necessarily require modifying their pretrained internal weights.

AI.tldr: Proposes Sandwich-Residuals: a lightweight test-time adaptation that freezes the pretrained world model and learns small residual corrections around the predictor, optimized online with self-supervised prediction error. It improves performance under distribution shifts with far fewer parameter updates and without needing rewards or source-domain data.
AI.motivation: Latent world models degrade when test-time conditions shift from training; existing methods adapt large portions of the model, which is costly and complex. A lightweight, data- and reward-free adaptation approach is desirable.
AI.method: Freeze the pretrained world model; attach and optimize small residuals around the predictor (Sandwich-Residuals) online using self-supervised prediction errors. No rewards, labels, or source-domain data required.
AI.result: On AdaJEPA across 21 conditions: 1.3x the success rate of the frozen model; 95% of the best AdaJEPA variant; 97–99% fewer parameters updated. Under compound shifts: 1.9x the frozen model's success rate, comparable to internal block adaptation. Also demonstrated on a DINO-WM model for 3D manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Effective test-time adaptation of world models can be achieved without modifying pretrained internal weights; residual corrections suffice and offer a lightweight, data-efficient alternative.

title: Assessment of Machine Learning-Based Critical Heat Flux Models in the CTF Subchannel Code for Square Rod Bundle Prediction
summary:
The prediction of critical heat flux (CHF), a key safety-related quantity in nuclear thermal hydraulics, remains an important challenge due to its direct relationship with fuel performance and reactor safety. Recent studies have demonstrated that relative to traditional empirical correlations and lookup tables (LUTs), machine learning (ML) methods can substantially improve CHF prediction accuracy. Most ML-based CHF models, however, have been developed and evaluated using tube databases, leaving their applicability to reactor-relevant rod bundle geometries largely unexplored.
  This study evaluates ML-based CHF models deployed within the CTF subchannel code using the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) rod bundle CHF database. Both pure and hybrid residual correction models are considered in local and semilocal formulations. The tube-trained ML CHF models generally transferred favorably to rod bundle applications and outperformed traditional CHF methods across most geometries and operating conditions. The local hybrid LUT model produced the strongest overall performance, and the semilocal pure ML model remained highly competitive. Comparison against the Bowring correlation, W-3 correlation, and 2006 Groeneveld LUT demonstrated that substantial improvements in rod bundle CHF prediction are possible even when models are trained exclusively on tube data. These findings provide one of the first large-scale assessments of ML-based CHF models in square rod bundles within a production-level subchannel analysis environment and support their broader application in reactor thermal hydraulic analysis.

AI.tldr: Tube-trained ML CHF models transfer to rod bundle applications, with a local hybrid LUT giving the strongest overall performance; semilocal pure ML remains competitive. They outperform traditional correlations/LUTs (Bowring, W-3, Groeneveld) in rod bundles, marking a large-scale assessment in production-level subchannel analysis.
AI.motivation: CHF is a safety-critical quantity in nuclear thermal hydraulics; ML can improve prediction accuracy over traditional correlations, but most models are trained on tube data. This study tests transferability of tube-trained ML CHF models to reactor-relevant rod-bundle geometries using a production code and EPRI data.
AI.method: Assess pure and hybrid residual-correction ML models in local and semilocal formulations within the CTF subchannel code. Train on tube CHF data, evaluate on the EPRI rod-bundle CHF database, compare against Bowring, W-3, and Groeneveld LUTs, across geometries and operating conditions.
AI.result: Tube-trained ML CHF models transfer favorably to rod bundles and outperform traditional CHF methods across most geometries/conditions. The local hybrid LUT model provides the strongest overall performance; semilocal pure ML is also highly competitive.
AI.conclusion: ML-based CHF models can be effectively applied to reactor-relevant rod-bundle geometries within production subchannel analysis, offering substantial prediction improvements and enabling broader adoption in reactor thermal-hydraulic analyses.

title: Understanding Engagement and Intrusiveness in Assistive Human-Robot Interaction Using Individual Traits
comment: Accepted for publication at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026)
summary: Robot assistance is particularly crucial in unfamiliar tasks, where users must understand task requirements while coordinating with the robot. Previous research offers mixed evidence on the role of robot proxemics in user engagement: some studies suggest closer proximity enhances interaction, while others report it can feel intrusive. In this work, we argue that perceptions of intrusiveness depend not only on proxemics but also on the frequency of robot interventions, and are strongly influenced by individual traits such as personality and demographics. We conducted an experiment with 32 participants who interacted with two assistive robots that provided similar task support but differed in their intervention strategies. Results indicate that overall engagement remains stable across conditions, yet affective responses and perceived intrusiveness vary significantly with personality traits. Moreover, personality shapes interaction dynamics differently depending on the robot's behavior. These findings emphasize that effective human-robot interaction should account for individual differences, tailoring robot behavior to maintain engagement while respecting each user's unique affective and behavioral profile.

AI.tldr: Examines how robot proxemics and intervention frequency interact with individual differences to affect engagement and perceived intrusiveness; results support personalized robot behavior.
AI.motivation: Addresses inconsistent findings on proxemics in HRI and highlights the role of user traits and intervention frequency in perceived intrusiveness.
AI.method: Experiment with 32 participants interacting with two assistive robots; robots deliver similar task support but differ in intervention strategies; measures include engagement, affective responses, perceived intrusiveness, and traits.
AI.result: Engagement remains stable across conditions; however affective responses and perceived intrusiveness vary with personality; personality modulates interaction dynamics based on robot behavior.
AI.conclusion: Robot behavior should be tailored to individual differences to maintain engagement while respecting users' affective and behavioral profiles.

title: Abstention and Noise Filtering: Two Missing Primitives of Softmax Attention
comment: 21 pages (8 pages main text plus appendices), 5 figures, 12 tables
summary: Gating the value pathway of attention reportedly improves language model pretraining, and prior studies disagree on why. We argue and provide experimental evidence that such gates supply two different things that softmax attention lacks: abstention and noise filtering. The first is abstention, which allows an attention head to output nothing, bypassing the requirement that attention weights must sum to one. The second is noise filtering, which allows the value pathway of an attention head to suppress interference from superposed features in the residual stream. In our experiments in matched models from 10M to 350M parameters, we supply abstention through a learned per-head sink logit in the softmax and noise filtering through a gate on each value. We report three empirical findings. First, the benefit of abstention, measured as the reduction in validation loss relative to a matched baseline, declines as models grow, whereas the benefit of noise filtering increases with scale. In particular, abstention accounts for nearly all of the gain from gating at 10M and filtering for most of it at 350M. Second, the best model at every scale is the one with both primitives built in. Third, injecting controlled interference into the values a head reads confirms that the gate removes such interference, and reveals that each of the two gate forms we study has a characteristic blind spot. Supplying both primitives adds negligible parameters and remains compatible with the key-value cache.

AI.tldr: Gated attention adds abstention and noise filtering; abstention helps small models; noise filtering scales with model size; best performance uses both; interference experiments confirm effects; negligible parameter cost; compatible with KV cache.
AI.motivation: Clarify why gating improves pretraining and disentangle two proposed mechanisms (abstention and noise filtering) and how each contributes across scales.
AI.method: Implement per-head sink logit for abstention and per-value gate for noise filtering in softmax-attention; evaluate on matched models from 10M to 350M params; compare to baselines; inject controlled interference into values to test gate; evaluate with and without both primitives.
AI.result: Abstention benefit declines with scale; noise filtering benefit grows with scale; best model at each scale uses both; gating removes interference; both gates have blind spots; adding both adds negligible parameters and remains KV-cache compatible.
AI.conclusion: Gating the value pathway provides two complementary mechanisms; optimal pretraining gains come from combining both; gating can be implemented with minimal overhead and retains cache compatibility.

title: ForceTwin: Physics-informed Digital Twins for Robotic Manipulation from Instrumented Human Interaction
summary: Manipulating objects requires understanding not only their motion, but also the physical properties that determine it. For articulated objects, these include inertia, friction, and mechanisms such as springs or door closers, whose effects can vary with configuration and velocity. Such properties are not directly observable from appearance: visually identical doors may require very different effort to manipulate. Existing digital-twin pipelines recover primarily kinematics or assign static physical parameters from visual and language priors, which can yield physically implausible estimates. As a result, state-dependent mechanism dynamics remain unidentified and are not represented in standard asset formats. We present ForceTwin, a system for identifying physics-informed digital twins of articulated objects from instrumented human interaction. A person probes an object using a handheld force-sensing gripper, providing synchronized poses and interaction forces from which we estimate the articulation, parametric dynamics including inertia, Coulomb friction, viscous damping, and a structured neural residual capturing state-dependent mechanism forces. ForceTwin nearly halves the inertial-parameter error of a VLM prior. As a feedforward dynamics model for impedance control on a Spot and a Franka FR3, ForceTwin achieves 87% goal completion across nine object-embodiment pairs, compared with 60% using VLM-prior and 57% using kinematics-only twins, with the largest gains on objects whose strong mechanisms cause both baselines to stall. We further use the identified twins to train whole-body door-traversal policies and deploy them in the real world. Project Page: https://timengelbracht.github.io/forcetwin-website/

AI.tldr: ForceTwin identifies physics-informed digital twins of articulated objects from interactive force data, improving inertial-parameter estimation and enabling effective impedance-control policies; demonstrated higher success than priors and kinematics-only twins, and extended to real-world door traversal.
AI.motivation: Visual appearance does not reveal state-dependent physical parameters; existing digital-twin pipelines underconstrain dynamics by focusing on kinematics or static priors, leaving state-dependent mechanisms underrepresented; need physically plausible, instrumented, dynamic models for articulated objects.
AI.method: Use a handheld force-sensing gripper to collect synchronized pose and interaction forces while a human probes the object. Estimate articulation and dynamic parameters (inertia, Coulomb friction, viscous damping) and learn a structured neural residual for state-dependent mechanism forces, forming ForceTwin; evaluate as a feedforward model for impedance control on a Spot and a Franka robot.
AI.result: Significant reduction in inertial-parameter error compared with a voxel-language-model (VLM) prior. Achieved 87% task success across nine object-embodiment pairs under impedance control vs. 60% (VLM-prior) and 57% (kinematics-only twins). Largest gains on objects with strong state-dependent mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: ForceTwin provides physically plausible, dynamics-aware digital twins enabling robust manipulation policies and real-world deployment (e.g., door traversal), by coupling instrumented interaction data with a structured dynamics model and a learned residual for state-dependent effects.

title: COMPLEX: A Closed-Form Certified Embedding of Multiparameter Persistence Modules
summary: Every multiparameter persistence vectorization we know of carries a one-sided Lipschitz upper bound and nothing below it: without a lower gauge there is no sense in which the features are faithful, and no per-prediction guarantee can be built on them. This paper supplies the missing side. COMPLEX is a closed-form, training-free embedding of multiparameter modules -- slice the module along a fixed near-diagonal net, embed each slice barcode by the certified PLACE/PALACE landmark map, concatenate. Under a checkable witnessing-slice coherence condition, holding on 100% of audited pairs on Orbit5k, a single slice carries a closed-form lower gauge: separated modules stay separated in the embedding. With the standard upper bound this gives, to our knowledge, the first two-sided distortion bound for a multiparameter feature map, making faithfulness measurable. Measuring it, we find the floor tight within a small factor of realized distances yet operationally local: an RBF-SVM reaches 91% where 1-NN reaches 78% on the same features. Local per-prediction certification therefore fails for a structural reason common to every landmark embedding whose lower gauge is witnessed by one coordinate. With no learned embedding and no held-out calibration -- only a cross-validated SVM head -- COMPLEX sets the state of the art on both Orbit benchmarks (91.95% on Orbit5k, 92.98% on Orbit100k), level with or above Euler-characteristic surfaces and above transformers and graphcode. On graphs it exceeds GRIL on all four shared molecular benchmarks with one fixed configuration, including the only multiparameter method to clear COX2's majority baseline by more than three points. Closed-form selection -- of the landmark radius, the kernel (certificate-preserving), and the bifiltration set -- buys further accuracy; gradient-shaped adaptation buys none.

AI.tldr: A closed-form, training-free embedding for multiparameter persistence modules (COMPLEX) provides a two-sided distortion bound and measurable faithfulness by slicing modules along a near-diagonal net and embedding each slice with certified landmark maps (PLACE/PALACE) under a witnessing coherence condition.
AI.motivation: To obtain faithful, two-sided guarantees for multiparameter persistence features, overcoming the lack of a lower gauge that has plagued existing one-sided Lipschitz bounds and enabling per-prediction certifiability.
AI.method: Slice the multiparameter module along a fixed near-diagonal net; embed each slice barcode using PLACE/PALACE landmark maps with a certificate-preserving kernel; concatenate slice embeddings; verify a witnessing-slice coherence condition on audited pairs (reported 100% on Orbit5k).
AI.result: Derives a closed-form, computable lower gauge; achieves a two-sided distortion bound for multiparameter feature maps; empirical evidence shows a small factor gap between measured and realized distances; SVM performance on Orbit benchmarks reaches ~92%, competitive with or surpassing Euler-characteristic surfaces, transformers, and graphcode; on graphs, beats GRIL on four molecular benchmarks; closed-form choices for landmark radius, kernel, and bifiltration improve accuracy; gradient-based adaptation provides no benefit.
AI.conclusion: Provides the first two-sided faithfulness guarantee for multiparameter feature maps without learned embeddings or held-out calibration, enabling measurable faithfulness and competitive performance with simple, training-free embeddings; highlights structural reasons for (limited) local per-prediction certification and establishes state-of-the-art results on multiple Orbit benchmarks.

title: PSR: Predictive Sensorimotor Representation Learning for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires policies to generate precise actions by reasoning over contact forces, robot configurations, and interaction histories beyond visual observations. Existing methods passively condition on force feedback rather than actively predicting future contact dynamics, limiting their ability to generate high-precision actions. To address this problem, we introduce Predictive Sensorimotor Representation (PSR) learning, a framework that learns a hierarchy of predictive representations from multimodal sensorimotor signals and integrates them into the action stream of a visuomotor policy. Specifically, during a pretraining stage, a multimodal Transformer is trained to learn a hierarchy of predictive representations by jointly forecasting future interaction dynamics. The learned hierarchy subsequently augments the action stream, enabling the resulting policy to exploit contact-relevant cues at multiple depths. We further instantiate PSR within a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, resulting in PSR-VLA, and evaluate it on six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks. Experimental results show that PSR-VLA achieves 91.7% overall success, improving over $π_{0.5}$, ForceVLA-$π_{0.5}$, and ForceVLA2-$π_{0.5}$ by 30.0, 22.5, and 19.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed PSR for force-aware, contact-rich manipulation. Videos of the tasks and stability tests are available at https://psr-vla.pages.dev/.

AI.tldr: PSR learning uses a multimodal Transformer to build a hierarchy of predictive sensorimotor representations that augment a visuomotor policy; instantiated as PSR-VLA, achieving 91.7% overall success on six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, outperforming baselines by notable margins.
AI.motivation: Current approaches mainly condition on force feedback without predicting future contact dynamics, hindering precision in contact-rich manipulation; a predictive, multi-depth representation could better exploit contact cues.
AI.method: Pretrain a multimodal Transformer to jointly forecast future interaction dynamics, learning a hierarchy of predictive representations; integrate the representations into the action stream of a visuomotor policy; instantiate as PSR-VLA within a Vision-Language-Action model; evaluate on six real-world tasks.
AI.result: PSR-VLA achieves 91.7% overall success; outperforms baseline pi_0.5, ForceVLA-pi_0.5, ForceVLA2-pi_0.5 by 30.0, 22.5, and 19.2 percentage points respectively.
AI.conclusion: Predictive sensorimotor representations effectively enhance force-aware, contact-rich manipulation; PSR-VLA demonstrates strong practical performance; video resources provide qualitative validation.

title: $λ$-Controlled GRPO: Turning Flow-Matching Ratio Instability into a Budgeted Resource
summary: Reinforcement learning is increasingly used to align image generators with reward signals, and Flow-GRPO recently extended this paradigm to flow-matching models by treating the denoising sampler as a stochastic policy that can be optimized from reward feedback. Training in this setting is unstable in a way specific to multi-step denoising: the policy update changes systematically across denoising steps, with importance ratios drifting below one, becoming increasingly dispersed, clipping at different rates, and leaving fewer usable samples late in training. Prior work treats these effects as separate failure modes and addresses each with a hand-tuned stabilizer. We show instead that they arise from a single per-step quantity, which we call path variance. This quantity is determined exactly by the sampler's Gaussian transition kernel and can be estimated cheaply during training. This reframes instability as a resource that can be measured and budgeted rather than a collection of symptoms to repair. Our method, $λ$-Controlled GRPO, calibrates importance-ratio behavior from this predicted law rather than from noisy empirical statistics, and allocates gradient effort across denoising steps according to their predicted cost. The two scales governing the update are fixed by standard policy choices rather than introduced as free tuning parameters. On a text-to-image model under two reward settings, rendering difficult target text scored by optical character recognition and matching human preferences scored by a preference model, $λ$-Controlled GRPO improves both text accuracy and preference reward over the strongest empirical stabilizer. It also keeps late-step path variance within its intended budget, precisely where the baseline systematically overshoots. The result is a Flow-GRPO update calibrated by its own transition law rather than stabilized after instability appears.

AI.tldr: A per-step stochastic policy instability in flow-based denoisers is governed by path variance, a quantity determined by the Gaussian transition kernel. The paper recasts instability as a budgeted resource and introduces λ-Controlled GRPO to calibrate updates from the transition law, improving text accuracy and human-preference rewards over empirical stabilizers.
AI.motivation: Flow-based image generation with reward signals (Flow-GRPO) suffers from multi-step denoising instability that degrades sample efficiency and reward optimization. A single, principled explanation—path variance—offers a unified stabilization target.
AI.method: Define path variance from the sampler's Gaussian transition kernel. Estimate it cheaply during training. Propose λ-Controlled GRPO that uses the predicted law to set importance-ratio behavior and allocate gradient updates across denoising steps. Two update scales are fixed by standard policy choices, removing ad-hoc tuning.
AI.result: In a text-to-image model with OCR-based text targets and a human-preference reward model, λ-Controlled GRPO improves text accuracy and preference rewards compared with the strongest empirical stabilizer. It bounds late-step path variance within budget and avoids the excessive late-step updates seen in baselines by aligning updates to the transition law.
AI.conclusion: Treat instability in Flow-GRPO as a controllable resource (path variance) governed by the Gaussian transition kernel. By budgeting and calibrating updates from this law, λ-Controlled GRPO achieves more stable and effective learning without ad-hoc stabilizers.

title: CRISP: Contact-Rich Robotic Simulation Platform with Extensive Geometries and Contact Solvers
summary: We present CRISP (Contact-RIch Simulation Platform), a high-fidelity physics engine tailored for complex multi-contact simulations such as tight-tolerance robotic manipulation. Achieving high physical fidelity in robotic simulation requires both expressive modeling of geometry and contact interactions, as well as accurate numerical resolution via robust collision detection and contact solvers. However, existing simulators often either rely on limited support for geometric representations and simplified modeling of contact interactions, or employ numerical resolution methods whose accuracy or robustness is inherently constrained. Accordingly, we develop a new simulator that supports diverse geometric representations with accurate optimization-based collision detection, and combines contact modeling with robust augmented Lagrangian-based contact solvers. This integration enables efficient and consistent detection of contact information across complex geometries while accurately resolving multi-contact constraints without problematic relaxations, which is essential for simulating contact-intensive and sharp interactions. We validate the physical fidelity of our simulator against state-of-the-art platforms and further demonstrate its capabilities through complex robotic manipulation scenarios. CRISP is publicly available at https://github.com/INRoL/crisp.

AI.tldr: CRISP is a high-fidelity multi-contact physics engine unifying expressive geometry, optimization-based collision detection, and augmented Lagrangian contact solvers to enable accurate, robust simulation for tight-tolerance robotic manipulation; validated vs. state-of-the-art platforms; open-source.
AI.motivation: Current simulators struggle to simultaneously support diverse geometric representations and robust, accurate multi-contact resolution; this limits fidelity in contact-intensive robotic manipulation.
AI.method: Develop a simulator with diverse geometry representations, accurate optimization-based collision detection, and robust augmented Lagrangian-based contact solvers; ensure consistent contact information across complex geometries and accurate multi-contact constraint resolution without relaxations.
AI.result: Empirical validation against leading platforms; demonstrations on complex robotic manipulation scenarios; CRISP is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: CRISP advances high-fidelity multi-contact simulation by bridging geometry expressiveness and solver robustness, enabling more reliable robotic manipulation research and applications.

title: Available Guardrails: Certifying Selective Prediction across ML Systems
summary: A selective predictor acts as a safety gate: it returns an output only when the prediction appears sufficiently trustworthy. Deployments increasingly require this reliability to be certified at a target precision for every reporting unit of interest, such as a tool, policy label, or patient subgroup. The main difficulty is often not whether a granted certificate is valid, but whether finite calibration data can produce one at all. As the gate becomes safer or more fine-grained, some units may receive too little evidence to certify. We make this notion of availability computable through classical exact-binomial inversion and formulate reporting-partition selection, under a fixed group order, as a dynamic program that exposes the trade-off among safety, granularity, and served traffic. The resulting frontier reveals a large population opportunity that finite-sample estimation nearly erases: a truth-informed planner gains $0.157$ mean coverage over support balancing, whereas a naive estimator recovers only $0.005$, making recovery from finite data the central challenge. Constructing candidate partitions on one planning split and selecting among them on another recovers part of this gap, improving mean coverage over support balancing by $0.060$, with the direction reproduced in $59$ of $60$ model effects across three intent-routing datasets and two architectures. A complementary validity-preserving lever, reallocating the familywise error budget across reporting units, recovers additional coverage both with population quantities and noisy estimates. The same frontier recurs, with predictor-specific ceilings, across LLM tool-calling, content moderation, lesion classification, and recommendation. Certified availability is therefore a plannable deployment resource that determines when a safety gate can be certified, at what granularity, and over how much traffic.

AI.tldr: A framework for certifying availability of selective predictors under finite data by exact-binomial inversion and dynamic programming, revealing a planning frontier among safety, granularity, and traffic, with substantial gains over naive estimation and cross-domain applicability.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable, unit-level certification of selective predictors (safety gates) when calibration data are limited, and to understand how to partition reporting units to balance safety, granularity, and served traffic.
AI.method: Compute availability via exact binomial inversion; formulate reporting-partition selection as a dynamic program with fixed group order; construct candidate partitions using a planning split and evaluate on a separate split; apply a validity-preserving lever by reallocating the familywise error budget; evaluate across multiple tasks and architectures.
AI.result: Identified a tractable frontier between safety and coverage: a truth-informed planner achieves 0.157 mean coverage over support balancing versus 0.005 for naive estimators; partition construction improves by 0.060; 59/60 model effects align across datasets and architectures; frontier recurs across LLM tool-calling, content moderation, lesion classification, and recommendation.
AI.conclusion: Certified availability is a plannable deployment resource that dictates when a safety gate can be certified, at what granularity, and over how much traffic.

title: Scaling Vision-Language Reward Learning for Robot Manipulation in Parallel Simulation
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can replace human annotators in preference-based reward learning, but sequential API requests and single-environment data collection make training slow and costly. We present RAPID (Reward learning with Adaptive Parallel Image Diversity), a system that couples GPU-parallel rollout with data-aware policy updates, single-request preference labeling, automatic reward stabilization, and representative image sampling. We evaluate these components on five Franka Panda manipulation tasks in IsaacLab. Parallel rollout and adaptive updates provide the first substantial reduction in training time: under matched two-stage prompting, mean runtime falls from 9.18 to 3.13 hours. With all RAPID components enabled, training completes in 1.15 hours using 896 rather than 19,840 API calls per run, and aggregate final success rises from 86.3\% to 98.7\%. This represents an 8.0$\times$ end-to-end speedup and a 95.5\% reduction in API usage. An offline evaluation with Gemma~3 12B and GPT-4.1 mini demonstrates that single-request prompting reduces labeling latency and cost across both models. Code is available at: https://github.com/rapid-vlm/rapid-vlm-rl.

AI.tldr: RAPID enables fast, cost-efficient VLM-based reward learning by combining GPU-parallel rollouts, data-aware policy updates, single-request labeling, automatic reward stabilization, and representative image sampling, achieving substantial speedups and API reductions while improving final success.
AI.motivation: Address the slow, costly training of preference-based reward learning with VLMs due to sequential API requests and single-environment data collection.
AI.method: Introduce RAPID with components: GPU-parallel rollout, data-aware policy updates, single-request preference labeling, automatic reward stabilization, and representative image sampling. Evaluate on five Franka Panda tasks in IsaacLab; compare under two-stage prompting; perform offline evaluation with Gemma 3 12B and GPT-4.1 mini; provide code link.
AI.result: Under matched two-stage prompting, training time drops from 9.18h to 3.13h. With all RAPID components: 1.15h and 896 API calls per run (vs 19,840). Final success rises from 86.3% to 98.7%. End-to-end speedup ~8x and API usage reduced ~95.5%. Offline evaluation confirms single-request prompting reduces labeling latency/cost for both models.
AI.conclusion: RAPID substantially accelerates and reduces the cost of VLM-based reward learning while improving performance; code is available for reproducibility.

title: Particle Competition and Cooperation for Robust Graph Convolutional Network Learning Under Label Noise
comment: Submitted to Neurocomputing. Code and experimental results are publicly available at https://github.com/fbreve/PCC-GCN and https://github.com/fbreve/NoisyGL
summary: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are highly sensitive to label noise, since corrupted supervision can propagate through the graph and degrade learned node representations. This work proposes PCC+GCN, a hybrid framework that uses Particle Competition and Cooperation (PCC) as a graph-based label-refinement stage before GCN training. PCC identifies suspicious labeled nodes through particle domination dynamics and determines whether their labels should be preserved, removed, or reassigned before GCN training. The framework also allows the graph used by PCC to be augmented with feature-based $k$-nearest-neighbor edges, while the GCN itself is trained on the original graph structure and node features. The proposed method was evaluated on ten graph datasets from the NoisyGL benchmark under conventional Uniform, Pair, and Random label noise, as well as under instance-dependent label noise.
